aaltje.label: Aaltje
aaltje.meaning: Dutch diminutive of Aleida or Adelheid, built on Germanic "adal", "noble".
aaltje.text: A typically Dutch familiar form, very common in the registers of Holland, Friesland and Groningen in the 18th and 19th centuries. It often alternates with Aleida, Aleid or Aeltje for the same person, so these spellings should be searched together.

aaron.label: Aaron
aaron.meaning: From Hebrew "Aharon", of disputed etymology, possibly Egyptian; sometimes interpreted as "exalted" or "mountain of strength".
aaron.text: The biblical name of Moses's brother and first high priest of Israel. Rare in Catholic registers, it is borne mainly in Jewish families and, after the Reformation, in Protestant circles in England, the Netherlands and North America.

abdul.label: Abdul
abdul.meaning: From Arabic "abd al-", "servant of", the first element of compound names whose second part is an attribute of God (Abdul Rahman, "servant of the Merciful").
abdul.text: A Muslim given name, virtually absent from older European registers; it appears in the United Kingdom mainly in the 20th century with immigration. In records it is often the first element of a compound name, also transcribed Abdel or Abdoul.

abel.label: Abel
abel.meaning: From Hebrew "Hevel", "breath, vapour", often understood as "that which is fleeting".
abel.text: The biblical name of the second son of Adam and Eve, killed by his brother Cain. Moderately used in France, Portugal and Spain, it was also favoured in Protestant circles. In France its name day is 5 August, the feast of Saint Abel, an 8th-century archbishop of Reims.

abigail.label: Abigail
abigail.text: The biblical name of one of King David's wives. Adopted by English Puritans in the 17th century, it is common in New England and English registers of the 17th and 18th centuries, often shortened to Abby or Nabby.

abilio.label: Abílio
abilio.text: A mainly Portuguese name (Abílio), found in the registers of Portugal and its diaspora in the 19th and 20th centuries. The accent is often dropped in transcriptions.

abner.label: Abner
abner.meaning: From Hebrew "Avner", understood as "my father is light".
abner.text: Abner is the commander of King Saul's army in the Book of Samuel. The name is found mainly among Protestants and in Jewish communities and remains rare in French Catholic registers.

abraham.label: Abraham
abraham.meaning: From Hebrew "Avraham", interpreted in the Bible as "father of a multitude".
abraham.text: The name of the biblical patriarch, widely used in Jewish families and, after the Reformation, among Protestants in the Netherlands, Switzerland, Germany and England. In Dutch registers it is often shortened to Bram.

achiel.label: Achiel
achiel.meaning: Flemish form of Achille, from Greek "Akhilleus", of uncertain etymology.
achiel.text: The Flemish form of Achille, common in Dutch-speaking Belgium in the 19th and early 20th centuries. The same person may appear as Achille in a French-language record and as Achiel in a Dutch one. It is linked to Saint Achilleus, a Roman martyr whose feast is 12 May.

achille.label: Achille
achille.meaning: From Greek "Akhilleus", the hero of the Iliad, of uncertain etymology.
achille.text: A name in fashion in France, Belgium and Italy (Achille) in the 19th century, reflecting the taste for classical names. It is linked to Saint Achilleus, a Roman martyr whose feast, shared with Saint Nereus, is 12 May.

ada.label: Ada
ada.meaning: Short form of Germanic names in "Adal-" ("noble"), such as Adelaide or Adela.
ada.text: A female name very fashionable in England and the United States in the late 19th century, also widespread in Italy. It may shorten Adelaide, Adela or Adeline, which explains why the same person is sometimes recorded under several forms.

adalbert.label: Adalbert
adalbert.text: A name widespread in Germany and Poland, borne by Saint Adalbert of Prague, martyred bishop and patron saint of Poland, whose feast is 23 April. In Poland it also corresponds to the Slavic name Wojciech, which the saint bore before his confirmation.

adam.label: Adam
adam.text: The name of the first man in the Bible, used throughout Europe since the Middle Ages, particularly in Poland, Germany and the Netherlands. It is also common as a surname, which can cause confusion in older records.

adela.label: Adela
adela.text: The Spanish, English and Polish form of Adèle, found in registers since the Middle Ages and fairly common in the 19th century. In Spain it is sometimes confused with Adelaida in records.

adelaida.label: Adelaida
adelaida.meaning: Spanish form of Adelaide, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "heit", "nature, kind".
adelaida.text: The Spanish form of Adelaide, found in Spanish registers mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. Depending on the record it may be shortened to Adela or Aida.

adelaide.label: Adelaide
adelaide.text: The Latinised form of Adelheid, used in Portugal, Italy, France (Adélaïde) and English-speaking countries, where Queen Adelaide made it popular in the 19th century. It is linked to Saint Adelaide, a 10th-century empress whose feast is 16 December.

adele.label: Adele
adele.text: A name very common in France, Belgium and Switzerland in the 19th century (Adèle), also found in Italy and Germany. In records it is sometimes confused with Adelaide or Adeline. In France its name day is 24 December, the feast of Saint Adela, an 8th-century abbess of Pfalzel.

adelheid.label: Adelheid
adelheid.text: The German form of Adelaide, common in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, with many diminutives (Aleid, Aaltje, Heidi). It was borne by Saint Adelaide, a 10th-century empress whose feast is 16 December.

adelina.label: Adelina
adelina.text: The Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Adeline, found mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. In records it often alternates with Adela, Adelia or Adelaide for the same person.

adeline.label: Adeline
adeline.text: A name already borne in the Middle Ages (Adeline, Adelina) and widely used again in France and Belgium in the 19th century. In France its name day is 20 October, the feast of Blessed Adeline, a 12th-century Norman abbess.

adolf.label: Adolf
adolf.text: A name common in Germany, Switzerland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands from the 17th to the early 20th century, then almost abandoned after 1945. It was borne by Saint Adolf, 13th-century bishop of Osnabrück, whose feast is 30 June.

adolfo.label: Adolfo
adolfo.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Adolf, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "wolf", "wolf".
adolfo.text: A name widespread in Portugal, Italy and Spain in the 19th and early 20th centuries. In Iberian registers the older spelling Adolpho also occurs.

adolph.label: Adolph
adolph.meaning: Latinising spelling of Adolf, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "wolf", "wolf".
adolph.text: A frequent spelling in German and Dutch registers of the 18th and 19th centuries, and among German-speaking emigrants to the United States. It alternates with Adolf, Adolphus or Adolphe depending on the language of the record.

adolphe.label: Adolphe
adolphe.meaning: French form of Adolf, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "wolf", "wolf".
adolphe.text: A name very widespread in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland in the 19th century. In France its name day is 30 June, the feast of Saint Adolf, 13th-century bishop of Osnabrück.

adolphine.label: Adolphine
adolphine.meaning: Feminine of Adolphe, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "wolf", "wolf".
adolphine.text: A female name fashionable in the 19th century in France, Belgium and the Netherlands, often given in honour of a godfather or father named Adolphe. It also occurs as Adolfine.

adoracion.label: Adoracion
adoracion.meaning: From Spanish "adoración", "adoration", from Latin "adoratio", referring to the adoration of the Magi or of the Blessed Sacrament.
adoracion.text: A typically Spanish devotional name (Adoración), used mainly from the 19th to the mid-20th century. In records it is often preceded by María, and familiarly shortened to Dora.

adriaan.label: Adriaan
adriaan.meaning: Dutch form of Adrian, from Latin "Hadrianus", "from Hadria".
adriaan.text: A very common name in the Netherlands and Flanders from the 16th to the 19th century, also written Adriaen, Adrianus (the Latin form used in Catholic registers) or shortened to Arie depending on the region. It is linked to Saint Adrian of Nicomedia, whose feast is 8 September.

adriaen.label: Adriaen
adriaen.meaning: Older Dutch spelling of Adriaan, from Latin "Hadrianus", "from Hadria".
adriaen.text: An older spelling of Adriaan, frequent in Dutch and Flemish registers of the 16th and 17th centuries, where the "e" marks a long vowel. It gradually gives way to Adriaan in the 18th century. It is linked to Saint Adrian of Nicomedia, whose feast is 8 September.

adrian.label: Adrian
adrian.meaning: From Latin "Hadrianus", "from Hadria", an Italian town that gave its name to the Adriatic.
adrian.text: The English, German, Spanish and Polish form of Adrien, found since the Middle Ages but most widespread in the 20th century. In Spain it appears as Adrián, in Catalonia as Adrià. It is linked to Saint Adrian of Nicomedia, whose feast is 8 September.

adriana.label: Adriana
adriana.meaning: Feminine of Adrianus, from Latin "Hadrianus", "from Hadria".
adriana.text: A female name common in the Netherlands and Flanders, where it is the Latin form used in Catholic registers, as well as in Italy and Spain. In Dutch records it often alternates with familiar diminutives.

adriano.label: Adriano
adriano.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Adrian, from Latin "Hadrianus", "from Hadria".
adriano.text: A name found in Italy, Portugal and Spain, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It is linked to Saint Adrian of Nicomedia, a martyr whose feast is 8 September.

adrianus.label: Adrianus
adrianus.meaning: Latin form of Adrian, from "Hadrianus", "from Hadria".
adrianus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic parish registers of the Netherlands and Flanders; the same person usually went by Adriaan or Arie in daily life and in civil records. It is linked to Saint Adrian of Nicomedia, whose feast is 8 September.

adrien.label: Adrien
adrien.meaning: From Latin "Hadrianus", "from Hadria", a town in Italy.
adrien.text: A name common in France, French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium, especially in the 19th century; the learned spelling Hadrien also occurs. Its feast is 8 September, that of Saint Adrian of Nicomedia, a 4th-century martyr.

adrienne.label: Adrienne
adrienne.meaning: Feminine of Adrien, from Latin "Hadrianus", "from Hadria".
adrienne.text: A female name widespread in France, Switzerland and Belgium in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also appears as Adrianne or Adriane.

afonso.label: Afonso
afonso.meaning: Portuguese form of Alphonse, from a Germanic name of disputed etymology, often explained by "adal" or "hild" and "funs", "ready, eager".
afonso.text: A royal name in Portugal since Afonso Henriques, the country's first king, and common in Portuguese registers of every period. It is sometimes written Affonso in older records.

agata.label: Agata
agata.text: The Polish and Italian form of Agatha, found in Polish and Italian registers from the 17th to the 20th century. It was borne by Saint Agatha of Sicily, virgin and martyr, whose feast is 5 February.

agatha.label: Agatha
agatha.text: The Latin and English form of Agathe, found in Dutch, German and English registers, often as the Latin form of Agaat or Agathe. It was borne by Saint Agatha of Sicily, virgin and martyr, whose feast is 5 February.

agathe.label: Agathe
agathe.text: A female name found in France, Germany and the Netherlands since the Middle Ages and fairly widespread in rural areas until the 19th century. Its feast is 5 February, that of Saint Agatha of Sicily, virgin and martyr.

aglae.label: Aglaé
aglae.meaning: From Greek "Aglaia", "splendour, brilliance", the name of one of the three Graces.
aglae.text: A mythological name fashionable in France in the late 18th and 19th centuries (Aglaé), reflecting neoclassical taste. In records the accent is often dropped or altered (Aglaé, Aglae).

agnes.label: Agnes
agnes.meaning: From Greek "hagnê", "pure, chaste", associated with Latin "agnus", "lamb".
agnes.text: A name widespread throughout Europe since the Middle Ages, frequent in English, Dutch, German and French (Agnès) registers. It was borne by Saint Agnes of Rome, virgin and martyr, whose feast is 21 January.

agnese.label: Agnese
agnese.meaning: Italian form of Agnes, from Greek "hagnê", "pure, chaste".
agnese.text: The Italian form of Agnes, found in Italian registers of every period. It was borne by Saint Agnes of Rome, virgin and martyr, whose feast is 21 January.

agneta.label: Agneta
agneta.meaning: Latinised form of Agnes, from Greek "hagnê", "pure, chaste".
agneta.text: A form of Agnes common in the Netherlands and northern Germany in the 17th and 18th centuries, as well as in Scandinavia. It also appears as Agnietje or Agnetta. It is linked to Saint Agnes of Rome, whose feast is 21 January.

agnieszka.label: Agnieszka
agnieszka.meaning: Polish form of Agnes, from Greek "hagnê", "pure, chaste".
agnieszka.text: The Polish form of Agnes, found in Polish registers since the Middle Ages. It was borne by Saint Agnes of Rome, virgin and martyr, whose feast is 21 January.

agostinho.label: Agostinho
agostinho.meaning: Portuguese form of Augustine, from Latin "Augustinus", derived from "Augustus", "venerable, majestic".
agostinho.text: The Portuguese form of Augustine, common in the registers of Portugal and Brazil. It is linked to Saint Augustine of Hippo, Doctor of the Church, whose feast is 28 August.

agostino.label: Agostino
agostino.meaning: Italian form of Augustine, from Latin "Augustinus", derived from "Augustus", "venerable, majestic".
agostino.text: The Italian form of Augustine, common in the registers of Italy and Ticino. It is linked to Saint Augustine of Hippo, Doctor of the Church, whose feast is 28 August.

agusti.label: Agustí
agusti.meaning: Catalan form of Augustine, from Latin "Augustinus", derived from "Augustus", "venerable, majestic".
agusti.text: The Catalan form (Agustí) of Augustine, found in the registers of Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands; in records written in Castilian the same person may appear as Agustín. It is linked to Saint Augustine of Hippo, whose feast is 28 August.

agustin.label: Agustín
agustin.meaning: Spanish form of Augustine, from Latin "Augustinus", derived from "Augustus", "venerable, majestic".
agustin.text: The Spanish form (Agustín) of Augustine, common in the registers of Spain and Latin America. It is linked to Saint Augustine of Hippo, Doctor of the Church, whose feast is 28 August.

agustina.label: Agustina
agustina.meaning: Spanish feminine of Agustín, from Latin "Augustinus", derived from "Augustus", "venerable".
agustina.text: A female name found in Spanish registers, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. In records it is often combined with María (María Agustina).

ahmed.label: Ahmed
ahmed.meaning: From Arabic "Ahmad", "most praiseworthy", one of the names of the Prophet Muhammad.
ahmed.text: A Muslim name very widespread in the Arab and Turkish world, rare in older European registers and found mainly in the 20th century with migration. Transcriptions vary by language: Ahmed, Ahmad, Amed.

aignan.label: Aignan
aignan.meaning: From Latin "Anianus", a Roman family name of uncertain origin.
aignan.text: Saint Aignan, bishop of Orléans, is said to have defended the city against Attila in 451; his feast is on 17 November. The name is mostly found around Orléans, in Berry and the Loire valley, where many parishes bear his name; Latin records write Anianus, and the spelling Agnan also occurs.

aime.label: Aimé
aime.text: A male name widespread in France, French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium, especially in the 19th century; the older spelling Aymé also occurs. Its feast is 13 September, that of Saint Amatus (Aimé), a 7th-century monk of Remiremont.

aimee.label: Aimée
aimee.text: A female name widespread in France, Switzerland and Belgium in the 19th century, also adopted in England (Aimee). In France its name day is 20 February, the feast of Blessed Amata of Assisi, niece of Saint Clare.

aires.label: Aires
aires.meaning: A medieval Iberian name of disputed origin, linked to the older form Arias, possibly of Germanic origin.
aires.text: A typically Portuguese name, frequent in the Middle Ages and the early modern period, which also became a surname. It appears in records as Ayres, Aires or Ayras.

alain.label: Alain
alain.meaning: Of disputed origin: an old Breton name, perhaps from the name of the Alans or from a Celtic word meaning "rock" or "handsome".
alain.text: A very old name in Brittany, borne by Breton dukes, later widespread throughout France, especially in the 20th century. In France its name day is 9 September, the feast of Blessed Alain de la Roche, a 15th-century Breton Dominican.

alan.label: Alan
alan.meaning: Of disputed origin: an old Breton name, perhaps from the name of the Alans or from a Celtic word meaning "rock" or "handsome".
alan.text: Brought to England by the Bretons who accompanied William the Conqueror, it is also traditional in Scotland. Its great popularity in the United Kingdom and the United States dates from the 20th century; Allan, Allen and, in Wales, Alun also occur.

alba.label: Alba
alba.text: A female name found in Spain and Italy, mainly in the 20th century. It should not be confused in records with the identical Spanish surname and ducal title.

alban.label: Alban
alban.meaning: From Latin "Albanus", "from Alba", the name of several ancient towns.
alban.text: The name of Saint Alban, the first martyr of Roman Britain, whose feast is 22 June. It is found in France, Germany, Switzerland and England, without ever being very frequent there.

albano.label: Albano
albano.text: A mainly Portuguese and Italian name, found in registers in the 19th and 20th centuries. In Italy it also evokes the Alban Hills and the town of Albano near Rome.

albert.label: Albert
albert.text: A name very widespread in France, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Germany and the United Kingdom in the 19th and early 20th centuries, borne by Prince Albert, the prince consort. Its feast is 15 November, that of Saint Albert the Great, Dominican and Doctor of the Church.

alberta.label: Alberta
alberta.meaning: Feminine of Albert, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "berht", "bright".
alberta.text: A female name found in the Netherlands, Belgium, England and the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, often given in honour of a father or godfather named Albert.

albertina.label: Albertina
albertina.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Albert, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "berht", "bright".
albertina.text: The Italian, Dutch and German form of Albertine, widespread in the 19th century. In registers it sometimes alternates with Alberta or Albertine for the same person.

albertine.label: Albertine
albertine.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Albert, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "berht", "bright".
albertine.text: A female name very widespread in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is often given in connection with a father or godfather named Albert.

alberto.label: Alberto
alberto.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Albert, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "berht", "bright".
alberto.text: A name common in Italy, Spain and Portugal, especially in the 19th and 20th centuries. Its feast is 15 November, that of Saint Albert the Great, Dominican and Doctor of the Church.

albertus.label: Albertus
albertus.meaning: Latin form of Albert, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "berht", "bright".
albertus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic registers of the Netherlands and Flanders; the same person often appears as Albert, Aalbert or Bertus in civil records. It is linked to Saint Albert the Great, whose feast is 15 November.

albin.label: Albin
albin.text: A name found in France, Switzerland, Germany and Poland, fairly common in the 19th century. In France its name day is 1 March, the feast of Saint Albinus (Aubin), 6th-century bishop of Angers.

albina.label: Albina
albina.text: A female name found in Italy, Poland and Spain, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It also occurs as Albine or Albinia.

albino.label: Albino
albino.text: A name found in Portugal, Italy and Spain, mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries. In records it should not be confused with the identical common noun.

albrecht.label: Albrecht
albrecht.meaning: German form of Albert, from Germanic "Adalberht", "noble and famous".
albrecht.text: The traditional German form of Albert, borne by many German princes and common in Germany and German-speaking Switzerland. It is linked to Saint Albert the Great, a Swabian Dominican whose feast is 15 November.

alcide.label: Alcide
alcide.meaning: From Greek "Alkeidês", "descendant of Alcaeus", an epithet of Heracles, related to "alkê", "strength".
alcide.text: A classical name fashionable in France and French-speaking Switzerland in the 19th century, also found in Italy. The form Alcides occurs in Iberian countries.

alda.label: Alda
alda.text: A female name found in Portugal and Italy, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries, with the diminutive Aldina. It is rarer elsewhere.

aldegonde.label: Aldegonde
aldegonde.text: Saint Aldegund, founder and abbess of Maubeuge in the 7th century, is celebrated on 30 January. The name is borne mostly in Hainaut and French Flanders.

aldo.label: Aldo
aldo.text: A typically Italian name, especially widespread in the late 19th and 20th centuries. It can also serve as a short form of names such as Ubaldo or Rinaldo.

alec.label: Alec
alec.meaning: Scottish short form of Alexander, from Greek "Alexandros", "defender of men".
alec.text: A familiar form of Alexander of Scottish origin, used in Britain especially in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. In official records the same person may be entered under the full name Alexander.

aleida.label: Aleida
aleida.meaning: Dutch form of Adelheid, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "heit", "nature, kind".
aleida.text: A typically Dutch and Frisian female name, frequent from the 17th to the 19th century, with the variants Aleid, Aleidis or Aaltje. It is close to Alida, with which it sometimes alternates for the same person.

alejandra.label: Alejandra
alejandra.meaning: Spanish feminine of Alejandro, from Greek "Alexandros", "defender of men".
alejandra.text: The Spanish form of Alexandra, found in the registers of Spain and Latin America, more frequent from the 20th century onward.

alejandro.label: Alejandro
alejandro.meaning: Spanish form of Alexander, from Greek "Alexandros", "defender of men".
alejandro.text: A name common in Spain and Latin America, found in registers of every period. The spelling Alexandro also occurs in older records.

aleksander.label: Aleksander
aleksander.meaning: Polish form of Alexander, from Greek "Alexandros", "defender of men".
aleksander.text: The Polish form of Alexander, found in Polish registers since the Middle Ages, with the diminutives Olek or Aleks. In registers kept in Latin or Russian, the same person may appear as Alexander or Aleksandr.

aleksandra.label: Aleksandra
aleksandra.meaning: Polish feminine of Aleksander, from Greek "Alexandros", "defender of men".
aleksandra.text: The Polish form of Alexandra, found in Polish registers, especially in the 19th and 20th centuries. In registers kept in Latin it often appears as Alexandra.

alessandra.label: Alessandra
alessandra.meaning: Italian feminine of Alessandro, from Greek "Alexandros", "defender of men".
alessandra.text: The Italian form of Alexandra, found in Italian registers of every period, with the diminutive Alessandrina.

alessandro.label: Alessandro
alessandro.meaning: Italian form of Alexander, from Greek "Alexandros", "defender of men".
alessandro.text: A name common in Italy and Ticino, often shortened to Sandro; dialect forms vary (Lissandro in Sicily). Its feast is 26 August, that of Saint Alexander of Bergamo, martyr and patron of the city.

aletta.label: Aletta
aletta.meaning: A Dutch form of disputed origin, usually linked to Adelheid (Germanic "adal", "noble").
aletta.text: A typically Dutch female name, found in Dutch registers and among Dutch settlers in South Africa in the 17th and 18th centuries. It appears as Aletta, Alette or Alet.

alex.label: Alex
alex.meaning: Short form of Alexander or Alexis, from Greek "alexein", "to defend".
alex.text: A short form of Alexander or Alexis, sometimes registered as an official given name, mainly in the 20th century, in Luxembourg, the United Kingdom, the United States and Germany. In older records the same person is usually entered under the full form.

alexander.label: Alexander
alexander.text: A name used throughout Europe, particularly traditional in Scotland (with Alasdair, Alistair, Sandy), Germany and the Netherlands. Its spread owes much to the prestige of Alexander the Great and to several popes and saints of the name.

alexandra.label: Alexandra
alexandra.meaning: Feminine of Alexander, from Greek "Alexandros", "defender of men".
alexandra.text: A female name found in Germany, the United Kingdom, Spain, France and Poland, rare before the 19th century and most widespread in the 20th century.

alexandre.label: Alexandre
alexandre.text: A name common in France, Portugal, Luxembourg, Belgium and French-speaking Switzerland, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. In France its name day is 22 April, the feast of Saint Alexander, a 2nd-century martyr of Lyon.

alexandrina.label: Alexandrina
alexandrina.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Alexander, from Greek "Alexandros", "defender of men".
alexandrina.text: A female name found in Portugal, the Netherlands and Britain, notably in the 19th century, when it was the first given name of Queen Victoria.

alexandrine.label: Alexandrine
alexandrine.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Alexander, from Greek "Alexandros", "defender of men".
alexandrine.text: A female name very widespread in France, French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium in the 19th century. In France its name day is 2 April, the feast of Blessed Alexandrina of Foligno, a 15th-century Poor Clare.

alexis.label: Alexis
alexis.meaning: From Greek "alexios", derived from "alexein", "to protect, defend".
alexis.text: A male name widespread in France, Luxembourg, Belgium and Switzerland, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. It was borne by Saint Alexius, known as the man of God, whose traditional feast is 17 July.

alfons.label: Alfons
alfons.meaning: German, Dutch and Polish form of Alphonse, from a Germanic name of disputed etymology, often explained by "adal" or "hild" and "funs", "ready, eager".
alfons.text: A name widespread in Belgium, Germany, Poland and Switzerland, mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries, with the Latin form Alfonsus or Alphonsus in Catholic registers. It is linked to Saint Alphonsus Liguori, Doctor of the Church, whose feast is 1 August.

alfonsina.label: Alfonsina
alfonsina.meaning: Italian feminine of Alfonso, from a Germanic name of disputed etymology.
alfonsina.text: A female name found in Italy and Belgium, mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It corresponds to the French Alphonsine.

alfonso.label: Alfonso
alfonso.meaning: From a Germanic name of disputed etymology, often explained by "adal" or "hild" and "funs", "ready, eager".
alfonso.text: The name of many kings of Castile, León and Aragon, very widespread in Spain and Italy; Alonso also occurs, while Ildefonso is a distinct name. It is linked to Saint Alphonsus Liguori, Neapolitan bishop and Doctor of the Church, whose feast is 1 August.

alfred.label: Alfred
alfred.text: The name of the Anglo-Saxon king Alfred the Great, revived in the 19th century in England and then in France, Switzerland, Germany and Belgium, where it became very common. Alfred the Great is commemorated on 26 October in the Anglican calendar.

alfredo.label: Alfredo
alfredo.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Alfred, from Old English "ælf", "elf", and "ræd", "counsel".
alfredo.text: A name widespread in Portugal, Italy and Spain from the 19th century onward, following the European vogue for Alfred.

algernon.label: Algernon
algernon.meaning: From Old Norman French "als grenons", "with moustaches", a nickname turned given name.
algernon.text: A rare name, mainly borne in the English aristocracy and upper middle class from the 18th to the early 20th century, notably in the Percy family. It is often shortened to Algy.

ali.label: Ali
ali.text: Borne by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad, it is one of the most widespread names in the Muslim world. In French records it appears mainly from the 19th century onward.

alice.label: Alice
alice.meaning: From Old French "Aalis", a form of Adelaide, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "heit", "nature, kind".
alice.text: A medieval name very widespread in France and England, strongly revived in the 19th century, notably in the United Kingdom, the United States, Switzerland and France. In France its name day is 16 December, the feast of Saint Adelaide, of whose name it is a form.

alicia.label: Alicia
alicia.meaning: Latinised form of Alice, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "heit", "nature, kind".
alicia.text: The medieval Latin form of Alice, used in older English records, and later a name in its own right in Spain and English-speaking countries, especially in the 20th century.

alicja.label: Alicja
alicja.meaning: Polish form of Alice, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "heit", "nature, kind".
alicja.text: The Polish form of Alice, infrequent in older registers and mainly widespread in the 20th century.

alida.label: Alida
alida.meaning: Dutch form derived from Adelheid, from Germanic "adal", "noble".
alida.text: A female name common in the Netherlands and Belgium, close to Aleida, also found in France in the 19th century. In France its name day is 26 April, the feast of Blessed Alda (Aldobrandesca) of Siena.

alina.label: Alina
alina.meaning: Of disputed origin: a short form of Adelina or of other names in "-lina", sometimes linked to Slavic or Latin roots.
alina.text: A female name found in Poland, Belgium and Spain, rare before the 19th century and mainly widespread in the 20th century, notably in Poland.

aline.label: Aline
aline.meaning: Short form of Adeline, from Germanic "adal", "noble".
aline.text: A female name widespread in France, French-speaking Switzerland, Luxembourg and Belgium in the 19th century. It may shorten Adeline or Alexandrine, so these forms are worth searching together.

alix.label: Alix
alix.meaning: Older form of Alice, from Germanic "adal", "noble", and "heit", "nature, kind".
alix.text: A medieval form of Alice, borne in the French nobility, and in use again in the 19th and 20th centuries in France and Belgium. Its feast is 9 January, that of Blessed Alix Le Clerc, a 17th-century foundress from Lorraine.

allan.label: Allan
allan.meaning: Variant of Alan, of disputed origin, perhaps from the name of the Alans or from a Celtic word meaning "rock" or "handsome".
allan.text: A spelling of Alan frequent in Scotland and English-speaking countries, mainly in the 20th century. It is also well known as a surname, especially in Scotland.

allen.label: Allen
allen.meaning: Variant of Alan, of disputed origin, perhaps from the name of the Alans or from a Celtic word meaning "rock" or "handsome".
allen.text: A mainly American spelling of Alan, often derived from a surname used as a given name. It is found in the United States and Britain from the 19th century onward.

alma.label: Alma
alma.meaning: From Latin "alma", "nurturing, kindly"; sometimes linked to Spanish "alma", "soul".
alma.text: A female name that became popular in Britain and France after the Battle of the Alma (1854) during the Crimean War, then spread in the United States, Germany and Switzerland in the late 19th century.

alois.label: Alois
alois.meaning: Germanic form of Aloysius, the Latinisation of Occitan "Aloys", a form of Louis ("Hlodwig", "glorious warrior").
alois.text: A name very widespread in Catholic southern Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Tyrol in the 18th and 19th centuries, under the influence of the cult of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga. Its feast is 21 June, that of this Italian Jesuit saint.

alojzy.label: Alojzy
alojzy.meaning: Polish form of Aloysius, the Latinisation of Occitan "Aloys", a form of Louis.
alojzy.text: The Polish form of Alois, found in Polish registers, notably in Silesia, in the 19th and 20th centuries. Its feast is 21 June, that of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga.

alonso.label: Alonso
alonso.meaning: Castilian form derived from Alfonso, from a Germanic name of disputed etymology.
alonso.text: A Spanish variant of Alfonso, very frequent in medieval and early modern Castile, which also became a surname. In records the same person may be called Alonso or Alfonso.

aloyse.label: Aloyse
aloyse.meaning: French and Luxembourgish form of Aloysius, the Latinisation of Occitan "Aloys", a form of Louis.
aloyse.text: A male name common in Luxembourg and Lorraine in the 18th and 19th centuries, often transcribed Aloys or Alois in German-language records. Its feast is 21 June, that of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga.

aloysius.label: Aloysius
aloysius.meaning: Latin form of Occitan "Aloys", a form of Louis ("Hlodwig", "glorious warrior").
aloysius.text: The Latin form of Alois, used in Catholic registers of Belgium and the Netherlands, and borne as a given name in Irish and American Catholic families. Its feast is 21 June, that of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga.

alphonse.label: Alphonse
alphonse.meaning: French form of Alfonso, from a Germanic name of disputed etymology, often explained by "adal" or "hild" and "funs", "ready, eager".
alphonse.text: A name very widespread in France, Luxembourg, Belgium and Switzerland in the 19th century. Its feast is 1 August, that of Saint Alphonsus Liguori, Neapolitan bishop and Doctor of the Church.

alphonsine.label: Alphonsine
alphonsine.meaning: Feminine of Alphonse, from a Germanic name of disputed etymology.
alphonsine.text: A female name very widespread in France, French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium in the 19th century, often given in connection with a father or godfather named Alphonse.

alphonsus.label: Alphonsus
alphonsus.meaning: Latin form of Alphonse, from a Germanic name of disputed etymology.
alphonsus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic registers of Flanders and the Netherlands; the same person usually appears as Alfons or Alphonse in civil records. It is linked to Saint Alphonsus Liguori, whose feast is 1 August.

alvaro.label: Álvaro
alvaro.meaning: Of disputed origin, usually linked to Germanic, perhaps "al", "all", and "wart", "guardian".
alvaro.text: An old Iberian name (Álvaro), frequent in Castile and Portugal since the Middle Ages, and the source of the surname Álvarez. The accent is often dropped in transcriptions.

alvin.label: Alvin
alvin.meaning: From Old English "Æthelwine", "noble friend", or "Ælfwine", "elf friend".
alvin.text: A mainly American name, widespread from the late 19th century onward. It is rare in older European registers.

alwin.label: Alwin
alwin.text: A name found in Germany and Poland, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It also occurs as Alwyn or Albuin.

alwine.label: Alwine
alwine.meaning: Feminine of Alwin, from Germanic "adal" or "alb" and "wini", "friend".
alwine.text: A German female name, mainly borne in the 19th and early 20th centuries and rarer afterwards.

alzira.label: Alzira
alzira.meaning: Of uncertain origin; sometimes linked to "Alzire", heroine of a tragedy by Voltaire, or to an Arabic root.
alzira.text: A mainly Portuguese and Brazilian female name, frequent in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is rare in other countries.

amalia.label: Amalia
amalia.meaning: From Germanic "amal", "vigour, industriousness", an element in the name of the Gothic Amal dynasty.
amalia.text: A name found in Italy, Portugal, Spain, Germany, the Netherlands and Poland, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. In records it alternates with Amélie, Amelia or Amalie.

amalie.label: Amalie
amalie.text: The German form of Amelia, widespread in Germany, Switzerland and Poland in the 18th and 19th centuries, notably in princely families. In French records the same person may appear as Amélie.

amand.label: Amand
amand.text: A name widespread in northern France and Belgium, where Saint Amand, the 7th-century evangeliser of Flanders, was greatly venerated. His feast is 6 February.

amanda.label: Amanda
amanda.text: A female name found in England from the 17th century in literature, and more widespread in the 19th and 20th centuries in the United States, Germany, Poland and Spain.

amandus.label: Amandus
amandus.meaning: Latin form of Amand, "worthy of being loved".
amandus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic registers of Flanders and Germany; the same person often appears as Amand or Amandus depending on the language of the record. Its feast is 6 February, that of Saint Amand, evangeliser of Flanders.

ambrogio.label: Ambrogio
ambrogio.text: A name closely associated with Milan, where Saint Ambrose was bishop in the 4th century, and common in Lombardy and Ticino. Its feast is 7 December, that of Saint Ambrose, the city's patron.

ambroise.label: Ambroise
ambroise.text: A name found in France and Belgium since the Middle Ages and fairly widespread in rural areas until the 19th century. Its feast is 7 December, that of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan and Doctor of the Church.

amedee.label: Amédée
amedee.text: A name of the House of Savoy, common in Savoy, French-speaking Switzerland and France in the 19th century. Its feast is 30 March, that of Blessed Amadeus IX, Duke of Savoy.

amedeo.label: Amedeo
amedeo.meaning: Italian form of Amédée, from Latin "ama Deum", "who loves God".
amedeo.text: A dynastic name of the House of Savoy, widespread in Piedmont and the rest of Italy in the 19th and 20th centuries. Its feast is 30 March, that of Blessed Amadeus IX, Duke of Savoy.

amelia.label: Amelia
amelia.meaning: From Germanic "amal", "vigour, industriousness", sometimes confused with Latin "Aemilia".
amelia.text: A name found in Portugal, Italy, Belgium, Poland, Spain and Britain, where it spread in the 18th century with the House of Hanover. It alternates with Amalia and Emilia in some records.

amelie.label: Amélie
amelie.meaning: French form of Amalia, from Germanic "amal", "vigour, industriousness".
amelie.text: A female name very widespread in France, Belgium and Switzerland in the 19th century, popularised notably by Queen Marie-Amélie. In records it alternates with Émilie, which is nevertheless a distinct name.

americo.label: Américo
americo.meaning: Portuguese and Italian form of Emmerich, from Germanic "Amalric" or "Haimirich", "powerful in his home".
americo.text: A mainly Portuguese name (Américo), widespread in the 19th and 20th centuries. It is associated with the navigator Amerigo Vespucci, who gave his name to America.

amice.label: Amice
amice.text: A medieval female name used in France and England in the 12th–14th centuries, notably among the nobility. Latin records write Amicia; it became rare after the end of the Middle Ages.

amilcar.label: Amílcar
amilcar.meaning: From Punic "Hamilcar", interpreted as "brother" or "servant of Melqart".
amilcar.text: The name of the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca, father of Hannibal, adopted as a given name in Portugal (Amílcar) in the 19th and 20th centuries, reflecting the taste for classical names.

amos.label: Amos
amos.meaning: From Hebrew "Amos", related to "amas", "to carry", often understood as "carried by God".
amos.text: The name of a biblical prophet, mainly used in Protestant circles in England and North America in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries. It is rare in Catholic registers.

amparo.label: Amparo
amparo.meaning: From Spanish "amparo", "protection, refuge", referring to Our Lady of the Forsaken (Virgen de los Desamparados).
amparo.text: A typically Spanish Marian devotional name, particularly widespread in the Valencia region, whose patroness is Our Lady of the Forsaken. In records it is often preceded by María.

amy.label: Amy
amy.text: A female name found in England since the Middle Ages, particularly widespread in Britain and the United States in the 19th century. It also appears as Amie or Aimee.

ana.label: Ana
ana.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Anne, from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
ana.text: An extremely common female name in Spain and Portugal in every period, often in compounds (Ana María, Ana Josefa). Its feast is 26 July, that of Saint Anne, mother of the Virgin Mary.

ana_maria.label: Ana Maria
ana_maria.meaning: Compound of Ana and María, both of Hebrew origin ("Hannah", "grace"; "Miryam", of disputed meaning).
ana_maria.text: A very common compound name in Spain, combining the Virgin Mary and her mother Saint Anne. In records the two elements are sometimes reversed, abbreviated or separated, and the person may appear under only one of them.

anais.label: Anaïs
anais.meaning: Of disputed origin: an Occitan or Catalan diminutive of Anne, sometimes linked to the Persian goddess Anahita.
anais.text: A name rare in older registers, found mainly in France in the 19th century (Anaïs), especially in the south. The diaeresis is often omitted in records.

anastasie.label: Anastasie
anastasie.text: A female name found in France in the 18th and 19th centuries, more frequent in the east and south. It is linked to several early martyr saints.

anastazja.label: Anastazja
anastazja.meaning: Polish form of Anastasia, from Greek "anastasis", "resurrection".
anastazja.text: The Polish form of Anastasia, found in Polish registers, notably in the 18th and 19th centuries. In registers kept in Latin it appears as Anastasia.

anatole.label: Anatole
anatole.text: A male name fashionable in France in the 19th century, especially in the middle classes. It is rare in earlier registers.

andre.label: André
andre.meaning: From Greek "Andreas", derived from "anêr, andros", "man, manly".
andre.text: A name very widespread in France, Luxembourg, Belgium, Switzerland and Portugal (André), especially in the late 19th and 20th centuries. Its feast is 30 November, that of Saint Andrew, apostle and brother of Saint Peter.

andrea.label: Andrea
andrea.meaning: From Greek "Andreas", derived from "anêr, andros", "man, manly".
andrea.text: In Italy Andrea is a male name, the Italian form of Andrew, very common in every period; elsewhere (Spain, Germany, the United States) it is mainly female and more recent. The Italian masculine is celebrated on 30 November, the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

andreas.label: Andreas
andreas.meaning: From Greek "Andreas", derived from "anêr, andros", "man, manly".
andreas.text: The Greek, Latin and German form of Andrew, very widespread in Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Belgium; in Catholic registers it is also the Latin form of André. Its feast is 30 November, that of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

andree.label: Andrée
andree.meaning: Feminine of André, from Greek "anêr, andros", "man, manly".
andree.text: A female name widespread in France and Luxembourg, especially in the late 19th and 20th centuries. It is rare in older registers.

andres.label: Andrés
andres.meaning: Spanish form of Andrew, from Greek "Andreas", "man, manly".
andres.text: The Spanish form (Andrés) of Andrew, common in Spain and Latin America in every period. Its feast is 30 November, that of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

andreu.label: Andreu
andreu.meaning: Catalan form of Andrew, from Greek "Andreas", "man, manly".
andreu.text: The Catalan form of Andrew, found in the registers of Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands; in records written in Castilian the same person may become Andrés. Its feast is 30 November, that of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

andrew.label: Andrew
andrew.meaning: English form of Andreas, from Greek "Andreas", "man, manly".
andrew.text: A very common name in Scotland, whose patron saint is Saint Andrew, as well as in England and the United States. Its feast is 30 November, that of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

andries.label: Andries
andries.meaning: Dutch form of Andrew, from Greek "Andreas", "man, manly".
andries.text: The Dutch form of Andrew, frequent in the Netherlands and Flanders from the 16th to the 19th century, often shortened to Dries; in Catholic registers it corresponds to Latin Andreas. It is linked to Saint Andrew the Apostle, whose feast is 30 November.

andrzej.label: Andrzej
andrzej.meaning: Polish form of Andrew, from Greek "Andreas", "man, manly".
andrzej.text: The Polish form of Andrew, very common in Poland since the Middle Ages; in Latin registers it appears as Andreas. Its feast is 30 November, that of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

aneta.label: Aneta
aneta.text: The Polish and Czech form of Annette, rare in older registers and mainly widespread in the 20th century.

ange.label: Ange
ange.text: A male name found in France, especially in Corsica and the south, and in Belgium. It corresponds to the Italian Angelo and often appears in compounds (Ange-Marie, Ange-Toussaint).

angel.label: Ángel
angel.text: A male name (Ángel) very widespread in Spain, especially from the 19th century, and found in France in families of Spanish origin. In Spain it is often celebrated on 2 October, the feast of the Holy Guardian Angels.

angela.label: Angela
angela.meaning: Feminine of Angelo, from Greek "angelos", "messenger", via Latin "angelus", "angel".
angela.text: A female name common in Italy, Spain and Portugal in every period, and in Britain in the 20th century. Its feast is 27 January, that of Saint Angela Merici, foundress of the Ursulines.

angele.label: Angèle
angele.meaning: French form of Angela, from Greek "angelos", "messenger", via Latin "angelus", "angel".
angele.text: A female name very widespread in France and Belgium in the 19th century (Angèle). Its feast is 27 January, that of Saint Angela Merici, foundress of the Ursulines.

angeles.label: Ángeles
angeles.meaning: From Spanish "ángeles", "angels", referring to Our Lady of the Angels (Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles).
angeles.text: A typically Spanish Marian devotional name (Ángeles), often preceded by María; Àngels in Catalan, Anxos in Galician. It is celebrated on 2 August, the feast of Our Lady of the Angels.

angelica.label: Angelica
angelica.text: A female name found in Italy, Belgium and Spain, popularised by the heroine of Ariosto's Orlando Furioso. It corresponds to the French Angélique.

angelika.label: Angelika
angelika.meaning: German and Polish form of Angelica, from Latin "angelica", "angelic".
angelika.text: A female name found in Germany, Switzerland and Poland, mainly in the 20th century. It is rare in older registers.

angelina.label: Angelina
angelina.meaning: Diminutive of Angela, from Greek "angelos", "messenger", via Latin "angelus", "angel".
angelina.text: A female name common in Italy, Belgium and Spain in the 19th and 20th centuries, and among Italian emigrants to the United States. In records it often alternates with Angela.

angeline.label: Angeline
angeline.meaning: Diminutive of Angèle, from Greek "angelos", "messenger", via Latin "angelus", "angel".
angeline.text: A female name widespread in France and Belgium in the 19th century, also found in the United States. It sometimes alternates with Angèle or Angélique in records.

angelique.label: Angélique
angelique.text: A female name widespread in France, Belgium and the Netherlands in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, notably in Catholic families. The Latin form Angelica also occurs.

angelo.label: Angelo
angelo.text: A male name very widespread in Italy and Ticino in every period, often in compounds (Angelo Maria); Italian emigrants spread it to France and the United States. The form Arcangelo, honouring Saint Michael, is close but distinct.

angiola.label: Angiola
angiola.meaning: Old Tuscan form of Angela, from Greek "angelos", "messenger".
angiola.text: An old regional form of Angela, frequent in Tuscany and central Italy in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, with the diminutive Angiolina. In records the same person may appear as Angela.

angus.label: Angus
angus.meaning: From Gaelic "Aonghas", often interpreted as "one choice" or "one strength".
angus.text: A traditional Scottish name, especially in the Highlands and Islands, borne by legendary kings of Ireland and Scotland. In registers it may appear as Gaelic Aonghas or as Aeneas, its learned rendering.

anibal.label: Aníbal
anibal.text: The name of the Carthaginian general Hannibal, adopted as a given name in Portugal and Spain (Aníbal) reflecting the taste for classical names, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries.

aniela.label: Aniela
aniela.meaning: Polish form of Angela, from Greek "angelos", "messenger".
aniela.text: The Polish form of Angela, found in Polish registers in the 18th and 19th centuries; in Latin registers it appears as Angela.

anita.label: Anita
anita.meaning: Spanish diminutive of Ana, from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
anita.text: A Spanish diminutive of Ana that became a name in its own right, spreading in the 20th century to Italy, the United States, Poland, Britain and France. In older Spanish records the same person is usually entered as Ana.

anke.label: Anke
anke.meaning: Low German and Dutch diminutive of Anna, from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
anke.text: A familiar form of Anna, originating in northern Germany, Friesland and the Netherlands. In older registers the same person may appear as Anna or Anneke.

ann.label: Ann
ann.meaning: English form of Anne, from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
ann.text: The English spelling of Anne, extremely common in English, Welsh and American registers from the 17th to the 20th century; the same person often appears as Ann, Anne, Anna or Nancy. Its feast is 26 July, that of Saint Anne, mother of the Virgin Mary.

anna.label: Anna
anna.meaning: Greek and Latin form of Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
anna.text: The Latin and international form of Anne, very common in Germany, Switzerland, Poland, Italy and the Netherlands; in Catholic registers it also renders French Anne. Its feast is 26 July, that of Saint Anne, mother of the Virgin Mary.

annabelle.label: Annabelle
annabelle.meaning: A medieval Scottish name of disputed origin, later associated with Anna and "belle" (beautiful).
annabelle.text: Annabel is recorded in Scotland from the Middle Ages; the spelling Annabelle spread in France in the 20th century, especially from the 1970s. It is rare in older French registers.

annaelle.label: Annaëlle
annaelle.meaning: A modern creation from Anne and the ending "-elle"; its sense is linked to Anne, "grace".
annaelle.text: A recent name that appeared in France at the end of the 20th century, part of the fashion for names ending in -elle with a Breton look. It does not occur in older registers.

anne.label: Anne
anne.text: One of the most frequent female names in France, England and Belgium from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, often in compounds (Anne-Marie, Marie-Anne). Its feast is 26 July, that of Saint Anne, mother of the Virgin Mary and patron saint of Brittany.

annemarie.label: Annemarie
annemarie.meaning: Compound of Anne and Marie, both of Hebrew origin ("Hannah", "grace"; "Miryam", of disputed meaning).
annemarie.text: A joined form of Anne-Marie, mainly widespread in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands in the 20th century. In older registers the two elements are usually separate (Anna Maria).

annet.label: Annet
annet.meaning: Disputed origin; usually linked to Saint Annemund (Ennemond), bishop of Lyon.
annet.text: A traditional male name of Auvergne, Limousin and Forez, frequent in 17th- and 18th-century registers. Despite its look it is not a diminutive of Anne: it is borne by men.

annetta.label: Annetta
annetta.meaning: Italian and Dutch diminutive of Anna, from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
annetta.text: A diminutive of Anna found in Italy and the Netherlands, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries; in records the same person may be entered as Anna. Its feast is 26 July, that of Saint Anne.

annette.label: Annette
annette.meaning: French diminutive of Anne, from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
annette.text: A diminutive of Anne that became a name in its own right in France in the early modern period, then spread to England, the Netherlands and Germany. In records it often alternates with Anne for the same person. Its feast is 26 July, that of Saint Anne.

annibale.label: Annibale
annibale.meaning: Italian form of Hannibal, from Punic "grace of Baal".
annibale.text: An Italian name inspired by the Carthaginian general Hannibal, found from the Renaissance onward in well-to-do families and more widely in the 19th and 20th centuries.

annick.label: Annick
annick.meaning: Breton diminutive of Anne, from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
annick.text: A Breton diminutive of Anne, long used familiarly and entered in civil records mainly in the 20th century, throughout France. Its feast is 26 July, that of Saint Anne, patron saint of Brittany.

anny.label: Anny
anny.meaning: Diminutive of Anne or Anna, from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
anny.text: A familiar form of Anna or Anne, sometimes registered as an official name in Switzerland, Germany, the Netherlands and France in the 20th century. Its feast is 26 July, that of Saint Anne.

anselme.label: Anselme
anselme.text: A name found in France since the Middle Ages, though never very frequent, more common in the east and south-east. Its feast is 21 April, that of Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury and Doctor of the Church.

anselmo.label: Anselmo
anselmo.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Anselm, from Germanic "ans", "god", and "helm", "helmet".
anselmo.text: A name found in Portugal, Spain and Italy, notably in Lombardy and the Aosta Valley, birthplace of Saint Anselm. Its feast is 21 April, that of Saint Anselm of Canterbury.

anszel.label: Anszel
anszel.meaning: A Yiddish form derived from German Anselm; etymology disputed.
anszel.text: A male Yiddish name, written Anszel in Polish records and Anschel in German records of the 19th century.

antao.label: Antão
antao.meaning: Old Portuguese form of Anthony, from Latin "Antonius", the name of a Roman family of obscure origin.
antao.text: A Portuguese form (Antão) reserved for Saint Anthony the Great, the Egyptian hermit, distinct from António, which usually refers to Saint Anthony of Padua. Its feast is 17 January.

anthelme.label: Anthelme
anthelme.text: Saint Anthelm, a Carthusian who became bishop of Belley, is celebrated on 26 June. The name is characteristic of Bugey and Savoy.

anthonie.label: Anthonie
anthonie.meaning: Old Dutch form of Anthony, from Latin "Antonius", the name of a Roman family of obscure origin.
anthonie.text: An older Dutch spelling of Anthony, frequent in 17th- and 18th-century registers, alongside Anthony, Antonie, Teunis or Toon depending on the region. It is linked to Saint Anthony of Padua, whose feast is 13 June.

anthony.label: Anthony
anthony.meaning: English form of Antonius, a Roman family name of obscure origin; the "th" spelling comes from a false link with Greek "anthos", "flower".
anthony.text: A name common in England, Ireland and the United States, more frequent in Catholic families, and an older spelling in Dutch. Its feast is 13 June, that of Saint Anthony of Padua.

antje.label: Antje
antje.meaning: Frisian and Dutch diminutive, usually linked to Anna (Hebrew "Hannah", "grace"), sometimes to Antonia.
antje.text: A female name typical of Friesland, Groningen and northern Germany in the 18th and 19th centuries. In records the same person may appear under a longer form, which makes identification tricky.

antoine.label: Antoine
antoine.meaning: From Latin "Antonius", the name of a Roman family of obscure origin.
antoine.text: One of the most frequent male names in France, Luxembourg, Belgium and French-speaking Switzerland from the 16th to the 19th century, often in compounds (Jean-Antoine, Antoine-Joseph). Its feast is 13 June, that of Saint Anthony of Padua; Saint Anthony the Great, celebrated on 17 January, was also much venerated in the countryside.

antoinette.label: Antoinette
antoinette.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Antoine, from Latin "Antonius".
antoinette.text: A female name very widespread in France, Belgium, Switzerland and the Netherlands from the 17th to the 19th century. In records it alternates with Antonia or Toinette for the same person.

anton.label: Anton
anton.meaning: German, Dutch and Slavic form of Anthony, from Latin "Antonius".
anton.text: A name common in Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and central Europe, especially in Catholic regions. Its feast is 13 June, that of Saint Anthony of Padua, sometimes also 17 January, that of Saint Anthony the Great.

antoni.label: Antoni
antoni.meaning: Polish and Catalan form of Anthony, from Latin "Antonius".
antoni.text: A name common in Poland, where it appears as Antonius in Latin registers, and in Catalonia, where it alternates with Castilian Antonio. Its feast is 13 June, that of Saint Anthony of Padua.

antonia.label: Antonia
antonia.meaning: Feminine of Antonius, a Roman family name of obscure origin.
antonia.text: A female name common in Spain, Portugal, Italy, the Netherlands and Germany; in Catholic registers it is also the Latin form of Antoinette. It often alternates with Antonina or Antoinette.

antonie.label: Antonie
antonie.meaning: Form of Antonius or Antonia, from Latin "Antonius".
antonie.text: In Germany and Poland Antonie is mainly a female name (a form of Antonia); in the Netherlands it is also an older male form of Anthony. The person's sex should therefore be checked in the record.

antonietta.label: Antonietta
antonietta.meaning: Italian diminutive of Antonia, from Latin "Antonius".
antonietta.text: An Italian female name, equivalent to Antoinette, common in the 19th and 20th centuries. In records it alternates with Antonia or Nietta.

antonin.label: Antonin
antonin.text: A male name widespread in France in the 19th century, notably in the south; in Czech, Antonín is simply the form of Anthony. Several saints Antoninus are venerated locally, including Saint Antoninus of Pamiers.

antonina.label: Antonina
antonina.meaning: Feminine of Antoninus, derived from Latin "Antonius".
antonina.text: A female name common in Poland, where it is the usual equivalent of Antoinette, and in Germany and Spain, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries.

antonine.label: Antonine
antonine.text: A female name widespread in France in the 19th century, especially in the south. In records it sometimes alternates with Antoinette.

antonino.label: Antonino
antonino.text: A name very widespread in Sicily and southern Italy, where it is often treated as an affectionate form of Antonio; it was borne by several local saints, including Saint Antoninus of Florence. In records it alternates with Antonio or Nino.

antonio.label: Antonio
antonio.meaning: From Latin "Antonius", the name of a Roman family of obscure origin.
antonio.text: One of the most frequent male names in Spain, Portugal and Italy in every period, often in compounds (José Antonio, Antonio María). Its feast is 13 June, that of Saint Anthony of Padua, who was born in Lisbon.

antonius.label: Antonius
antonius.meaning: Latin form of Anthony, a Roman family name of obscure origin.
antonius.text: The Latin form used in Catholic registers of the Netherlands, Flanders, Germany and Switzerland; in daily life the same person appears as Antoon, Anton, Teunis or Antoine. It is linked to Saint Anthony of Padua, whose feast is 13 June.

antony.label: Antony
antony.text: A spelling of Antoine or Anthony found in France, the Netherlands and Switzerland, rare in older registers. Its feast is 13 June, that of Saint Anthony of Padua.

antoon.label: Antoon
antoon.meaning: Flemish and Dutch form of Anthony, from Latin "Antonius".
antoon.text: A common form in Flanders and the Netherlands, often shortened to Toon; in Catholic registers the same person appears as Antonius. It is linked to Saint Anthony of Padua, whose feast is 13 June.

apolline.label: Apolline
apolline.meaning: From Greek "Apollonia", derived from the name of the god Apollo.
apolline.text: The French form of Apollonia, the virgin martyr of Alexandria (249) invoked against toothache, whose feast is on 9 February. It is found in French registers from the 17th to the 19th century, often spelled Appoline or Appolline.

apolonia.label: Apolonia
apolonia.meaning: From Greek "Apollônia", derived from the name of the god Apollo.
apolonia.text: A female name common in Poland (Apolonia) and Spain, especially in rural areas in the 18th and 19th centuries. It was borne by Saint Apollonia of Alexandria, a martyr invoked against toothache, whose feast is 9 February.

araceli.label: Araceli
araceli.meaning: From Latin "ara coeli", "altar of heaven", referring to Our Lady of Araceli.
araceli.text: A Spanish Marian devotional name, linked notably to the cult of Our Lady of Araceli at Lucena in Andalusia. It is mainly widespread in the 20th century and often preceded by María.

archibald.label: Archibald
archibald.text: A traditional name in Scotland, notably in the Campbell and Douglas families, later spread to England and the United States in the 19th century. It is often shortened to Archie.

arend.label: Arend
arend.meaning: From Dutch "arend", "eagle", often used as a short form of Arnold (Germanic "arn", "eagle", and "wald", "ruler").
arend.text: A typically Dutch and Low German male name, found in Dutch registers from the 16th to the 19th century, also written Arent. It may alternate with Arnoldus in Catholic registers.

arie.label: Arie
arie.meaning: In the Netherlands, a short form of Adriaan (Latin "Hadrianus", "from Hadria"); elsewhere sometimes from Hebrew "Aryeh", "lion".
arie.text: A very common male name in the Netherlands, especially in South Holland, in the 19th and 20th centuries, where it shortens Adriaan; in records the same person may appear as Adrianus or Adriaan. In Poland and Israel it corresponds rather to the Hebrew Aryeh.

aristide.label: Aristide
aristide.text: A classical name fashionable in France, Belgium and Italy in the 19th century, recalling the Athenian statesman Aristides the Just. In France its name day is 31 August, the feast of Saint Aristides, a 2nd-century Christian apologist of Athens.

arkadiusz.label: Arkadiusz
arkadiusz.meaning: Polish form of Arcadius, from Greek "Arkadios", "from Arcadia".
arkadiusz.text: A Polish name rare in older registers and mainly widespread in the second half of the 20th century.

arlene.label: Arlene
arlene.meaning: Of uncertain origin; sometimes linked to Arline, heroine of the opera The Bohemian Girl (1843), or formed on names such as Charlene.
arlene.text: An American female name, mainly widespread in the 20th century, with many spellings (Arleen, Arline, Arlena). It is absent from older European registers.

arlette.label: Arlette
arlette.meaning: Of disputed origin, perhaps Germanic; the name traditionally given to the mother of William the Conqueror.
arlette.text: A name associated with medieval Normandy, rare for centuries and then mainly widespread in France in the first half of the 20th century.

armand.label: Armand
armand.text: A name widespread in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland in the 18th and 19th centuries, popularised by Armand Jean du Plessis, Cardinal Richelieu. In France its name day is 23 December, the feast of Saint Hartmann, 12th-century bishop of Brixen.

armande.label: Armande
armande.meaning: Feminine of Armand, from Germanic "hari", "army", and "man", "man".
armande.text: A female name found in France in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, often in connection with a godfather named Armand. It remained less frequent than Armandine.

armandine.label: Armandine
armandine.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Armand, from Germanic "hari", "army", and "man", "man".
armandine.text: A typically French female name, fashionable in the 19th century and rarer afterwards. In records it sometimes alternates with Armande.

armando.label: Armando
armando.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Armand, from Germanic "hari", "army", and "man", "man".
armando.text: A name widespread in Portugal, Italy and Spain, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries.

armel.label: Armel
armel.meaning: From Breton; often explained as "arzh", "bear", and "mael", "prince", though this is disputed.
armel.text: Saint Armel, a monk who came from Britain in the 6th century, gave his name to Ploërmel; his feast is on 16 August. The name is found mostly in Brittany, as Armel or Arzel.

armida.label: Armida
armida.meaning: Of uncertain origin; the name of the enchantress in Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered (1581).
armida.text: An Italian literary name, inspired by Tasso's heroine and the many operas about her, mainly used in the 19th and 20th centuries. It also appears as Armide or Arminda.

arnaldo.label: Arnaldo
arnaldo.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Arnold, from Germanic "arn", "eagle", and "wald", "ruler".
arnaldo.text: A name found in Portugal, Italy and Italian-speaking Switzerland, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries.

arnaud.label: Arnaud
arnaud.text: A medieval name very widespread in south-western France (Arnaud, Arnaut, Arnauld), where it also gave rise to many surnames. In France its name day is 10 February, the feast of Blessed Arnaldo of Limena, a Benedictine of Padua.

arnaudine.label: Arnaudine
arnaudine.meaning: Feminine of Arnaud, from Germanic "arn", "eagle", and "wald", "rule".
arnaudine.text: A feminine form of Arnaud, mostly recorded in south-western France (Gascony, Béarn). It remains uncommon and records sometimes give Arnaude instead.

arno.label: Arno
arno.meaning: Short form of Germanic names in "arn", "eagle", such as Arnold.
arno.text: A name found in Luxembourg, Germany and Poland, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It may shorten Arnold or Arnulf, so these forms are worth searching together.

arnold.label: Arnold
arnold.text: A name widespread in Switzerland, the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg and Britain, especially in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. In Catholic registers it appears as Arnoldus.

arnoldus.label: Arnoldus
arnoldus.meaning: Latin form of Arnold, from Germanic "arn", "eagle", and "wald", "ruler".
arnoldus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic registers of the Netherlands and Flanders; in daily life the same person appears as Arnout, Arnoud, Arend or Nol.

arrigo.label: Arrigo
arrigo.meaning: Old Italian form of Henry, from Germanic "Heimirich", "ruler of the home".
arrigo.text: An older, literary form of Enrico, common in medieval Tuscany and revived in the 19th century in educated circles. In records the same person may appear as Enrico.

arsene.label: Arsène
arsene.text: A name widespread in France and Belgium in the 19th century (Arsène), rarer before. It was borne by Saint Arsenius the Great, a hermit of the Egyptian desert, whose feast is 19 July.

artheme.label: Arthème
artheme.meaning: From Greek "Artemios", derived from the name of the goddess Artemis.
artheme.text: A rare name, found mostly in 19th-century French registers. Records spell it Arthème or Artème, and Artemius in Latin.

arthur.label: Arthur
arthur.meaning: Of disputed origin: perhaps from Celtic "artos", "bear", or from the Roman family name "Artorius".
arthur.text: The name of the legendary king of the Round Table, very widespread in Britain and the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries, as well as in Belgium, Luxembourg and France. It was also found in the Breton aristocracy from the Middle Ages.

artur.label: Artur
artur.meaning: Portuguese, Polish, German and Spanish form of Arthur, of disputed origin.
artur.text: A name found in Portugal, Poland, Germany and Spain, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. The older form Artus also occurs.

arturo.label: Arturo
arturo.meaning: Italian and Spanish form of Arthur, of disputed origin.
arturo.text: A name widespread in Italy and Spain, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries.

ascanio.label: Ascanio
ascanio.meaning: From Latin "Ascanius", the name of Aeneas's son in the Aeneid, of uncertain etymology.
ascanio.text: An Italian name of classical inspiration, borne mainly in the nobility and middle classes from the Renaissance onward. It remains rare in ordinary registers.

ascension.label: Ascensión
ascension.meaning: From Spanish "ascensión", "ascension", referring to the Ascension of Christ.
ascension.text: A typically Spanish devotional name (Ascensión), often preceded by María and sometimes given to children born around the feast of the Ascension, whose date varies each year.

assunta.label: Assunta
assunta.meaning: From Italian "assunta", "taken up (into heaven)", referring to the Assumption of the Virgin.
assunta.text: A Marian devotional name very widespread in Italy, especially in the south, often preceded by Maria. It is celebrated on 15 August, the feast of the Assumption.

asuncion.label: Asunción
asuncion.meaning: From Spanish "asunción", "assumption", referring to the Assumption of the Virgin.
asuncion.text: A typically Spanish Marian devotional name (Asunción), often preceded by María; Assumpció in Catalan. It is celebrated on 15 August, the feast of the Assumption.

athanase.label: Athanase
athanase.text: A name found in France in the 18th and 19th centuries, notably in the south-east, in Brittany and in Quebec. It was borne by Saint Athanasius of Alexandria, Doctor of the Church, whose feast is 2 May.

attilio.label: Attilio
attilio.meaning: From Latin "Atilius", the name of a Roman family, of uncertain etymology; often wrongly linked to Attila.
attilio.text: An Italian name mainly widespread in the late 19th and 20th centuries, reflecting the taste for Roman names.

aubin.label: Aubin
aubin.text: Saint Aubin, bishop of Angers in the 6th century, is celebrated on 1 March; many Saint-Aubin parishes dot western France. The name was common in Anjou, Brittany and Normandy under the Ancien Régime; the Latin Albinus is shared with Albin.

aubine.label: Aubine
aubine.text: An uncommon feminine form of Aubin, found mostly in western France. It should not be confused with Albine, which has its own sheet.

audrey.label: Audrey
audrey.meaning: Norman and English form of "Æthelthryth", from Old English "æthel", "noble", and "thryth", "strength".
audrey.text: An English name derived from Saint Æthelthryth (Audrey), abbess of Ely, mainly widespread in Britain and the United States in the first half of the 20th century. Its feast is 23 June, that of this saint.

august.label: August
august.text: A name widespread in Germany, Switzerland, Belgium, Poland, the Netherlands and Luxembourg in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Its name day is most often 28 August, the feast of Saint Augustine of Hippo.

augusta.label: Augusta
augusta.meaning: Feminine of Augustus, from Latin "augustus", "venerable, majestic".
augusta.text: A female name found in Italy, Portugal, Belgium, Switzerland, Germany and Britain, especially in the 19th century, notably in German princely families.

auguste.label: Auguste
auguste.text: In France, Belgium, Switzerland and Luxembourg, Auguste is a male name very widespread in the 19th century; in Germany and Poland it is instead a female form (Augusta). In France its name day is 29 February, the feast of Saint Auguste Chapdelaine, a missionary martyred in China.

augustin.label: Augustin
augustin.text: A name widespread in France, Belgium, Switzerland, Germany and Poland, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. Its feast is 28 August, that of Saint Augustine of Hippo, Doctor of the Church.

augustine.label: Augustine
augustine.text: A female name very widespread in France, Belgium and Switzerland in the 19th century. In English, however, Augustine is a male form, which should be checked in the records.

augustinus.label: Augustinus
augustinus.meaning: Latin form of Augustine, derived from "Augustus", "venerable, majestic".
augustinus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic registers of Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany; in daily life the same person appears as Augustijn, Augustin or Stijn. It is linked to Saint Augustine of Hippo, whose feast is 28 August.

augusto.label: Augusto
augusto.text: A name widespread in Portugal, Italy and Spain in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is often celebrated on 28 August, the feast of Saint Augustine of Hippo.

augustus.label: Augustus
augustus.meaning: From Latin "Augustus", "venerable, majestic", the title of the first Roman emperor.
augustus.text: The Latin form of Auguste, used as a given name in Britain, the United States, the Netherlands and Germany, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries; it is also the Latin form of August in Catholic registers. It is often shortened to Gus.

aurelia.label: Aurelia
aurelia.meaning: From Latin "Aurelia", the name of a Roman family, associated with "aureus", "golden".
aurelia.text: A female name found in Italy, Spain, the Netherlands, Poland and the United States, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. In French records it corresponds to Aurélie.

aurelie.label: Aurélie
aurelie.meaning: From Latin "Aurelia", the name of a Roman family, associated with "aureus", "golden".
aurelie.text: A female name found in France in the 19th century (Aurélie), and very fashionable again in the late 20th century. In France its name day is 15 October, the feast of Saint Aurelia, an 11th-century recluse in Regensburg.

aurelio.label: Aurelio
aurelio.meaning: From Latin "Aurelius", the name of a Roman family, associated with "aureus", "golden".
aurelio.text: A name found in Spain, Italy and Portugal, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. The forms Aureliano or, in Catalan, Aureli also occur.

auriane.label: Auriane
auriane.meaning: Linked to Latin "aurum", "gold", or to Aurelian; disputed origin.
auriane.text: A modern name that appeared in France at the end of the 20th century. It does not occur in older registers.

aurora.label: Aurora
aurora.text: A female name found in Spain and Italy, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. In Spain it may also refer to a Marian devotion (Virgen de la Aurora).

aurore.label: Aurore
aurore.text: A female name found in France in the 19th century, made famous by Aurore Dupin (George Sand), and fashionable again in the late 20th century.

austremoine.label: Austremoine
austremoine.text: Saint Austremonius, regarded as the apostle of Auvergne and first bishop of Clermont, is celebrated on 1 November. The name is specific to Auvergne.

aviv.label: Aviv
aviv.text: A modern Hebrew name, given mainly in Israel from the 20th century, more often to boys. It is absent from older registers.

avoye.label: Avoye
avoye.meaning: Generally regarded as an old French form of Hedwig; disputed origin.
avoye.text: A medieval female name that survives in the Rue Sainte-Avoye in Paris. It still appears in some 16th- and 17th-century registers, spelled Avoye or Avoie, before disappearing.

babette.label: Babette
babette.meaning: Diminutive of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "God is my oath"; sometimes also of Barbara.
babette.text: A familiar form of Elizabeth, common in Germany, Alsace and France in the 18th and 19th centuries. In official records the same person is usually entered as Élisabeth, Elisabetha or Barbara.

baldassarre.label: Baldassarre
baldassarre.meaning: Italian form of Balthazar, the traditional name of one of the Magi, linked to Akkadian "Bel-shar-usur", "Bel protect the king".
baldassarre.text: An Italian name used since the Renaissance, more frequent in the north and in Sicily. It is celebrated on 6 January, at Epiphany, with the Magi.

baltasar.label: Baltasar
baltasar.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Balthazar, the traditional name of one of the Magi, linked to Akkadian "Bel-shar-usur", "Bel protect the king".
baltasar.text: A name found in Spain and Portugal since the Middle Ages, especially in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries. It is celebrated on 6 January, at Epiphany, with the Magi.

balthasar.label: Balthasar
balthasar.meaning: The traditional name of one of the Magi, linked to Akkadian "Bel-shar-usur", "Bel protect the king".
balthasar.text: A name widespread in Germany, Switzerland, Belgium and the Netherlands in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, notably in the Rhineland, where the relics of the Magi are venerated in Cologne; Balthazar and the short form Baltes also occur. It is celebrated on 6 January, at Epiphany.

baptist.label: Baptist
baptist.meaning: From Greek "baptistês", "one who baptises", the epithet of Saint John the Baptist.
baptist.text: A name found in Switzerland, Germany and Belgium, often as the second element of Johann Baptist; the person may therefore appear as Johann, Baptist or both. It is linked to Saint John the Baptist, whose feast is 24 June.

baptiste.label: Baptiste
baptiste.meaning: From Greek "baptistês", "one who baptises", the epithet of Saint John the Baptist.
baptiste.text: A name very widespread in France, Belgium, Switzerland and Luxembourg, mostly as part of Jean-Baptiste; the same person may appear as Jean, Baptiste or Jean-Baptiste depending on the record. Its feast is 24 June, that of Saint John the Baptist.

baptistin.label: Baptistin
baptistin.meaning: Diminutive of Baptiste, from Greek "baptistês", "one who baptises".
baptistin.text: A typically Provençal name, widespread in Provence and south-eastern France in the 19th century. In records the same person may also be entered as Jean-Baptiste. It is linked to Saint John the Baptist, whose feast is 24 June.

baptistine.label: Baptistine
baptistine.meaning: Feminine of Baptistin, from Greek "baptistês", "one who baptises".
baptistine.text: A typically Provençal female name, widespread in south-eastern France in the 19th century; the Italian Battistina is its equivalent.

barbara.label: Barbara
barbara.text: A female name very widespread in Poland, Germany, Switzerland and Belgium in every period, and in the United States and Britain in the 20th century. It was borne by Saint Barbara, a martyr and patron saint of gunners and miners, whose feast is 4 December.

barbe.label: Barbe
barbe.meaning: French form of Barbara, from Greek "barbaros", "foreign".
barbe.text: An old French form of Barbara, frequent in the registers of Lorraine, Belgium and northern France from the 16th to the 18th century, rarer afterwards. Its feast is 4 December, that of Saint Barbara, patron saint of miners.

barend.label: Barend
barend.meaning: Dutch form of Bernard, from Germanic "bern", "bear", and "hard", "strong, hardy".
barend.text: A typically Dutch name, common in the Netherlands from the 16th to the 19th century; in Catholic registers it appears as Bernardus. It is linked to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, whose feast is 20 August.

barrie.label: Barrie
barrie.meaning: Variant of Barry, from Irish "Barra", a short form of "Fionnbharr", "fair-headed".
barrie.text: A mainly British spelling of Barry, widespread in the mid-20th century. It is rare in older registers.

barry.label: Barry
barry.meaning: From Irish "Barra", a short form of "Fionnbharr", "fair-headed"; also an Anglo-Norman surname.
barry.text: A name of Irish origin, also used as a surname, mainly widespread in Britain, Ireland and the United States in the 20th century.
