barthelemy.label: Barthélemy
barthelemy.meaning: From Aramaic "bar Talmai", "son of Talmai", via Greek "Bartholomaios".
barthelemy.text: A name found in France, French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium since the Middle Ages (Barthélemy, Barthélémy), fairly common until the 18th century. Its feast is 24 August, that of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.

bartholomaus.label: Bartholomäus
bartholomaus.meaning: German form of Bartholomew, from Aramaic "bar Talmai", "son of Talmai".
bartholomaus.text: The German form (Bartholomäus) common in Germany, Switzerland and Silesia, often shortened to Bartel, Barthel or Mewes depending on the region. Its feast is 24 August, that of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.

bartholomeus.label: Bartholomeus
bartholomeus.meaning: Latin and Dutch form of Bartholomew, from Aramaic "bar Talmai", "son of Talmai".
bartholomeus.text: The form used in Dutch and Flemish registers, where the same person often appears as Bartel, Bart or Meeus. It is linked to Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, whose feast is 24 August.

bartlomiej.label: Bartłomiej
bartlomiej.meaning: Polish form of Bartholomew, from Aramaic "bar Talmai", "son of Talmai".
bartlomiej.text: The Polish form (Bartłomiej) common since the Middle Ages, with the diminutives Bartek and Bartosz; in Latin registers it appears as Bartholomaeus. Its feast is 24 August, that of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.

bartolome.label: Bartolomé
bartolome.meaning: Spanish form of Bartholomew, from Aramaic "bar Talmai", "son of Talmai".
bartolome.text: The Spanish form (Bartolomé) common in Spain since the Middle Ages, often shortened to Bartolo. Its feast is 24 August, that of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.

bartolomeo.label: Bartolomeo
bartolomeo.meaning: Italian form of Bartholomew, from Aramaic "bar Talmai", "son of Talmai".
bartolomeo.text: The Italian form, common in Italy and Ticino in every period, often shortened to Bartolo, Meo or Baccio. Its feast is 24 August, that of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.

bartolomeu.label: Bartolomeu
bartolomeu.meaning: Portuguese form of Bartholomew, from Aramaic "bar Talmai", "son of Talmai".
bartolomeu.text: The Portuguese form, borne notably by the navigator Bartolomeu Dias, and found in Portuguese registers of every period. Its feast is 24 August, that of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.

bartomeu.label: Bartomeu
bartomeu.meaning: Catalan form of Bartholomew, from Aramaic "bar Talmai", "son of Talmai".
bartomeu.text: The Catalan form, particularly frequent in Majorca and the Balearic Islands, where it is often shortened to Tomeu; in records written in Castilian the same person becomes Bartolomé. Its feast is 24 August, that of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.

baruch.label: Baruch
baruch.text: Baruch is the scribe of the prophet Jeremiah. The name is common in Jewish communities; Boruch or Borouch reflect the Yiddish pronunciation, and Barouch the French transcription.

basil.label: Basil
basil.text: The English form of Basile, found in Britain mainly in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is linked to Saint Basil of Caesarea, Doctor of the Church, whose feast is 2 January.

basile.label: Basile
basile.text: A name found in France and Belgium since the Middle Ages, fairly common in rural areas in the 17th and 18th centuries. Its feast is 2 January, that of Saint Basil of Caesarea, Doctor of the Church.

battista.label: Battista
battista.meaning: Italian form of Baptiste, from Greek "baptistês", "one who baptises".
battista.text: A very widespread Italian name, mostly as part of Giovanni Battista; the same person may appear as Giovanni, Battista or Giovanni Battista depending on the record, and also as Giobatta in Liguria. It is linked to Saint John the Baptist, whose feast is 24 June.

baudouin.label: Baudouin
baudouin.text: The name of the counts of Flanders and the kings of Jerusalem, widely used in northern France and Flanders in the Middle Ages. Latin records write Balduinus; it became rarer after the 16th century.

beat.label: Beat
beat.text: Saint Beatus, a hermit on the shores of Lake Thun regarded as the apostle of Switzerland, is celebrated on 9 May. The name is frequent in German-speaking Switzerland; Latin registers write Beatus.

beata.label: Beata
beata.text: A female name found in Poland, the Netherlands and Germany, rare in older registers and mainly widespread in Poland in the 20th century.

beatrice.label: Beatrice
beatrice.meaning: From Latin "Beatrix", associated with "beatus", "happy"; perhaps an alteration of "Viatrix", "traveller".
beatrice.text: A name found in Italy since the Middle Ages, made famous by Dante's Beatrice, then in Britain, Switzerland and France in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is often shortened to Bice in Italy.

beatrix.label: Beatrix
beatrix.meaning: From Latin "Beatrix", associated with "beatus", "happy"; perhaps an alteration of "Viatrix", "traveller".
beatrix.text: The Latin and medieval form of Beatrice, borne in the European nobility and found in Belgium, Britain, France, Italy and Germany. It is linked to Saint Beatrice of Silva, a Portuguese nun whose feast is 17 August.

beatriz.label: Beatriz
beatriz.meaning: Iberian form of Beatrice, from Latin "Beatrix", associated with "beatus", "happy".
beatriz.text: A female name common in Portugal and Spain since the Middle Ages; in Portugal the old form Brites also occurs. Its feast is 17 August, that of Saint Beatrice of Silva, foundress of the Conceptionists.

beila.label: Beila
beila.meaning: From Yiddish, linked to the sense "beautiful"; disputed origin.
beila.text: A female name of the Jewish communities of Central and Eastern Europe. Polish registers transcribe it Bajla or Bejla, German and French records Beila or Beile.

belen.label: Belen
belen.meaning: From Spanish "Belén", "Bethlehem", from Hebrew "Beit Lehem", "house of bread".
belen.text: A Spanish devotional name referring to the Nativity, often preceded by María; Betlem in Catalan. It is mainly widespread in the 20th century.

bella.label: Bella
bella.meaning: Short form of Isabella or Annabella, associated with Italian "bella", "beautiful".
bella.text: A short form, sometimes registered as a given name, found in Germany, Poland and Britain, notably in Jewish families of central Europe. In records the same person may be entered as Isabella or Isabelle.

belle.label: Belle
belle.meaning: Short form of Isabel or Annabel, associated with French "belle", "beautiful".
belle.text: A short form of Isabel or Arabella, used as a given name in the United States and Britain in the 19th and early 20th centuries. In official records the same person may be entered under the full form.

benedetta.label: Benedetta
benedetta.meaning: Italian feminine of Benedetto, from Latin "benedicta", "blessed".
benedetta.text: An Italian female name found in every period, though never very frequent. It corresponds to the French Benoîte.

benedetto.label: Benedetto
benedetto.meaning: Italian form of Benedict, from Latin "benedictus", "blessed".
benedetto.text: An Italian name common in every period, often shortened to Betto or Bettino. Its feast is 11 July, that of Saint Benedict of Nursia, father of Western monasticism and patron saint of Europe.

benedictus.label: Benedictus
benedictus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic registers of Belgium, the Netherlands, France and Germany; in daily life the same person appears as Benoît, Benedikt or Bennet. It is linked to Saint Benedict of Nursia, whose feast is 11 July.

benedikt.label: Benedikt
benedikt.meaning: German form of Benedict, from Latin "benedictus", "blessed".
benedikt.text: A name found in Germany, Switzerland (where Bendicht also occurs) and Poland, especially in Catholic regions. Its feast is 11 July, that of Saint Benedict of Nursia.

benigne.label: Bénigne
benigne.text: Saint Benignus, a martyr regarded as the apostle of Burgundy, is venerated in Dijon and celebrated on 1 November. The name is characteristic of Burgundy, mostly borne by men (Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet) and more rarely by women.

benita.label: Benita
benita.meaning: Spanish feminine of Benito, from Latin "benedicta", "blessed".
benita.text: A Spanish female name, found mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries. In Latin registers it may appear as Benedicta.

benito.label: Benito
benito.meaning: Spanish form of Benedict, from Latin "benedictus", "blessed".
benito.text: A Spanish name common since the Middle Ages; Benedicto and, in Galicia, Bieito also occur. Its feast is 11 July, that of Saint Benedict of Nursia.

benjamin.label: Benjamin
benjamin.meaning: From Hebrew "Binyamin", "son of the right hand", that is "favourite son" or "son of the south".
benjamin.text: The name of Jacob's youngest son, used in France, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Germany and, very widely, in English-speaking countries, notably among Protestants. In France its name day is 31 March, the feast of Saint Benjamin, a deacon martyred in Persia in the 5th century.

benno.label: Benno
benno.meaning: Germanic short form of names in "Bern-" ("bear"), sometimes also of Benedikt.
benno.text: A name found in Germany, Poland and Switzerland, particularly in Bavaria. It was borne by Saint Benno, bishop of Meissen and patron saint of Munich, whose feast is 16 June.

benoit.label: Benoît
benoit.text: A name found in France, Belgium and French-speaking Switzerland since the Middle Ages (Benoît, Benoist), which also gave rise to many surnames. Its feast is 11 July, that of Saint Benedict of Nursia, father of Western monasticism.

bento.label: Bento
bento.meaning: Portuguese form of Benedict, from Latin "benedictus", "blessed".
bento.text: A Portuguese name common from the Middle Ages to the 19th century. Its feast is 11 July, that of Saint Benedict of Nursia.

berek.label: Berek
berek.meaning: From Yiddish "ber", "bear", with a Polish diminutive suffix.
berek.text: The Polish form of Yiddish Ber or Berl, associated with Issachar, very frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. German and Alsatian records write Beer.

berend.label: Berend
berend.meaning: Low German and Dutch form of Bernard, from Germanic "bern", "bear", and "hard", "strong".
berend.text: A name typical of northern Germany and the eastern Netherlands, frequent from the 16th to the 19th century, also written Berendt or Behrend. It is linked to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, whose feast is 20 August.

bernadette.label: Bernadette
bernadette.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Bernard, from Germanic "bern", "bear", and "hard", "strong".
bernadette.text: A name made famous by Bernadette Soubirous, the visionary of Lourdes, and mainly widespread in France in the 20th century. It is celebrated on 18 February in France; the Roman calendar commemorates the saint on 16 April.

bernard.label: Bernard
bernard.text: A name widespread in France, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Britain since the Middle Ages, which gave rise to many surnames. Its feast is 20 August, that of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, Doctor of the Church.

bernarde.label: Bernarde
bernarde.meaning: Feminine of Bernard, from Germanic "bern", "bear", and "hard", "strong".
bernarde.text: A feminine form of Bernard, mostly recorded in south-western France (Gascony, Béarn, the Pyrenees) under the Ancien Régime. It is distinct from Bernardine, which has its own sheet.

bernardina.label: Bernardina
bernardina.meaning: Feminine of Bernardino, from Germanic "bern", "bear", and "hard", "strong".
bernardina.text: A female name found in the Netherlands, Spain and Germany, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. It is also the Latin form of Bernardine in Catholic registers.

bernardino.label: Bernardino
bernardino.meaning: Italian diminutive of Bernardo, from Germanic "bern", "bear", and "hard", "strong".
bernardino.text: A name widespread in Italy, Portugal, Spain and Ticino, popularised by Saint Bernardino of Siena, a 15th-century Franciscan preacher whose feast is 20 May.

bernardo.label: Bernardo
bernardo.meaning: Iberian and Italian form of Bernard, from Germanic "bern", "bear", and "hard", "strong".
bernardo.text: A name common in Portugal, Spain, Italy and Ticino since the Middle Ages. Its feast is 20 August, that of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux.

bernardus.label: Bernardus
bernardus.meaning: Latin form of Bernard, from Germanic "bern", "bear", and "hard", "strong".
bernardus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic registers of the Netherlands and Flanders; in daily life the same person appears as Barend, Berend, Bernard or Ben. It is linked to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, whose feast is 20 August.

bernhard.label: Bernhard
bernhard.meaning: German form of Bernard, from Germanic "bern", "bear", and "hard", "strong".
bernhard.text: A name common in Germany, Switzerland, Poland and the Netherlands since the Middle Ages. Its feast is 20 August, that of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux.

bernice.label: Bernice
bernice.meaning: From Greek "Berenikê", the Macedonian form of "Pherenikê", "bringer of victory".
bernice.text: A mainly American female name, widespread in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; the French equivalent is Bérénice.

bert.label: Bert
bert.meaning: Short form of Germanic names containing "berht", "bright, famous" (Albert, Herbert, Bertram, Hubert...).
bert.text: A short form used as a given name in Britain, the United States and the Netherlands, especially in the late 19th and 20th centuries. The same person should be searched under the full form, which varies from one individual to another.

berta.label: Berta
berta.text: The German, Portuguese, Polish and Spanish form of Bertha, common in the 19th and early 20th centuries. In records it may alternate with Bertha.

bertha.label: Bertha
bertha.text: A name very widespread in Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Poland, and in English-speaking countries in the 19th century; it goes back to the Middle Ages (Bertrada, known as Bertha Broadfoot, mother of Charlemagne). In records it alternates with Berta or Berthe.

berthe.label: Berthe
berthe.meaning: French form of Bertha, from Germanic "berht", "bright, famous".
berthe.text: A medieval name (Bertrada, known as Bertha Broadfoot, mother of Charlemagne), which became very fashionable again in France, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Belgium in the late 19th century.

berthold.label: Berthold
berthold.text: An old German name, borne by dukes of Zähringen and Bavaria, found in Germany, Switzerland and Poland; the forms Barthold or Bertold also occur.

bertie.label: Bertie
bertie.meaning: English diminutive of names in "-bert", from Germanic "berht", "bright" (Albert, Herbert, Bertram...).
bertie.text: An English diminutive used as a given name in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, mostly for boys, more rarely for girls (Bertha, Roberta). The full form should be searched for in other records.

bertin.label: Bertin
bertin.text: Saint Bertin, abbot of the monastery at Saint-Omer in the 7th century, is celebrated on 5 September. The name is found mostly in Artois and French Flanders.

bertram.label: Bertram
bertram.text: A name found in England since the Norman Conquest, fashionable again in the 19th century, also used in Germany. It is often shortened to Bert.

bertrand.label: Bertrand
bertrand.text: A medieval name widespread in France, especially in the south, borne by Bertrand du Guesclin, and the source of many surnames. In France its name day is 6 September, the feast of Blessed Bertrand de Garrigues, a companion of Saint Dominic.

bertrande.label: Bertrande
bertrande.meaning: Feminine of Bertrand, from Germanic "berht", "bright", and "hramn", "raven".
bertrande.text: A feminine form of Bertrand, frequent in south-western France and Languedoc in the 16th and 17th centuries. Records also spell it Bertranne.

beryl.label: Beryl
beryl.meaning: From Greek "bêryllos", the name of a gemstone (beryl).
beryl.text: An English female name, from the vogue for gemstone names, mainly widespread in Britain in the 1920s and 1930s.

beulah.label: Beulah
beulah.meaning: From Hebrew "be'ulah", "married", a symbolic name for the land of Israel in the Book of Isaiah.
beulah.text: A biblical name, mainly American, widespread in Protestant circles in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

beverly.label: Beverly
beverly.meaning: From Old English "beofor", "beaver", and "leac", "stream", a Yorkshire place name that became a surname and then a given name.
beverly.text: A mainly American name, first male and then almost exclusively female in the 20th century; in Britain it is more often spelt Beverley.

biagio.label: Biagio
biagio.meaning: Italian form of Blaise, from Latin "Blasius", perhaps from "blaesus", "stammering".
biagio.text: A common Italian name, especially in the south. Its feast is 3 February, that of Saint Blaise of Sebaste, a martyred bishop invoked against throat ailments.

bianca.label: Bianca
bianca.meaning: From Italian "bianca", "white", of Germanic origin ("blank", "bright, white").
bianca.text: The Italian form of Blanche, found in Italy since the Middle Ages and spread to Germany, Poland and France in the 20th century.

bianka.label: Bianka
bianka.meaning: Polish and German form of Bianca, from Italian "bianca", "white", of Germanic origin.
bianka.text: A female name found in Poland and Germany, mainly in the 20th century; the form Blanka also occurs there. It is rare in older registers.

blaise.label: Blaise
blaise.text: A name found in France and Switzerland since the Middle Ages, fairly common in rural areas until the 18th century. Its feast is 3 February, that of Saint Blaise of Sebaste, a martyred bishop invoked against throat ailments.

blanca.label: Blanca
blanca.meaning: Spanish form of Blanche, of Germanic origin ("blank", "bright, white").
blanca.text: A female name borne by queens of Castile and Navarre, common in Spain in every period. It corresponds to French Blanche and Portuguese Branca.

blanche.label: Blanche
blanche.meaning: From French "blanche", "white", of Germanic origin ("blank", "bright, white").
blanche.text: A medieval name, borne notably by Blanche of Castile, mother of Saint Louis, which became very fashionable again in France, Belgium and Switzerland in the 19th century.

blas.label: Blas
blas.meaning: Spanish form of Blaise, from Latin "Blasius", perhaps from "blaesus", "stammering".
blas.text: A Spanish name common since the Middle Ages; Brais also occurs in Galicia. Its feast is 3 February, that of Saint Blaise of Sebaste, invoked against throat ailments.

blima.label: Blima
blima.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Blume, frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. Blima and Bluma alternate for the same person.

bogdan.label: Bogdan
bogdan.text: A Slavic name found in Poland, Ukraine and the Balkans; it is equivalent to the Greek Theodore. In Poland it is mainly widespread in the 20th century.

boguslaw.label: Bogusław
boguslaw.text: A Polish name (Bogusław) borne by dukes of Pomerania (Bogislaw), mainly widespread in Poland in the 20th century.

boleslaw.label: Bolesław
boleslaw.text: A dynastic name of the Piasts, the first rulers of Poland (Bolesław), used in Poland in every period. It appears as Boleslas in French and Boleslaus in Latin.

bonaventura.label: Bonaventura
bonaventura.text: A name found in Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Germany and Belgium, especially in Catholic circles. Its feast is 15 July, that of Saint Bonaventure, Franciscan and Doctor of the Church.

bonne.label: Bonne
bonne.text: A medieval name borne notably by Bonne of Luxembourg and Bonne of Bourbon, still present in registers until the 17th century. Saint Bona of Pisa is celebrated on 29 May; Latin records write Bona.

bonnie.label: Bonnie
bonnie.text: A mainly American female name, widespread in the 20th century. It is absent from older European registers.

borromaus.label: Borromäus
borromaus.meaning: From the family name of Saint Charles Borromeo, archbishop of Milan.
borromaus.text: Mostly used as a second given name after Karl or Carl (Karl Borromäus) in German-speaking Catholic regions, in honour of Saint Charles Borromeo, celebrated on 4 November. Records also write Boromäus or Borromaeus.

bozena.label: Bożena
bozena.text: A Polish (Bożena) and Czech (Božena) female name, rare in older registers and mainly widespread in Poland in the 20th century.

brajna.label: Brajna
brajna.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Breyne, with the diminutive Brajndla, found in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century.

branca.label: Branca
branca.meaning: Portuguese form of Blanche, of Germanic origin ("blank", "bright, white").
branca.text: A Portuguese and Galician female name, borne in the royal family in the Middle Ages and found in Portuguese registers of every period.

bras.label: Brás
bras.meaning: Portuguese form of Blaise, from Latin "Blasius", perhaps from "blaesus", "stammering".
bras.text: A Portuguese name (Brás) common from the Middle Ages to the 18th century, which also became a surname. Its feast is 3 February, that of Saint Blaise of Sebaste.

brenda.label: Brenda
brenda.meaning: Of disputed origin: perhaps from Old Norse "brandr", "sword, flame", or from a Celtic name.
brenda.text: A name first used in Shetland, popularised in the 19th century by a novel by Walter Scott, then very widespread in Britain and the United States in the mid-20th century.

brian.label: Brian
brian.meaning: Of disputed Celtic origin, often linked to "bre", "height", hence "noble, exalted".
brian.text: An Irish name borne by King Brian Boru, also brought to England by Bretons in the Middle Ages, and very widespread in Britain and the United States in the 20th century. Bryan also occurs.

brice.label: Brice
brice.meaning: From Latin "Brictius", probably of Celtic origin; disputed meaning.
brice.text: Saint Brice succeeded Saint Martin as bishop of Tours and is celebrated on 13 November. An old name in France, it was rare under the Ancien Régime and became fashionable again in the second half of the 20th century.

bridget.label: Bridget
bridget.meaning: From Irish "Brighid", linked to Celtic "brig", "strength, exaltation".
bridget.text: A name very widespread in Ireland and, through Irish emigration, in Britain and the United States; Bride, Biddy or Bridie also occur. Its feast is 1 February, that of Saint Brigid of Kildare, patron saint of Ireland.

brieuc.label: Brieuc
brieuc.meaning: From Old Breton or Welsh "Brioc"; disputed meaning.
brieuc.text: Saint Brieuc, a 5th-century Welsh monk, gave his name to the town of Saint-Brieuc; his feast is on 1 May. The name is mainly borne in Brittany.

brigida.label: Brigida
brigida.meaning: Italian and Spanish form of Bridget, from Irish "Brighid", linked to Celtic "brig", "strength".
brigida.text: A female name found in Italy and Spain in every period. Its feast is 23 July, that of Saint Bridget of Sweden, who lived and died in Rome.

brigitte.label: Brigitte
brigitte.meaning: French and German form of Brigid, from Irish "Brighid", linked to Celtic "brig", "strength".
brigitte.text: A name long found in France and Germany, but mainly very widespread in the mid-20th century. In France its name day is 23 July, the feast of Saint Bridget of Sweden.

bronislaw.label: Bronisław
bronislaw.text: A Polish name (Bronisław) widespread in the 19th and early 20th centuries; in French, Bronislas occasionally occurs.

bronislawa.label: Bronisława
bronislawa.meaning: Feminine of Bronisław, from Slavic "broni", "defend", and "slava", "glory".
bronislawa.text: A Polish female name (Bronisława) widespread in the 19th and early 20th centuries, particularly in Lesser Poland.

bruce.label: Bruce
bruce.meaning: From a Norman surname taken from a place in Normandy (probably Brix), borne by Robert the Bruce, King of Scots.
bruce.text: A Scottish surname turned given name, mainly widespread in the United States, Australia and Britain in the 20th century.

bruno.label: Bruno
bruno.text: An old Germanic name, used in Germany, Italy, Poland, Belgium, France and Switzerland. Its feast is 6 October, that of Saint Bruno of Cologne, founder of the Carthusian order.

burkhard.label: Burkhard
burkhard.text: Saint Burchard, first bishop of Würzburg, is celebrated on 14 October. The name is common in German and Swiss registers, spelled Burkard, Burkart, or Burchardus in Latin.

cacilie.label: Cäcilie
cacilie.meaning: German form of Cecilia, from Latin "Caecilia", a Roman family name often linked to "caecus", "blind".
cacilie.text: The German form (Cäcilie) common in Germany, Switzerland and Silesia, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries; the umlaut is often transcribed "ae" or dropped. Its feast is 22 November, that of Saint Cecilia, patron saint of musicians.

caetano.label: Caetano
caetano.meaning: Portuguese form of Cajetan, from Latin "Caietanus", "from Gaeta".
caetano.text: A Portuguese (Caetano) and Brazilian name, widespread in the 18th and 19th centuries. Its feast is 7 August, that of Saint Cajetan of Thiene, founder of the Theatines.

calvin.label: Calvin
calvin.meaning: From the surname of the reformer John Calvin, from Latin "calvus", "bald".
calvin.text: An American name adopted first in Protestant circles in honour of the reformer, then more widely used in the 19th and 20th centuries.

camilla.label: Camilla
camilla.meaning: From Latin "Camilla", the name of a warrior queen in the Aeneid, linked to "camillus", a young attendant at religious rites.
camilla.text: A female name found in Italy, Switzerland, Belgium, Germany and Britain, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. It corresponds to the feminine French Camille.

camille.label: Camille
camille.meaning: From Latin "Camillus" or "Camilla", a young attendant at religious rites.
camille.text: A unisex name: mainly male in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland until the early 20th century, it then became predominantly female; the person's sex should therefore be checked in the record. The masculine is celebrated on 14 July, the feast of Saint Camillus de Lellis, founder of the Camillians.

camillo.label: Camillo
camillo.meaning: From Latin "Camillus", a young attendant at religious rites.
camillo.text: An Italian name, borne notably by Camillo Benso di Cavour, also found in Germany and Switzerland. Its feast is 14 July, that of Saint Camillus de Lellis, founder of the Camillians.

camilo.label: Camilo
camilo.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Camillus, from Latin "Camillus".
camilo.text: A name found in Spain and Portugal, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. Its feast is 14 July, that of Saint Camillus de Lellis.

candida.label: Cándida
candida.text: A female name found in Portugal (Cândida), Spain and Italy, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries.

candido.label: Cándido
candido.text: A name found in Portugal (Cândido), Spain and Italy, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. The Portuguese accent is often dropped in transcriptions.

cannelle.label: Cannelle
cannelle.meaning: From the name of the spice, cinnamon.
cannelle.text: A recent name, given in France from the end of the 20th century. It does not occur in older registers.

carel.label: Carel
carel.meaning: Older Dutch form of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carel.text: An older Dutch spelling of Karel, frequent in the Netherlands and Flanders in the 17th and 18th centuries; in Catholic registers it corresponds to Latin Carolus. It is linked to Saint Charles Borromeo, whose feast is 4 November.

carine.label: Carine
carine.meaning: French form of Karin, a Scandinavian diminutive of Catherine.
carine.text: A name that spread in France in the 1960s and 1970s, spelled Carine or Karine. It is absent from older registers, where Catherine is the expected form.

carl.label: Carl
carl.meaning: German form of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carl.text: The traditional German spelling of Karl, very widespread in Germany, Switzerland and Luxembourg, and spread to the United States by German emigration. It is linked to Saint Charles Borromeo, whose feast is 4 November.

carles.label: Carles
carles.meaning: Catalan form of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carles.text: The Catalan form of Charles, found in the registers of Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands; in records written in Castilian the same person becomes Carlos. Its feast is 4 November, that of Saint Charles Borromeo.

carlo.label: Carlo
carlo.meaning: Italian form of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carlo.text: A very common Italian name, particularly in Lombardy, where Saint Charles Borromeo was archbishop of Milan. Its feast is 4 November, that of this saint.

carlos.label: Carlos
carlos.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carlos.text: A royal name in Spain and Portugal, very widespread in Iberian registers of every period. Its feast is 4 November, that of Saint Charles Borromeo.

carlota.label: Carlota
carlota.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Charlotte, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carlota.text: A female name found in Portugal and Spain, borne by queens and infantas, and more widely used in the 19th and 20th centuries.

carlotta.label: Carlotta
carlotta.meaning: Italian form of Charlotte, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carlotta.text: An Italian female name, found mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries, also adopted in Germany and the United States.

carme.label: Carme
carme.meaning: Catalan form of Carmen, from Hebrew "Karmel", "garden, orchard", the name of Mount Carmel.
carme.text: The Catalan form of Carmen, found in the registers of Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands, often preceded by Maria. It is celebrated on 16 July, the feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel.

carmela.label: Carmela
carmela.meaning: From Hebrew "Karmel", "garden, orchard", the name of Mount Carmel, via Our Lady of Mount Carmel.
carmela.text: A Marian devotional name very widespread in southern Italy and Spain, often preceded by Maria, with the diminutives Carmelina or Melina. It is celebrated on 16 July, the feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel.

carmelo.label: Carmelo
carmelo.meaning: From Hebrew "Karmel", "garden, orchard", the name of Mount Carmel, via Our Lady of Mount Carmel.
carmelo.text: A male Marian devotional name, very widespread in Sicily, southern Italy and Spain. It is celebrated on 16 July, the feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel.

carmen.label: Carmen
carmen.meaning: From Spanish "Carmen", an alteration of "Carmel", from Hebrew "Karmel", "garden, orchard", influenced by Latin "carmen", "song".
carmen.text: A Marian devotional name extremely widespread in Spain, often in compounds (María del Carmen), and spread to France, Portugal and Italy. It is celebrated on 16 July, the feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel.

carol.label: Carol
carol.meaning: Short form of Caroline, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carol.text: An English and American female name, mainly widespread in the mid-20th century. It is rare in older registers, where the same person may be entered as Caroline.

carola.label: Carola
carola.meaning: Latin feminine of Carolus, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carola.text: A female name found in Italy, Germany and Britain; in Catholic registers it is also the Latin form of Caroline or Charlotte.

carole.label: Carole
carole.meaning: French form of Carola, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carole.text: A female name mainly widespread in the mid-20th century in Britain, the United States and France. It is rare in older registers.

carolina.label: Carolina
carolina.meaning: Feminine of Carolus, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carolina.text: A female name common in Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Belgium, Spain and Germany, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries; in Catholic registers it is also the Latin form of Caroline.

caroline.label: Caroline
caroline.meaning: Feminine of Charles via Latin "Carolus", from Germanic "karl", "free man".
caroline.text: A female name very widespread in the 19th century in Luxembourg, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Germany, France and English-speaking countries. In records it alternates with Carolina, Charlotte or Lina for the same person.

carolus.label: Carolus
carolus.meaning: Latin form of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carolus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic registers of Belgium, the Netherlands, France and Germany; in daily life the same person appears as Karel, Charles or Karl. It is linked to Saint Charles Borromeo, whose feast is 4 November.

carolyn.label: Carolyn
carolyn.meaning: English variant of Caroline, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carolyn.text: A mainly American female name, widespread in the mid-20th century. It is rare in older registers.

carrie.label: Carrie
carrie.meaning: English diminutive of Caroline, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
carrie.text: A diminutive of Caroline used as a given name in the United States, especially in the late 19th century. In other records the same person may be entered as Caroline.

casilda.label: Casilda
casilda.meaning: Of disputed origin: perhaps Arabic, perhaps Germanic ("hild", "battle").
casilda.text: A Spanish female name, linked to the cult of Saint Casilda of Toledo, said by legend to be the daughter of a Muslim ruler, whose shrine is near Burgos. Her feast is 9 April.

casimir.label: Casimir
casimir.meaning: From Polish "Kazimierz", from "kazić", "to destroy", and "mir", "peace", also understood as "proclaimer of peace".
casimir.text: The name of several kings of Poland, spread to France, Switzerland, Germany and Belgium, especially in the 19th century, notably in Catholic circles. Its feast is 4 March, that of Saint Casimir, a Polish prince and patron saint of Lithuania.

caspar.label: Caspar
caspar.meaning: The traditional name of one of the Magi, often linked to Persian "ganzabara", "treasurer", an uncertain etymology.
caspar.text: A name widespread in Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Belgium in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, as Caspar, Kaspar or Jasper. It is celebrated on 6 January, at Epiphany, with the Magi.

cassandra.label: Cassandra
cassandra.meaning: From Greek "Kassandra", a Trojan prophetess in mythology, of disputed etymology.
cassandra.text: A mythological name found in Italy and Britain, notably in the English gentry of the 17th and 18th centuries. It remains rare in ordinary registers.

catalina.label: Catalina
catalina.meaning: Spanish form of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", of obscure etymology, associated with "katharos", "pure".
catalina.text: A female name very common in Spain in every period, borne by Catherine of Aragon. Its feast is 25 November, that of Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

catarina.label: Catarina
catarina.meaning: Portuguese form of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", of obscure etymology, associated with "katharos", "pure".
catarina.text: A female name common in Portugal in every period, also written Catharina in older records. Its feast is 25 November, that of Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

caterina.label: Caterina
caterina.meaning: Italian form of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", of obscure etymology, associated with "katharos", "pure".
caterina.text: A female name very common in Italy in every period, often shortened to Rina or Nina. Its feast is 29 April, that of Saint Catherine of Siena, patron saint of Italy.

cathalina.label: Cathalina
cathalina.meaning: Older spelling of Catalina, the Spanish form of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê".
cathalina.text: An older spelling of Catalina, frequent in Spanish registers of the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, where the "h" is purely graphic. It is linked to Saint Catherine of Alexandria, whose feast is 25 November.

catharina.label: Catharina
catharina.meaning: Latin, Dutch and German form of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", associated with "katharos", "pure".
catharina.text: An extremely common female name in the Netherlands, Flanders, Germany and Switzerland, with many diminutives (Trijntje, Kaatje, Katrin, Cato); it is also the Latin form used in Catholic registers. Its feast is 25 November, that of Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

catharine.label: Catharine
catharine.meaning: Variant of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", associated with "katharos", "pure".
catharine.text: A frequent spelling in Dutch, English and American registers of the 17th and 18th centuries, where it alternates with Catherine, Catharina or Katherine. It is linked to Saint Catherine of Alexandria, whose feast is 25 November.

catherine.label: Catherine
catherine.meaning: From Greek "Aikaterinê", of obscure etymology, associated with "katharos", "pure".
catherine.text: One of the most frequent female names in France, England, Luxembourg, Belgium and Switzerland from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, spelt Catherine, Katherine or Catharine. Its feast is 25 November, that of Saint Catherine of Alexandria, patron saint of young unmarried women; in France Saint Catherine of Siena is also celebrated on 29 April.

cato.label: Cato
cato.meaning: Dutch diminutive of Catharina, from Greek "Aikaterinê".
cato.text: A familiar form of Catharina, common in the Netherlands in the 18th and 19th centuries; in official records the same person often appears as Catharina. It should not be confused with the Roman male name Cato.

cayetano.label: Cayetano
cayetano.meaning: Spanish form of Cajetan, from Latin "Caietanus", "from Gaeta".
cayetano.text: A Spanish name widespread in the 18th and 19th centuries; Gaietà in Catalan. Its feast is 7 August, that of Saint Cajetan of Thiene, founder of the Theatines.

cecil.label: Cecil
cecil.meaning: From Latin "Caecilius", a Roman family name, via the English surname Cecil, of Welsh origin.
cecil.text: An English male name, taken from the Cecil family surname, very widespread in Britain and the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

cecile.label: Cécile
cecile.meaning: From Latin "Caecilia", a Roman family name often linked to "caecus", "blind".
cecile.text: A female name widespread in France, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Belgium and the Netherlands since the Middle Ages (Cécile), with a revival in the 19th century. Its feast is 22 November, that of Saint Cecilia, a Roman martyr and patron saint of musicians.

cecilia.label: Cecilia
cecilia.meaning: From Latin "Caecilia", a Roman family name often linked to "caecus", "blind".
cecilia.text: The Latin and international form of Cecile, common in the Netherlands, Italy, Spain, Belgium and English-speaking countries; it is also the form used in Catholic registers. Its feast is 22 November, that of Saint Cecilia, patron saint of musicians.

cecylia.label: Cecylia
cecylia.meaning: Polish form of Cecilia, from Latin "Caecilia".
cecylia.text: The Polish form of Cecilia, found in Polish registers in the 18th and 19th centuries; in Latin registers it appears as Caecilia. Its feast is 22 November, that of Saint Cecilia.

celeste.label: Celeste
celeste.text: A name found in Portugal (Celeste), Italy, France (Céleste), Belgium and the United States. In France and Italy it could be borne by men as well as women, which should be checked in the record.

celestin.label: Célestin
celestin.text: A name widespread in France and Belgium in the 19th century (Célestin), rarer before. In France its name day is 19 May, the feast of Saint Celestine V, a 13th-century hermit pope.

celestine.label: Celestine
celestine.text: A female name very widespread in France and Belgium in the 19th century (Célestine). In records it sometimes alternates with Céleste.

celestino.label: Celestino
celestino.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Célestin, from Latin "Caelestinus", "heavenly".
celestino.text: A name found in Spain, Portugal and Italy, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. Its feast is 19 May, that of Saint Celestine V, a 13th-century hermit pope.

celia.label: Celia
celia.meaning: From Latin "Caelia", a Roman family name, associated with "caelum", "sky, heaven".
celia.text: A female name found in Spain, the Netherlands and English-speaking countries, popularised in England by Shakespeare (As You Like It). It is sometimes used as a short form of Cecilia, from which it is nevertheless distinct.

celina.label: Celina
celina.meaning: Of disputed origin: from Latin "Caelina", linked to "caelum", "sky, heaven", or a form of Céline.
celina.text: A female name found in Poland (Celina), Belgium and France, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. In Poland it was particularly widespread between the two world wars.

celine.label: Céline
celine.meaning: From Latin "Caelina", linked to "caelum", "sky, heaven", or a short form of Marceline.
celine.text: A female name found in France and Belgium in the 19th century (Céline), and very fashionable in the second half of the 20th century. In France its name day is 21 October, the feast of Saint Céline, mother of Saint Remigius.

cesar.label: César
cesar.meaning: From Latin "Caesar", a surname of the Julian family, of disputed etymology ("caesaries", "head of hair"?).
cesar.text: A name found in Portugal (César), Spain, France, Belgium, Switzerland and Italy, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. In records it sometimes alternates with the Latin form Caesar.

cesare.label: Cesare
cesare.meaning: Italian form of Caesar, from Latin "Caesar", of disputed etymology.
cesare.text: An Italian name found since the Renaissance (Cesare Borgia), more widely used in the 19th and 20th centuries, also in Ticino.

cesarine.label: Césarine
cesarine.text: A female name widespread in France and Belgium in the 19th century (Césarine), rarer afterwards.

cesira.label: Cesira
cesira.meaning: Of uncertain origin; sometimes linked to Latin "Caesar".
cesira.text: An Italian female name, mainly borne in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, notably in central Italy.

cezary.label: Cezary
cezary.meaning: Polish form of Caesar, from Latin "Caesar".
cezary.text: A Polish name rare in older registers and mainly widespread in the second half of the 20th century.

chaim.label: Chaïm
chaim.text: A very widespread name in Jewish communities, often given as a wish for long life. Central European records write Chaim, those from North Africa and France more often Haïm.

chaja.label: Chaja
chaja.text: One of the most frequent Jewish female names in 19th-century Polish records, often in compounds (Chaja Sura, Chaja Ruchla). It was sometimes given to a sick child to ward off death; after 1868 records in Russian write Хая.

chantal.label: Chantal
chantal.meaning: From the surname of Saint Jane de Chantal, taken from a Burgundian place name, perhaps from Provençal "cantal", "stone, boundary".
chantal.text: A name taken from Saint Jane Frances de Chantal, foundress of the Visitation, mainly widespread in France in the mid-20th century. Its feast is 12 August, that of this saint.

charlemagne.label: Charlemagne
charlemagne.text: The name of the Carolingian emperor, occasionally used as a given name in France, mostly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It remains rare in registers.

charlene.label: Charlène
charlene.meaning: A modern feminine of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
charlene.text: A form borrowed from English Charlene, widely given in France in the 1980s and 1990s. It is absent from older registers.

charles.label: Charles
charles.text: A royal and imperial name (Charlemagne), among the most common in France, Belgium, Luxembourg, England and the United States, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. Its feast is 4 November, that of Saint Charles Borromeo, archbishop of Milan.

charlotte.label: Charlotte
charlotte.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
charlotte.text: A female name widespread in Germany, Luxembourg, Switzerland, the Netherlands, France and Britain, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. In records it alternates with Caroline, Carlota or Lotte.

chaskiel.label: Chaskiel
chaskiel.meaning: The Yiddish form of Ezekiel, "God strengthens".
chaskiel.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Khatskl, a diminutive of Ezekiel, common in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century.

chawa.label: Chawa
chawa.text: The Hebrew and Yiddish form of Eve, written Chawa in 19th-century Polish records. The diminutive Chawka is common.

chester.label: Chester
chester.meaning: From the English city of Chester, from Latin "castra", "military camp".
chester.text: A place name turned given name, mainly American, widespread in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

chiara.label: Chiara
chiara.meaning: Italian form of Clare, from Latin "clara", "bright, famous".
chiara.text: An Italian female name found in every period, borne by Saint Clare of Assisi. Its feast is 11 August, that of this saint, foundress of the Poor Clares.

christiaan.label: Christiaan
christiaan.meaning: Dutch form of Christian, from Latin "christianus", "Christian", from Greek "Khristos".
christiaan.text: A Dutch name found in the Netherlands and Flanders from the 17th to the 19th century; in Catholic registers it appears as Christianus.

christian.label: Christian
christian.text: A name widespread in Germany, Switzerland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Scandinavia in every period, and in France mainly in the 20th century. It is very frequent in Lutheran registers.

christiana.label: Christiana
christiana.text: A female name found in Germany, the Netherlands, Britain and Poland, especially in the 17th and 18th centuries; in Latin registers it also corresponds to Christiane.

christiane.label: Christiane
christiane.text: A female name found in Germany since the early modern period, and very widespread in France in the mid-20th century.

christina.label: Christina
christina.text: A female name common in the Netherlands, Germany, Britain, Italy, Belgium and Poland; in registers it often alternates with Christine or Stina. Its feast is 24 July, that of Saint Christina of Bolsena, martyr.

christine.label: Christine
christine.text: A female name found since the Middle Ages in France, Germany and the Netherlands, and very widespread in the mid-20th century in Britain and France. Its feast is 24 July, that of Saint Christina of Bolsena, martyr.

christoffel.label: Christoffel
christoffel.meaning: Dutch form of Christopher, from Greek "Christophoros", "bearer of Christ".
christoffel.text: The Dutch form of Christopher, Christoffel appears mainly in records from the Netherlands between the 16th and 19th centuries. Latin entries write it Christophorus, and everyday usage often shortened it to Stoffel. The name refers to Saint Christopher, patron of travellers.

christoph.label: Christoph
christoph.text: The German form of Christopher, Christoph is frequent in records from the German-speaking lands and German-speaking Switzerland from the late Middle Ages onward. It is also spelt Christof or Christoff, latinised as Christophorus, and shortened to Stoffel in popular use. The name honours Saint Christopher, patron of travellers.

christophe.label: Christophe
christophe.text: Used in France, Belgium and French-speaking Switzerland since the Middle Ages, Christophe is steady but moderately common in pre-Revolutionary records. Latin entries write it Christophorus, and older spellings include Christofle and Cristophe. It honours Saint Christopher, a legendary martyr who became patron of travellers.

christopher.label: Christopher
christopher.text: The English form of the name, Christopher is common in English parish registers from the 16th century and spread widely in the United States. It is often abbreviated Christ., Kit or Chris, and latinised as Christophorus. The name honours Saint Christopher, patron of travellers.

chrysostome.label: Chrysostome
chrysostome.text: The epithet of Saint John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, celebrated on 13 September. In France it is mostly borne as the second part of the compound Jean-Chrysostome; records often spell it Chrisostome.

claire.label: Claire
claire.text: A French female name spread by the cult of Saint Clare of Assisi, founder of the Poor Clares, Claire appears in records from the Middle Ages without being among the most frequent names. Latin entries write it Clara, and the spelling Clère occurs in some older records. Its name day is the feast of Saint Clare.

clara.label: Clara
clara.text: The Latin, German, Dutch, Spanish and Portuguese form of Claire, Clara is widespread in records across Catholic Europe. It saw a revival in the 19th century in the German-speaking countries and the United States. The name honours Saint Clare of Assisi, founder of the Poor Clares.

clarence.label: Clarence
clarence.meaning: From the English ducal title of Clarence, itself named after the town of Clare in Suffolk; "Clarence" comes from medieval Latin "Clarentia".
clarence.text: A noble title turned given name in the 19th century, Clarence was mostly used in England and the United States between the 1870s and 1930s. It is rare before the 19th century and almost absent from continental European records.

clarisse.label: Clarisse
clarisse.meaning: Derived from Claire, from Latin "clarus", "clear, famous".
clarisse.text: A French derivative of Claire, linked to the name of the Poor Clare nuns, Clarisse is found mainly in 19th-century French records. It also appears as Clarice or Clarissa. Lacking a well-established saint of its own, it traditionally takes its name day from Saint Clare of Assisi.

clasina.label: Clasina
clasina.meaning: Dutch feminine of Klaas, a short form of Nicolaas, from Greek "Nikolaos", "victory of the people".
clasina.text: A typically Dutch female name, Clasina is found mainly in records from the Netherlands in the 18th and 19th centuries. It also appears as Klazina or Claasje. It has no well-established saint of its own.

claude.label: Claude
claude.meaning: From the Roman family name "Claudius", linked by folk etymology to Latin "claudus", "lame".
claude.text: Very common in France before the Revolution, especially in Franche-Comté, Burgundy, Lorraine and the Lyon area, Claude was then mostly masculine but also given to women. Latin entries write it Claudius or Claudia, and the sex is often shown only by the article or an agreement. Its early popularity came from the cult of Saint Claude, bishop of Besançon, whose abbey in the Jura drew many pilgrims.

claudette.label: Claudette
claudette.meaning: French feminine diminutive of Claude, from the Roman name "Claudius".
claudette.text: A French diminutive of Claude, Claudette appears in records before the Revolution but only became common in the 20th century, especially from the 1920s to the 1940s. It has no well-established saint of its own.

claudia.label: Claudia
claudia.meaning: Feminine of the Roman family name "Claudius".
claudia.text: The Latin and Italian feminine form, Claudia appears in Italian and Spanish records and, in Latin, in French records where it renders a woman called Claude. It spread widely across Europe in the 20th century. There is no Saint Claudia with a well-established cult.

claudine.label: Claudine
claudine.meaning: Feminine derivative of Claude, from the Roman name "Claudius".
claudine.text: A feminine derivative of Claude, Claudine was common in France before the Revolution, especially in the East, in Burgundy and around Lyon, where Claude was widespread. Regional forms include Glaudine and Claudie. Its name day is the feast of Saint Claudine Thévenet, a foundress from Lyon canonised in 1993.

claudio.label: Claudio
claudio.text: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Claude, Claudio has been used in records from those countries since the Renaissance without ranking among the most common names. It became more frequent in the 20th century. Several early martyrs bore the name, but no single cult dominates.

claudius.label: Claudius
claudius.meaning: A Roman family name, linked by folk etymology to Latin "claudus", "lame".
claudius.text: The Latin form of Claude, Claudius appears mainly in Latin-language records from France, Belgium, the Netherlands and the German-speaking lands. In the 19th century it was sometimes given as such, especially in France. In registers it should usually be read as Claude.

claus.label: Claus
claus.meaning: German short form of Nikolaus, from Greek "Nikolaos", "victory of the people".
claus.text: A short form of Nicholas, Claus (or Klaus) was very widespread in northern Germany, where it often stands as a name in its own right in the records. Clas, Claes and Klaas are its Scandinavian and Dutch counterparts. The name goes back to Saint Nicholas of Myra.

clelia.label: Clelia
clelia.meaning: From the Roman name "Cloelia", a legendary heroine of ancient Rome.
clelia.text: An Italian name inspired by Roman history, Clelia is found mainly in Italian records of the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is rare elsewhere. Its name day is the feast of Saint Clelia Barbieri, a foundress from Emilia canonised in 1989.

clemence.label: Clémence
clemence.text: A virtue name, Clémence is found in France and Belgium from the Middle Ages and stayed moderately common until the early 20th century. Latin entries write it Clementia. It has no well-established saint of its own.

clemens.label: Clemens
clemens.text: The German, Dutch and Latin form of Clement, Clemens is frequent in Catholic records from Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Switzerland. It also appears as Klemens and, in popular use, shortened to Clem or Mens. It honours Pope Saint Clement I.

clement.label: Clément
clement.text: Clément has been used in France and Belgium since the Middle Ages, steadily but not very frequently. Latin entries write it Clemens, and the English form Clement is found in England. It honours Pope Saint Clement I, one of the first bishops of Rome.

clemente.label: Clemente
clemente.text: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Clement, Clemente is found in records from those countries and Ticino from the late Middle Ages. It honours Pope Saint Clement I.

clementia.label: Clementia
clementia.text: The Latin form of Clémence, Clementia appears mainly in Latin-language records from Belgium and the Netherlands, where it can also render Clementine. It should be read according to the family's everyday language. There is no well-established saint of its own.

clementina.label: Clementina
clementina.meaning: Feminine of Clementinus, derived from Latin "clemens", "merciful".
clementina.text: The Italian, Spanish and Latin form of Clementine, Clementina became common in the 19th century in Italy, Spain and Belgium. It is rarer in earlier records. There is no well-established saint of its own.

clementine.label: Clémentine
clementine.meaning: Feminine of Clementinus, derived from Latin "clemens", "merciful".
clementine.text: Mainly a 19th-century name, Clémentine was frequent in France and Belgium and is also found in Germany and the Netherlands. Latin entries write it Clementina. It has no well-established saint of its own.

cleophea.label: Cleophea
cleophea.meaning: Probably derived from Greek "kleos", "glory", by analogy with Cleophas; the etymology is uncertain.
cleophea.text: A rare name characteristic of German-speaking Switzerland, Cleophea appears in records from that region from the 16th to the 19th century. It is also spelt Kleophea. It has no well-established saint of its own.

clifford.label: Clifford
clifford.meaning: From an English place name, "ford by a cliff" (Old English "clif" and "ford").
clifford.text: An English place and family name turned given name in the 19th century, Clifford was mostly used in England and the United States between the 1880s and 1940s. It is rare in earlier records.

clinton.label: Clinton
clinton.meaning: From an English place name ending in "-ton" (Old English "tun", "farmstead, settlement"), passed down as a surname; the first element is disputed.
clinton.text: An English surname turned given name, Clinton spread mainly in the United States from the 19th century, partly in honour of politicians bearing the name. It is rare in Europe before the 20th century.

clive.label: Clive
clive.meaning: From Old English "clif", "cliff", through a place name and surname.
clive.text: An English surname turned given name, Clive was popularised in the 19th century in memory of Robert Clive, governor of Bengal. It is mostly found in Britain in the 20th century and is rare in older records.

clotaire.label: Clotaire
clotaire.text: The name of several Merovingian kings, Clotaire remained rare as a given name and appears mainly in 19th-century French records, reflecting a taste for national history. Lothaire and Chlotarius are its historical equivalents. It has no well-established saint.

clotilde.label: Clotilde
clotilde.text: The name of Clovis's wife, Clotilde was used in France, Belgium, Switzerland and Italy, especially in the 19th century. It is also spelt Clothilde or latinised as Clotildis. Its name day is the feast of Saint Clotilde, queen of the Franks.

clovis.label: Clovis
clovis.meaning: From Frankish "Chlodowig", "glorious warrior", the same root as Louis.
clovis.text: The name of the first Christian king of the Franks, Clovis is an old form of Louis; it only became a usual given name in France and Belgium in the 19th century. It remains uncommon in the records. Clovis is not venerated as a saint.

clyde.label: Clyde
clyde.meaning: From the Scottish River Clyde, of Celtic origin; meaning uncertain.
clyde.text: A Scottish river name turned given name, Clyde was mostly used in the United States between the 1880s and 1930s. It is rare in Europe and in records before the 19th century.

coenraad.label: Coenraad
coenraad.text: The Dutch form of Conrad, Coenraad is found in records from the Netherlands from the 16th to the 19th century, also spelt Koenraad or Coenraet. Everyday usage often shortened it to Coen or Koen. Its name day is the feast of Saint Conrad, bishop of Constance.

coleta.label: Coleta
coleta.meaning: Diminutive of Nicole, feminine of Nicholas, from Greek "Nikolaos", "victory of the people".
coleta.text: The Spanish and Latin form of Colette, Coleta appears in some records from Belgium and Spain. It honours Saint Colette of Corbie, reformer of the Poor Clares.

colette.label: Colette
colette.meaning: Diminutive of Nicole, feminine of Nicholas, from Greek "Nikolaos", "victory of the people".
colette.text: A diminutive of Nicole, Colette is found in France and Belgium from the late Middle Ages, particularly in Picardy and the North, but only became very common in the 20th century. It is also spelt Collette. Its name day is the feast of Saint Colette of Corbie, reformer of the Poor Clares.

colin.label: Colin
colin.meaning: Depending on the case, a medieval diminutive of Nicholas ("victory of the people") or an anglicised form of Gaelic "Cailean", "young dog"; the two origins have merged.
colin.text: A medieval diminutive of Nicholas in both France and England, Colin is also, in Scotland, the anglicised form of Gaelic Cailean. As a given name it is mostly found in Britain in the 20th century; in France it survives mainly as a surname. It has no saint of its own.

colomba.label: Colomba
colomba.text: An Italian name, Colomba appears in records from the peninsula without being very frequent. The masculine Colombano and the French forms Colombe and Coulombe are closely related. Several saints bore the name, with no single dominant cult for the Italian form.

colombe.label: Colombe
colombe.text: Saint Columba of Sens, a martyr, is celebrated on 31 December. The name appears in French registers under the Ancien Régime, notably in Burgundy and Champagne.

come.label: Côme
come.text: Saints Cosmas and Damian, martyred physicians, are celebrated on 26 September. The name is mostly spelled Cosme in Ancien Régime registers.

conan.label: Conan
conan.meaning: From Celtic; explained by a root meaning "hound" or "high", disputed.
conan.text: The name of several medieval dukes of Brittany (Conan I to Conan IV), used in Brittany in the Middle Ages. It is rare in modern registers.

concepcio.label: Concepció
concepcio.meaning: From Latin "conceptio", "conception", referring to the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary.
concepcio.text: The Catalan form of Concepción, Concepció is a Marian name given mainly in Catalonia and the Catalan-speaking lands from the 19th century, after the Immaculate Conception was proclaimed a dogma in 1854. It is often shortened to Ció. Its name day is the feast of the Immaculate Conception.

concepcion.label: Concepción
concepcion.meaning: From Latin "conceptio", "conception", referring to the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary.
concepcion.text: A Spanish Marian name, Concepción is often preceded by María in the records (María de la Concepción) and spread strongly in the 19th century. The diminutives Concha and Conchita are very common. Its name day is the feast of the Immaculate Conception, a major feast in Spain.

conrad.label: Conrad
conrad.text: A Germanic name borne by emperors and dukes, Conrad is common in records from Switzerland, Germany and Luxembourg, as Konrad, Conradt or latinised Conradus. The familiar forms Kunz and Kuno are frequent in German-speaking areas. Its name day is the feast of Saint Conrad, bishop of Constance.

constance.label: Constance
constance.text: A virtue name, Constance was borne from the Middle Ages by French and English nobility, then spread moderately to all social groups. Latin entries write it Constantia. It has no well-established saint of its own.

constant.label: Constant
constant.text: A virtue name mostly used in the 19th century in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, Constant is often rendered Constantius or Constans in Latin records. It can be confused with Constantine in transcriptions. It has no well-established saint of its own.

constantia.label: Constantia
constantia.text: The Latin form of Constance, Constantia appears mainly in Latin-language records from Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany, and sometimes as an everyday name in the Netherlands. It should be read according to the family's language (Constance, Konstanze, Stanzi). There is no well-established saint of its own.

constantin.label: Constantin
constantin.text: The name of the emperor Constantine the Great, Constantin is found in Germany, Belgium, France and Switzerland, more often in Catholic families, as Konstantin or latinised Constantinus. It can be confused with Constant in transcriptions. The emperor is venerated as a saint in the Eastern Churches but has no feast in the Roman calendar.

constantino.label: Constantino
constantino.text: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Constantine, Constantino appears in Iberian records without being very frequent. Catalan writes it Constantí. It has no well-established saint of its own in the Roman calendar.

constantinus.label: Constantinus
constantinus.text: The Latin form of Constantine, Constantinus appears mainly in Latin-language records from Belgium and the Netherlands, where everyday usage says Constantijn. It should not be confused with Constantius, the Latin form of Constant. It has no well-established saint of its own in the Roman calendar.

consuelo.label: Consuelo
consuelo.meaning: From Spanish "consuelo", "consolation", referring to Our Lady of Consolation.
consuelo.text: A Spanish Marian name, Consuelo shortens María del Consuelo and spread mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries, in Spain as well as Latin America. Catalan says Consol. The devotion to Our Lady of Consolation is celebrated on different dates depending on the shrine.

cora.label: Cora
cora.meaning: Probably from Greek "korê", "maiden", an epithet of Persephone; sometimes a short form of Cordelia or Corinne.
cora.text: A literary name, Cora became common in the United States in the second half of the 19th century and is less frequent in France. It is rare in earlier records. It has no saint of its own.

coralie.label: Coralie
coralie.meaning: Probably from Greek "korê", "maiden", or associated with the word for "coral"; the etymology is uncertain.
coralie.text: A French name that appeared at the end of the 18th century, Coralie is found in France and Belgium in the 19th century and had a strong revival in the late 20th century. It is absent from older records. It has no saint of its own.

corentin.label: Corentin
corentin.meaning: From Breton, perhaps from "korventenn", "hurricane"; the etymology is disputed.
corentin.text: A Breton name, Corentin was used mainly in Brittany, especially in Cornouaille around Quimper, before the Revolution. It only spread to the rest of France in the late 20th century. It honours Saint Corentin, first bishop of Quimper.

corinne.label: Corinne
corinne.text: The name of a Greek poetess, popularised in France by Madame de Staël's novel Corinne (1807). It was mainly given in the 1960s and 1970s.

cornelia.label: Cornelia
cornelia.meaning: Feminine of the Roman family name "Cornelius", perhaps related to "cornu", "horn".
cornelia.text: The feminine form of Cornelius, Cornelia is common in the Netherlands and Belgium, where Dutch usage shortens it to Neeltje, Kee or Cor. It is also found in Italy, Germany and the United States. There is no well-established saint of its own.

cornelie.label: Cornélie
cornelie.meaning: Feminine of the Roman family name "Cornelius".
cornelie.text: The French form of Cornelia, Cornélie is found mainly in Belgium, northern France and the Netherlands, often alternating with the Latin form depending on the language of the record. There is no well-established saint of its own.

cornelis.label: Cornelis
cornelis.meaning: From the Roman family name "Cornelius", perhaps related to "cornu", "horn".
cornelis.text: The Dutch form of Cornelius, Cornelis was one of the most frequent male names in the Netherlands and Flanders from the 16th to the 19th century. Everyday usage shortens it to Kees, Cees, Cor, Knelis or Neel, and Latin entries write it Cornelius. It honours the martyr Pope Saint Cornelius, celebrated together with Saint Cyprian.

cornelius.label: Cornelius
cornelius.meaning: From the Roman family name "Cornelius", perhaps related to "cornu", "horn".
cornelius.text: The Latin form of Cornelis, Cornelius is very frequent in Latin-language records from Belgium and the Netherlands, and used as such in Germany, Ireland, England and the United States. In Ireland it also served to render Gaelic Conchobhar. It honours the martyr Pope Saint Cornelius.

corrado.label: Corrado
corrado.text: The Italian form of Conrad, Corrado appears in Italian records from the Middle Ages without ranking among the most common names. Its name day is the feast of Saint Conrad of Piacenza, a hermit venerated at Noto in Sicily.

cosimo.label: Cosimo
cosimo.text: The Italian form of Cosmas, Cosimo was popularised in Florence by the Medici and is found mainly in Tuscany and southern Italy. Latin entries write it Cosmas. It honours Saint Cosmas, a physician martyr celebrated with his brother Saint Damian.

costantino.label: Costantino
costantino.text: The Italian form of Constantine, Costantino appears in Italian and Ticino records, especially in the South and Sardinia, where the emperor is the object of popular devotion. It has no feast in the general Roman calendar.

costanza.label: Costanza
costanza.text: The Italian form of Constance, Costanza has been used in Italy since the Middle Ages, notably among the nobility, then more widely. It has no well-established saint of its own.

crepin.label: Crépin
crepin.text: Saints Crispin and Crispinian, martyred shoemakers of Soissons and patrons of shoemakers, are celebrated on 25 October. The name was mostly borne in Picardy and Champagne.

cristian.label: Cristian
cristian.text: The Spanish, Italian and Romanian form of Christian, Cristian is rare in older Iberian records and only became common in the 20th century. It has no well-established saint of its own.

cristina.label: Cristina
cristina.text: The Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Christine, Cristina has appeared in records from those countries since the Middle Ages. It honours Saint Christina of Bolsena, a virgin martyr venerated in Italy and Spain.

cristobal.label: Cristóbal
cristobal.text: The Spanish form of Christopher, Cristóbal has been used in Spanish records since the late Middle Ages; the Catalan form Cristòfol and the latinised Christophorus also occur. In Spain, Saint Christopher is traditionally celebrated on 10 July.

cristoforo.label: Cristoforo
cristoforo.text: The Italian form of Christopher, Cristoforo appears in Italian and Ticino records from the Middle Ages, sometimes as Cristofano or Tofano in Tuscany. It honours Saint Christopher, patron of travellers.

cristovao.label: Cristóvão
cristovao.text: The Portuguese form of Christopher, Cristóvão has been found in Portuguese records since the late Middle Ages, also spelt Christovão or Christovam in older entries. It honours Saint Christopher, patron of travellers.

curtis.label: Curtis
curtis.meaning: From Old French "curteis", "courteous", through an English surname.
curtis.text: An English surname turned given name, Curtis spread mainly in the United States from the late 19th century. It is rare in European records. It has no saint of its own.

cynthia.label: Cynthia
cynthia.meaning: From Greek "Kynthia", an epithet of Artemis, who was said to be born on Mount Kynthos on Delos.
cynthia.text: A name drawn from mythology, Cynthia is rare before the 19th century and spread mainly in the 20th century in Britain and the United States. It has no saint of its own.

cypora.label: Cypora
cypora.text: The name of Moses's wife in the Bible, written Cypora or Cypojra in 19th-century Polish records. The English biblical form is Zipporah.

cyprien.label: Cyprien
cyprien.text: A rare but steady name in France and French-speaking Switzerland, Cyprien appears in records before the Revolution, Latin entries writing it Cyprianus. It honours Saint Cyprian, bishop of Carthage and martyr, celebrated together with Pope Saint Cornelius.

cyr.label: Cyr
cyr.text: Saint Cyricus, a child martyred with his mother Saint Julitta, is celebrated on 16 June. The name is rare, but many Saint-Cyr parishes exist in France.

cyril.label: Cyril
cyril.text: The English form of Cyril, it spread in Britain mostly in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, having previously been rare. It honours one of the saints named Cyril; the feast given here is that of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, Doctor of the Church.

cyrille.label: Cyrille
cyrille.text: A rare name before the Revolution, Cyrille is found in France and Belgium, more often in the 19th century, Latin entries writing it Cyrillus. It only became common in the 20th century. Its name day is the feast of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, Doctor of the Church.

czeslaw.label: Czesław
czeslaw.text: A traditional Polish name, Czesław (without diacritic: Czeslaw) has been used in Poland since the Middle Ages and became very common in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Latin records render it Ceslaus. It is associated with Blessed Ceslaus, a Silesian Dominican who has not been canonised.

czeslawa.label: Czesława
czeslawa.meaning: Feminine of Czesław, from Old Slavic "čьstь", "honour", and "slava", "glory".
czeslawa.text: The Polish feminine of Czesław, Czesława (Czeslawa) is found mainly in Polish records of the late 19th and 20th centuries. It has no well-established saint of its own.

daisy.label: Daisy
daisy.meaning: From Old English "dæges eage", "day's eye", the name of the daisy; also used as a pet form of Margaret.
daisy.text: A traditional pet form of Margaret (a play on French "marguerite", "daisy"), Daisy became a name in its own right in Britain and the United States in the late 19th century. A Daisy in the records may therefore be a Margaret. It has no saint of its own.

dale.label: Dale
dale.meaning: From Old English "dæl", "valley", through a surname.
dale.text: An English surname turned given name, Dale spread mainly in the United States in the 20th century. It is rare in older records and in Europe. It has no saint of its own.

damian.label: Damian
damian.meaning: From Greek "Damianos", perhaps from "damazein", "to tame"; the etymology is disputed.
damian.text: The Polish, Spanish and German form of Damien, Damian appears in Catholic records from those countries, without being very frequent before the 20th century. Latin entries write it Damianus. It honours Saint Damian, a physician martyr celebrated with his brother Saint Cosmas.

daniel.label: Daniel
daniel.text: The name of an Old Testament prophet, Daniel was used throughout Europe and was particularly favoured in Protestant circles (the Netherlands, Switzerland, England, the United States). Latin entries write it Daniel, or Danielis in the genitive. It honours the prophet Daniel, listed in the Roman Martyrology.

daniele.label: Daniele
daniele.text: In Italian, Daniele is the masculine form of Daniel, common in records from the peninsula and Ticino; in French, Danièle (or Daniele without accent) is a female name widespread in the 20th century. The sex must therefore be read from the language of the record. No single name day covers both uses.

danielle.label: Danielle
danielle.meaning: Feminine of Daniel, from Hebrew "Daniyyel", "God is my judge".
danielle.text: The French feminine of Daniel, Danielle is rare before the 20th century and became very common in France between the 1930s and 1960s. It is also spelt Danièle. It has no well-established saint of its own.

dante.label: Dante
dante.meaning: Short form of Durante, from Latin "durans", "enduring, lasting".
dante.text: An Italian name associated with the poet Dante Alighieri (whose full name was Durante), Dante appears in Italian records, especially in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

danuta.label: Danuta
danuta.meaning: Of disputed origin, perhaps Lithuanian or Slavic, associated with "dana", "gift".
danuta.text: A Polish name that was previously rare, Danuta spread after Sienkiewicz's novel "The Knights of the Cross" (1900), whose heroine is called Danusia. It is mostly found in 20th-century Polish records. It has no saint of its own.

daphne.label: Daphne
daphne.meaning: From Greek "daphnê", "laurel", the name of a nymph in mythology.
daphne.text: A mythological name, Daphne spread in Britain in the late 19th and 20th centuries and remains rare elsewhere. It is almost absent from older records. It has no saint of its own.

daria.label: Daria
daria.meaning: Feminine of Darius, from Old Persian "Darayavahush", "he who holds the good".
daria.text: A rare name in early Western Europe, Daria is found in Poland, Italy and Spain, mainly in the 20th century. It honours Saint Daria, a Roman martyr celebrated with her husband Saint Chrysanthus.

david.label: David
david.text: The name of the king of Israel, David was used throughout Europe and was especially widespread in Wales (Dafydd, Dewi), Scotland and in English, Dutch and Swiss Protestant circles. Latin entries write it David, or Davidis in the genitive. In Britain its name day is the feast of Saint David, patron of Wales.

davide.label: Davide
davide.text: The Italian form of David, Davide appears in Italian and Ticino records, more frequently in the 19th and 20th centuries. The old Tuscan form Davit occasionally appears. It honours King David, listed in the Roman Martyrology.

dawid.label: Dawid
dawid.text: The Polish form of David, Dawid has been used in Poland since the Middle Ages without being very frequent in older Catholic records. It became very common in the late 20th century. It honours King David, listed in the Roman Martyrology.

dean.label: Dean
dean.meaning: An English surname, either from Old English "denu", "valley", or from Latin "decanus", "dean".
dean.text: An English surname turned given name, Dean spread mainly in the United States in the 20th century. It is rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

deborah.label: Deborah
deborah.text: Deborah is a prophetess and judge of Israel in the Book of Judges. The name is found in Protestant registers and in Jewish communities; Dwojra is the Polish transcription of Yiddish Dvoyre.

delfim.label: Delfim
delfim.text: The Portuguese form of Delphinus, Delfim appears in Portuguese records, mainly from the 19th century, without being frequent. The bishop Saint Delphinus of Bordeaux has no widespread cult there.

delphine.label: Delphine
delphine.meaning: From Latin "Delphina", related to Greek "delphis", "dolphin", or to the town of Delphi.
delphine.text: A rare name before the Revolution, Delphine spread in France and Belgium in the 19th century, then had a strong revival in the 20th. Latin entries write it Delphina. Its name day is the feast of Blessed Delphine of Sabran, a 14th-century Provençal noblewoman.

denis.label: Denis
denis.text: The name of the first bishop of Paris, Denis has been common in France since the Middle Ages, especially in the Île-de-France and the North, and is also found in Belgium and Switzerland. Latin entries write it Dionysius, and the spellings Denys and Denis both occur. It honours Saint Denis, martyr and patron saint of France.

denise.label: Denise
denise.meaning: Feminine of Denis, from Greek "Dionysios", "devoted to Dionysus".
denise.text: The feminine of Denis, Denise is found in France from the Middle Ages, but became very common above all between the 1920s and 1950s. Latin entries write it Dionysia. It has no well-established saint of its own.

dennis.label: Dennis
dennis.text: The English form of Denis, Dennis has been used in England since the Middle Ages and was widespread in Ireland, where it also rendered Gaelic Donnchadh. It became common in Britain and the United States in the 20th century. It honours Saint Denis, first bishop of Paris.

deolinda.label: Deolinda
deolinda.meaning: A Portuguese name, perhaps formed from Latin "Deus", "God", and Portuguese "linda", "beautiful"; the etymology is uncertain.
deolinda.text: A typically Portuguese name, Deolinda is found mainly in Portuguese records of the late 19th and 20th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

derek.label: Derek
derek.meaning: English form of Theodoric, from Germanic "theud", "people", and "ric", "powerful".
derek.text: An English form of Dutch origin (Dirk, Diederik), Derek is rare before the 19th century and spread mainly in Britain in the mid-20th century. It has no well-established saint of its own.

derrick.label: Derrick
derrick.meaning: English form of Theodoric, from Germanic "theud", "people", and "ric", "powerful".
derrick.text: A variant of Derek, Derrick is found in England as a surname from the 16th century, but became a given name mainly in the 20th century. It has no well-established saint of its own.

desire.label: Désiré
desire.text: A name expressing joy at a longed-for birth, Désiré was common in France, Belgium and the Netherlands in the 19th century. Latin entries write it Desideratus, and the accents are often missing (Desire). Its name day is the feast of Saint Desideratus, a 6th-century bishop of Bourges.

desiree.label: Désirée
desiree.text: The feminine of Désiré, Désirée is found in France and Belgium in the 19th century and later in Spain and elsewhere. Latin entries write it Desiderata. It has no well-established saint of its own.

desmond.label: Desmond
desmond.meaning: From Irish "Deasmhumhain", "South Munster", the name of a region and a family.
desmond.text: An Irish surname turned given name, Desmond spread in Ireland and Britain mainly in the 20th century. It is rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

diana.label: Diana
diana.meaning: From the name of the Roman goddess Diana, perhaps related to Latin "dius", "divine, bright".
diana.text: A name of mythological origin, Diana is found in Italy from the Renaissance, then in Britain, Poland and Spain mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no well-established saint of its own.
