diane.label: Diane
diane.meaning: From the name of the Roman goddess Diana, perhaps related to Latin "dius", "divine, bright".
diane.text: Popularised in the Renaissance by Diane de Poitiers, Diane remained a rare name in French records until the 20th century, when it also spread in the United States and Britain. Blessed Diana degli Andalò, a Dominican of Bologna, has not been canonised, so the name has no well-established saint.

didier.label: Didier
didier.text: An old name, Didier was used in France from the early Middle Ages but stayed moderately frequent until its great vogue in the mid-20th century. Latin entries write it Desiderius. Its name day is the feast of Saint Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, martyred in the 7th century.

didiere.label: Didière
didiere.text: A feminine form of Didier, found in registers of eastern France under the Ancien Régime.

diedrich.label: Diedrich
diedrich.text: The Low German form of Dietrich, Diedrich is found mainly in northern Germany (East Frisia, Oldenburg, Bremen), also spelt Diederich, Diderich or Dierk. It has no well-established saint of its own.

diego.label: Diego
diego.meaning: Of disputed origin: from Santiago ("Saint James") by splitting "Sant Yago", or from medieval Latin "Didacus", perhaps from Greek "didachê", "teaching".
diego.text: A very old Spanish name, Diego is common in records throughout Spain; Latin entries write it Didacus. It should be kept distinct from Jaime and Santiago, even though its etymology may link them. Its name day is the feast of Saint Didacus (Diego) of Alcalá, a 15th-century Franciscan friar.

dietrich.label: Dietrich
dietrich.text: An old Germanic name, Dietrich has been used in Germany and German-speaking Switzerland since the Middle Ages, Latin entries writing it Theodoricus. The short form Dieter spread mainly in the 20th century. It has no well-established saint of its own.

dina.label: Dina
dina.meaning: From Hebrew "Dinah", "judged" or "justice", daughter of Jacob; also a short form of names ending in "-dina" (Claudina, Bernardina).
dina.text: A biblical name used in Dutch and English Protestant circles, Dina is also, in Italy and Germany, the short form of names such as Bernardina or Geraldina. It has no well-established saint of its own.

dino.label: Dino
dino.meaning: Italian short form of names ending in "-dino" (Bernardino, Aldino, Corradino).
dino.text: An Italian diminutive that became a name in its own right, Dino is found mainly in Italian records of the 19th and 20th centuries. In older records, look for the full name it comes from. It has no saint of its own.

diogo.label: Diogo
diogo.meaning: Portuguese form of Diego, either from Santiago ("Saint James") or from medieval Latin "Didacus"; the etymology is disputed.
diogo.text: A very old Portuguese name, Diogo has been common in Portuguese records since the Middle Ages; Latin entries write it Didacus. It honours Saint Didacus (Diego) of Alcalá, a 15th-century Franciscan friar.

dionisio.label: Dionisio
dionisio.text: The Spanish and Italian form of Denis, Dionisio has appeared in records from those countries since the Middle Ages; Catalan writes it Dionís. It honours Saint Denis, first bishop of Paris, also celebrated in the Roman calendar.

dirk.label: Dirk
dirk.meaning: Dutch short form of Diederik, from Germanic "theud", "people", and "ric", "powerful".
dirk.text: A Dutch name widespread since the Middle Ages, Dirk is also spelt Dirck, Derk or Dierk, and Latin entries render it Theodoricus. It is frequent in records from the Netherlands, Flanders and northern Germany. It has no well-established saint of its own.

dirkje.label: Dirkje
dirkje.meaning: Dutch feminine of Dirk, from Germanic "theud", "people", and "ric", "powerful".
dirkje.text: A Dutch feminine formed on Dirk, Dirkje is found mainly in records from the Netherlands from the 17th to the 19th century. It has no saint of its own.

dmytro.label: Dmytro
dmytro.meaning: Ukrainian form of Demetrius, from Greek "Dêmêtrios", "devoted to Demeter".
dmytro.text: A Ukrainian name, Dmytro appears in records from former eastern Poland and Galicia, often for Greek Catholic or Orthodox faithful; Polish or Latin entries write it Dymitr or Demetrius. It honours Saint Demetrius of Thessaloniki, celebrated on 26 October in the Byzantine calendar.

dolores.label: Dolores
dolores.meaning: From Spanish "dolores", "sorrows", referring to Our Lady of Sorrows (María de los Dolores).
dolores.text: A Spanish Marian name, Dolores shortens María de los Dolores and spread mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries, in Spain as well as in Hispanic communities in the United States. Its common diminutives are Lola and Loles. Its name day is the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows.

dolors.label: Dolors
dolors.meaning: From Catalan "dolors", "sorrows", referring to Our Lady of Sorrows.
dolors.text: The Catalan form of Dolores, Dolors is a Marian name given mainly in Catalonia and the Catalan-speaking lands from the 19th century. Its name day is the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows.

domenec.label: Domènec
domenec.text: The Catalan form of Dominic, Domènec (Domenec) appears in Catalan records from the Middle Ages; Castilian or Latin entries write it Domingo or Dominicus. It honours Saint Dominic, founder of the Order of Preachers.

domenica.label: Domenica
domenica.meaning: Feminine of Dominicus, from Latin "dominicus", "belonging to the Lord".
domenica.text: The Italian feminine of Domenico, Domenica is frequent in Italian records, notably in the South. The word also means Sunday, and the name was sometimes given to a girl born on that day. It has no well-established saint of its own.

domenico.label: Domenico
domenico.text: The Italian form of Dominic, Domenico is one of the most common male names in Italy, especially in the South, and is also found in Ticino. It honours Saint Dominic, founder of the Order of Preachers.

dominga.label: Dominga
dominga.meaning: Feminine of Domingo, from Latin "dominicus", "belonging to the Lord".
dominga.text: The Spanish feminine of Domingo, Dominga is found in Spanish records, mainly before the 19th century and during it. It has no well-established saint of its own.

domingo.label: Domingo
domingo.text: The Spanish form of Dominic, Domingo has been common in Spanish records since the Middle Ages; Saint Dominic himself was Castilian (Domingo de Guzmán). It honours Saint Dominic, founder of the Order of Preachers.

domingos.label: Domingos
domingos.text: The Portuguese form of Dominic, Domingos has been widespread in Portuguese records since the Middle Ages. It honours Saint Dominic, founder of the Order of Preachers.

dominicus.label: Dominicus
dominicus.text: The Latin form of Dominic, Dominicus appears mainly in Latin-language records from Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and France. It should be read as Dominique, Dominik or Dominicus depending on the family's language. It honours Saint Dominic, founder of the Order of Preachers.

dominik.label: Dominik
dominik.text: The Polish, German and Czech form of Dominic, Dominik appears in Catholic records from those countries and Switzerland, also spelt Dominikus. It honours Saint Dominic, founder of the Order of Preachers.

dominique.label: Dominique
dominique.text: Mostly masculine before the Revolution, Dominique was common in Lorraine, Luxembourg, Belgium and eastern France, where it was sometimes also given to girls. Latin entries write it Dominicus or Dominica depending on the sex. It honours Saint Dominic, founder of the Order of Preachers.

donald.label: Donald
donald.text: A traditional Gaelic name of the Scottish Highlands and Islands, Donald is very frequent in Scotland and spread to England and the United States mainly in the 20th century. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

donatien.label: Donatien
donatien.text: Saints Donatian and Rogatian, martyrs of Nantes, are celebrated on 24 May. The name is characteristic of the Nantes area and western France, notably in the 18th and 19th centuries.

donato.label: Donato
donato.text: A frequent Italian name, notably in the South and Tuscany, Donato is also found in Ticino and Spain; Latin entries write it Donatus. It honours Saint Donatus, bishop of Arezzo and martyr.

donna.label: Donna
donna.text: Mainly an American name, Donna spread in the United States in the 20th century, especially between the 1930s and 1960s. It is rare in older European records. It has no saint of its own.

dora.label: Dora
dora.meaning: Short form of Dorothea, Theodora or Isidora, from Greek "dôron", "gift".
dora.text: A short form of Dorothea, Theodora or Isidora, Dora became a name in its own right in the 19th century in Switzerland, Germany, Britain and the United States. In the records, a Dora often hides one of those full names. It has no saint of its own.

doreen.label: Doreen
doreen.meaning: Probably derived from Dora, or from Irish "Doireann"; the etymology is uncertain.
doreen.text: An early 20th-century English name, Doreen was very popular in Britain between the 1910s and 1940s. It is absent from older records. It has no saint of its own.

dorian.label: Dorian
dorian.meaning: From Greek "Dôrieus", "Dorian", an inhabitant of Doris.
dorian.text: Popularised by Oscar Wilde's novel The Picture of Dorian Gray, it spread in France at the end of the 20th century. It is absent from older registers.

doris.label: Doris
doris.meaning: From Greek "Dôris", "Dorian woman", the name of a sea nymph.
doris.text: A name of mythological origin, Doris spread in the late 19th and early 20th centuries in Britain, the United States and Germany. It is rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

dorota.label: Dorota
dorota.text: The Polish form of Dorothy, Dorota has been used in Poland since the Middle Ages and appears regularly in the records, sometimes in the Latin form Dorothea. It honours Saint Dorothy of Caesarea, virgin martyr.

dorothea.label: Dorothea
dorothea.text: The German, Dutch and Latin form of Dorothy, Dorothea was very widespread in German-speaking lands from the 16th to the 19th century, shortened to Dorle, Dörte, Thea or Dora. It is also found in Poland, Switzerland and England. It honours Saint Dorothy of Caesarea, virgin martyr.

dorothee.label: Dorothee
dorothee.text: The French form of Dorothea, Dorothée is found in France and Belgium without being very frequent, and more often in Alsace and Lorraine. It honours Saint Dorothy of Caesarea, virgin martyr.

dorothy.label: Dorothy
dorothy.text: The English form of the name, Dorothy has been used in England since the 16th century and was very popular in Britain and the United States in the early 20th century. Its diminutives Dolly and Dot are common. It honours Saint Dorothy of Caesarea, virgin martyr.

douglas.label: Douglas
douglas.meaning: From Gaelic "dubh glas", "dark water", a Scottish river and clan name.
douglas.text: The name of a great Scottish family turned given name, Douglas was first used in Scotland, then spread to England and the United States mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

douwe.label: Douwe
douwe.meaning: An old Frisian name of uncertain meaning.
douwe.text: A typically Frisian name, Douwe is frequent in records from Dutch Friesland from the 16th to the 19th century, often followed by a patronymic ending in "-s" or "-es" (Douwes). It has no saint of its own.

duarte.label: Duarte
duarte.meaning: Portuguese form of Edward, from Old English "ead", "wealth", and "weard", "guardian".
duarte.text: Introduced in Portugal by King Duarte (15th century), grandson of John of Gaunt through his mother Philippa of Lancaster, Duarte remains a steady Portuguese name in the records. It honours Saint Edward the Confessor, king of England.

duncan.label: Duncan
duncan.text: A Scottish name borne by medieval kings, Duncan is common in Scotland and spread to the United States and Canada with Scottish emigration. It is rare in continental European records. It has no well-established saint of its own.

durand.label: Durand
durand.text: A medieval given name common in southern and central France, which became one of the country's most frequent surnames. As a given name it grew rare after the 16th century; Latin records write Durandus.

dwight.label: Dwight
dwight.meaning: An English surname, probably from the medieval name Diot, a diminutive of Dionisia (Denise).
dwight.text: An English surname turned given name, Dwight spread in the United States from the 19th century, mostly in the 20th. It is rare in Europe. It has no saint of its own.

earl.label: Earl
earl.meaning: From Old English "eorl", "nobleman, warrior", which became the title of earl.
earl.text: An English noble title turned given name, Earl spread mainly in the United States between the 1880s and 1930s. It is rare in older British and European records. It has no saint of its own.

ebe.label: Ebe
ebe.meaning: Italian form of Hebe, from Greek "hêbê", "youth", the goddess of youth.
ebe.text: A rare mythological name, Ebe is found mainly in Italian records of the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

ebenezer.label: Ebenezer
ebenezer.meaning: From Hebrew "Even ha-Ezer", "stone of help", the name of a memorial stone in the Bible.
ebenezer.text: A biblical name adopted by Puritans and Nonconformists, Ebenezer was used mainly in England, Wales, Scotland and New England from the 17th to the 19th century. It is rare in continental Europe. It has no saint of its own.

eberhard.label: Eberhard
eberhard.text: An old Germanic name, Eberhard has been used in Germany and Switzerland since the Middle Ages, notably in the House of Württemberg; Latin entries write it Eberhardus and the Dutch form is Evert. It has no saint with a widely established cult.

edgar.label: Edgar
edgar.text: The name of an Anglo-Saxon king, Edgar almost disappeared after the Norman Conquest, then came back into fashion in the 19th century in England, France, Germany and the United States. It honours Saint Edgar the Peaceful, 10th-century king of England.

edgard.label: Edgard
edgard.meaning: French form of Edgar, from Old English "ead", "wealth", and "gar", "spear".
edgard.text: The French and Belgian spelling of Edgar, Edgard is found mainly in records of the 19th and early 20th centuries, in Belgium and northern France. It honours Saint Edgar the Peaceful, king of England.

edith.label: Edith
edith.text: An Anglo-Saxon name, Edith was revived in the 19th century and became very common in Britain, the United States, Germany and France in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It honours Saint Edith of Wilton, daughter of King Edgar.

edme.label: Edme
edme.meaning: Burgundian form of Edmund, from Old English "ead", "wealth", and "mund", "protection".
edme.text: A name characteristic of Burgundy and Champagne (Yonne, Aube, Côte-d'Or), Edme was very frequent there before the Revolution and became rare after the 19th century. It honours Saint Edmund of Abingdon (Edmund Rich), archbishop of Canterbury, who died in France in 1240 and was buried at Pontigny Abbey.

edmee.label: Edmée
edmee.meaning: Feminine of Edme, from Old English "ead", "wealth", and "mund", "protection".
edmee.text: The feminine of Edme, Edmée is found mainly in Burgundy and Champagne before the Revolution, in the same regions as the masculine. It has no saint of its own.

edmond.label: Edmond
edmond.text: The French form of Edmund, Edmond is rare before the Revolution but became common in the 19th century in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland. In the Yonne and Aube, the old form Edme is its equivalent. Its name day is the feast of Saint Edmund, king of East Anglia, martyred by the Vikings.

edmund.label: Edmund
edmund.text: An Anglo-Saxon name that stayed in use after the Norman Conquest, Edmund has been used in England since the Middle Ages, and also in Germany and Poland in the 19th century. It honours Saint Edmund, king of East Anglia, martyred by the Vikings in 869.

edna.label: Edna
edna.meaning: Either from Hebrew "ednah", "delight" (Book of Tobit), or from Irish "Eithne"; the etymology is disputed.
edna.text: Mainly an English-speaking name, Edna spread in Britain and the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is rare in older records and in continental Europe. It has no saint of its own.

edoardo.label: Edoardo
edoardo.meaning: Italian form of Edward, from Old English "ead", "wealth", and "weard", "guardian".
edoardo.text: The Italian form of Edward, Edoardo appears in Italian records mainly from the 19th century; the older form Odoardo is more frequent before then. It honours Saint Edward the Confessor, king of England.

edouard.label: Édouard
edouard.text: A name of English origin, Édouard is rare in France before the Revolution and became common in the 19th century in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland. Latin entries write it Eduardus, and the accent is often missing (Edouard). Its name day is the feast of Saint Edward the Confessor, king of England.

eduard.label: Eduard
eduard.meaning: German and Dutch form of Edward, from Old English "ead", "wealth", and "weard", "guardian".
eduard.text: The German, Dutch, Catalan and Polish form of Edward, Eduard spread mainly in the 19th century in Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. Latin entries write it Eduardus. It honours Saint Edward the Confessor, king of England.

eduarda.label: Eduarda
eduarda.meaning: Feminine of Eduardo, from Old English "ead", "wealth", and "weard", "guardian".
eduarda.text: The Portuguese and Spanish feminine of Eduardo, Eduarda is found mainly in Portugal and Brazil, more rarely in Spain, from the 19th century. It has no saint of its own.

eduardo.label: Eduardo
eduardo.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Edward, from Old English "ead", "wealth", and "weard", "guardian".
eduardo.text: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Edward, Eduardo spread mainly from the 19th century; in Portugal the older traditional form is Duarte. It honours Saint Edward the Confessor, king of England.

eduardus.label: Eduardus
eduardus.meaning: Latin form of Edward, from Old English "ead", "wealth", and "weard", "guardian".
eduardus.text: The Latin form of Edward, Eduardus appears mainly in Latin-language records from Belgium and the Netherlands, where everyday usage says Edouard or Eduard. It should be read according to the family's language. It honours Saint Edward the Confessor, king of England.

edvige.label: Edvige
edvige.meaning: Italian form of Hedwig, from Germanic "hadu", "battle", and "wig", "fight".
edvige.text: The Italian form of Hedwig, Edvige is found in Italian records mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It honours Saint Hedwig of Silesia, duchess and patron saint of Silesia.

edward.label: Edward
edward.text: The name of several kings of England, Edward has been one of the most common male names in England since the Middle Ages and is widespread in the United States; it is abbreviated Ed., Edw., Ned or Ted. It is also found in Poland and Belgium, mainly in the 19th century. It honours Saint Edward the Confessor, king of England.

edwin.label: Edwin
edwin.text: An Anglo-Saxon name revived in the 19th century, Edwin is common in Britain and the United States and is also found in Switzerland, Germany and the Netherlands. It honours Saint Edwin, king of Northumbria, who converted to Christianity.

egbert.label: Egbert
egbert.text: An old Germanic name, Egbert appears in Dutch and German records without being very frequent. It was borne by Anglo-Saxon kings and early medieval bishops, but no single cult dominates for the name.

egidio.label: Egidio
egidio.meaning: From Latin "Aegidius", itself from Greek "aigidion", "young goat"; the etymology is disputed.
egidio.text: The Italian form of Giles, Egidio has appeared in Italian records since the Middle Ages, sometimes as Gilio. It honours Saint Giles, a Provençal hermit greatly venerated in the Middle Ages.

egidius.label: Egidius
egidius.meaning: Latin form of Giles, from Greek "aigidion", "young goat"; the etymology is disputed.
egidius.text: The Latin form of Giles, Egidius is frequent in Latin records and as an everyday name in Belgium and the Netherlands, where usage shortens it to Gielis or Gillis. In French-speaking families it should be read as Gilles. It honours Saint Giles, a Provençal hermit.

eileen.label: Eileen
eileen.meaning: From Irish "Eibhlín", from Norman Aveline or associated with Helen; the etymology is disputed.
eileen.text: An Irish name, Eileen spread in Britain and the United States mainly in the early 20th century. In older Irish records it may be rendered as Ellen or Helena. It has no well-established saint of its own.

elaine.label: Elaine
elaine.meaning: An Old French form of Helen, from Greek "Helenê", of disputed meaning ("brightness, torch").
elaine.text: A name taken from the Arthurian romances, Elaine spread mainly in the 20th century in Britain and the United States. It is rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

elda.label: Elda
elda.meaning: An Italian name of uncertain origin, perhaps Germanic ("hild", "battle") or a short form.
elda.text: An Italian name, Elda is found mainly in records from northern Italy in the late 19th and 20th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

elea.label: Éléa
elea.meaning: A modern creation of uncertain origin, associated with Greek or Hebrew.
elea.text: A recent name, widely given in France at the start of the 21st century. It does not occur in older registers.

eleanor.label: Eleanor
eleanor.meaning: From Occitan "Aliénor", of disputed etymology; sometimes linked to Helen.
eleanor.text: Popularised in England by Eleanor of Aquitaine and Eleanor of Provence, Eleanor has been used since the Middle Ages and saw a revival in the 19th century in the United States and Britain. The diminutives Nell and Nora are frequent. No saint bears this name, so it has no name day of its own.

elena.label: Elena
elena.meaning: From Greek "Helenê", of disputed meaning ("brightness, torch").
elena.text: The Italian and Spanish form of Helen, Elena has been common in records from those countries since the Middle Ages. It honours Saint Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine.

eleonora.label: Eleonora
eleonora.meaning: From Occitan "Aliénor", of disputed etymology; sometimes linked to Helen.
eleonora.text: The Italian, Polish and Latin form of Eleanor, Eleonora appears in Italian and Central European records, often among the nobility, then more widely in the 19th century. No saint bears this name, so it has no well-established name day.

eleonore.label: Eleonore
eleonore.meaning: From Occitan "Aliénor", of disputed etymology; sometimes linked to Helen.
eleonore.text: The French and German form of Eleanor, Éléonore is found in France, Belgium and Germany, mostly among the nobility before the Revolution, then more widely in the 19th century. The accents are often missing in records (Eleonore). No saint bears this name, so it has no well-established name day.

elfriede.label: Elfriede
elfriede.meaning: German form of Old English "Ælfthryth", from "ælf", "elf", and "thryth", "strength".
elfriede.text: A German name of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Elfriede was very common in Germany between the 1900s and 1930s, often shortened to Friedel or Elfi. It is rare in earlier records. It has no well-established saint of its own.

elia.label: Elia
elia.meaning: Italian form of Elijah, from Hebrew "Eliyahu", "my God is Yahweh".
elia.text: Used in Italy and Italian-speaking Switzerland in honour of the prophet Elijah, celebrated on 20 July. In these registers it is a male name.

elian.label: Élian
elian.meaning: Linked to Latin "Aelianus", a Roman family name.
elian.text: A modern name, mostly given from the end of the 20th century. It is rare in older registers.

eliane.label: Eliane
eliane.meaning: From Latin "Aeliana", derived from the Roman family name "Aelius".
eliane.text: A 20th-century French name, Éliane (Eliane) became common in France between the 1920s and 1950s. It is very rare in older records. It has no well-established saint of its own.

elias.label: Elias
elias.text: The Greek and Latin form of Elijah, Elias was used in the German-speaking lands, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Poland, notably in Protestant circles. Elijah (English) and Elia (Italian) are close forms. It honours the prophet Elijah, celebrated on 20 July.

elie.label: Élie
elie.text: The French form of Elijah, Élie (Elie) is found in France, French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium, more often among Protestants and in the South-West; the old form Hélie is frequent in the Middle Ages. Latin entries write it Elias. It honours the prophet Elijah.

elisa.label: Elisa
elisa.meaning: Short form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
elisa.text: A short form of Elizabeth that became a name in its own right, Elisa is common in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Belgium, especially in the 19th century. In the records it may refer to a woman called Elizabeth in other entries. Its name day is the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

elisabet.label: Elisabet
elisabet.meaning: From Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
elisabet.text: The Catalan, Scandinavian and sometimes German form of Elizabeth, Elisabet appears notably in Catalan records; the usual Castilian form is Isabel. It honours Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

elisabeth.label: Elisabeth
elisabeth.meaning: From Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
elisabeth.text: The name of John the Baptist's mother, Elisabeth is one of the most frequent female names in Germany, Switzerland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Belgium, and common in France (Élisabeth, Élizabeth). Its diminutives are very numerous: Lisette, Élise, Else, Lise, Liesel, Betje, Bep. Its name day is the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

elisabetha.label: Elisabetha
elisabetha.meaning: From Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
elisabetha.text: A German, Swiss and Dutch spelling of Elizabeth, Elisabetha (also Elisabeta) is frequent in records from the 17th to the 19th century, notably in German-speaking Switzerland and southern Germany. It should be grouped with Elisabeth in searches. Its name day is the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

elisabetta.label: Elisabetta
elisabetta.meaning: From Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
elisabetta.text: The Italian form of Elizabeth, Elisabetta has been common in Italian records since the Middle Ages, often shortened to Betta, Bettina or Lisa. It honours Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

elise.label: Elise
elise.meaning: Short form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
elise.text: A diminutive of Elizabeth that became a name in its own right, Élise (Elise) is common in the 19th century in France, Switzerland, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands. The same woman may appear as Élisabeth and as Élise in different records. Its name day is the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

elisee.label: Élisée
elisee.text: The name of an Old Testament prophet, Élisée (Elisee) was used mainly by Protestants in France and French-speaking Switzerland, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries. It remains rare elsewhere. It honours the prophet Elisha, disciple of Elijah.

eliza.label: Eliza
eliza.meaning: Short form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
eliza.text: A short form of Elizabeth, Eliza was very common in Britain and the United States in the 18th and 19th centuries, often as a name in its own right. The same woman may appear as Elizabeth and as Eliza in different records. Its name day is the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

elizabeth.label: Elizabeth
elizabeth.meaning: From Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
elizabeth.text: The name of John the Baptist's mother and of several queens, Elizabeth has been one of the most common female names in England and the United States since the 16th century. Its diminutives are very numerous (Eliza, Betty, Bess, Betsy, Beth, Lizzie), often used alone in the records. Its name day is the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

ella.label: Ella
ella.meaning: Probably from Germanic "ali", "other, foreign", or a short form of Elizabeth, Eleanor or Helen; the etymology is uncertain.
ella.text: A short name, Ella spread in the late 19th century in the United States, Germany, Switzerland and Britain, often as a short form of other names. In the records it may stand for an Elisabeth, an Eleonore or a Helena. It has no well-established saint of its own.

ellen.label: Ellen
ellen.meaning: English form of Helen, from Greek "Helenê", of disputed meaning ("brightness, torch").
ellen.text: An old English form of Helen, Ellen was very common in England, Ireland and the United States in the 19th century; the diminutives Nell and Nellie are frequent. It is also found in Germany, the Netherlands and Scandinavia. It honours Saint Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine.

elly.label: Elly
elly.meaning: Short form of Elizabeth, Helen or Eleonore; the etymology varies.
elly.text: A diminutive that became a given name in the early 20th century, Elly is found mainly in Germany, the Netherlands and Poland. In the records, look for the full name (Elisabeth, Helena, Eleonore). It has no saint of its own.

elmer.label: Elmer
elmer.text: An English surname turned given name, Elmer was mostly used in the United States between the 1870s and 1930s. It is rare in Europe. It has no saint of its own.

elodie.label: Elodie
elodie.meaning: From the name of Saint Alodia, a Spanish martyr, of uncertain etymology (perhaps Germanic "al", "all", and "od", "wealth").
elodie.text: A rare name before the Revolution, Élodie (Elodie) is found in France and Belgium in the 19th century, then became very popular in the late 20th century. Its name day is the feast of Saint Alodia (Élodie), martyred at Huesca in the 9th century with her sister Nunilo.

eloi.label: Éloi
eloi.text: An old name, Éloi (Eloi, Eloy) is found in France, Belgium and the North, where the saint is very popular as patron of goldsmiths, blacksmiths and farriers. Latin entries write it Eligius. It honours Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon and adviser to King Dagobert.

eloisa.label: Eloísa
eloisa.meaning: Spanish and Italian form of Héloïse, probably from Germanic "Helewidis", from "heil", "healthy", and "wid", "wide"; the etymology is disputed.
eloisa.text: Mainly a 19th-century name, Eloísa (Eloisa) is found in Spain and Italy. It has no well-established saint of its own.

eloy.label: Eloy
eloy.text: The Spanish form of Eligius, Eloy has appeared in Spanish records since the Middle Ages; Catalan says Eloi. It honours Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon and patron of goldsmiths.

elsa.label: Elsa
elsa.meaning: Short form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
elsa.text: A diminutive of Elizabeth that became a name in its own right, Elsa spread in the 19th century in Switzerland, Germany and Italy, partly thanks to Wagner's opera "Lohengrin". In the records it may refer to a woman called Elisabeth in other entries. Its name day is the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

elsbeth.label: Elsbeth
elsbeth.meaning: Contracted form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
elsbeth.text: A contracted German and Swiss form of Elizabeth, Elsbeth (or Elsbet, Elßbeth) is frequent in German-speaking records from the 16th to the 18th century. It should be grouped with Elisabeth in searches. Its name day is the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

else.label: Else
else.meaning: Short form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
else.text: A German, Dutch and Scandinavian diminutive of Elizabeth, Else became a name in its own right in the 19th and 20th centuries, especially in Germany. In older records Else (or Elß) often stands for an Elisabeth. Its name day is the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

elvira.label: Elvira
elvira.meaning: Probably from a Visigothic name; the etymology is disputed.
elvira.text: A name of Visigothic origin used in Spain since the Middle Ages, Elvira also spread in Italy and Germany in the 19th century, partly thanks to opera. The French form is Elvire. It has no well-established saint of its own.

elzbieta.label: Elżbieta
elzbieta.meaning: From Hebrew "Elisheva", "my God is an oath".
elzbieta.text: The Polish form of Elizabeth, Elżbieta (without diacritic: Elzbieta) has been one of the most common female names in Poland since the Middle Ages. Latin entries write it Elisabetha or Elisabeth. Its name day is the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

ema.label: Ema
ema.meaning: Portuguese and Slavic form of Emma, from Germanic "ermen", "whole, universal".
ema.text: The Portuguese, Polish and Slovene form of Emma, Ema is found mainly in records from Portugal and Central Europe in the 19th and 20th centuries. It is rare before then. There is no saint with an established cult for this form.

emanuel.label: Emanuel
emanuel.text: The name given to the Messiah in Isaiah's prophecy, Emanuel was used in Switzerland, Portugal, Germany and the Netherlands, notably in German-speaking Protestant families. Portuguese and Spanish also use the short form Manuel. As it designates Christ himself, the name has no saint of its own.

emanuele.label: Emanuele
emanuele.text: The Italian form of Emmanuel, Emanuele appears in Italian records, notably in the House of Savoy (Emanuele Filiberto, Vittorio Emanuele), which helped it spread in the 19th century. As it designates Christ himself, the name has no saint of its own.

emelie.label: Emelie
emelie.meaning: Variant of Émilie, from the Roman family name "Aemilius"; sometimes confused with Amélie.
emelie.text: A spelling of Émilie or Amélie frequent in Belgium and northern France in the 19th century, Emelie should be grouped with both names in searches, as registers often confuse them. It has no well-established saint of its own.

emiel.label: Emiel
emiel.meaning: Dutch form of Émile, from the Roman family name "Aemilius".
emiel.text: The Flemish and Dutch form of Émile, Emiel was used mainly in Flemish Belgium in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Depending on the language of the record, the same man may be entered as Emile or Emiel. It has no well-established saint of its own.

emil.label: Emil
emil.meaning: From the Roman family name "Aemilius", perhaps related to "aemulus", "rival".
emil.text: The German, Polish and Scandinavian form of Émile, Emil spread mainly in the 19th century in Switzerland, Germany, Luxembourg and Poland. It is rare in earlier records. It has no well-established saint of its own.

emile.label: Émile
emile.meaning: From the Roman family name "Aemilius", perhaps related to "aemulus", "rival".
emile.text: A rare name before the Revolution, Émile (Emile) became one of the most common male names in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland in the 19th century, after Rousseau's "Emile" (1762). Latin entries write it Aemilius or Emilius. It has no well-established saint of its own.

emili.label: Emili
emili.meaning: Catalan form of Émile, from the Roman family name "Aemilius".
emili.text: The Catalan form of Émile, Emili is found mainly in Catalan records of the 19th and 20th centuries; Castilian entries write it Emilio. It has no well-established saint of its own.

emilia.label: Emilia
emilia.meaning: Feminine of the Roman family name "Aemilius".
emilia.text: The Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and Polish form of Émilie, Emilia appears in records from those countries, mainly from the 18th century. Several saints bear the name, but none has a dominant cult.

emiliano.label: Emiliano
emiliano.meaning: From Latin "Aemilianus", derived from the family name "Aemilius".
emiliano.text: A Spanish and Italian name, Emiliano appears in records from those countries, often linked to the cult of Saint Aemilianus (San Millán), a hermit of La Rioja whose monastery of San Millán de la Cogolla was a major pilgrimage site. In Castile the popular form of the name is Millán.

emilie.label: Emilie
emilie.meaning: Feminine of the Roman family name "Aemilius".
emilie.text: A rare name before the Revolution, Émilie (Emilie) became very common in the 19th century in France, Belgium, Switzerland and Germany. It is often confused with Amélie and Emelie in the records. Several 19th-century saints bear the name, with no dominant feast.

emilien.label: Émilien
emilien.meaning: From Latin "Aemilianus", derived from the family name "Aemilius".
emilien.text: A rare name, Émilien (Emilien) is found in France mainly in the 19th century and had a revival in the late 20th century. It has no saint with an established cult in France.

emilienne.label: Emilienne
emilienne.text: A French name of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Émilienne (Emilienne) was common in France between the 1880s and 1930s. It is rare before then. It has no well-established saint of its own.

emilio.label: Emilio
emilio.meaning: From the Roman family name "Aemilius", perhaps related to "aemulus", "rival".
emilio.text: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Émile, Emilio spread mainly in the 19th century. Latin entries write it Aemilius. It has no well-established saint of its own.

emily.label: Emily
emily.meaning: English form of Émilie, from the Roman family name "Aemilius".
emily.text: The English form of Émilie, Emily became common in Britain and the United States from the 18th century and very frequent in the 19th. It is sometimes confused with Amelia in the records. There is no saint whose feast dominates for this name.

emma.label: Emma
emma.meaning: From Germanic "ermen" or "irmin", "whole, universal", often a short form of names beginning with "Ermen-".
emma.text: A medieval name borne by queens and noblewomen, Emma was revived in the 19th century and became common in Switzerland, Germany, Italy, Belgium and the United States. The old forms Hemma and Imma are found in German-speaking areas. Its name day is the feast of Saint Emma (Hemma) of Gurk, a foundress venerated in Carinthia.

emmanuel.label: Emmanuel
emmanuel.text: The name given to the Messiah in Isaiah's prophecy, Emmanuel is found in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland, more frequently from the 19th century; Portugal also uses Manuel. As it designates Christ himself, the name has no saint of its own and is sometimes celebrated at Christmas.

emmanuelle.label: Emmanuelle
emmanuelle.meaning: Feminine of Emmanuel, from Hebrew "Immanu El", "God with us".
emmanuelle.text: Rare before the 20th century, this name was most fashionable in France in the 1960s and 1970s.

emmy.label: Emmy
emmy.meaning: Diminutive of Emma or Emilie; see Emma, from Germanic "ermen", "whole".
emmy.text: A diminutive that became a given name in the late 19th century, Emmy (or Emmi) is found mainly in Switzerland, Germany and the Netherlands. In the records it may refer to a woman entered elsewhere as Emma or Emilie. It has no saint of its own.

encarnacion.label: Encarnación
encarnacion.meaning: From Latin "incarnatio", "incarnation", referring to the mystery of the Incarnation of Christ.
encarnacion.text: A Spanish Marian name, Encarnación shortens María de la Encarnación and spread mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries; the diminutives Encarna and Encarnita are common, and Catalan says Encarnació. Its name day is the Annunciation, which celebrates the Incarnation.

engelbert.label: Engelbert
engelbert.meaning: From Germanic "Angil", the name of the Angles, and "berht", "bright".
engelbert.text: An old Germanic name, Engelbert has been used in Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium since the Middle Ages, mainly in Catholic regions. Latin entries write it Engelbertus. It honours Saint Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, murdered in 1225.

engelina.label: Engelina
engelina.meaning: A Dutch derivative of Germanic names beginning with "Engel-", associated with the word "engel", "angel".
engelina.text: A Dutch name, Engelina is found mainly in records from the Netherlands from the 17th to the 19th century, also as Engeltje or Angelina. It has no saint of its own.

engeltrude.label: Engeltrude
engeltrude.meaning: From Germanic "engil", linked to the Angles, and "trud", "strength".
engeltrude.text: A Germanic name of the early Middle Ages, found mostly in medieval genealogies. Latin records write Engeltrudis.

enid.label: Enid
enid.meaning: From Welsh, perhaps from "enaid", "soul", or "enid", "purity"; the etymology is disputed.
enid.text: A Welsh name taken from the Arthurian legends, Enid spread in Britain in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, after Tennyson's poems. It is rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

enric.label: Enric
enric.meaning: Catalan form of Henry, from Germanic "haim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
enric.text: The Catalan form of Henry, Enric appears in Catalan records; Castilian entries write it Enrique and Latin ones Henricus. It honours Saint Henry II, Holy Roman Emperor.

enrica.label: Enrica
enrica.meaning: Feminine of Enrico, from Germanic "haim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
enrica.text: The Italian feminine of Enrico, Enrica is found in Italian records mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no well-established saint of its own.

enrichetta.label: Enrichetta
enrichetta.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Enrico, from Germanic "haim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
enrichetta.text: The Italian form of Henrietta, Enrichetta is found in Italian records mainly in the 19th century. It has no well-established saint of its own.

enrico.label: Enrico
enrico.meaning: Italian form of Henry, from Germanic "haim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
enrico.text: The Italian form of Henry, Enrico has been used in Italy and Ticino since the Middle Ages and became very common in the 19th century. Latin entries write it Henricus. It honours Saint Henry II, Holy Roman Emperor.

enrique.label: Enrique
enrique.meaning: Spanish form of Henry, from Germanic "haim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
enrique.text: The name of several kings of Castile, Enrique has been used in Spain since the Middle Ages; Latin entries write it Henricus. It honours Saint Henry II, Holy Roman Emperor.

enriqueta.label: Enriqueta
enriqueta.meaning: Feminine of Enrique, from Germanic "haim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
enriqueta.text: The Spanish form of Henrietta, Enriqueta is found in Spanish records mainly in the 19th century. It has no well-established saint of its own.

erasmus.label: Erasmus
erasmus.text: Used in Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and England since the late Middle Ages, Erasmus is associated with the humanist Erasmus of Rotterdam; the short form Asmus is frequent in northern Germany. It honours Saint Erasmus (Saint Elmo), bishop and martyr, one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers.

ercole.label: Ercole
ercole.meaning: Italian form of Hercules, from Greek "Hêraklês", "glory of Hera".
ercole.text: A name inspired by antiquity, Ercole has been used in Italy since the Renaissance, notably in the House of Este at Ferrara. It appears in Italian records without being very frequent. It has no well-established saint of its own.

erhard.label: Erhard
erhard.text: An old Germanic name, Erhard was used mainly in Bavaria, Alsace and southern Germany, where the saint is venerated; it is also found in Switzerland and Poland. Latin entries write it Erhardus. It honours Saint Erhard, a missionary bishop venerated at Regensburg.

eric.label: Eric
eric.text: A Scandinavian name, Eric spread in Britain and the United States in the 19th century, then in France in the second half of the 20th century, where it became very common. It is rare in older Western European records. Its name day is the feast of Saint Eric, 12th-century king of Sweden.

erich.label: Erich
erich.meaning: German form of Eric, from Old Norse "Eiríkr", "ever powerful".
erich.text: The German form of Eric, Erich spread mainly in the late 19th and early 20th centuries in Germany, Switzerland and German-speaking Poland. It is rare in earlier records. Its name day is the feast of Saint Eric, king of Sweden.

erika.label: Erika
erika.meaning: Feminine of Erik, from Old Norse "Eiríkr", "ever powerful"; also associated with the Latin name of heather ("erica").
erika.text: Mainly a 20th-century name, Erika was very common in Germany between the 1920s and 1950s and is also found in Poland and Spain. It is rare in earlier records. It has no saint of its own.

erminia.label: Erminia
erminia.meaning: Of disputed origin: the Italian feminine of Herminius (a Roman name) or linked to Germanic "ermen", "whole".
erminia.text: An Italian name mainly of the 19th century, Erminia was popularised by the heroine of Tasso's "Jerusalem Delivered". It is also found in Germany. It has no well-established saint of its own.

erna.label: Erna
erna.meaning: Short form of Ernestine, or derived from Germanic "ernust", "struggle, earnestness"; the etymology is disputed.
erna.text: A German name of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Erna was very common in Germany between the 1890s and 1930s and is also found in Poland. It is rare in earlier records. It has no saint of its own.

ernest.label: Ernest
ernest.text: The French and English form of Ernst, Ernest became common in the 19th century in France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Britain and the United States. It is rare before the Revolution. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

ernesta.label: Ernesta
ernesta.meaning: Italian feminine of Ernesto, from Germanic "ernust", "struggle, earnestness".
ernesta.text: The Italian feminine of Ernesto, Ernesta is found in Italian records mainly in the 19th century. It has no saint of its own.

ernestina.label: Ernestina
ernestina.meaning: Feminine of Ernesto, from Germanic "ernust", "struggle, earnestness".
ernestina.text: The Italian and Spanish form of Ernestine, Ernestina is found in records from those countries and Germany, mainly in the 19th century. It has no saint of its own.

ernestine.label: Ernestine
ernestine.meaning: Feminine of Ernest, from Germanic "ernust", "struggle, earnestness".
ernestine.text: The feminine of Ernest, Ernestine is found in Germany, Poland, France, Belgium and Switzerland, mainly in the 19th century. It is rare before the Revolution. It has no saint of its own.

ernesto.label: Ernesto
ernesto.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Ernst, from Germanic "ernust", "struggle, earnestness".
ernesto.text: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Ernest, Ernesto spread mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It is rare in earlier records. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

ernst.label: Ernst
ernst.text: A name borne by dukes of Saxony and Brunswick, Ernst is common in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands, especially from the 17th century and very frequent in the 19th. Latin entries write it Ernestus. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

ersilia.label: Ersilia
ersilia.meaning: From Latin "Hersilia", the name of Romulus's wife in Roman legend; the etymology is uncertain.
ersilia.text: A name inspired by antiquity, Ersilia is found in Italian records, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

erwin.label: Erwin
erwin.text: A Germanic name, Erwin spread mainly in the late 19th and 20th centuries in Germany, Switzerland and Alsace, notably in memory of Erwin von Steinbach, architect of Strasbourg cathedral. It is rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

esperanza.label: Esperanza
esperanza.meaning: From Spanish "esperanza", "hope", one of the theological virtues.
esperanza.text: A virtue name and a Marian name, Esperanza often shortens María de la Esperanza and spread in Spain mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries; Catalan says Esperança. Its name day is the feast of Our Lady of Hope (or of the Expectation), celebrated on 18 December in Spain.

esteban.label: Esteban
esteban.text: The Spanish form of Stephen, Esteban has been used in Spain since the Middle Ages; Catalan says Esteve and Latin entries write Stephanus. It honours Saint Stephen, the first martyr.

estefania.label: Estefanía
estefania.text: The Spanish form of Stephanie, Estefanía (Estefania) appears in Spanish records from the Middle Ages without being frequent, and spread more in the 20th century. It has no well-established saint of its own.

estelle.label: Estelle
estelle.text: A name of Provençal origin, Estelle is found mainly in southern France and spread in the 19th century, then in the United States and Britain; the star is the emblem of the Félibrige. It is rare in older records from the North. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

ester.label: Ester
ester.meaning: From Hebrew "Ester", probably from Persian "stara", "star"; the etymology is disputed.
ester.text: The Italian, Polish, Spanish and German form of Esther, Ester is found in records from those countries, notably in Jewish and Protestant communities. It has no well-established feast in the Roman calendar.

estera.label: Estera
estera.meaning: Polish form of Esther, probably a Persian name ("star").
estera.text: The form in which Polish records register the biblical Esther, frequent among the Jews of Poland in the 19th century, with the diminutive Esterka. The Yiddish equivalent is Ester.

estevao.label: Estêvão
estevao.text: The Portuguese form of Stephen, Estêvão (Estevao) has been used in Portugal since the Middle Ages; Latin entries write it Stephanus. It honours Saint Stephen, the first martyr.

esther.label: Esther
esther.meaning: From Hebrew "Ester", probably from Persian "stara", "star"; the etymology is disputed.
esther.text: The name of the biblical queen, Esther was used mainly in Protestant circles (the Netherlands, Switzerland, England, the United States) and in Jewish communities. It is rarer in older Catholic records. It has no well-established feast in the Roman calendar.

ethel.label: Ethel
ethel.meaning: From Old English "æthel", "noble", originally a short form of names such as Etheldreda.
ethel.text: An English name of the late 19th century, Ethel was very common in Britain and the United States between the 1870s and 1920s. It is rare in earlier records. It has no saint of its own.

etienne.label: Étienne
etienne.text: A very common name in France, French-speaking Switzerland, Belgium and Luxembourg since the Middle Ages, Étienne (Etienne) appears in old forms such as Estienne; Latin entries write it Stephanus. It honours Saint Stephen, deacon and first martyr.

etiennette.label: Etiennette
etiennette.text: The feminine of Étienne, Étiennette (Etiennette) is found in France before the Revolution, with the old forms Estiennette and Tiennette. It became rare after the 19th century. It has no well-established saint of its own.

ettore.label: Ettore
ettore.meaning: Italian form of Hector, from Greek "Hektôr", "he who holds fast, protector".
ettore.text: A name inspired by Homer, Ettore has been used in Italy since the Renaissance and spread mainly in the 19th century. It has no saint of its own.

eugen.label: Eugen
eugen.text: The German, Polish and Romanian form of Eugene, Eugen spread mainly in the 19th century in Germany, Switzerland and Central Europe, partly in memory of Prince Eugene of Savoy. It is rare in earlier records. Several saints and popes bore the name, with no dominant feast.

eugene.label: Eugène
eugene.text: A rare name before the Revolution, Eugène (Eugene) became very common in the 19th century in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland, then in the United States, where it is often shortened to Gene. Latin entries write it Eugenius. Several saints and popes bore the name, with no dominant feast.

eugenia.label: Eugenia
eugenia.text: The Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and Polish form of Eugénie, Eugenia appears in records from those countries, mainly in the 19th century. It honours Saint Eugenia, a Roman virgin martyr.

eugenie.label: Eugénie
eugenie.text: Mainly a 19th-century name, Eugénie (Eugenie) was very common in France and Belgium under the Second Empire, echoing Empress Eugénie. It is also found in Switzerland and Germany. It honours Saint Eugenia, a Roman virgin martyr.

eugenio.label: Eugenio
eugenio.text: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Eugene, Eugenio appears in records from those countries and Ticino, mainly from the 18th century. Several saints and popes bore the name, with no dominant feast.

eugenius.label: Eugenius
eugenius.meaning: Latin form of Eugene, from Greek "Eugenios", "well-born".
eugenius.text: The Latin form of Eugene, Eugenius appears mainly in Latin-language records from Belgium and the Netherlands. It should be read as Eugène or Eugeen depending on the family's language. Several saints and popes bore the name, with no dominant feast.

eugeniusz.label: Eugeniusz
eugeniusz.meaning: Polish form of Eugene, from Greek "Eugenios", "well-born".
eugeniusz.text: The Polish form of Eugene, Eugeniusz spread in Poland mainly in the late 19th and 20th centuries. Latin entries write it Eugenius. Several saints and popes bore the name, with no dominant feast.

eulalia.label: Eulalia
eulalia.text: An old Spanish name, Eulalia honours two much-venerated martyrs: Eulalia of Mérida and Eulalia of Barcelona, patron of that city, hence the Catalan form Laia and the old Spanish Olalla. It is also found in Belgium and Germany. The feast given is that of Eulalia of Mérida.

eulalie.label: Eulalie
eulalie.text: The French form of Eulalia, Eulalie is found in France, Belgium and the South-West, mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It honours Saint Eulalia of Mérida, virgin martyr.

eunice.label: Eunice
eunice.text: The name of Timothy's mother in the New Testament, Eunice was adopted by the Puritans and remained mainly in use in England and the United States. It is rare in continental Europe. It has no well-established feast.

euphrasie.label: Euphrasie
euphrasie.text: A rare name, Euphrasie is found in France and Belgium mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries. Latin entries write it Euphrasia. Its name day is the feast of Saint Euphrasia, a 5th-century nun in the Thebaid.

euphrosine.label: Euphrosine
euphrosine.text: The name of one of the three Graces and of Saint Euphrosyne of Alexandria. It was fashionable in France in the late 18th and 19th centuries; Frosine and Phrosine are shortened forms.

eusebio.label: Eusebio
eusebio.text: The Spanish, Portuguese and Italian form of Eusebius, Eusebio has appeared in records from those countries since the Middle Ages; Latin entries write it Eusebius. It honours Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli.

eustache.label: Eustache
eustache.text: An old name, Eustache is found in France before the Revolution, without being very frequent. Latin entries write it Eustachius. It honours Saint Eustace, a legendary Roman martyr, patron of hunters.

eutrope.label: Eutrope
eutrope.text: Saint Eutropius, first bishop of Saintes, is celebrated on 30 April. The name is characteristic of Saintonge and Aunis.

eva.label: Eva
eva.text: The name of the first woman in the Bible, Eva was used throughout Europe, notably in the Netherlands, Germany and Spain; it became very common in the 19th and 20th centuries. The French form is Ève. It has no saint of its own in the Roman calendar.

evan.label: Evan
evan.meaning: Welsh form of John (Ieuan), from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
evan.text: An anglicised form of Welsh Ieuan, Evan is very common in Wales, where it also gave the surname Evans. It is found in England and the United States, mainly in families of Welsh origin. It honours Saint John the Baptist.

evaristo.label: Evaristo
evaristo.text: The Spanish and Italian form of Evaristus, Evaristo appears in records from those countries, mainly in the 19th century. It honours Saint Evaristus, a 1st-century pope and martyr.

evelina.label: Evelina
evelina.meaning: Latinised form of Aveline, of Germanic origin ("avi", meaning disputed); sometimes linked to Eve.
evelina.text: Mainly a 19th-century name, Evelina is found in Italy, Belgium, Britain and Poland, partly thanks to Fanny Burney's novel "Evelina" (1778). It has no saint of its own.

evelyn.label: Evelyn
evelyn.meaning: From an English surname derived from Aveline, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
evelyn.text: An English surname first given as a male name, Evelyn became mostly feminine in the late 19th century and very common in the United States and Britain in the early 20th. In older records the sex should therefore be checked. It has no saint of its own.

evelyne.label: Evelyne
evelyne.meaning: French form of Evelyn, from Aveline, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
evelyne.text: A 20th-century French name, Évelyne (Evelyne, Eveline) became common in France between the 1940s and 1960s. It is rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

everett.label: Everett
everett.meaning: From an English surname derived from Eberhard, from Germanic "ebur", "boar", and "hard", "strong".
everett.text: An English surname turned given name, Everett spread mainly in the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is rare in Europe. It has no saint of its own.

evert.label: Evert
evert.meaning: Dutch form of Eberhard, from Germanic "ebur", "boar", and "hard", "strong".
evert.text: The Dutch form of Eberhard, Evert is common in records from the Netherlands from the 16th to the 19th century, also spelt Evart or Everd; Latin entries write it Everardus. It has no saint with a widely established cult.

evrard.label: Évrard
evrard.text: The French equivalent of Eberhard, used in northern France and Flanders in the Middle Ages. Records spell it Everard or Évrart, and Everardus in Latin.

ewa.label: Ewa
ewa.meaning: Polish form of Eve, from Hebrew "Hawwah", "living".
ewa.text: The Polish form of Eve, Ewa has been used in Poland since the Middle Ages and became very common in the 20th century. Latin entries write it Eva. It has no saint of its own in the Roman calendar.

ewald.label: Ewald
ewald.text: A Germanic name, Ewald is found in Germany and in German-speaking Poland; it became more frequent in the 19th century. It honours the two Saints Ewald, Anglo-Saxon missionaries martyred in Saxony in the late 7th century.

ezio.label: Ezio
ezio.meaning: Italian form of the Roman name "Aetius", perhaps from Greek "aetos", "eagle".
ezio.text: An Italian name inspired by antiquity, Ezio spread mainly in the late 19th and 20th centuries. It is rare in earlier records. It has no saint of its own.

fabian.label: Fabian
fabian.meaning: From Latin "Fabianus", derived from the Roman family name "Fabius", itself linked to "faba", "bean".
fabian.text: The Polish, German and Spanish form of Fabian, it appears in Catholic records from those countries, often linked to the feast of Saints Fabian and Sebastian. It became more common in the 20th century. It honours Saint Fabian, pope and martyr.

fabien.label: Fabien
fabien.meaning: From Latin "Fabianus", derived from "Fabius", a Roman family name.
fabien.text: Saint Fabian, a martyred pope, is celebrated on 20 January. The name appears under the Ancien Régime and became very popular again in France in the 1970s and 1980s.

fabienne.label: Fabienne
fabienne.meaning: Feminine of Fabien, from Latin "Fabius", a Roman family name.
fabienne.text: Rare before the 20th century, this name was mostly given in France in the 1960s.

fabio.label: Fabio
fabio.meaning: From the Roman family name "Fabius", linked to Latin "faba", "bean".
fabio.text: An Italian name inspired by antiquity, Fabio has been used in Italy since the Renaissance and became very common in the 20th century. It is a name distinct from Fabiano (Fabian). It has no well-established saint of its own.

fabrice.label: Fabrice
fabrice.meaning: From Latin "Fabricius", a Roman family name linked to "faber", "craftsman".
fabrice.text: Rare in older registers, this name became very popular in France in the 1960s and 1970s.

fabrizio.label: Fabrizio
fabrizio.meaning: From the Roman family name "Fabricius", linked to Latin "faber", "craftsman".
fabrizio.text: An Italian name inspired by antiquity, Fabrizio has been used in Italy since the Renaissance, mainly among the nobility, and became common in the 20th century. The French form is Fabrice. It has no well-established saint of its own.

fajwel.label: Fajwel
fajwel.meaning: Disputed: from Latin Phoebus or Vivus.
fajwel.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Fayvl, common in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. German records write Feiwel.

fatima.label: Fatima
fatima.meaning: From Arabic "Fâtima", "one who weans", the name of the daughter of the prophet of Islam.
fatima.text: In the Iberian countries, Fátima (Fatima) is a Christian Marian name given in honour of the apparitions of Our Lady of Fátima (1917), widespread in Portugal and Spain from the 1930s. It is also very common in the Muslim world. In Iberian usage its name day is the feast of Our Lady of Fátima.

fausta.label: Fausta
fausta.meaning: Feminine of Faustus, from Latin "faustus", "favourable, fortunate".
fausta.text: An Italian name of Latin inspiration, Fausta appears in Italian records without being frequent, mainly in the 19th century. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

faustina.label: Faustina
faustina.meaning: Feminine of Faustinus, derived from Latin "faustus", "favourable, fortunate".
faustina.text: An Italian and Spanish name, Faustina appears in records from those countries, mainly in the 19th century. Saint Faustina Kowalska, a Polish nun canonised in 2000, could not have influenced names given before the 20th century. It has no long-established feast.

faustino.label: Faustino
faustino.text: A Spanish, Portuguese and Italian name, Faustino appears in records from those countries, mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It honours Saint Faustinus, a martyr of Brescia celebrated with his brother Saint Jovita.

fausto.label: Fausto
fausto.text: An Italian, Portuguese and Spanish name of Latin inspiration, Fausto appears in records from those countries mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

federico.label: Federico
federico.meaning: Italian and Spanish form of Frederick, from Germanic "frid", "peace", and "ric", "powerful".
federico.text: The Italian and Spanish form of Frederick, Federico has been used since the Middle Ages, notably by the Hohenstaufen emperors, and became common in the 19th century. The older form Federigo is found in Tuscany. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frederick, bishop of Utrecht, martyred in the 9th century.

feiga.label: Feiga
feiga.text: A female name of the Jewish communities of Central and Eastern Europe. Polish registers write Fajga, others Faiga or Feige.

felice.label: Felice
felice.text: In Italian, Felice is mainly the masculine form of Felix, common in Italian and Ticino records; it is also, more rarely, given to women, and in English Felice is a female name. The sex should therefore be checked in the record. No single name day covers both uses.

felicie.label: Félicie
felicie.text: A French name mainly of the 19th century, Félicie (Felicie) is found in France and Belgium. It is sometimes confused with Félicité in the records. It has no well-established saint of its own.

felicien.label: Félicien
felicien.text: A rare name, Félicien (Felicien) is found in France and Belgium, mainly in the 19th century. Latin entries write it Felicianus. It has no saint with a well-established cult in France.

felicita.label: Felicita
felicita.text: The Italian form of Félicité, Felicita (Felicità) appears in Italian and Spanish records, mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It honours Saint Felicity, a martyr of Carthage celebrated with Saint Perpetua.

felicitas.label: Felicitas
felicitas.text: The Latin and German form of Felicity, Felicitas appears in Catholic records from Germany, Belgium and Spain. In Latin records it may render Félicité or Félicie. It honours Saint Felicity, a martyr of Carthage celebrated with Saint Perpetua.

felicite.label: Félicité
felicite.text: A French name mainly of the 18th and 19th centuries, Félicité (Felicite) is found in France and Belgium. Latin entries write it Felicitas. It honours Saint Felicity, a martyr of Carthage celebrated with Saint Perpetua.

felicja.label: Felicja
felicja.meaning: Polish form of Felicia, feminine of Felix, from Latin "felix", "happy".
felicja.text: The Polish feminine of Feliks, Felicja is found in Polish records, mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Latin entries write it Felicia or Felicitas. It has no well-established saint of its own.

feliks.label: Feliks
feliks.meaning: Polish form of Felix, from Latin "felix", "happy, fruitful".
feliks.text: The Polish form of Felix, Feliks appears in Polish records from the Middle Ages; Latin entries write it Felix. Several saints bear the name; the feast given is that of Saint Felix of Nola, a priest of Campania.

felipa.label: Felipa
felipa.meaning: Feminine of Felipe, from Greek "Philippos", "lover of horses".
felipa.text: The Spanish feminine of Felipe, Felipa is found in Spanish records, mainly in the early modern period and the 19th century. It has no well-established saint of its own.

felipe.label: Felipe
felipe.meaning: Spanish form of Philip, from Greek "Philippos", "lover of horses".
felipe.text: The name of several kings of Spain, Felipe has been common in Spanish and Portuguese records since the 16th century; Catalan says Felip and Latin entries write Philippus. It honours Saint Philip the Apostle, celebrated with Saint James the Less.

felisa.label: Felisa
felisa.meaning: Spanish form of Felicia, feminine of Felix, from Latin "felix", "happy".
felisa.text: The Spanish feminine of Felix, Felisa is found mainly in Spanish records of the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no well-established saint of its own.

felix.label: Félix
felix.text: A name used throughout Catholic Europe, Félix (Felix) is common in France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Spain, Switzerland and Germany, especially in the 19th century. Several saints bear the name; the feast given is that of Saint Felix of Nola, a priest of Campania.

fenna.label: Fenna
fenna.meaning: A Frisian name, feminine of Fenne or Feen; meaning uncertain.
fenna.text: A typically Frisian name, Fenna is found mainly in records from Friesland and Groningen from the 17th to the 19th century. It has no saint of its own.

ferdinand.label: Ferdinand
ferdinand.meaning: Germanic, probably from "fard", "journey", and "nand", "daring"; the etymology is disputed.
ferdinand.text: A name brought to Central Europe by the Habsburgs of Spanish origin, Ferdinand is common in Germany, Austria, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland, especially from the 17th century. Latin entries write it Ferdinandus. It honours Saint Ferdinand III, king of Castile.

ferdinanda.label: Ferdinanda
ferdinanda.meaning: Feminine of Ferdinand, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
ferdinanda.text: The Italian feminine of Ferdinando, Ferdinanda appears in Italian records without being frequent, mainly in the 19th century. It has no saint of its own.

ferdinando.label: Ferdinando
ferdinando.meaning: Italian form of Ferdinand, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
ferdinando.text: The Italian form of Ferdinand, Ferdinando was borne notably by the Medici and the Bourbons of Naples, and appears in Italian and Ticino records. Everyday usage shortens it to Nando. It honours Saint Ferdinand III, king of Castile.

ferdinandus.label: Ferdinandus
ferdinandus.meaning: Latin form of Ferdinand, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
ferdinandus.text: The Latin form of Ferdinand, Ferdinandus appears mainly in Latin-language records from Belgium and the Netherlands. It should be read as Ferdinand according to the family's language. It honours Saint Ferdinand III, king of Castile.

fermin.label: Fermín
fermin.text: Mainly a Navarrese and Basque name, Fermín (Fermin) is linked to the cult of Saint Firmin, by tradition the first bishop of Amiens, a native of Pamplona and patron of Navarre. Catalan says Fermí. In Pamplona his feast is kept on 7 July (the San Fermín festival).

fernand.label: Fernand
fernand.meaning: French form of Ferdinand, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
fernand.text: The French form of Ferdinand, Fernand became very common in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is rare before the Revolution. Its name day is the feast of Saint Ferdinand III, king of Castile.

fernanda.label: Fernanda
fernanda.meaning: Feminine of Fernando, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
fernanda.text: The Portuguese, Spanish and Italian feminine of Fernando, Fernanda is found mainly in records from Portugal, Spain and Italy in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

fernande.label: Fernande
fernande.meaning: Feminine of Fernand, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
fernande.text: The French feminine of Fernand, Fernande was mostly common in France and Belgium between the 1890s and 1930s. It is rare before then. It has no saint of its own.

fernando.label: Fernando
fernando.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Ferdinand, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
fernando.text: The name of several kings of Castile, Aragon and Portugal, Fernando has been very common in Spanish and Portuguese records since the Middle Ages; the older forms Hernando and Fernán also occur. It honours Saint Ferdinand III, king of Castile.

fernao.label: Fernão
fernao.meaning: Old Portuguese form of Ferdinand, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
fernao.text: A medieval and early modern Portuguese form of Fernando, Fernão (Fernao) is found mainly in Portuguese records from the 15th to the 18th century, before being replaced by Fernando. It honours Saint Ferdinand III, king of Castile.

ferran.label: Ferran
ferran.meaning: Catalan form of Ferdinand, of Germanic origin; the etymology is disputed.
ferran.text: The Catalan form of Ferdinand, Ferran appears in Catalan records; Castilian entries write it Fernando and Latin ones Ferdinandus. It honours Saint Ferdinand III, king of Castile.

ferreol.label: Ferréol
ferreol.text: Saint Ferreolus, a martyr of Vienne, is celebrated on 18 September. The name is found mostly in Dauphiné, the Lyonnais and Auvergne.

ferruccio.label: Ferruccio
ferruccio.meaning: Italian diminutive of Ferro, from Latin "ferrum", "iron"; sometimes linked to Ferdinando.
ferruccio.text: An Italian name, Ferruccio spread mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is rare in older records. It has no well-established saint of its own.

fiacre.label: Fiacre
fiacre.text: Saint Fiacre, a 7th-century Irish hermit settled near Meaux and patron of gardeners, is celebrated on 30 August. The name is found mostly in Brie and Île-de-France under the Ancien Régime.

fidel.label: Fidel
fidel.text: A Spanish and German name, Fidel appears in records from those countries, mainly from the 18th century; the German form is also Fidelis. It honours Saint Fidelis of Sigmaringen, a Capuchin martyred in Switzerland in 1622.

fidela.label: Fidela
fidela.text: The Spanish feminine of Fidel, Fidela is found in Spanish records, mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

filip.label: Filip
filip.text: The Polish, Dutch, German and Scandinavian form of Philip, Filip appears in records from Poland, Flemish Belgium and Germany. Latin entries write it Philippus. It honours Saint Philip the Apostle.

filipe.label: Filipe
filipe.text: The Portuguese form of Philip, Filipe (formerly Filippe or Phelippe) is common in Portuguese records, notably since the union of the crowns under the Philips (1580-1640). It honours Saint Philip the Apostle.

filippo.label: Filippo
filippo.text: The Italian form of Philip, Filippo has been common in Italian and Ticino records since the Middle Ages, often shortened to Pippo. It honours Saint Philip the Apostle; Saint Philip Neri, celebrated on 26 May, is also very popular in Italy.

filomena.label: Filomena
filomena.text: A name widespread in the 19th century in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Poland, Filomena owes its popularity to the cult of Saint Philomena, whose presumed relics were found in Rome in 1802 and venerated at Mugnano. Her cult was removed from the calendar in 1961. Her traditional feast was on 11 August.

firmin.label: Firmin
firmin.text: Mainly a Picard name, Firmin was much used around Amiens and in northern France, as well as in Belgium and French-speaking Switzerland. Latin entries write it Firminus. It honours Saint Firmin, martyr, by tradition first bishop of Amiens and the city's patron saint.

fiszel.label: Fiszel
fiszel.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Fishl, "little fish", common in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. German records write Fischel.

fleurie.label: Fleurie
fleurie.text: A rare name formed on the word "fleur", comparable to Flore. It appears occasionally in French registers.

flora.label: Flora
flora.meaning: From Latin "flos, floris", "flower", the name of the Roman goddess of flowers.
flora.text: A name used throughout Europe, Flora is common in Italy, Spain, Germany, Poland and Scotland, where it also renders Gaelic Fionnghal. It spread mainly in the 19th century. It honours Saint Flora, a 9th-century martyr of Córdoba.

flore.label: Flore
flore.text: The French form of Flora, Flore is found in France and Belgium, mainly in the 19th century. Latin entries write it Flora. It honours Saint Flora, a 9th-century martyr of Córdoba.

florence.label: Florence
florence.text: In France, Florence is a female name used from the Middle Ages but rare until the 20th century; in England and the United States it spread in the second half of the 19th century in honour of Florence Nightingale. In older English records it may also designate a man. It has no saint with a widely established cult.

florencio.label: Florencio
florencio.text: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Florent, Florencio appears in records from those countries, mainly in the 19th century; Catalan says Florenci. Several saints bear the name, with no dominant cult.

florent.label: Florent
florent.text: An old name, Florent has been found in France and Belgium since the Middle Ages; Latin entries write it Florentius, and it should not be confused with Florian or Florentin. It became common mainly in the late 20th century. Several saints bear the name, with no dominant cult.

florentin.label: Florentin
florentin.text: A rare name, Florentin is found in France, Switzerland and Belgium, mainly in the 19th century. Latin entries write it Florentinus. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

florentina.label: Florentina
florentina.meaning: Feminine of Florentinus, derived from Latin "florens", "flourishing".
florentina.text: A Spanish, Belgian and Polish name, Florentina appears in records from those countries, mainly in the 19th century; Polish writes it Florentyna. Saint Florentina of Cartagena, sister of Isidore of Seville, is venerated in Spain, but her cult remains local.

florentine.label: Florentine
florentine.meaning: Feminine of Florentin, derived from Latin "florens", "flourishing".
florentine.text: A rare name, Florentine is found in France, Germany and Poland, mainly in the 19th century. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

florentino.label: Florentino
florentino.text: The Spanish form of Florentin, Florentino appears in Spanish records, mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

floyd.label: Floyd
floyd.meaning: An English variant of Welsh "Lloyd", from "llwyd", "grey".
floyd.text: A surname of Welsh origin turned given name, Floyd spread mainly in the United States between the 1880s and 1930s. It is rare in Europe. It has no saint of its own.

fortunata.label: Fortunata
fortunata.text: An Italian name, Fortunata appears in Italian records, mainly in the South and in the 19th century. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

fortunato.label: Fortunato
fortunato.text: A Portuguese, Italian and Spanish name, Fortunato appears in records from those countries, mainly in the 19th century; Latin entries write it Fortunatus. Several saints bear the name, with no dominant cult.

fortune.label: Fortuné
fortune.text: The French form of Fortunatus, Fortuné (Fortune) is found in France, mainly in the South and in the 19th century. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

fortunee.label: Fortunée
fortunee.text: A name found mostly in southern France in the 19th century and in the Jewish communities of North Africa. It is distinct from the Italian Fortunata.

foy.label: Foy
foy.text: Saint Faith, a martyr of Agen whose relics are venerated at Conques, is celebrated on 6 October. The name is found mostly in south-western France.

frajda.label: Frajda
frajda.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Freyde, with the diminutive Frejdla, frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century.

france.label: France
france.meaning: From the name of the country, itself derived from the Germanic people of the Franks; sometimes a short form of Françoise.
france.text: Mostly a female name, France spread in France in the 19th and early 20th centuries, sometimes as a short form of Françoise; it was also given to some men. It is rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

frances.label: Frances
frances.meaning: English feminine of Francis, from Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman", itself from the name of the Franks.
frances.text: The English form of Françoise, Frances has been common in England since the 16th century and widespread in the 19th and 20th centuries in Britain, Ireland and the United States; its diminutives Fanny and Fran are frequent. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frances of Rome, a 15th-century Roman foundress.

francesc.label: Francesc
francesc.meaning: Catalan form of Francis, from Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
francesc.text: The Catalan form of Francis, Francesc (Francesch in older records) is very common in Catalan records; the diminutives Cesc and Xesc are frequent. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi.

francesca.label: Francesca
francesca.text: The Italian form of Frances, Francesca has been one of the most common female names in Italy since the late Middle Ages, often shortened to Checca or Franca. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frances of Rome, a 15th-century Roman foundress.

francesco.label: Francesco
francesco.meaning: Italian form of Francis, from Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
francesco.text: The name of the saint of Assisi, Francesco has been one of the most frequent male names in Italy since the 13th century, shortened to Cecco, Checco or Franco. Latin entries write it Franciscus. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi.

francina.label: Francina
francina.meaning: Dutch form of Frances, from Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
francina.text: The Dutch form of Frances, Francina (also Fransina, Frankje) appears in records from the Netherlands from the 17th to the 19th century. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frances of Rome.

francine.label: Francine
francine.text: A diminutive of Françoise, Francine is found in France before the Revolution but became common mainly between the 1930s and 1960s. The same woman may appear as Françoise and as Francine in different records. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frances of Rome.

francis.label: Francis
francis.meaning: English form of François, from Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
francis.text: The English form of the name, Francis is common in England, Ireland and the United States, especially in Catholic families; in France it spread in the 20th century. Latin entries write it Franciscus. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi.

francisca.label: Francisca
