francisca.text: The Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch and Latin form of Frances, Francisca is one of the most common female names in Spanish and Portuguese records; the diminutives Paca, Paquita, Pancha and Curra are frequent. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frances of Rome.

francisca_de_assis.label: Francisca de Assis
francisca_de_assis.meaning: A Portuguese compound name formed from Francisca, from Latin "Franciscus", and the name of Assisi, home of Saint Francis.
francisca_de_assis.text: A Portuguese compound name, Francisca de Assis was given in direct honour of Saint Francis of Assisi, like its male counterpart Francisco de Assis; it is found in Portugal and Brazil. In indexes it may be reduced to Francisca. Its name day is the feast of Saint Francis of Assisi, whom it explicitly names.

francisco.label: Francisco
francisco.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Francis, from Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
francisco.text: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Francis, Francisco has been one of the most frequent male names in Iberian records since the 16th century, often in compounds (Francisco Javier, Francisco de Paula). The diminutives Paco, Pancho, Curro and Chico are common. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi.

francisco_javier.label: Francisco Javier
francisco_javier.meaning: A Spanish compound name: Francisco, from Latin "Franciscus", and Javier, from Basque "etxe berri", "new house", the name of the saint's native castle.
francisco_javier.text: A very common compound name in Spain, Francisco Javier (Francesc Xavier in Catalan) is given in honour of Saint Francis Xavier, a Jesuit missionary born at the castle of Javier in Navarre. In indexes it may be reduced to Francisco or Javier. Its name day is the feast of Saint Francis Xavier.

franciscus.label: Franciscus
franciscus.meaning: Latin form of Francis, from medieval Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
franciscus.text: The Latin form of Francis, Franciscus is very frequent in Latin-language records from Belgium, the Netherlands, France and Germany, and was used as an everyday name in the Netherlands and Flanders, where people said Frans. It should be read according to the family's language. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi.

francisque.label: Francisque
francisque.meaning: A Latinising French form of François, from Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
francisque.text: A variant of François, Francisque is found mainly around Lyon and in east-central France in the 19th century. The same man may be entered as François in other records. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi.

franciszek.label: Franciszek
franciszek.meaning: Polish form of Francis, from Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
franciszek.text: The Polish form of Francis, Franciszek is very common in Polish records, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries; Latin entries write it Franciscus. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi.

franciszka.label: Franciszka
franciszka.text: The Polish form of Frances, Franciszka appears in Polish records, mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries; Latin entries write it Francisca. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frances of Rome.

franck.label: Franck
franck.meaning: From Germanic "frank", the name of the Franks, "free".
franck.text: The French spelling of Frank, Franck spread in France mainly in the second half of the 20th century. It is rare in older records, where it survives mostly as a surname. It has no saint of its own.

franco.label: Franco
franco.meaning: From Germanic "frank", "Frank, free", often used as a short form of Francesco.
franco.text: An Italian name, Franco is both an old Germanic name and the short form of Francesco; it spread mainly in the 20th century. In the records, a Franco may have been baptised Francesco. Its name day is traditionally that of Saint Francis of Assisi.

francois.label: François
francois.meaning: From medieval Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman", itself from the name of the Franks.
francois.text: A very common name in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland since the 16th century, François (Francois) is also spelt Françoys or Francoys in older records; Latin entries write it Franciscus. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi; Saint Francis de Sales, celebrated on 24 January, is also popular in Savoy.

francoise.label: Françoise
francoise.meaning: Feminine of François, from medieval Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
francoise.text: A very common female name in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland since the 16th century, Françoise (Francoise) is often latinised as Francisca; Breton says Soizic. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frances of Rome, a 15th-century Roman foundress.

frank.label: Frank
frank.meaning: From Germanic "frank", the name of the Franks, "free"; also a short form of Francis or Franklin.
frank.text: A Germanic name and a short form of Francis or Franz, Frank is common in the United States, Britain, Germany and Switzerland, especially in the late 19th and 20th centuries. In the records a Frank may have been baptised Francis, Franz or Franciscus. It has no saint of its own.

franklin.label: Franklin
franklin.meaning: From Middle English "frankeleyn", "freeholder", of Anglo-Norman origin; unrelated to Francis.
franklin.text: An English surname turned given name, Franklin spread mainly in the United States from the 18th century, in honour of Benjamin Franklin, and again in the 20th century. It is not a form of Francis, despite frequent associations. It has no saint of its own.

frans.label: Frans
frans.meaning: Dutch form of Francis, from Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
frans.text: The Dutch form of Francis, Frans has been very common in the Netherlands and Flanders since the 16th century; Latin entries write it Franciscus, and the same man may appear under both forms. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi.

franz.label: Franz
franz.meaning: German form of Francis, from Latin "Franciscus", "Frenchman".
franz.text: The German form of Francis, Franz is very common in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Luxembourg, especially in Catholic regions, notably in compounds (Franz Xaver, Franz Josef). Latin entries write it Franciscus. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi.

franziska.label: Franziska
franziska.text: The German form of Frances, Franziska appears in Catholic records from Germany, Austria and Switzerland, shortened to Fanny or Franzi. Latin entries write it Francisca. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frances of Rome.

freda.label: Freda
freda.meaning: Short form of Frederica or Winifred, or from Germanic "frid", "peace".
freda.text: An English name of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Freda is found mainly in Britain and the United States. It is rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

frederic.label: Frédéric
frederic.text: A name of Germanic origin, Frédéric (Frederic) is rare in France before the Revolution, except in Alsace and among Protestants, then became common in the 19th century in France, Switzerland and Belgium. Latin entries write it Fridericus. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frederick, bishop of Utrecht, martyred in the 9th century.

frederick.label: Frederick
frederick.meaning: English form of Frederick, from Germanic "frid", "peace", and "ric", "powerful".
frederick.text: Introduced into England mainly with the House of Hanover, Frederick became very common in Britain and the United States in the 19th century, shortened to Fred or Freddie. It is also found in families of German origin. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frederick, bishop of Utrecht.

frederico.label: Frederico
frederico.meaning: Portuguese form of Frederick, from Germanic "frid", "peace", and "ric", "powerful".
frederico.text: The Portuguese form of Frederick, Frederico appears in Portuguese records mainly from the 19th century; it is rare before then. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frederick, bishop of Utrecht, martyred in the 9th century.

frederik.label: Frederik
frederik.meaning: Dutch and Scandinavian form of Frederick, from Germanic "frid", "peace", and "ric", "powerful".
frederik.text: The Dutch, Flemish and Danish form of Frederick, Frederik is common in the Netherlands and Belgium, shortened to Frits, Freek or Frerik; the Frisian form is Freerk. Latin entries write it Fredericus. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frederick, bishop of Utrecht.

frederika.label: Frederika
frederika.meaning: Feminine of Frederik, from Germanic "frid", "peace", and "ric", "powerful".
frederika.text: The Dutch and German feminine of Frederick, Frederika (also Frederica, Fredrika) is found in the Netherlands and Germany, mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

frederique.label: Frédérique
frederique.meaning: Feminine of Frédéric, from Germanic "frid", "peace", and "ric", "powerful".
frederique.text: The French feminine of Frédéric, Frédérique (Frederique) is found in France and Belgium, rarely before the 19th century, and became common mainly in the mid-20th century. It has no saint of its own.

frida.label: Frida
frida.meaning: From Germanic "frid", "peace", often a short form of Frederika or Elfriede.
frida.text: A Germanic and Scandinavian name, Frida is found in Germany, Switzerland and Poland, mainly in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. In the records it may be the short form of a longer name (Friederike, Elfriede). It has no saint of its own.

fridolin.label: Fridolin
fridolin.text: A name characteristic of south-western Germany and Switzerland, particularly the canton of Glarus, whose patron saint he is, Fridolin is frequent in Catholic records from those regions. Latin entries write it Fridolinus. It honours Saint Fridolin, a missionary who founded Säckingen Abbey.

frieda.label: Frieda
frieda.meaning: From Germanic "frid", "peace", often a short form of Friederike or Elfriede.
frieda.text: A German name of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Frieda was very common in Germany and Switzerland and is also found in the United States in families of German origin. In the records it may be the short form of Friederike. It has no saint of its own.

friederike.label: Friederike
friederike.meaning: Feminine of Friedrich, from Germanic "frid", "peace", and "ric", "powerful".
friederike.text: The German feminine of Friedrich, Friederike was very common in Germany, especially in Prussia and the Protestant North, in the 18th and 19th centuries; the short forms Rike, Frieda and Fritzi are frequent. It has no saint of its own.

friedrich.label: Friedrich
friedrich.text: The name of emperors and kings of Prussia, Friedrich is one of the most common male names in Germany, German-speaking Switzerland and Luxembourg, shortened to Fritz. Latin entries write it Fridericus. Its name day is the feast of Saint Frederick, bishop of Utrecht, martyred in the 9th century.

froim.label: Froim
froim.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Froyim, Joseph's son in the Bible, common in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. French or German records write Ephraim.

frymet.label: Frymet
frymet.text: A female Yiddish name written Frymet or Frumet in 19th-century Polish records; Fruma is a closely related form.

fulgence.label: Fulgence
fulgence.text: Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa in the 6th century, is celebrated on 1 January. The name is uncommon; records also spell it Fulgance or Fulgent.

fulvia.label: Fulvia
fulvia.meaning: From the Roman family name "Fulvius", linked to Latin "fulvus", "tawny, reddish-yellow".
fulvia.text: An Italian name inspired by antiquity, Fulvia has appeared in Italian records since the Renaissance without being frequent, and more often in the 20th century. It has no saint of its own.

gabriel.label: Gabriel
gabriel.text: The name of the archangel of the Annunciation, Gabriel was used throughout Catholic Europe, in France, Spain, Portugal, Switzerland and Belgium; Latin entries write it Gabriel, or Gabrielis in the genitive. It honours the archangel Saint Gabriel, celebrated together with the archangels Michael and Raphael.

gabriela.label: Gabriela
gabriela.meaning: Feminine of Gabriel, from Hebrew "Gavri'el", "God is my strength".
gabriela.text: The Portuguese, Spanish, Polish and German form of Gabrielle, Gabriela spread mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no well-established saint of its own.

gabriele.label: Gabriele
gabriele.text: In Italian, Gabriele is the masculine form of Gabriel; in German, by contrast, Gabriele is a female name, very common in the mid-20th century. The sex must therefore be read from the language and context of the record. No single name day covers both uses.

gabriella.label: Gabriella
gabriella.meaning: Feminine of Gabriel, from Hebrew "Gavri'el", "God is my strength".
gabriella.text: The Italian form of Gabrielle, Gabriella appears in Italian and Belgian records, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no well-established saint of its own.

gabrielle.label: Gabrielle
gabrielle.meaning: Feminine of Gabriel, from Hebrew "Gavri'el", "God is my strength".
gabrielle.text: The feminine of Gabriel, Gabrielle is found in France from the 16th century (Gabrielle d'Estrées) and became more common in the 19th and early 20th centuries, in France and Belgium. It has no well-established saint of its own.

gael.label: Gaël
gael.meaning: Linked to the name of the Gaels, Celtic peoples of Ireland and Scotland; disputed meaning.
gael.text: A modern name with a Breton look, widely given in France from the 1970s. It is absent from older registers.

gaelle.label: Gaëlle
gaelle.meaning: Feminine of Gaël, linked to the name of the Gaels; disputed meaning.
gaelle.text: A modern name, widely given in France in the 1970s and 1980s. It is absent from older registers.

gaetan.label: Gaëtan
gaetan.meaning: From Latin "Caietanus", "from Gaeta", a town in Italy.
gaetan.text: The French form of Gaetano, Gaétan (Gaetan) is rare in France before the 19th century and became more common in the 20th century, in France as in Quebec. It honours Saint Cajetan of Thiene, founder of the Theatines.

gaetano.label: Gaetano
gaetano.meaning: From Latin "Caietanus", "from Gaeta", a town in Italy.
gaetano.text: A widespread Italian name, especially in the South (Naples, Sicily), Gaetano is also found in Ticino; Latin entries write it Caietanus. It honours Saint Cajetan of Thiene, founder of the Theatines, much venerated in Naples.

gall.label: Gall
gall.meaning: From Latin "Gallus", the Irish saint's name; disputed meaning.
gall.text: Saint Gall, a companion of Saint Columbanus, founded the hermitage that became St. Gallen and is celebrated on 16 October. The name is used in eastern Switzerland and southern Germany; Latin registers write Gallus.

gary.label: Gary
gary.meaning: From an English surname, probably from Germanic "gar", "spear".
gary.text: A surname turned given name, Gary spread mainly in the United States and Britain in the mid-20th century. It is absent from older records. It has no saint of its own.

gaspar.label: Gaspar
gaspar.meaning: The traditional name of one of the Three Kings, perhaps from Persian "ganzabara", "treasurer"; the etymology is disputed.
gaspar.text: A Spanish, Portuguese and Dutch name, Gaspar appears in records from those countries from the late Middle Ages, linked to the cult of the Three Kings. Latin entries write it Caspar or Gaspar. Its name day is the Epiphany, which celebrates the Three Kings.

gaspard.label: Gaspard
gaspard.meaning: The traditional name of one of the Three Kings, perhaps from Persian "ganzabara", "treasurer"; the etymology is disputed.
gaspard.text: The French form of Caspar, Gaspard has been used in France, Switzerland, Belgium and Luxembourg since the late Middle Ages, linked to the cult of the Three Kings, without being very frequent. Latin entries write it Gaspardus or Caspar. Its name day is the Epiphany, which celebrates the Three Kings.

gasparde.label: Gasparde
gasparde.meaning: Feminine of Gaspard, the traditional name of one of the Magi; disputed origin.
gasparde.text: A feminine form of Gaspard, found in French registers of the 16th–18th centuries.

gaspare.label: Gaspare
gaspare.meaning: The traditional name of one of the Three Kings, perhaps from Persian "ganzabara", "treasurer"; the etymology is disputed.
gaspare.text: The Italian form of Caspar, Gaspare appears in Italian and Ticino records from the late Middle Ages, linked to the cult of the Three Kings. Its name day is the Epiphany, which celebrates the Three Kings.

gaston.label: Gaston
gaston.meaning: Of disputed origin: perhaps from "Gascon", or derived from Vaast (Latin "Vedastus"), of which it would be a popular form.
gaston.text: A name borne by the counts of Foix-Béarn in the Middle Ages, Gaston became very common in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its name day is the feast of Saint Vedast, bishop of Arras, of whose name Gaston is traditionally considered a form.

gatien.label: Gatien
gatien.text: Saint Gatian, first bishop of Tours, is celebrated on 18 December. The name is characteristic of Touraine.

gautier.label: Gautier
gautier.text: The French equivalent of Walter, widely used in the Middle Ages before becoming mostly a surname. Saint Walter of Pontoise is celebrated on 8 April; records also spell it Gauthier or Gaultier.

gebhard.label: Gebhard
gebhard.text: Saint Gebhard, bishop of Constance in the 10th century, is celebrated on 27 August. The name is common around Lake Constance, in Vorarlberg and eastern Switzerland; records also write Gebhart.

geertruid.label: Geertruid
geertruid.meaning: Dutch form of Gertrude, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "trud", "strength".
geertruid.text: The Dutch form of Gertrude, Geertruid (also Geertruy, Geertrui) is common in records from the Netherlands from the 16th to the 19th century, often shortened to Geertje or Truus. It honours Saint Gertrude of Nivelles, a Brabant abbess much venerated in the Low Countries.

geertruida.label: Geertruida
geertruida.meaning: Dutch form of Gertrude, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "trud", "strength".
geertruida.text: A Latinising Dutch form of Gertrude, Geertruida is very common in records from the Netherlands in the 18th and 19th centuries, with many variants (Geertruyda, Gertruida) and the diminutives Geertje, Truida or Truus. It honours Saint Gertrude of Nivelles, a Brabant abbess much venerated in the Low Countries.

geesje.label: Geesje
geesje.meaning: A Dutch diminutive, probably of Gesina or Geertruida; the etymology is uncertain.
geesje.text: A Dutch name typical of the north-eastern Netherlands, Geesje is found mainly in 18th- and 19th-century records. It has no saint of its own.

gema.label: Gema
gema.text: The Spanish form of Gemma, Gema spread in Spain mainly in the second half of the 20th century. It is absent from older records. Its name day is the feast of Saint Gemma Galgani, an Italian mystic canonised in 1940.

gemma.label: Gemma
gemma.text: An Italian name used since the Middle Ages (Gemma Donati, Dante's wife), Gemma spread mainly in the 20th century in Italy and Spain. Its name day is the feast of Saint Gemma Galgani, a mystic from Lucca canonised in 1940.

genara.label: Genara
genara.meaning: Spanish feminine of Genaro, from Latin "Januarius", "of January".
genara.text: A name found in Spanish and Spanish-American registers. It is the feminine form of Genaro.

gene.label: Gene
gene.meaning: English short form of Eugene, from Greek "Eugenios", "well-born".
gene.text: A short form of Eugene that became a given name, Gene spread mainly in the United States in the 20th century. In the records a Gene may have been registered as Eugene. It has no saint of its own.

genevieve.label: Geneviève
genevieve.meaning: Of disputed origin, probably Germanic or Celtic; meaning uncertain.
genevieve.text: The name of the patron saint of Paris, Geneviève (Genevieve) has been used in France since the Middle Ages, notably in the Île-de-France, and remained common until the 20th century. Latin entries write it Genovefa. It honours Saint Genevieve, patron saint of Paris.

gennaro.label: Gennaro
gennaro.meaning: From Latin "Ianuarius", "of January", itself linked to the god Janus.
gennaro.text: A typically Neapolitan name, Gennaro is very common in Campania and southern Italy; Latin entries write it Ianuarius or Januarius. It honours Saint Januarius (San Gennaro), martyred bishop of Benevento and patron of Naples.

genowefa.label: Genowefa
genowefa.meaning: Polish form of Genevieve, of disputed origin, probably Germanic or Celtic.
genowefa.text: The Polish form of Genevieve, Genowefa spread in Poland mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries, partly thanks to the popular legend of Genevieve of Brabant. Latin entries write it Genovefa. Its name day is the feast of Saint Genevieve, patron saint of Paris.

geoffrey.label: Geoffrey
geoffrey.meaning: Germanic, perhaps from "gawia", "territory", or "walah", "foreigner", and "frid", "peace"; the etymology is disputed.
geoffrey.text: Brought to England by the Normans (Geoffroy), Geoffrey has been used since the Middle Ages and had a revival in Britain in the 20th century; Jeffrey and Geoffry are also found. The French form is Geoffroy. It has no saint with a well-established cult.

georg.label: Georg
georg.meaning: From Greek "geôrgos", "farmer, one who works the land".
georg.text: The German form of George, Georg has been very common in Germany, Switzerland, Austria and Alsace since the late Middle Ages; the popular forms Jörg, Jürgen and Görg also occur. Latin entries write it Georgius. It honours Saint George, soldier and martyr.

george.label: George
george.meaning: From Greek "geôrgos", "farmer, one who works the land".
george.text: The name of England's patron saint and of several Hanoverian kings, George became one of the most common male names in Britain and the United States from the 18th century. Latin entries write it Georgius. It honours Saint George, soldier and martyr, patron saint of England.

georges.label: Georges
georges.meaning: From Greek "geôrgos", "farmer, one who works the land".
georges.text: Used in France since the Middle Ages, Georges remained moderately common before the Revolution, then became one of the most common names in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Latin entries write it Georgius. It honours Saint George, soldier and martyr.

georgette.label: Georgette
georgette.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Georges, from Greek "geôrgos", "farmer".
georgette.text: The French feminine of Georges, Georgette was mostly common in France and Belgium between the 1900s and 1930s. It is rare before then. It has no saint of its own.

georgia.label: Georgia
georgia.text: The English feminine of George, Georgia is found in the United States mainly in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is rare in older European records. It has no well-established saint of its own.

georgiana.label: Georgiana
georgiana.meaning: Latinised feminine of George, from Greek "geôrgos", "farmer".
georgiana.text: An English feminine formed on George, Georgiana was fashionable in Britain in the 18th and 19th centuries, notably among the aristocracy, then in the United States. Georgina is also found. It has no saint of its own.

georgina.label: Georgina
georgina.meaning: English feminine form of George, from Greek "geôrgos", "farmer, tiller of the soil".
georgina.text: A mainly British name that arose in the 18th century in the wake of the Hanoverian kings George and remained common in English records until the mid-20th century. It also appears in the Netherlands, Belgium and France, where Georgette or Georgine are the more usual forms.

gerald.label: Gerald
gerald.meaning: From Germanic "ger", "spear", and "wald", "rule": "one who rules by the spear".
gerald.text: A Norman name brought to England after 1066, it later became rare before returning to fashion in the 19th century; it was very common in the United States and Britain in the first half of the 20th century. Its old French form is Géraud, and Saint Gerald of Aurillac, whose feast is 13 October, is the usual patron.

geraldine.label: Geraldine
geraldine.meaning: Feminine of Gerald, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "wald", "rule".
geraldine.text: The name first referred to a woman of the Irish FitzGerald family and was popularised in the 16th century by the "fair Geraldine" of the poet Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey. It became a given name in the 19th century and was most frequent in the United States and Britain from the 1920s to the 1950s.

gerard.label: Gérard
gerard.text: A widespread medieval name in northern France, Belgium and the Netherlands, where it gives Geert and Gerrit; in France it had a strong revival in the 20th century. Old records also spell it Girard or Gérart, forms that produced many surnames. Its name day is 3 October, the feast of Saint Gerard of Brogne, a 10th-century abbot.

gerarda.label: Gerarda
gerarda.meaning: Feminine form of Gerard, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "hard", "strong".
gerarda.text: A mainly Dutch female name, found in records from the Netherlands from the 17th to the early 20th century and often shortened in everyday use. It appears alongside the variant Gerardina, with which it is practically interchangeable.

gerardina.label: Gerardina
gerardina.meaning: Feminine derivative of Gerard, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "hard", "strong".
gerardina.text: A Dutch form of Gerarda, frequent in records from the Netherlands in the 18th and 19th centuries. It is often shortened to Dina or Ardina, a short form worth linking to it when searching.

gerardo.label: Gerardo
gerardo.meaning: Spanish and Italian form of Gerard, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "hard", "strong".
gerardo.text: A name common in Italy, especially in the south, and in Spain, where the Galician spelling Xerardo also occurs. Its popularity in southern Italy owes much to Saint Gerard Majella, an 18th-century Redemptorist invoked by mothers, whose feast is 16 October.

gerardus.label: Gerardus
gerardus.meaning: Latin form of Gerard, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "hard", "strong".
gerardus.text: A Latinised form used in Catholic baptismal registers in the Netherlands and Belgium, and sometimes in 19th-century Dutch civil records. The same man often appears elsewhere as Gerard, Gerrit or Geert, or under the spelling Gerhardus.

gerda.label: Gerda
gerda.meaning: Of disputed meaning: linked to the Norse giantess Gerd ("enclosure, protection") or a short form of Gertrud.
gerda.text: A name in fashion in Germany and Scandinavia in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, helped by Andersen's tale "The Snow Queen", whose heroine is called Gerda. It also occurs in German-speaking families in Poland and the Netherlands.

gerhard.label: Gerhard
gerhard.meaning: German form of Gerard, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "hard", "strong".
gerhard.text: A German name used since the Middle Ages that became very popular again in the early 20th century, in Germany, German-speaking Switzerland and German-speaking families in Poland. Old records also spell it Gerhardt or Gerhardus, and the short form Gerd is frequent.

germain.label: Germain
germain.meaning: From Latin "Germanus", "brother" in the sense of "of the same stock", also understood as "German, inhabitant of Germania".
germain.text: An old French name, common in parish registers and still frequent among men born in the 19th century, in France, French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium. It honours Saint Germanus of Auxerre and above all Saint Germain of Paris, a 6th-century bishop whose feast is 28 May.

germaine.label: Germaine
germaine.meaning: Feminine of Germain, from Latin "Germanus", "brother, of the same stock".
germaine.text: A female name very widespread in France in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, among the most given to girls born before 1900; it also occurs in Belgium and French-speaking Switzerland. Its spread followed the canonisation in 1867 of Saint Germaine Cousin, the shepherdess of Pibrac, whose feast is 15 June.

german.label: Germán
german.meaning: Spanish form of Germain, from Latin "Germanus", "brother, of the same stock".
german.text: A Spanish name attested in records since the Middle Ages and still common in the 20th century; the Galician form is Xermán. It should not be confused with the German Hermann, which has a different origin, although the two are sometimes linked.

gerolamo.label: Gerolamo
gerolamo.meaning: Italian variant of Girolamo (Jerome), from Greek "hieros", "holy", and "onoma", "name".
gerolamo.text: An Italian spelling of Girolamo, frequent in northern Italian records in the 16th and 17th centuries and used interchangeably with it. The name honours Saint Jerome, Doctor of the Church and translator of the Bible into Latin, whose feast is 30 September.

gerrit.label: Gerrit
gerrit.meaning: Dutch and Frisian short form of Gerard, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "hard", "strong".
gerrit.text: A male name very widespread in the Netherlands from the 17th to the 20th century, especially in the eastern and northern provinces, and in neighbouring German areas. In Latin baptismal records the same man is often entered as Gerardus, and he may also appear as Geert.

gershon.label: Gershon
gershon.meaning: From Hebrew "Gershon", the name of Levi's eldest son; disputed meaning.
gershon.text: A biblical name used in Jewish communities across Europe. Records also spell it Gerson or Gershen.

gertrud.label: Gertrud
gertrud.meaning: From Germanic "ger", "spear", and "trud", "strength": "strength of the spear".
gertrud.text: A female name common in German-speaking lands since the Middle Ages, with many regional forms: Gertraud in Bavaria and Austria, Geertruid in the Netherlands, Gesche or Trude in familiar use. In German-speaking countries and Belgium it honours Saint Gertrude of Nivelles, a 7th-century abbess whose feast is 17 March.

gertruda.label: Gertruda
gertruda.meaning: Polish form of Gertrude, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "trud", "strength".
gertruda.text: A Polish and Czech form of Gertrude, well attested in Polish records of the 19th and 20th centuries, notably in Silesia and Pomerania. The most widely kept feast is that of Saint Gertrude the Great, a 13th-century German mystic, on 16 November, Saint Gertrude of Nivelles being celebrated on 17 March.

gertrude.label: Gertrude
gertrude.meaning: From Germanic "ger", "spear", and "trud", "strength": "strength of the spear".
gertrude.text: A name borne since the Middle Ages in France, Belgium and German-speaking lands, and very fashionable in Britain and the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Records also spell it Geertrude or Gertrudis, and it appears under the pet forms Gertie or Trudy. Its name day is 16 November, the feast of Saint Gertrude the Great, a 13th-century German mystic.

gertrudes.label: Gertrudes
gertrudes.meaning: Portuguese form of Gertrude, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "trud", "strength".
gertrudes.text: The Portuguese form of the name, uncommon but present in parish registers of Portugal and Brazil. It honours Saint Gertrude the Great, a 13th-century German mystic, whose feast is 16 November.

gertrudis.label: Gertrudis
gertrudis.meaning: Spanish and Latin form of Gertrude, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "trud", "strength".
gertrudis.text: The Spanish form of the name, and also the Latin form used in baptismal registers in Belgium and the Netherlands, where the same woman may appear elsewhere as Geertruida. In Spain its spread owes much to devotion to Saint Gertrude the Great, whose feast is 16 November.

gervais.label: Gervais
gervais.meaning: From Latin "Gervasius", of obscure origin, possibly Greek or Germanic.
gervais.text: An old French name found in parish registers, especially in Normandy and western France, and also a surname. It honours Saint Gervasius, a martyr of Milan paired with his brother Saint Protasius, both celebrated on 19 June.

gervaise.label: Gervaise
gervaise.text: A feminine form of Gervais, found in French registers under the Ancien Régime. In older records the spelling Gervaise sometimes also denotes a man, so the sex should be checked.

gesina.label: Gesina
gesina.meaning: Low German and Dutch form, generally considered a pet form of Gertrud, from Germanic "ger", "spear", and "trud", "strength".
gesina.text: A female name of the north-eastern Netherlands and northern Germany, frequent in records from Groningen, Drenthe and Overijssel in the 18th and 19th centuries. It often alternates with Gesine, Geesje or Gesche for the same person.

ghislain.label: Ghislain
ghislain.meaning: Probably from Germanic "gisil", "hostage, pledge", hence the disputed meaning "pledge, guarantor".
ghislain.text: A name typical of Belgium and northern France, linked to Saint Ghislain, a 7th-century hermit in Hainaut, where a town bears his name. Fairly rare before the 20th century, it has its name day on 10 October.

ghislaine.label: Ghislaine
ghislaine.meaning: Feminine of Ghislain, probably from Germanic "gisil", "hostage, pledge".
ghislaine.text: A mainly Belgian and French female name, rare before 1900 and widespread in the mid-20th century. It is also spelled Ghyslaine or Gislaine.

giacinta.label: Giacinta
giacinta.meaning: Italian feminine of Giacinto, from Greek "hyakinthos", the hyacinth flower.
giacinta.text: An Italian female name found in records from the 17th century, especially in Lazio and the south. Its name day is 30 January, the feast of Saint Hyacintha Mariscotti, a Franciscan nun of Viterbo.

giacinto.label: Giacinto
giacinto.meaning: Italian form of Hyacinth, from Greek "hyakinthos", the hyacinth flower.
giacinto.text: An Italian name common in records since the Counter-Reformation, notably in the south and in Piedmont. It chiefly honours Saint Hyacinth of Poland (Jacek), a 13th-century Dominican preacher whose feast is 17 August.

giacomo.label: Giacomo
giacomo.meaning: Italian form of James, from Hebrew "Ya'aqov", often interpreted as "he who holds the heel" or "may God protect".
giacomo.text: One of the most common male names in Italy and Ticino since the Middle Ages; old records also give Jacopo, Giacomino or the Latin form Jacobus. Its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint James the Greater.

giambattista.label: Giambattista
giambattista.meaning: Italian contraction of Giovanni Battista, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious", and Greek "baptistês", "one who baptises".
giambattista.text: A contracted form of Giovanni Battista, very frequent in Italy from the 16th to the 19th century, also written Gian Battista or Giovambattista depending on the record. Its name day is 24 June, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist.

gian.label: Gian
gian.meaning: Italian and Romansh short form of Giovanni, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
gian.text: A short form of Giovanni, mostly used in Italy in compound names (Gian Battista, Gian Domenico, Gian Maria) and as a name in its own right in Romansh-speaking Graubünden. Like Giovanni, its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

giancarlo.label: Giancarlo
giancarlo.meaning: Italian compound of Gian (John) and Carlo (Charles).
giancarlo.text: An Italian compound name, mostly given in the 20th century. It is found in Italy and Italian-speaking Switzerland.

gijsbert.label: Gijsbert
gijsbert.meaning: Dutch form of Gisbert, from Germanic "gisil", "hostage, pledge", and "berht", "bright, famous".
gijsbert.text: A typically Dutch male name, common in records from the provinces of Utrecht, Holland and Gelderland from the 17th to the 19th century. It is often shortened to Gijs and Latinised as Gijsbertus or Gisbertus in baptismal records.

gijsbertus.label: Gijsbertus
gijsbertus.meaning: Latinised form of Gijsbert, from Germanic "gisil", "hostage, pledge", and "berht", "bright, famous".
gijsbertus.text: The Latin form of Gijsbert, used in Catholic baptismal registers in the Netherlands and sometimes carried into 19th-century civil records. The same man may appear elsewhere as Gijsbert, Gisbertus or simply Gijs.

gilbert.label: Gilbert
gilbert.text: A name widespread in France and England since the Middle Ages, where it also gave many surnames; it returned to fashion in France in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The best-known saint is Saint Gilbert of Sempringham, the English founder of a religious order, whose feast is 4 February; the French calendar also honours Saint Gilbert of Neuffontaines in June.

gilberte.label: Gilberte
gilberte.meaning: Feminine of Gilbert, from Germanic "gisil", "hostage, pledge", and "berht", "bright".
gilberte.text: A French female name, rare in older records and mostly given in the late 19th and first half of the 20th century. It is often borne as a second given name or as Gilbertine.

gilda.label: Gilda
gilda.meaning: Of disputed origin: perhaps from Germanic "gild", "worth, offering", or a short form of names such as Ermenegilda.
gilda.text: An Italian name rare before the 19th century, popularised by Gilda, the heroine of Verdi's opera "Rigoletto" (1851). It then appears in Italy and in Italian emigrant communities, notably in the United States in the early 20th century.

gildas.label: Gildas
gildas.text: Saint Gildas the Wise, a 6th-century Briton monk settled at Rhuys, is celebrated on 29 January. The name is used in Brittany, where its Breton form is Gweltaz.

gilles.label: Gilles
gilles.meaning: From Latin "Aegidius", itself linked to Greek "aigis", "goatskin, aegis"; the meaning is disputed.
gilles.text: An old French name, frequent in records from the Middle Ages and the Ancien Régime, notably in Belgium, where the Gilles of the Binche carnival keep the name alive. In Latin records it appears as Aegidius or Egidius, which often surprises researchers. Its name day is 1 September, the feast of Saint Giles the Hermit.

gillette.label: Gillette
gillette.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Gilles, from Greek "aigis", "aegis".
gillette.text: A feminine form of Gilles, frequent in French registers from the 15th to the 17th century. Records also spell it Gilette.

gillian.label: Gillian
gillian.meaning: Medieval English form of Juliana, from Latin "Julius", the name of a Roman family.
gillian.text: An English name common in the Middle Ages, to the point that "Jill" was used familiarly for any young woman, then rare before a strong revival in Britain in the mid-20th century. It is also spelled Jillian or Gilian.

gillonne.label: Gillonne
gillonne.text: A feminine form of Gilles, found in French registers of the 16th and 17th centuries. Records also spell it Gilonne.

gina.label: Gina
gina.meaning: Short form of Italian names ending in "-gina", such as Luigina, Georgina or Regina, whose origin it shares.
gina.text: An Italian pet form that became a name in its own right in the 19th century, then spread to France and the United States in the 20th century. In the records the same woman may appear under the full form (Luigina, Regina) and under this pet form.

ginette.label: Ginette
ginette.meaning: French pet form, usually linked to Geneviève, sometimes to Virginie.
ginette.text: A 20th-century French female name, mostly given in the 1920s to 1940s and practically absent from older records. It was also very common in Quebec in the same period.

ginevra.label: Ginevra
ginevra.meaning: Italian form of Guinevere, from Welsh "Gwenhwyfar", often interpreted as "white, shining"; also associated with "ginepro", the juniper.
ginevra.text: An Italian name of literary tradition, taken from the queen of the Arthurian romances and attested since the Renaissance, notably in Florence. It remains uncommon in records before the 20th century.

gino.label: Gino
gino.meaning: Short form of Italian names ending in "-gino", such as Luigino or Giorgino, whose origin it shares.
gino.text: An Italian pet form that became a name in its own right in the late 19th century, common in Tuscany and northern Italy as well as among Italian emigrants. The same person may appear under the full name (Luigi, Giorgio) in other records.

gioacchino.label: Gioacchino
gioacchino.meaning: Italian form of Joachim, from Hebrew "Yehoyaqim", "God raises up" or "God establishes".
gioacchino.text: An Italian name common in records, especially in the south and Sicily, sometimes spelled Gioachino or shortened to Nino. It honours Saint Joachim, father of the Virgin Mary, celebrated with Saint Anne on 26 July.

giorgio.label: Giorgio
giorgio.meaning: Italian form of George, from Greek "geôrgos", "farmer, tiller of the soil".
giorgio.text: A name found throughout Italy and Ticino since the Middle Ages, notably in Venice and Genoa, of which Saint George is patron. Its name day is 23 April, the feast of Saint George the martyr.

giovanna.label: Giovanna
giovanna.meaning: Italian feminine of Giovanni, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
giovanna.text: One of the most common female names in Italy since the Middle Ages, with many pet forms in the records (Giannetta, Giovannina, Nanna, Vanna). The Italian calendar often marks its name day on 30 May, the feast of Saint Joan of Arc.

giovanni.label: Giovanni
giovanni.meaning: Italian form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
giovanni.text: The most widespread male name in Italy for centuries, alone or in compounds (Giovanni Battista, Giovanni Maria), with many regional and short forms: Gianni, Giovan, Nanni, Zuanne in Venice. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

giovanni_battista.label: Giovanni Battista
giovanni_battista.meaning: Italian compound name: Giovanni, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious", and Battista, from Greek "baptistês", "one who baptises".
giovanni_battista.text: A compound name extremely frequent in Italy from the 16th to the 19th century, appearing in the records under various spellings: Giovan Battista, Giovanbattista, Giambattista, or the Latin Joannes Baptista. Its name day is 24 June, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist.

giovannina.label: Giovannina
giovannina.meaning: Italian pet form of Giovanna, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
giovannina.text: An affectionate pet form of Giovanna, sometimes entered as the official name in 19th-century Italian records. The same woman may appear elsewhere simply as Giovanna, or as Nina or Vannina.

girolama.label: Girolama
girolama.meaning: Italian feminine of Girolamo (Jerome), from Greek "hieros", "holy", and "onoma", "name".
girolama.text: An uncommon Italian female name, attested in records mainly in the 16th and 17th centuries. It appears under many spellings: Gerolama, Geronima, Geromina.

girolamo.label: Girolamo
girolamo.meaning: Italian form of Jerome, from Greek "hieros", "holy", and "onoma", "name": "holy name".
girolamo.text: An Italian name very widespread in the Renaissance and early modern period, also written Gerolamo, Geronimo or Hieronymus in Latin records. It honours Saint Jerome, Doctor of the Church and translator of the Bible, whose feast is 30 September.

gisela.label: Gisela
gisela.meaning: From Germanic "gisil", "hostage, pledge", hence the disputed meaning "pledge, promise".
gisela.text: A Germanic name borne from Carolingian times, notably by a sister of Charlemagne, and revived in Germany in the 20th century. In German-speaking countries its name day is 7 May, the feast of Blessed Gisela of Hungary, wife of King Saint Stephen.

gisele.label: Gisèle
gisele.meaning: French form of Gisela, from Germanic "gisil", "hostage, pledge".
gisele.text: A medieval name, borne in Carolingian families, which fell out of use before returning in France in the early 20th century, peaking in the 1920s to 1940s. Its name day is 7 May, the feast of Blessed Gisela of Hungary.

gitla.label: Gitla
gitla.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Gitl, frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. German records write Gittel.

giuditta.label: Giuditta
giuditta.meaning: Italian form of Judith, from Hebrew "Yehudit", "woman of Judea, Jewess".
giuditta.text: An Italian name inspired by the biblical heroine of the Book of Judith, found in Catholic records as well as in Italian Jewish communities. It remains uncommon and is not tied to a widely celebrated saint.

giulia.label: Giulia
giulia.meaning: Italian form of Julia, from Latin "Julia", the name of a great Roman family (gens Julia).
giulia.text: An old Italian female name, common in records since the Renaissance and very widespread in the 19th and 20th centuries. Its name day is 22 May, the feast of Saint Julia of Corsica, a martyr venerated notably in Brescia and Livorno.

giuliano.label: Giuliano
giuliano.meaning: Italian form of Julian, from Latin "Julianus", "of the Julii family".
giuliano.text: An Italian name attested since the Middle Ages, borne notably in the great families of Renaissance Florence, and common in records until the 20th century. Several Saints Julian exist, so the feast day varies by region and calendar.

giulio.label: Giulio
giulio.meaning: Italian form of Julius, from Latin "Julius", the name of Julius Caesar's Roman family.
giulio.text: An Italian name very widespread since the Renaissance, in all regions and in Ticino, sometimes written Gilio or Giulietto in older records. Its name day is 12 April, the feast of Pope Saint Julius I.

giuseppa.label: Giuseppa
giuseppa.meaning: Italian feminine of Giuseppe, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
giuseppa.text: A female name very common in Sicily and southern Italy in the 18th and 19th centuries, often under the pet forms Peppa or Peppina. It alternates in the records with Giuseppina for the same woman.

giuseppe.label: Giuseppe
giuseppe.meaning: Italian form of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
giuseppe.text: One of the most frequent male names in Italy since the 17th century, especially in the south. Records and familiar usage give it many forms: Beppe, Peppino, Pino, Iseppo in Venetian, or the Latin Josephus. Its name day is 19 March, the feast of Saint Joseph, husband of the Virgin Mary.

giuseppina.label: Giuseppina
giuseppina.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Giuseppe, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
giuseppina.text: A female name extremely widespread in Italy in the 19th and early 20th centuries, in every region, often shortened to Pina or Peppina. In the records it sometimes alternates with Giuseppa or the Latin Josepha for the same woman.

giustina.label: Giustina
giustina.meaning: Italian form of Justina, from Latin "justus", "just, righteous".
giustina.text: An old Italian female name, frequent especially in the Veneto, where Saint Justina is patroness of Padua. Her feast is 7 October, a date also associated with the victory of Lepanto (1571), which fell on her feast day.

gladys.label: Gladys
gladys.meaning: Anglicised form of Welsh "Gwladys", perhaps from "gwlad", "country", sometimes linked to Latin Claudia; the meaning is disputed.
gladys.text: An old Welsh name that became very fashionable in Britain around 1900 and in the United States in the 1910s to 1920s. It also appears in Spain and Latin America in the 20th century, sometimes spelled Gladis.

glenn.label: Glenn
glenn.meaning: From Scottish Gaelic "gleann", "narrow valley", first a surname.
glenn.text: A Scottish surname that became a given name in the 19th century, mainly in the United States, where it was common in the mid-20th century. It is also spelled Glen and rarely appears in records before 1880.

gloria.label: Gloria
gloria.meaning: From Latin "gloria", "glory", referring to divine glory.
gloria.text: A mainly Spanish and Portuguese name of religious inspiration, linked notably to the Marian title "Our Lady of Glory". Rare before the 19th century, it spread in the 20th century in Spain, Portugal and English-speaking countries.

godefroy.label: Godefroy
godefroy.text: Borne by Godfrey of Bouillon, this name was common among the northern French nobility in the Middle Ages. Saint Godfrey, bishop of Amiens, is celebrated on 8 November; Latin records write Godefridus.

golda.label: Golda
golda.text: A Yiddish name common in Poland, Lithuania and Ukraine in the 18th and 19th centuries. Polish records write Golda or Gołda.

goncalo.label: Gonçalo
goncalo.meaning: Portuguese form of Gonzalo, from a Visigothic name Latinised as "Gundisalvus", whose first element is "gund", "battle"; the second is disputed.
goncalo.text: An old Portuguese name, borne since the Middle Ages and still common in parish registers of northern Portugal. Its popularity owes much to Blessed Gonçalo of Amarante, a 13th-century Dominican much venerated in Portugal and Brazil, celebrated on 10 January.

gonzaga.label: Gonzaga
gonzaga.meaning: Name of the princely family of Mantua, taken as a given name in honour of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga.
gonzaga.text: A devotional name, mainly Portuguese and Brazilian, usually borne as a second element (Luís Gonzaga, sometimes Maria Gonzaga). It honours Saint Aloysius Gonzaga, a young 16th-century Italian Jesuit and patron of youth, whose feast is 21 June.

gonzalo.label: Gonzalo
gonzalo.meaning: From a Visigothic name Latinised as "Gundisalvus", whose first element is "gund", "battle"; the second is disputed.
gonzalo.text: An old Spanish name, borne since the Middle Ages in Castile and northern Iberia, which gave the patronymic surname González. In Latin records it appears as Gundisalvus, and in Catalan or Basque as Gonçal and Gontzal.

gordon.label: Gordon
gordon.meaning: From a Scottish place name in Berwickshire that became a clan name; its meaning is uncertain, perhaps "great hill" in Brittonic.
gordon.text: A Scottish clan name that became a given name in the 19th century, popularised after the death of General Charles Gordon at Khartoum in 1885. It was mostly frequent in Britain and the United States in the first half of the 20th century.

gottfried.label: Gottfried
gottfried.text: A German name common since the Middle Ages in German-speaking lands, Switzerland and Silesia; its French form is Godefroy, and it is Latinised as Godefridus. It is sometimes shortened to Götz in familiar use.

gotthelf.label: Gotthelf
gotthelf.meaning: German name formed from "Gott", "God", and "helf", "help": "may God help".
gotthelf.text: A devotional name typical of German Lutheran Pietism in the 17th and 18th centuries, like Gottlieb or Gottlob. It is found mostly in Saxony, Silesia and among German-speaking Protestants in Poland, often as a second given name.

gotthold.label: Gotthold
gotthold.meaning: German name formed from "Gott", "God", and "hold", "gracious, devoted": "devoted to God".
gotthold.text: A devotional name born in German Protestant circles in the 17th and 18th centuries, borne by the writer Gotthold Ephraim Lessing. It appears mostly in Lutheran records from Saxony and Silesia, often as a second given name.

gottlieb.label: Gottlieb
gottlieb.meaning: German name formed from "Gott", "God", and "lieb", "dear, beloved": "beloved of God", a translation of Greek Theophilus.
gottlieb.text: A name very widespread among German-speaking Protestants in the 18th and 19th centuries, notably in Württemberg, Switzerland and among German settlers in Poland. It is the equivalent of Greek Theophilus and Latin Amadeus, with which it is sometimes interchanged in records.

gottlob.label: Gottlob
gottlob.meaning: German name formed from "Gott", "God", and "Lob", "praise": "praise God".
gottlob.text: A devotional name typical of Lutheran Pietism, frequent in Württemberg and Saxony in the 18th and 19th centuries, and among German settlers in Poland. It is often borne as a second given name (Johann Gottlob, Christian Gottlob).

gozelon.label: Gozelon
gozelon.meaning: A Germanic name built on the element "Gauz-"; disputed meaning.
gozelon.text: The name of several 11th-century dukes of Lotharingia, found mostly in medieval genealogies. Sources write Gozelon, Gothelon or Gozelo.

gozlin.label: Gozlin
gozlin.meaning: A Germanic name built on the element "Gauz-"; disputed meaning.
gozlin.text: An early medieval name, borne notably by Gozlin, bishop of Paris during the Viking siege of 885–886. It is often linked to the origin of Josselin.

grace.label: Grace
grace.meaning: From English "grace", from Latin "gratia", "grace" in the religious sense.
grace.text: A virtue name adopted by English Puritans in the 17th century, frequent in England, Scotland, Ireland and the United States in the 19th and 20th centuries. It often appears under the pet form Gracie.

gracia.label: Gracia
gracia.text: A Spanish name of religious inspiration, linked to the Marian title "Our Lady of Grace", attested since the Middle Ages and mostly borne by women born before 1960. It also appears as Graciela or the Latin form Gratia.

graham.label: Graham
graham.meaning: From a Scottish surname derived from the English town of Grantham, whose Old English name roughly means "gravelly homestead"; the meaning is disputed.
graham.text: The name of a great Scottish family of Anglo-Norman origin, which became a given name in the 19th century and was very common in Britain in the mid-20th century. It also occurs as Graeme and Grahame, especially in Scotland.

gregoire.label: Grégoire
gregoire.meaning: From Greek "grêgorein", "to watch, to be vigilant".
gregoire.text: An old French name found in records of every period in France, Belgium and French-speaking Switzerland, without ever being among the most frequent. In Latin records it appears as Gregorius. Its name day is 3 September, the feast of Pope Saint Gregory the Great.

gregor.label: Gregor
gregor.meaning: German and Slavic form of Gregory, from Greek "grêgorein", "to watch, to be vigilant".
gregor.text: A name borne in German-speaking lands, especially Catholic ones (Bavaria, Austria, Switzerland), and in Central Europe. Latin records write it Gregorius. Its name day is 3 September, the feast of Pope Saint Gregory the Great.

gregoria.label: Gregoria
gregoria.meaning: Spanish feminine of Gregorio, from Greek "grêgorein", "to watch, to be vigilant".
gregoria.text: A Spanish female name, frequent in rural records of the 18th and 19th centuries and mostly borne by women born before 1950. It was often chosen after the saint of the day of birth, a common practice in Spain.

gregorio.label: Gregorio
gregorio.meaning: Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Gregory, from Greek "grêgorein", "to watch".
gregorio.text: A name common in Spain and Italy since the Middle Ages, particularly in rural Spanish records of the 18th and 19th centuries. Its name day is 3 September, the feast of Pope Saint Gregory the Great.

gregory.label: Gregory
gregory.meaning: English form of Gregory, from Greek "grêgorein", "to watch, to be vigilant".
gregory.text: A name attested in England since the Middle Ages, rare after the Reformation, then very popular in the United States in the mid-20th century. Its name day is 3 September, the feast of Pope Saint Gregory the Great, who sent the first missionaries to England.

griffith.label: Griffith
griffith.meaning: Anglicised form of Welsh "Gruffudd", whose second element is thought to mean "lord"; the meaning is disputed.
griffith.text: A Welsh name borne by medieval princes, common in Wales and the border counties, and the source of the surname Griffiths. Welsh records also write it Gruffydd or Griffin.

grzegorz.label: Grzegorz
grzegorz.meaning: Polish form of Gregory, from Greek "grêgorein", "to watch, to be vigilant".
grzegorz.text: A Polish name present since the Middle Ages in Catholic records, Latinised as Gregorius. Long fairly modest, it became very frequent in Poland in the second half of the 20th century. Its name day is notably 3 September, the feast of Pope Saint Gregory the Great.

guadalupe.label: Guadalupe
guadalupe.meaning: From a place name in Extremadura whose first element is Arabic "wadi", "river"; the second, sometimes linked to Latin "lupus", "wolf", is disputed.
guadalupe.text: A Spanish Marian name, from the shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Extremadura and later the Mexican cult of the Virgin of Guadalupe; it is mainly female but also borne by men, notably in Mexico (José Guadalupe). Its name day is 12 December, Extremadura celebrating its patroness on 8 September.

guenole.label: Guénolé
guenole.text: Saint Winwaloe, founder of Landévennec abbey, is celebrated on 3 March. The name is used in Brittany, notably in Cornouaille.

guglielmo.label: Guglielmo
guglielmo.meaning: Italian form of William, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
guglielmo.text: An Italian name borne since the Middle Ages, first among the nobility, then found in records from every region. In Italy its name day is 25 June, the feast of Saint William of Vercelli, founder of the abbey of Montevergine.

guido.label: Guido
guido.meaning: From Germanic "wid", understood as "wood" or "wide"; the meaning is disputed.
guido.text: A medieval name very widespread in Italy, where it was borne by the musician monk Guido of Arezzo, and found in Germany, Switzerland and Belgium; it corresponds to French Guy. Its name day is 12 September, the feast of Saint Guy of Anderlecht, an 11th-century pilgrim venerated near Brussels.

guilherme.label: Guilherme
guilherme.meaning: Portuguese form of William, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
guilherme.text: An old Portuguese name, borne since the Middle Ages and found in parish registers without being among the most frequent before the 20th century. Latin records render it as Guilielmus or Gulielmus.

guilielmus.label: Guilielmus
guilielmus.meaning: Latin form of William, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
guilielmus.text: The Latinised form of William used in Catholic parish registers, especially in Belgium and the Netherlands. The same man may appear elsewhere as Guillaume, Willem, Wilhelm or Gulielmus depending on the language of the record.

guillaume.label: Guillaume
guillaume.meaning: From Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection": "protected by will".
guillaume.text: A medieval name very widespread in France, Belgium and Luxembourg, borne by William the Conqueror and many princes; it gave rise to a host of surnames. Latin records write it Guillelmus or Gulielmus, and southern France has the Occitan form Guilhem. Its name day is 10 January, the feast of Saint William of Bourges.

guillem.label: Guillem
guillem.meaning: Catalan form of William, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
guillem.text: A Catalan name very widespread in the Middle Ages in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands, later displaced in records by the Castilian form Guillermo. It revived strongly in Catalonia in the late 20th century.

guillemette.label: Guillemette
guillemette.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Guillaume, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet".
guillemette.text: A feminine form of Guillaume, very frequent in French registers from the 14th to the 17th century, notably in Brittany, Normandy and Anjou. Records also spell it Guillaumette.

guillemine.label: Guillemine
guillemine.meaning: Feminine of Guillaume, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet".
guillemine.text: Another feminine form of Guillaume, alongside Guillemette, found in French registers under the Ancien Régime. Records also write Guillaumine.

guillermo.label: Guillermo
guillermo.meaning: Spanish form of William, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
guillermo.text: A Spanish name attested since the Middle Ages, found in records throughout Spain and Latin America, and more frequent in the 20th century than before. Latin records render it as Guillelmus or Gulielmus.

guiomar.label: Guiomar
guiomar.meaning: From a Germanic name of Visigothic times, "Wigmar", from "wig", "battle", and "mar", "famous".
guiomar.text: An old Iberian female name, borne mainly by the Portuguese and Castilian nobility in the 15th and 16th centuries, also written Giomar. It is rare in later parish registers.

gulielmus.label: Gulielmus
gulielmus.meaning: Latin form of William, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
gulielmus.text: A Latin spelling of William used in Catholic parish registers in Belgium and the Netherlands, as well as in old English records. It alternates with Guilielmus or Guillelmus, and corresponds, depending on the language, to Guillaume, Willem, Wilhelm or William.

gunther.label: Günther
gunther.text: A German name from the Nibelung legend, where Gunther is king of the Burgundians, and borne since the Middle Ages. It was very fashionable in Germany in the first half of the 20th century; it is also spelled Günter or Guenther.

gustaaf.label: Gustaaf
gustaaf.meaning: Dutch form of Gustav, from a Swedish name of disputed meaning, perhaps "staff of the Geats".
gustaaf.text: A mainly Flemish name, frequent in Belgium in the 19th and early 20th centuries, often shortened to Staf or Guust. It corresponds to French Gustave, which may be used for the same person in bilingual records.

gustav.label: Gustav
gustav.meaning: From a Swedish name of disputed meaning, perhaps "staff of the Geats", sometimes linked to a Slavic name.
gustav.text: A Swedish royal name (Gustav Vasa, Gustavus Adolphus), spread to Germany after the Thirty Years' War and very widespread in German-speaking lands and Poland in the 19th century. It also appears as Gustaf, the Swedish spelling, or as the Latin Gustavus.

gustave.label: Gustave
gustave.meaning: French form of Gustav, from a Swedish name of disputed meaning, perhaps "staff of the Geats".
gustave.text: A name rare in France before 1800 that became very fashionable in the 19th century in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland, among the most given to boys born before 1900. It is not tied to any well-established saint.

gustavo.label: Gustavo
gustavo.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Gustav, from a Swedish name of disputed meaning, perhaps "staff of the Geats".
gustavo.text: A name of Nordic origin that spread to Italy, Spain and Portugal in the 19th century, during the Romantic era. It is more frequent in the 20th century, notably in Latin America.

gustavus.label: Gustavus
gustavus.meaning: Latin form of Gustav, from a Swedish name of disputed meaning, perhaps "staff of the Geats".
gustavus.text: A Latinised form of the name, used in Catholic records in Belgium and the Netherlands, but also as an everyday name in Britain and the United States in the 19th century, in memory of Gustavus Adolphus. Depending on the language, the same man may appear elsewhere as Gustave, Gustaaf or Gustav.

gustaw.label: Gustaw
gustaw.meaning: Polish form of Gustav, from a Swedish name of disputed meaning, perhaps "staff of the Geats".
gustaw.text: A name widespread in Poland in the 19th and early 20th centuries, in Catholic and Protestant families alike, notably those of German origin. In Latin records it appears as Gustavus.

guy.label: Guy
guy.meaning: From Germanic "wid", understood as "wood" or "wide"; the meaning is disputed.
guy.text: A medieval name borne by the French nobility, notably counts and lords, then revived in France and Belgium in the 20th century; it is also common in England. It corresponds to Italian Guido, and Latin records write it Guido or Wido. Saint Guy of Anderlecht, an 11th-century pilgrim, is celebrated on 12 September; the popular French calendar marks the name on 12 June.

guyonne.label: Guyonne
guyonne.meaning: Feminine of Guyon, a diminutive of Guy.
guyonne.text: A female name borne notably in the Laval family, several of whose heiresses took the name Guyonne. It remains rare in registers.

gwenael.label: Gwenaël
gwenael.text: Saint Gwenaël, abbot of Landévennec in the 6th century, is celebrated on 3 November. An old name in Brittany, it spread widely from the 1970s.

gwendoline.label: Gwendoline
gwendoline.meaning: From Welsh "gwen", "white, blessed", and a second element often interpreted as "ring, bow"; the meaning is disputed.
gwendoline.text: A name of Welsh origin that became fashionable in Britain in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, often shortened to Gwen. It appears under many spellings: Gwendolen, Gwendolyn, Gwendolin.

halina.label: Halina
halina.meaning: Of disputed origin: a Polish form of Helena or from Greek "galênê", "calm, serenity".
halina.text: A Polish name very widespread in the 20th century, especially among women born between the 1920s and 1950s, and much rarer in older records. It is often used as the pet form Halinka.

hamelin.label: Hamelin
hamelin.text: A medieval name of western France and Anglo-Norman England that later became a surname. It is found mostly in sources earlier than the 16th century.

hanna.label: Hanna
hanna.meaning: From Hebrew "Hannah", "grace, favour", the common source of Anne and Anna.
hanna.text: A form common in Poland, Germany, the Netherlands and Scandinavia, where it is treated as a variant of Anna; in Poland it was very widespread in the 20th century. Its name day there is 26 July, the feast of Saint Anne, mother of the Virgin Mary.

hannah.label: Hannah
hannah.text: A biblical name, that of the mother of the prophet Samuel, adopted by English and Dutch Protestants after the Reformation and frequent in England and North America in the 18th and 19th centuries. It is also borne in Jewish communities across Europe. In English records it sometimes alternates with Anna or Ann for the same woman.

hannchen.label: Hannchen
hannchen.meaning: German diminutive of Johanna or Hanna, from Hebrew, "God is gracious" or "grace".
hannchen.text: An affectionate diminutive ("little Hanne") used in German-speaking lands in the 18th and 19th centuries, sometimes entered as such in records, including in Jewish communities. The same woman may appear elsewhere under the full name Johanna or Hanna.

hanns.label: Hanns
hanns.meaning: Old German spelling of Hans, the short form of Johannes, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
hanns.text: A short form of Johannes, extremely widespread in German-speaking lands since the late Middle Ages; the double-n spelling is found mainly in older records. The same man may be entered as Johannes, Johann or Hans depending on the record. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

hanspeter.label: Hanspeter
hanspeter.text: A compound name typical of 20th-century German-speaking Switzerland and Germany, written as one word or hyphenated.

hansruedi.label: Hansruedi
hansruedi.meaning: Compound of Hans (John) and Ruedi, a Swiss diminutive of Rudolf.
hansruedi.text: A compound name specific to German-speaking Switzerland, mostly given in the 20th century. In official records it may correspond to Hans Rudolf.

harm.label: Harm
harm.meaning: Dutch and Frisian short form of Herman, from Germanic "heri", "army", and "man", "man".
harm.text: A name typical of the northern and eastern Netherlands (Groningen, Drenthe, Friesland) and German East Frisia, frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries. In the records it alternates with Harmen, Herman or the Latin Harmannus for the same person.

harold.label: Harold
harold.meaning: From Old English "Hereweald" and Old Norse "Haraldr", from "here", "army", and "weald", "power": "army ruler".
harold.text: The name of the last Anglo-Saxon king, killed at Hastings in 1066, which remained rare after the Norman Conquest and was brought back into fashion in the Victorian era. It was among the most given names in Britain and the United States around 1900, often shortened to Harry.

harriet.label: Harriet
harriet.meaning: English form of Henriette, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
harriet.text: An English name that appeared in the 17th century as an adaptation of Henriette, very common in England and the United States in the 18th and 19th centuries. It is often shortened to Hattie or Hatty, and also spelled Harriett.

harrison.label: Harrison
harrison.meaning: English surname meaning "son of Harry", that is, of Henry.
harrison.text: An English surname used as a given name, mainly in the United States from the 19th century, sometimes in honour of Presidents William Henry Harrison and Benjamin Harrison. It remained uncommon until the late 20th century.

hartwig.label: Hartwig
hartwig.text: A medieval name of northern Germany, borne by bishops of Bremen and Hamburg, and still present in records from Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony. It is relatively rare elsewhere.

harvey.label: Harvey
harvey.meaning: From Breton "Haerviu", an old form of Hervé, from "haer", "battle", and "viu", "worthy"; the meaning is disputed.
harvey.text: A name brought to England by Bretons who came with the Normans, at first mainly a surname, then a common given name in the United States and Britain in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It corresponds to French Hervé.

hazel.label: Hazel
hazel.meaning: From English "hazel", the hazel tree, a plant name.
hazel.text: An English name from the late 19th-century wave of plant names, very popular in the United States and Britain between 1890 and 1930. It is practically absent from earlier records.

heather.label: Heather
heather.meaning: From English "heather", the heath plant, a plant name.
heather.text: An English name that appeared in the late 19th century with the fashion for plant names, mostly widespread in Britain in the mid-20th century. It is practically absent from records before 1880.

hector.label: Hector
hector.meaning: From Greek "Hektôr", the name of the Trojan hero, linked to "ekhein", "to hold": "he who holds fast".
hector.text: A name taken from the Iliad, borne from the Middle Ages among the nobility, then very fashionable in France and Belgium in the 19th century. It is also common in Spain (Héctor) and in Scotland, where it was used to anglicise a Gaelic name.

hedwig.label: Hedwig
hedwig.text: A Germanic name borne since the Middle Ages in Germany, Silesia and Poland, where it gives Jadwiga; older records also write it Hadewig or Hedewig. It honours Saint Hedwig of Silesia, a 13th-century duchess and patron saint of Silesia, whose feast is 16 October.

heinrich.label: Heinrich
heinrich.meaning: From Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful": "ruler of the home".
heinrich.text: One of the most widespread names in German-speaking lands from the Middle Ages to the 20th century, borne by many emperors. It appears under a host of short forms: Heinz, Hein, Heini, Henning; Latin records write it Henricus. Its name day is 13 July, the feast of Emperor Saint Henry II.

helen.label: Helen
helen.meaning: From Greek "Helenê", of disputed meaning, often linked to "hêlê", "sunlight, torch".
helen.text: The English form of Helena, in use since the Middle Ages and among the most given female names in the United States in the early 20th century. It is often written Helena or Ellen in the records. Its name day is 18 August, the feast of Saint Helena, mother of Emperor Constantine.

helena.label: Helena
helena.meaning: From Greek "Helenê", of disputed meaning, often linked to "hêlê", "sunlight, torch".
helena.text: The Latin and Central European form of Helen, extremely widespread in Poland, where it is among the most borne names, and common in the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal and German-speaking lands. In Latin records it often stands for Hélène, Helene or Helen. Its name day is 18 August, the feast of Saint Helena, mother of Emperor Constantine.

helene.label: Helene
helene.meaning: From Greek "Helenê", of disputed meaning, often linked to "hêlê", "sunlight, torch".
helene.text: The French (Hélène) and German (Helene) form of the name, very widespread in France and German-speaking lands, and among the frequent female names of women born before 1900. In Latin records it appears as Helena. Its name day is 18 August, the feast of Saint Helena, mother of Emperor Constantine.

helmuth.label: Helmuth
helmuth.meaning: From Germanic, perhaps "helm", "helmet, protection", and "muot", "mind, courage"; the meaning is disputed.
helmuth.text: A German name borne in the 19th century notably by Field Marshal von Moltke, and very widespread in the first half of the 20th century. It appears under the spellings Helmut, Hellmut or Hellmuth, which should be linked when searching.

heloise.label: Héloïse
heloise.meaning: Of disputed Germanic origin, perhaps from "heil", "healthy, whole", and "wid", "wide"; sometimes linked to Elijah or Louis.
heloise.text: A name made famous by Héloïse, wife of Abelard in the 12th century, and brought back into fashion in France in the 19th century, notably after Rousseau's "Julie, or the New Heloise". It is also spelled Éloïse. The French calendar marks it on 11 February, the feast of Saint Héloïse, a recluse at Coulombs.

hendricus.label: Hendricus
hendricus.meaning: Dutch Latinised form of Hendrik (Henry), from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
hendricus.text: A Latin spelling of Hendrik used in Catholic records in the Netherlands and sometimes kept in civil registration. The same man may appear elsewhere as Hendrik, Henricus or Hendrikus. Its name day is 13 July, the feast of Emperor Saint Henry II.

hendrik.label: Hendrik
hendrik.meaning: Dutch form of Henry, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
hendrik.text: One of the most frequent male names in the Netherlands and Flanders from the 16th to the 20th century, often shortened to Henk, Hein or Rik. Records also give Hendrick, Henderik or the Latin Henricus. Its name day is 13 July, the feast of Emperor Saint Henry II.

hendrika.label: Hendrika
hendrika.meaning: Dutch feminine of Hendrik, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
hendrika.text: A female name very common in the Netherlands and Flanders in the 18th and 19th centuries, often shortened to Riek, Rika or Henny. In the records it alternates with Hendrina, Henrica or Henriette for the same woman.

hendrikus.label: Hendrikus
hendrikus.meaning: Dutch Latinised form of Hendrik (Henry), from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
hendrikus.text: A Latinised form of Hendrik, frequent in Dutch Catholic records and in civil registration of the 19th and early 20th centuries. It alternates with Hendricus, Henricus or Hendrik for the same man. Its name day is 13 July, the feast of Emperor Saint Henry II.

hendrina.label: Hendrina
hendrina.meaning: Dutch feminine derivative of Hendrik, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
hendrina.text: A Dutch female name, frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries, notably in the eastern and northern provinces. It alternates with Hendrika or Henderina in the records, and is shortened to Drien or Rina.

henning.label: Henning
henning.meaning: Low German and Scandinavian short form, most often of Johannes ("God is gracious"), sometimes of Heinrich.
henning.text: A name of northern Germany and Scandinavia, attested since the late Middle Ages and found in records from Schleswig-Holstein, Mecklenburg and Pomerania. The same man may appear elsewhere as Johannes.

henny.label: Henny
henny.meaning: Pet form of names such as Henriette, Hendrika or Johanna, whose origin it shares.
henny.text: A familiar form used in the Netherlands and Germany in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, sometimes entered as the official name. It is mostly female but can also refer to a man (Hendrik). The full name often appears in other records.

henri.label: Henri
henri.meaning: From Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful": "ruler of the home".
henri.text: A royal name (notably Henri IV), very common in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland, and among the male names most given to boys born before 1900. Old records also spell it Henry or the Latin Henricus. Its name day is 13 July, the feast of Emperor Saint Henry II.

henrica.label: Henrica
henrica.meaning: Latin feminine form of Henry, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
henrica.text: A Latinised form used in Catholic registers in Belgium and the Netherlands for women called Hendrika or Henriette in daily life. It occurs mainly in the 17th and 18th centuries.

henricus.label: Henricus
henricus.meaning: Latin form of Henry, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
henricus.text: The Latin form of Henry used in Catholic records in Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany, and sometimes kept in Dutch civil registration. The same man may appear elsewhere as Henri, Hendrik or Heinrich depending on the language. Its name day is 13 July, the feast of Emperor Saint Henry II.

henrietta.label: Henrietta
henrietta.meaning: Latinised and English form of Henriette, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
henrietta.text: A name spread in England in the 17th century by Queen Henrietta Maria of France, then common in Britain, the United States and the Netherlands in the 18th and 19th centuries. It is often shortened to Hetty or Etta.

henriette.label: Henriette
henriette.meaning: Feminine of Henri, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
henriette.text: A female name very widespread in France in the 19th century, among the most given to girls born before 1900, and also common in Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Germany. It is often borne in compounds (Marie-Henriette) and has counterparts such as Henriqueta or Hendrika in neighbouring countries.

henrique.label: Henrique
henrique.meaning: Portuguese form of Henry, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
henrique.text: A Portuguese name borne since the founding of the kingdom, notably by Prince Henry the Navigator, and found in parish registers of every period. Its name day is 13 July, the feast of Emperor Saint Henry II.

henriqueta.label: Henriqueta
henriqueta.meaning: Portuguese form of Henriette, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
henriqueta.text: A Portuguese female name, uncommon before the 19th century, which then spread in Portugal and Brazil. It corresponds to French Henriette.

henry.label: Henry
henry.meaning: English form of Henri, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
henry.text: An English royal name borne by eight kings, among the most frequent in England and the United States from the Middle Ages to the early 20th century, often under the familiar form Harry. In France, Henry is also an old spelling of Henri. Its name day is 13 July, the feast of Emperor Saint Henry II.

henryk.label: Henryk
henryk.meaning: Polish form of Henry, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
henryk.text: A Polish name borne by medieval dukes of Silesia and very widespread in the 20th century, especially among men born between the 1920s and 1950s. In Latin records it appears as Henricus. Its name day is notably 13 July, the feast of Emperor Saint Henry II.

henryka.label: Henryka
henryka.meaning: Polish feminine of Henryk, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
henryka.text: A Polish female name mostly borne by women born in the first half of the 20th century. In Latin records it appears as Henrica or Henrietta.

herbert.label: Herbert
herbert.text: An old name borne in England and Germany in the Middle Ages, then brought back into fashion in the late 19th century; it was very common in Britain, the United States and Germany around 1900. It honours Saint Herbert of Derwentwater, a 7th-century English hermit whose feast is 20 March.

herman.label: Herman
herman.text: The Dutch, English and Scandinavian form of Hermann, very common in the Netherlands and among Germanic emigrants in the United States in the 19th and 20th centuries. In the Netherlands it alternates with Harm, Harmen or the Latin Hermanus for the same person.

hermann.label: Hermann
