hermann.text: A German name borne since the Middle Ages and very widespread in the 19th century, in Germany, Switzerland, Luxembourg and German-speaking families in Poland. It should not be confused with Germain, which is of Latin origin. Its name day is 24 September, the feast of Blessed Hermann of Reichenau, an 11th-century scholar monk.

hermanus.label: Hermanus
hermanus.meaning: Dutch Latinised form of Herman, from Germanic "heri", "army", and "man", "man".
hermanus.text: A Latinised form frequent in Catholic records and Dutch civil registration in the 18th and 19th centuries. The same man may appear elsewhere as Herman, Harmen, Harm or Harmanus.

hermina.label: Hermina
hermina.meaning: Feminine of Herman, from Germanic "heri", "army", and "man", "man".
hermina.text: A Dutch and Central European female name, common in the 19th and 20th centuries, often shortened to Mina or Mien. It alternates with Hermine or Harmina in the records.

hermine.label: Hermine
hermine.meaning: Feminine of Hermann, from Germanic "heri", "army", and "man", "man".
hermine.text: A German and French female name, widespread in the 19th century in Germany, Switzerland, Belgium and France. It is also spelled Hermina or shortened to Herma or Minna.

herminia.label: Herminia
herminia.meaning: From Latin "Herminius", the name of a Roman family, sometimes linked to the Greek god Hermes; the meaning is disputed.
herminia.text: A Spanish name mostly borne by women born in the first half of the 20th century, also widespread in Latin America. It corresponds to Italian Erminia, the name of a heroine of Tasso's "Jerusalem Delivered".

herminie.label: Herminie
herminie.meaning: French form of Herminia, from Latin "Herminius", the name of a Roman family; the meaning is disputed.
herminie.text: A French Romantic name, inspired by the heroine Herminia of Tasso's "Jerusalem Delivered", mostly given in the 19th century. It is sometimes confused with Hermine in the records.

hertha.label: Hertha
hertha.meaning: Name of a Germanic goddess, from an old misreading of "Nerthus" in Tacitus; sometimes linked to "erda", "earth".
hertha.text: A German name that appeared in the 19th century with the Romantic taste for Germanic antiquity, very widespread in Germany around 1900-1930. It is also spelled Herta.

herve.label: Hervé
herve.meaning: From Breton "Haerviu", from "haer", "battle", and "viu", "worthy"; the meaning is disputed.
herve.text: An old Breton name, linked to Saint Hervé, a blind 6th-century hermit much venerated in Brittany, whose feast is 17 June. It is found in Breton records of the Ancien Régime, then spread throughout France in the mid-20th century.

hervee.label: Hervée
hervee.meaning: Feminine of Hervé, from Breton "houarn", "iron", and "vi", "ardent"; disputed meaning.
hervee.text: A rare feminine form of Hervé, found mostly in Brittany in the 20th century.

hester.label: Hester
hester.meaning: Variant of Esther, of disputed meaning: from Persian "stâra", "star", or from the name of the goddess Ishtar.
hester.text: The English and Dutch form of Esther, common among Protestants in the 17th and 18th centuries, then in the United States until the early 20th century. It alternates with Esther in the records for the same woman and is shortened to Hetty.

hetty.label: Hetty
hetty.meaning: Pet form of Hester, Henrietta or Hendrika, whose origin it shares.
hetty.text: A pet form common in England, the United States and the Netherlands in the 18th and 19th centuries, sometimes entered as the official name. The full name, to be sought in other records, varies from family to family.

hieronymus.label: Hieronymus
hieronymus.meaning: Latin form of Jerome, from Greek "hieros", "holy", and "onoma", "name": "holy name".
hieronymus.text: The Latin form of Jerome, used in Catholic records and as an everyday name in German-speaking lands and the Netherlands in the 16th to 18th centuries (the painter Hieronymus Bosch bore it). Its name day is 30 September, the feast of Saint Jerome, translator of the Bible into Latin.

hilaire.label: Hilaire
hilaire.text: An old French name found in records from the Middle Ages to the late 19th century, notably in western France, Belgium and Luxembourg. It honours Saint Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop and Doctor of the Church, whose feast is 13 January.

hilda.label: Hilda
hilda.meaning: From Germanic "hild", "battle", often a short form of names such as Hildegard or Mathilde.
hilda.text: An Anglo-Saxon name brought back into fashion in the Victorian era, among the most given in England around 1900, and also common in Germany and the United States. It honours Saint Hilda of Whitby, a 7th-century Anglo-Saxon abbess, whose feast is 17 November.

hilde.label: Hilde
hilde.meaning: German short form of names such as Hildegard or Brunhilde, from Germanic "hild", "battle".
hilde.text: A German and Dutch name mostly borne by women born in the first half of the 20th century. The full name (Hildegard, Mathilde) may appear in other records of the same person.

hildegard.label: Hildegard
hildegard.text: A medieval German name, borne by a wife of Charlemagne and by the mystic Hildegard of Bingen, then revived in Germany in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its name day is 17 September, the feast of Saint Hildegard of Bingen.

hinda.label: Hinda
hinda.text: A female Yiddish name, the counterpart of Hirsch ("stag"), frequent in Jewish records of Poland and Lithuania in the 19th century. The diminutive Hindla is common.

hinrich.label: Hinrich
hinrich.meaning: Low German form of Heinrich, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
hinrich.text: A form typical of northern Germany (Holstein, Hamburg, Lower Saxony, Mecklenburg), frequent in Lutheran records of the 17th to 19th centuries. The same man may appear elsewhere as Heinrich. Its name day is 13 July, the feast of Emperor Saint Henry II.

hippolyte.label: Hippolyte
hippolyte.meaning: From Greek "hippos", "horse", and "luein", "to loose": "one who unleashes horses".
hippolyte.text: A French name widespread in the 18th and especially the 19th century, in France and Belgium alike; it is also borne by women in a few older records. Its name day is 13 August, the feast of Saint Hippolytus of Rome, a 3rd-century priest and martyr.

hiram.label: Hiram
hiram.meaning: From Hebrew and Phoenician, understood as "my brother is exalted"; the meaning is disputed.
hiram.text: A biblical name, that of the king of Tyre who was Solomon's ally, adopted by English-speaking Protestants and frequent in the United States in the 19th century. It is also known in Masonic tradition.

hirsch.label: Hirsch
hirsch.text: A common name in the Jewish communities of Germany and Eastern Europe, associated with the tribe of Naphtali and often paired with Hebrew Zvi. Records write Hersch, Hirsz or, as a diminutive, Herschel.

homer.label: Homer
homer.meaning: From Greek "Homêros", the name of the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey, of disputed meaning ("hostage" in one interpretation).
homer.text: A name of classical taste, mainly widespread in the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is rare in Europe, where the French form Homère appears in a few records.

honorat.label: Honorat
honorat.text: Saint Honoratus, founder of the monastery of Lérins and later archbishop of Arles, is celebrated on 16 January. The name is characteristic of Provence.

honore.label: Honoré
honore.text: A French name common in the Ancien Régime and the 19th century, notably in Provence, Picardy and Belgium, with the Latin form Honoratus in records. Its name day is 16 May, the feast of Saint Honoratus of Amiens, a 6th-century bishop and patron saint of bakers.

honoree.label: Honorée
honoree.text: A feminine form of Honoré, found in French registers, notably in Provence and Picardy, under the Ancien Régime.

honorine.label: Honorine
honorine.text: A French female name, frequent in the 19th century, notably in Normandy and Belgium. It honours Saint Honorina, a Gallo-Roman martyr venerated in Normandy and at Conflans-Sainte-Honorine, whose feast is 27 February.

horace.label: Horace
horace.meaning: From Latin "Horatius", the name of a Roman family, borne by the poet Horace; meaning unknown.
horace.text: A name of classical taste, common in England and the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries, where it alternates with Horatio (in memory of Admiral Nelson). It also appears in France and French-speaking Switzerland in the 19th century.

horst.label: Horst
horst.meaning: From German "Horst", "thicket, grove" or "eyrie (of a bird of prey)".
horst.text: A German name that appeared in the late 19th century and was very widespread between the 1920s and 1950s. It is practically absent from records before 1880.

hortense.label: Hortense
hortense.meaning: From Latin "Hortensia", the name of a Roman family, associated with "hortus", "garden".
hortense.text: A name made popular by Hortense de Beauharnais, Queen of Holland and mother of Napoleon III, widely given in France and Belgium in the 19th century. It appears as Hortensia or Hortenzia in other languages.

howard.label: Howard
howard.meaning: English surname of disputed etymology: perhaps from Germanic "hug", "mind", and "hard", "strong", or from a Norse name.
howard.text: The name of the family of the Dukes of Norfolk, which became a given name in the 19th century and was very common in the United States in the 1910s to 1930s. It is rare in records before 1850.

hubert.label: Hubert
hubert.text: A name very widespread in Belgium, Luxembourg and north-eastern France because of the cult of Saint Hubert in the Ardennes; it also occurs in the Netherlands, Germany and England. Latin records write it Hubertus. Its name day is 3 November, the feast of Saint Hubert of Liège, patron saint of hunters.

hubertine.label: Hubertine
hubertine.meaning: Feminine of Hubert, from Germanic "hug", "mind", and "berht", "bright".
hubertine.text: A female name found mainly in Belgium, Dutch Limburg and eastern France, regions with a strong cult of Saint Hubert, in the 18th and 19th centuries. It alternates with the Latin form Huberta.

hubertus.label: Hubertus
hubertus.meaning: Latin form of Hubert, from Germanic "hug", "mind", and "berht", "bright, famous".
hubertus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic records and as an everyday name in the Netherlands (especially Limburg), Belgium and the Rhineland. The same man may appear elsewhere as Hubert. Its name day is 3 November, the feast of Saint Hubert of Liège, patron saint of hunters.

hugh.label: Hugh
hugh.meaning: English form of Hugues, from Germanic "hug", "mind, intellect".
hugh.text: A name brought to England by the Normans, common in England, Scotland and Ireland, where it was also used to anglicise Gaelic names. Welsh records give the form Huw. Its name day is 17 November, the feast of Saint Hugh of Lincoln, a 12th-century bishop.

hugo.label: Hugo
hugo.meaning: Latin and Germanic form of Hugh, from Germanic "hug", "mind, intellect".
hugo.text: The form used in Latin records for Hugues and as an everyday name in Germany, the Netherlands, Poland and Iberia, common in the 19th century. Its name day is 29 April, the feast of Saint Hugh of Cluny, a great 11th-century abbot.

hugues.label: Hugues
hugues.text: A medieval name borne by Hugh Capet and many lords, frequent in records until the 16th century and rarer afterwards, and the source of many surnames (Hugon, Huet). Latin records write it Hugo. Its name day is 1 April, the feast of Saint Hugh of Grenoble, the bishop who sheltered the Carthusians.

huguette.label: Huguette
huguette.meaning: Feminine of Hugues, from Germanic "hug", "mind, intellect".
huguette.text: A female name attested in the Middle Ages, then mostly given in France in the 1920s to 1950s. It is rare in records of the 17th to 19th centuries.

hulda.label: Hulda
hulda.meaning: Of disputed origin: from the biblical prophetess Huldah (Hebrew "weasel"), or from Scandinavian "huld", "gracious, lovely".
hulda.text: A name mostly borne in Protestant circles in Germany, Scandinavia and Poland in the 19th century, as well as among Scandinavian and German emigrants in the United States. It is rare in Catholic regions.

humberto.label: Humberto
humberto.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Humbert, from Germanic "hun", of disputed meaning, and "berht", "bright, famous".
humberto.text: A name uncommon in Iberia before the 19th century, which spread in the 20th century in Portugal, Spain and Latin America. It corresponds to Italian Umberto, the name of kings of the House of Savoy.

humphrey.label: Humphrey
humphrey.meaning: From Germanic "hun", of disputed meaning, and "fridu", "peace".
humphrey.text: A name brought to England by the Normans, common among the English nobility and gentry from the Middle Ages to the 17th century, then rarer. Welsh derived the form Wmffre from it, and it is written Humfrey or Humphry in older records.

hyacinthe.label: Hyacinthe
hyacinthe.meaning: From Greek "hyakinthos", the hyacinth flower, name of a young hero of mythology.
hyacinthe.text: A French name common in the 18th and 19th centuries, borne mostly by men but also by women in some records. Its name day is 17 August, the feast of Saint Hyacinth of Poland (Jacek), a 13th-century Dominican preacher.

ian.label: Ian
ian.meaning: Scottish form (Iain) of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
ian.text: An anglicised form of Scottish Gaelic Iain, long limited to Scotland, then very widespread throughout Britain in the mid-20th century. In older Scottish records the same man is usually entered as John. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

icek.label: Icek
icek.meaning: A Yiddish diminutive of Isaac, "he will laugh".
icek.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Itsik, a diminutive of Isaac, among the most frequent Jewish male names in 19th-century Poland. The variant Ajzyk (Eisik) also stands for Isaac.

ida.label: Ida
ida.meaning: From Germanic "id", often understood as "work, activity"; the meaning is disputed.
ida.text: A medieval name revived in the 19th century, very widespread in Germany, Switzerland, Italy, the Netherlands, Scandinavia and the United States around 1880-1910; it is also frequent in France among women born before 1900. In German-speaking countries its name day is 4 September, the feast of Saint Ida of Herzfeld; the French calendar marks it on 13 April.

ignace.label: Ignace
ignace.meaning: From Latin "Egnatius", a Roman family name of obscure origin, later associated with "ignis", "fire".
ignace.text: A Catholic name that spread from the 17th century with the influence of the Jesuits, found in records from France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland. Its name day is 31 July, the feast of Saint Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Society of Jesus.

ignacio.label: Ignacio
ignacio.meaning: Spanish form of Ignatius, from Latin "Egnatius", a Roman family name later associated with "ignis", "fire".
ignacio.text: A Spanish name very widespread since the canonisation of Ignatius of Loyola in 1622, especially in the Basque Country, where Iñaki also occurs. Its name day is 31 July, the feast of Saint Ignatius of Loyola.

ignacy.label: Ignacy
ignacy.meaning: Polish form of Ignatius, from Latin "Egnatius", a Roman family name later associated with "ignis", "fire".
ignacy.text: A Polish name common from the 17th to the 19th century, among the nobility and in the countryside alike. In Latin records it appears as Ignatius. Its name day is 31 July, the feast of Saint Ignatius of Loyola.

ignasi.label: Ignasi
ignasi.meaning: Catalan form of Ignatius, from Latin "Egnatius", a Roman family name later associated with "ignis", "fire".
ignasi.text: A Catalan name borne in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands, where older records often use the Castilian form Ignacio for the same person. Its name day is 31 July, the feast of Saint Ignatius of Loyola.

ignatius.label: Ignatius
ignatius.meaning: Latin form of Ignatius, from "Egnatius", a Roman family name later associated with "ignis", "fire".
ignatius.text: The Latin form used in Catholic records in Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Poland, and as an everyday name among English-speaking Catholics. Depending on the language, the same man may appear elsewhere as Ignace, Ignaz or Ignacy. Its name day is 31 July, the feast of Saint Ignatius of Loyola.

ignaz.label: Ignaz
ignaz.meaning: German form of Ignatius, from Latin "Egnatius", a Roman family name later associated with "ignis", "fire".
ignaz.text: A name of the Catholic German-speaking regions (Bavaria, Austria, Switzerland, Silesia), frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries. Latin records write it Ignatius. Its name day is 31 July, the feast of Saint Ignatius of Loyola.

ignazio.label: Ignazio
ignazio.meaning: Italian form of Ignatius, from Latin "Egnatius", a Roman family name later associated with "ignis", "fire".
ignazio.text: An Italian name widespread since the 17th century, particularly in Sicily and Sardinia. Its name day is 31 July, the feast of Saint Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits.

igor.label: Igor
igor.meaning: Russian form of Old Norse "Ingvarr", from the god Ing and "varr", "guardian"; the meaning is disputed.
igor.text: A name of medieval Rus', rare in Western and Central Europe before the 20th century, then widespread in Poland and other Slavic countries in the second half of the 20th century. It seldom appears in older records.

ilda.label: Ilda
ilda.meaning: Short form of Germanic names in "-hild", "battle", such as Brunilda or Matilda.
ilda.text: A mainly Portuguese and Italian female name, uncommon before the late 19th century and borne chiefly in the 20th century. It also appears as Hilda.

ildefonso.label: Ildefonso
ildefonso.meaning: From a Visigothic name, "Hildefuns", from "hild", "battle", and "funs", "ready, eager".
ildefonso.text: A Spanish name of Visigothic origin, found in records from Castile and Andalusia, and sometimes shortened to Alfonso or Fonso. It honours Saint Ildefonsus of Toledo, a 7th-century archbishop, whose feast is 23 January.

ilona.label: Ilona
ilona.meaning: Hungarian form generally linked to Helen (Greek "Helenê"); the meaning is disputed.
ilona.text: An old Hungarian name that spread to Poland and other Central European countries in the 20th century, especially from the 1960s. It is rare in earlier Polish records.

ilse.label: Ilse
ilse.meaning: German diminutive of Elisabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "God is my oath".
ilse.text: A diminutive of Elisabeth that became a name in its own right in the late 19th century, very widespread in Germany and among German speakers in Poland between 1900 and 1940. The name also appears as Ilsa or Ilsabe. Its name day follows Elisabeth, the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary on 17 November.

immanuel.label: Immanuel
immanuel.meaning: From Hebrew "Immanu El", "God is with us".
immanuel.text: The German form of Emmanuel, mostly borne among German and Swiss Protestants in the 18th and 19th centuries, like the philosopher Immanuel Kant. It also occurs in Jewish communities.

ina.label: Ina
ina.meaning: Short form of female names ending in "-ina" (Wilhelmina, Katharina, Hendrina), whose origin it shares.
ina.text: A pet form that became an official name in the Netherlands, Germany, Scandinavia and the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The full name may appear in other records of the same woman.

inacio.label: Inácio
inacio.meaning: Portuguese form of Ignatius, from Latin "Egnatius", a Roman family name later associated with "ignis", "fire".
inacio.text: A Portuguese name found in parish registers since the 17th century, under Jesuit influence. Its name day is 31 July, the feast of Saint Ignatius of Loyola.

ines.label: Ines
ines.meaning: Spanish form of Agnes, from Greek "hagnê", "pure, chaste", associated with Latin "agnus", "lamb".
ines.text: A very old name in Iberia (Inés, Inês), borne notably by Inês de Castro in the 14th century, and later spread to Italy, France and Germany. Its name day is 21 January, the feast of Saint Agnes, virgin martyr of Rome.

inez.label: Inez
inez.meaning: English and Dutch form of Inés, itself the Spanish form of Agnes, from Greek "hagnê", "pure, chaste".
inez.text: A name mainly widespread in the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and also found in Poland and the Netherlands. Its name day is 21 January, the feast of Saint Agnes, virgin martyr of Rome.

inigo.label: Íñigo
inigo.meaning: From Basque "Eneko", of disputed meaning, sometimes understood as "my little one".
inigo.text: A Navarrese and Basque name borne by medieval kings of Pamplona, and the baptismal name of Saint Ignatius of Loyola; it is often confused with Ignacio in the records. Its name day is 1 June, the feast of Saint Íñigo, 11th-century abbot of Oña.

inocencio.label: Inocencio
inocencio.text: A Spanish and Portuguese name borne by several popes (Innocent), frequent in rural records of the 18th and 19th centuries and mostly among men born before 1950. It was sometimes given to children born around the feast of the Holy Innocents on 28 December.

ippolita.label: Ippolita
ippolita.meaning: Italian feminine of Ippolito, from Greek "hippos", "horse", and "luein", "to loose".
ippolita.text: A name of the Italian Renaissance, borne in the great families (Sforza, Gonzaga), then found more modestly in the records. It also recalls Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons.

ippolito.label: Ippolito
ippolito.meaning: Italian form of Hippolytus, from Greek "hippos", "horse", and "luein", "to loose".
ippolito.text: An Italian name borne in princely families during the Renaissance (Este, Medici), then found in records from all regions. Its name day is 13 August, the feast of Saint Hippolytus of Rome, a 3rd-century priest and martyr.

ira.label: Ira
ira.meaning: From Hebrew "Ira", a biblical name often understood as "watchful"; the meaning is disputed.
ira.text: A biblical name adopted by English-speaking Protestants, mostly frequent in the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is masculine in that context, whereas Ira is feminine in Eastern Europe as a pet form of Irina.

irena.label: Irena
irena.meaning: Polish form of Irene, from Greek "eirênê", "peace".
irena.text: A name very widespread in Poland in the 20th century, especially among women born between the 1920s and 1950s, and rarer in earlier records. Several Saints Irene exist, so the feast day varies by calendar.

irene.label: Irene
irene.text: A name of Greek origin borne by several Byzantine empresses, found in Italy, Spain and Portugal, and very fashionable in Britain and the United States from the 1900s to the 1930s. In France it is spelled Irène. Several Saints Irene exist, so the feast day varies by calendar.

irenee.label: Irénée
irenee.text: A French name, particularly found around Lyon, and mostly given in the 19th century. It honours Saint Irenaeus, 2nd-century bishop of Lyon and Doctor of the Church, whose feast is 28 June.

ireneusz.label: Ireneusz
ireneusz.meaning: Polish form of Irenaeus, from Greek "Eirênaios", "peaceful".
ireneusz.text: A Polish name rare in older records that became very widespread among men born in the 1950s to 1970s. Its name day is notably 28 June, the feast of Saint Irenaeus of Lyon.

iris.label: Iris
iris.meaning: From Greek "Iris", messenger of the gods and personification of the rainbow, also the name of the flower.
iris.text: A name that appeared in the late 19th century with the fashion for flower names, mainly in Britain, where it was very common in the 1920s and 1930s. It is rare in earlier records.

irma.label: Irma
irma.meaning: Short form of Germanic names in "Irm-" (Irmgard, Irmtraud), from "irmin", "great, universal".
irma.text: A name that became fashionable in the late 19th century in Germany, Switzerland, Belgium, France and Italy, and fairly frequent among women born before 1900. The original full name (Irmgard, Irmine) may appear in other records.

irmgard.label: Irmgard
irmgard.text: A medieval German name, borne by women of the Carolingian nobility (Ermengarde), then revived in Germany in the early 20th century. Older records also write it Irmengard or Ermgard.

irving.label: Irving
irving.meaning: From a Scottish surname taken from a place name (Irvine), of disputed Celtic origin.
irving.text: A Scottish surname that became a given name in the 19th century, mainly in the United States, where it was frequent in the early 20th century, notably in immigrant families from Central and Eastern Europe. It also appears as Irvin or Irwin.

isaac.label: Isaac
isaac.text: The name of the biblical patriarch, son of Abraham, widely borne in Jewish communities across Europe and among Protestants in the Netherlands, Switzerland, England and North America. The records give many spellings: Isack, Izaak, Isaak. It is not tied to a widely kept saint's feast in the West.

isabel.label: Isabel
isabel.meaning: Iberian form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "God is my oath".
isabel.text: A name very widespread in Spain and Portugal since the Middle Ages, borne by many queens; it passed to England and Scotland, where Isobel is found. Its name day is 4 July, the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Portugal (the "Rainha Santa Isabel").

isabella.label: Isabella
isabella.meaning: Italian and Latinised form of Isabel, itself a form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "God is my oath".
isabella.text: A name common in Italy since the Renaissance and used as the Latin form of Isabelle in records from Belgium and the Netherlands; it is also in use in England. Like other forms of Elizabeth, its name day is often 4 July, the feast of Saint Elizabeth of Portugal.

isabelle.label: Isabelle
isabelle.meaning: French form of Isabel, itself a form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "God is my oath".
isabelle.text: A name borne in princely families in the Middle Ages, common in France, Belgium and Switzerland under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century, then extremely popular in France in the mid-20th century. Older records also write it Ysabeau or Ysabelle. Its name day is 22 February, the feast of Blessed Isabelle of France, sister of Saint Louis.

isidore.label: Isidore
isidore.text: A name widespread in France and Belgium in the 19th century, especially in the countryside; it also occurs in Jewish communities across Europe. Latin records write it Isidorus. Its name day is 4 April, the feast of Saint Isidore of Seville, bishop and Doctor of the Church.

isidoro.label: Isidoro
isidoro.meaning: Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Isidore, from Greek "Isidôros", "gift of Isis".
isidoro.text: A name common in Spain, Portugal and Italy, mostly among men born before 1950. It honours Saint Isidore of Seville, 7th-century bishop and Doctor of the Church, whose feast is 4 April; in Spain the popular form Isidro rather refers to Saint Isidore the Farmer.

isidro.label: Isidro
isidro.meaning: Popular Spanish form of Isidore, from Greek "Isidôros", "gift of Isis".
isidro.text: A Spanish name very common in the countryside, linked to Saint Isidore the Farmer, patron of Madrid and of farmers, whose feast is 15 May. The Catalan form is Isidre, and the spelling Ysidro also occurs.

ismael.label: Ismael
ismael.text: A biblical name, that of the son of Abraham and Hagar, found in Spain since the Middle Ages and in France in the 19th century, as well as in Jewish communities and among some Protestants. It was mainly widespread in Spain in the late 20th century.

itala.label: Itala
itala.meaning: Feminine of Italo, from Latin "Italus", "Italian", the name of a legendary king.
itala.text: An Italian patriotic name that appeared after the country's unification (1861) and was mostly given in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is absent from earlier records.

italia.label: Italia
italia.meaning: From the name of Italy, Latin "Italia".
italia.text: A patriotic name given in Italy after unification (1861), mostly in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and also among Italian emigrants. It is practically absent from earlier records.

italo.label: Italo
italo.meaning: From Latin "Italus", "Italian", the name of a legendary king said to have given his name to Italy.
italo.text: An Italian patriotic name that spread after unification (1861), mostly among men born between 1880 and 1940. It is rare in older records.

ivan.label: Ivan
ivan.meaning: Slavic form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
ivan.text: The Russian, Ukrainian and South Slavic form of John, found in Poland mainly in the eastern regions and spread to Western Europe in the 20th century (Yvan in France, Iván in Spain). Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

ivo.label: Ivo
ivo.meaning: From Germanic "iv", "yew" (the tree used to make bows).
ivo.text: The Latin and Italian form of Yves, borne in Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy and Germany; in Latin records it often corresponds to French Yves. Its name day is 19 May, the feast of Saint Ivo of Kermartin, a 13th-century Breton priest and patron saint of lawyers.

ivor.label: Ivor
ivor.meaning: From Welsh "Ifor" or Old Norse "Ívarr", of disputed meaning ("lord" or "yew-bow warrior").
ivor.text: A mainly Welsh name, revived in Wales in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and found elsewhere in Britain. Welsh records also give the form Ifor.

ivy.label: Ivy
ivy.text: An English name from the late 19th-century wave of plant names, among the most given in England around 1900. It is practically absent from records before 1870.

izabela.label: Izabela
izabela.meaning: Polish form of Isabella, itself a form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheva", "God is my oath".
izabela.text: A name borne by the Polish nobility from the 18th century, then very widespread in Poland in the second half of the 20th century, often shortened to Iza. In older records the same woman may be entered as Elżbieta or the Latin Elisabetha; the feast day varies by calendar.

izrael.label: Izrael
izrael.text: The name given to Jacob in the Bible, very frequent among the Jews of Poland in the 19th century. Polish records write Izrael or the shortened Yiddish form Srul.

jacek.label: Jacek
jacek.meaning: Polish form of Hyacinth, from Greek "hyakinthos", the hyacinth flower.
jacek.text: An old Polish name, linked to Saint Hyacinth (Jacek Odrowąż), a 13th-century Dominican and apostle of Poland, whose feast is 17 August. In Latin records it appears as Hyacinthus, and sometimes as Jacenty. It became very widespread in Poland in the second half of the 20th century.

jacinta.label: Jacinta
jacinta.meaning: Spanish feminine of Jacinto, from Greek "hyakinthos", the hyacinth flower.
jacinta.text: A Spanish and Portuguese female name, mostly borne by women born before 1950. Its name day is 30 January, the feast of Saint Hyacintha Mariscotti, an Italian Franciscan nun.

jacinto.label: Jacinto
jacinto.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Hyacinth, from Greek "hyakinthos", the hyacinth flower.
jacinto.text: A name common in Portugal and Spain in 18th- and 19th-century records, and today borne mostly by men born before 1960. Its name day is 17 August, the feast of Saint Hyacinth of Poland, a Dominican preacher.

jackie.label: Jackie
jackie.meaning: English pet form of Jack (John) or Jacqueline, sharing their Hebrew origin.
jackie.text: A unisex 20th-century name, given to boys and girls alike in the United States and Britain, and in France mostly as a pet form of Jacques or Jacqueline (Jacky). It is practically absent from older records.

jacob.label: Jacob
jacob.meaning: From Hebrew "Ya'aqov", often interpreted as "he who holds the heel" or "may God protect".
jacob.text: The name of the biblical patriarch, very widespread in the Netherlands, Switzerland, Germany and Belgium, among Protestants and Catholics alike, as well as in Jewish communities. Latin records write it Jacobus, and it is often shortened to Jaap in the Netherlands. In Catholic areas its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint James the Greater, whose original name is Jacob.

jacoba.label: Jacoba
jacoba.meaning: Dutch feminine of Jacob, from Hebrew "Ya'aqov".
jacoba.text: A female name very common in the Netherlands and Flanders from the 17th to the 19th century, often shortened to Coba, Co or Jaapje. In the records it alternates with Jacomina or Jacobina for the same woman.

jacobee.label: Jacobée
jacobee.text: An old feminine form of Jacques, found in French registers mostly before the 18th century. It recalls Mary Jacobe, one of the Holy Marys venerated at Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer.

jacobus.label: Jacobus
jacobus.meaning: Latin form of James and Jacob, from Hebrew "Ya'aqov".
jacobus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic records throughout Europe, and also an everyday name in the Netherlands and Flanders, where it remains common in 19th-century civil registration. The same man may appear elsewhere as Jacques, Jacob, Jaak or Koos. Its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint James the Greater.

jacopo.label: Jacopo
jacopo.meaning: Old Italian form of James, from Hebrew "Ya'aqov".
jacopo.text: The Tuscan and medieval form of the name, frequent in Florence and central Italy, alternating with Giacomo and also written Iacopo. Its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint James the Greater.

jacqueline.label: Jacqueline
jacqueline.text: A female name borne from the Middle Ages (Jacqueline of Bavaria, Countess of Hainaut), then extremely popular in France, Belgium and the Netherlands in the 1920s to 1950s; it is also found in Britain and the United States. The French calendar marks it on 8 February, the feast of Blessed Jacoba of Settesoli, a disciple of Saint Francis of Assisi.

jacquemine.label: Jacquemine
jacquemine.meaning: Feminine of Jacquemin, a diminutive of Jacques.
jacquemine.text: A feminine form of Jacquemin, frequent in Lorraine, Champagne and northern France in the 16th and 17th centuries. Records also spell it Jacmine.

jacques.label: Jacques
jacques.meaning: From Hebrew "Ya'aqov" through Latin "Jacobus", often interpreted as "he who holds the heel" or "may God protect".
jacques.text: A name very widespread in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland since the Middle Ages, spurred by the pilgrimage to Compostela, and extremely popular in the mid-20th century. Latin records write it Jacobus. Its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint James the Greater.

jacquette.label: Jacquette
jacquette.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Jacques, from Hebrew "Yaakov".
jacquette.text: A feminine form of Jacques, frequent in French registers from the 15th to the 17th century. Records also spell it Jaquette.

jacquine.label: Jacquine
jacquine.text: A feminine form of Jacques found in French registers under the Ancien Régime, before it was superseded by Jacqueline.

jadwiga.label: Jadwiga
jadwiga.meaning: Polish form of Hedwig, from Germanic "hadu", "battle", and "wig", "battle".
jadwiga.text: A very widespread Polish female name, borne by Queen Jadwiga (Hedwig of Anjou) in the 14th century and frequent in records of every period. In Latin records it appears as Hedvigis. Its name day is 16 October, the feast of Saint Hedwig of Silesia.

jaime.label: Jaime
jaime.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of James, from Hebrew "Ya'aqov".
jaime.text: An Iberian name borne by kings of Aragon (James I the Conqueror), common in Spain and Portugal and formerly spelled Jayme. It coexists with Santiago and Diego, other forms derived from the same name. Its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint James the Greater.

jakob.label: Jakob
jakob.meaning: German form of Jacob and James, from Hebrew "Ya'aqov".
jakob.text: A name very common in Germany, Switzerland and Austria from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, among Catholics and Protestants alike, and also among German speakers in Poland. Latin records write it Jacobus. Its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint James the Greater.

jakub.label: Jakub
jakub.meaning: Polish and Czech form of James, from Hebrew "Ya'aqov".
jakub.text: A Polish name found in records of every period, Latinised as Jacobus, and very widespread again in the late 20th century; its familiar form is Kuba. Its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint James the Greater.

james.label: James
james.meaning: English form of Jacques and Jacob, from Hebrew "Ya'aqov" through Late Latin "Jacomus".
james.text: One of the most frequent male names in England, Scotland, Ireland and the United States, borne by the Stuart kings, and among the most given in Britain in the early 20th century; familiar forms are Jim, Jimmy or Jamie. In France, James is a name borrowed from English, mostly in the 19th century. Its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint James the Greater.

jan.label: Jan
jan.meaning: Dutch, Polish, Czech and Scandinavian form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
jan.text: One of the most widespread names of northern and Central Europe: extremely frequent in the Netherlands, Flanders and Poland, where it is among the most borne male names. Latin records write it Joannes or Johannes, and it appears in compounds (Jan Baptist, Jan Willem). Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

jane.label: Jane
jane.meaning: English form of Jeanne, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
jane.text: An English name that appeared in the 16th century (Jane Seymour, Jane Grey), gradually displacing Joan and becoming very common in Britain and the United States; it is often borne as a middle name. In France, Jane is a rarer borrowed form. Its name day is 12 August, the feast of Saint Jane Frances de Chantal.

janet.label: Janet
janet.meaning: Scottish and English diminutive of Jane or Jean, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
janet.text: A very old name in Scotland, where it also appears as Jonet or Jennet in parish registers, then very widespread in Britain and the United States in the mid-20th century. It corresponds to French Jeannette.

janice.label: Janice
janice.meaning: Modern English derivative of Jane, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
janice.text: A name that appeared in the late 19th century, mostly widespread in the United States and Britain between the 1930s and 1960s. It is absent from older records.

janina.label: Janina
janina.meaning: Polish feminine of Jan, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
janina.text: A Polish female name extremely widespread in the 20th century, especially among women born between the 1910s and 1950s, and rarer in earlier records, where Joanna is more usual. It is shortened to Janka or Janeczka.

janine.label: Janine
janine.meaning: French diminutive of Jeanne, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
janine.text: A 20th-century French female name, mostly given between the 1920s and 1950s; it is also spelled Jeannine. It is rare in earlier records.

jankiel.label: Jankiel
jankiel.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Yankl, a diminutive of Jacob, frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. The same man may be called Jankiel or Jakub in different entries.

janusz.label: Janusz
janusz.meaning: Polish derivative of Jan (John), from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
janusz.text: An old Polish name, borne by medieval dukes of Masovia, then very widespread among men born between the 1930s and 1960s. It should not be confused with Januariusz (Januarius), despite the resemblance.

jaroslaw.label: Jarosław
jaroslaw.text: An old Slavic name, borne by princes of medieval Rus', rare in Polish records before the 20th century, then very widespread among men born between the 1950s and 1970s. It also occurs as Jaroslav or Yaroslav.

jaume.label: Jaume
jaume.meaning: Catalan form of James, from Hebrew "Ya'aqov".
jaume.text: A Catalan name very widespread since the Middle Ages, borne by King James I of Aragon, and common in Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands. In Castilian records the same man may be entered as Jaime. Its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint James the Greater.

javier.label: Javier
javier.meaning: From the Basque place name "Etxeberri", "new house", the name of Saint Francis Xavier's birthplace castle.
javier.text: A Spanish name born of the cult of Saint Francis Xavier, the Navarrese Jesuit missionary, first borne as a second element (Francisco Javier) and then alone; the Basque form is Xabier. It was very widespread in Spain in the 20th century. Its name day is 3 December, the feast of Saint Francis Xavier.

jay.label: Jay
jay.meaning: Short form of names beginning with J (James, Jason), or from English "jay", the bird; the meaning is disputed.
jay.text: A mainly American name, borne in the 19th and 20th centuries and very common in the mid-20th century. It often appears as a short form of a full name that other records may reveal.

jean.label: Jean
jean.text: Borne by both Saint John the Baptist and Saint John the Evangelist, this was the most common male given name in France for centuries, alone or in compound forms (Jean-Baptiste, Jean-Pierre, Jean-Marie).

jean_baptiste.label: Jean-Baptiste
jean_baptiste.meaning: Compound name: Jean, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious", and Baptiste, from Greek "baptistês", "one who baptises".
jean_baptiste.text: A compound name extremely frequent in France, Belgium and Luxembourg from the 17th to the 19th century, often written without a hyphen or abbreviated "J. Bte" in the records. It appears in Flemish (Jan Baptist), German (Johann Baptist) and Latin (Joannes Baptista). Its name day is 24 June, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist.

jean_pierre.label: Jean-Pierre
jean_pierre.meaning: Compound name: Jean, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious", and Pierre, from Greek "petros", "stone, rock".
jean_pierre.text: A compound name frequent in Luxembourg and Lorraine from the 18th century, then extremely popular throughout France in the mid-20th century. In older records it is often written without a hyphen, or even as one word, and the bearer may appear elsewhere simply as Jean or Pierre.

jeanette.label: Jeanette
jeanette.meaning: Diminutive of Jeanne, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
jeanette.text: A single-n spelling of Jeannette, mainly widespread in Germany, the Netherlands, Britain and the United States, where it was frequent in the 1920s to 1940s. Like Jeanne, its name day is 30 May, the feast of Saint Joan of Arc.

jeanne.label: Jeanne
jeanne.meaning: Feminine form of Jean, "God is gracious".
jeanne.text: Popularised in particular by Joan of Arc (Jeanne d'Arc), this female name is common in French records from the 14th century onward, with several regional variants (Jehanne, Jeannette).

jeannette.label: Jeannette
jeannette.meaning: French diminutive of Jeanne, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
jeannette.text: A diminutive of Jeanne used since the Middle Ages (Joan of Arc was called Jeannette in her village), which became a name in its own right in the 19th and 20th centuries in France, Belgium and the Netherlands. Its name day is 30 May, the feast of Saint Joan of Arc.

jeannine.label: Jeannine
jeannine.meaning: French diminutive of Jeanne, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
jeannine.text: A 20th-century French female name, widely given between the 1920s and 1950s, also spelled Jeanine or Janine. It is rare in earlier records.

jechiel.label: Jechiel
jechiel.text: A Jewish name frequent in 19th-century Poland, often shortened to Chil in civil records. The same man may appear under both forms.

jeffrey.label: Jeffrey
jeffrey.meaning: English form of Geoffrey, of disputed Germanic origin: "gawia", "territory", or "god", "god", combined with "fridu", "peace".
jeffrey.text: A name brought to England by the Normans (Geoffrey), then very widespread in the United States in the mid-20th century under the spelling Jeffrey or Jeffery. It is often confused with German Gottfried, to which it is close without being identical.

jennie.label: Jennie
jennie.meaning: English pet form of Jane or Janet, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
jennie.text: A pet form that became an official name in the United States and Britain in the late 19th century, very frequent around 1880-1910. The full name (Jane, Janet) may appear in other records of the same woman.

jennifer.label: Jennifer
jennifer.meaning: Cornish form of Guinevere, from Welsh "Gwenhwyfar", often interpreted as "white, shining".
jennifer.text: A name long confined to Cornwall, spread in Britain in the early 20th century and very popular by the 1940s, then in the United States. It is rare in records before 1900.

jenny.label: Jenny
jenny.meaning: Pet form of Jeanne, Johanna or Jane, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
jenny.text: A pet form common in English- and German-speaking countries, which became an official name in the 19th century in Switzerland, Germany, France and the Netherlands. The full name (Johanna, Jeanne, Jane) may appear in other records of the same woman.

jenta.label: Jenta
jenta.meaning: From Old French or Italian "gentile", "noble, gracious".
jenta.text: An old Yiddish name of Romance origin, written Jenta in 19th-century Polish records. The Yiddish form is Yente.

jeremias.label: Jeremias
jeremias.meaning: Latin and Germanic form of Jeremiah, from Hebrew "Yirmeyahu", "God exalts".
jeremias.text: The name of the biblical prophet, borne mostly among Protestants in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands in the 16th to 18th centuries, and also in Latin Catholic records. The English and French forms are Jeremiah and Jérémie.

jeremie.label: Jérémie
jeremie.text: The name of the prophet Jeremiah, celebrated on 1 May, found in both Protestant and Catholic registers under the Ancien Régime. The spelling Jérémy spread in France in the 1980s and 1990s.

jerome.label: Jérôme
jerome.text: A French name found in records of every period, written Hieronymus in Latin records, then very popular in France in the 1960s to 1980s; it was also common in the United States in the mid-20th century. Its name day is 30 September, the feast of Saint Jerome, translator of the Bible into Latin.

jeronimo.label: Jerónimo
jeronimo.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Jerome, from Greek "hieros", "holy", and "onoma", "name".
jeronimo.text: A name common in Spain and Portugal since the 16th century, often linked to the Hieronymite order. Its name day is 30 September, the feast of Saint Jerome.

jerry.label: Jerry
jerry.meaning: English pet form of Gerald, Gerard or Jeremiah, whose origin it shares.
jerry.text: A pet form that became a name in its own right in the United States, very frequent in the 1930s to 1950s. The original full name may appear in other records.

jerzy.label: Jerzy
jerzy.meaning: Polish form of George, from Greek "geôrgos", "farmer, tiller of the soil".
jerzy.text: A Polish name borne by the nobility since the 16th century, found in records under the Latin form Georgius, then very widespread in the 20th century, especially among men born between the 1920s and 1950s. Its name day is 23 April, the feast of Saint George.

jesse.label: Jesse
jesse.meaning: From Hebrew "Yishay", of disputed meaning, often understood as "gift".
jesse.text: A biblical name, that of King David's father, adopted by English-speaking Protestants and frequent in the United States in the 19th century. In France its form is Jessé, rare in the records.

jessie.label: Jessie
jessie.meaning: Scottish pet form of Janet (Jean), from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious"; sometimes also of Jessica.
jessie.text: A name very common in Scotland in the 18th and 19th centuries, where the same woman may be entered as Janet or Jessie depending on the record, then widespread in England and the United States around 1880-1920. It is also borne by men in the United States as a variant of Jesse.

jesuina.label: Jesuína
jesuina.meaning: Portuguese devotional name derived from Jesus, from Hebrew "Yehoshua", "God saves".
jesuina.text: An uncommon Portuguese female name, found mainly in 19th- and early 20th-century records in Portugal and Brazil. It does not correspond to any particular saint.

jesus.label: Jesús
jesus.text: A devotional name very widespread in Spain and Latin America, whereas it is avoided out of reverence in most other Catholic countries. It is often borne in compounds (Jesús María, José de Jesús); the Galician form is Xesús.

jesusa.label: Jesusa
jesusa.meaning: Spanish feminine of Jesús, from Hebrew "Yehoshua", "God saves".
jesusa.text: A Spanish devotional female name, mostly borne by women born in the first half of the 20th century. It does not correspond to any particular saint.

jette.label: Jette
jette.meaning: Danish and Low German pet form of Henriette, from Germanic "heim", "home", and "ric", "powerful".
jette.text: A pet form used in Denmark and northern Germany, sometimes entered as the official name in the 19th century. The same woman may appear elsewhere as Henriette.

jill.label: Jill
jill.meaning: Short form of Gillian, itself from Juliana, from Latin "Julius".
jill.text: An old English name (the nursery rhyme "Jack and Jill"), common again in Britain and the United States in the mid-20th century. It is rare in 18th- and 19th-century records.

jo.label: Jo
jo.meaning: Short form of names beginning with Jo- (Joanna, Josephine, Johanna, Joseph), whose origin it shares.
jo.text: A unisex pet form, borne by women and men alike, and sometimes entered as the official name in the United States and the Netherlands in the 20th century. It is often combined (Mary Jo, Jo Ann).

joachim.label: Joachim
joachim.meaning: From Hebrew "Yehoyaqim", "God raises up" or "God establishes".
joachim.text: A name widespread in German-speaking lands and Poland, and found in France, notably in Alsace and Lorraine; the German short forms are Jochen and Achim. Its name day is 26 July, together with Saint Anne, the feast of Saint Joachim, father of the Virgin Mary.

joan.label: Joan
joan.meaning: From Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious": a female form in English, a male form in Catalan.
joan.text: Beware of sex: in English, Joan is a female name (Jeanne), common in the Middle Ages and very popular again in Britain and the United States in the 1920s and 1930s; in Catalan, Joan is the male form of John, very frequent in Catalonia, the Balearic Islands and Valencia. The name day therefore depends on the bearer: Saint Joan of Arc (30 May) or Saint John the Baptist (24 June).

joana.label: Joana
joana.meaning: Portuguese, Catalan and Occitan form of Jeanne, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
joana.text: A female name very common in Portugal since the Middle Ages, and found in Catalonia and Occitania. In Portugal it also recalls Blessed Joan of Portugal, the princess of Aveiro. Its name day is generally 30 May, the feast of Saint Joan of Arc.

joanes.label: Joanes
joanes.meaning: Basque form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
joanes.text: A Basque name in use on both sides of the Pyrenees, in records from the French and Spanish Basque Country, where the same person may be entered as Jean or Juan. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

joanna.label: Joanna
joanna.meaning: Latin, Polish and English form of Joan, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
joanna.text: The Latin form used in Catholic records in Belgium and the Netherlands, and a very widespread everyday name in Poland, especially in the second half of the 20th century; it also occurs in England. Poland has several name days for it; the most usual elsewhere is 30 May, the feast of Saint Joan of Arc.

joanne.label: Joanne
joanne.meaning: English form of Johanna, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
joanne.text: A name mainly widespread in the United States and Britain in the mid-20th century, also spelled Joann or Jo Anne. It is rare in earlier records.

joannes.label: Joannes
joannes.meaning: Latin form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
joannes.text: A Latin form extremely frequent in Catholic records across Europe, especially in Belgium, the Netherlands, France and Poland, alone or in compounds (Joannes Baptista). The same man may appear elsewhere as Jean, Jan, Johann or Juan depending on the language of the record. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

joanny.label: Joanny
joanny.meaning: Regional form of Jean, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
joanny.text: A form typical of the Lyon area, Forez and Beaujolais, frequent in the 19th century, where the same person may be entered as Jean in other records. It is also borne by a few women. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

joao.label: João
joao.meaning: Portuguese form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
joao.text: The most widespread male name in Portugal for centuries, borne by many kings, alone or in compounds (João Baptista, João Maria). Latin records write it Joannes. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist, which is very popular in Portugal.

joaquim.label: Joaquim
joaquim.meaning: Portuguese and Catalan form of Joachim, from Hebrew "Yehoyaqim", "God raises up".
joaquim.text: A name very common in Portugal and Catalonia in the 18th and 19th centuries, often shortened to Quim in Catalan. Its name day is 26 July, the feast of Saint Joachim, father of the Virgin Mary.

joaquin.label: Joaquín
joaquin.meaning: Spanish form of Joachim, from Hebrew "Yehoyaqim", "God raises up".
joaquin.text: A very widespread Spanish name, mostly among men born before 1960, with regional forms (Xoaquín in Galician, Jokin in Basque). Its name day is 26 July, the feast of Saint Joachim, father of the Virgin Mary.

joaquina.label: Joaquina
joaquina.meaning: Spanish feminine of Joaquín, from Hebrew "Yehoyaqim", "God raises up".
joaquina.text: A Spanish female name common in the 18th and 19th centuries, today mostly borne by women born before 1950; the Catalan form is Joaquima. It is sometimes shortened to Quina.

jocelyne.label: Jocelyne
jocelyne.meaning: Feminine of Jocelyn (Josselin), from a Germanic name "Gauzelin", derived from the tribal name of the Geats; the meaning is disputed.
jocelyne.text: A 20th-century French female name, mostly given between the 1940s and 1960s, and practically absent from earlier records. It has many spellings: Joceline, Josseline, Jocelyne.

jock.label: Jock
jock.meaning: Scottish pet form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
jock.text: A familiar Scottish form of John, equivalent to English Jack, sometimes entered as such in records. The same man usually appears as John in official documents.

joel.label: Joel
joel.text: The name of the biblical prophet, borne among Protestants and in Jewish communities, and common in France in the 1940s to 1960s (Joël). It also spread in English-speaking and Iberian countries in the late 20th century. Its feast day varies by calendar.

joelle.label: Joëlle
joelle.meaning: Feminine of Joël, from Hebrew "Yo'el", "Yahweh is God".
joelle.text: A 20th-century French female name, mostly given between the 1940s and 1960s, and absent from older records. It is not tied to any particular saint.

johan.label: Johan
johan.meaning: Dutch, Scandinavian and German form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
johan.text: A name common in the Netherlands, Flanders, Scandinavia and Luxembourg, often in compounds (Johan Hendrik, Johan Frederik). In the records it alternates with Johannes, Jan or Johann. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

johann.label: Johann
johann.meaning: German form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
johann.text: The most widespread male name in German-speaking lands from the 16th to the 19th century, very often the first element of a compound (Johann Georg, Johann Friedrich) in which the second name was the one used. It alternates with Johannes, Hans or the Latin Joannes. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

johanna.label: Johanna
johanna.meaning: Latin and Germanic form of Joan, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
johanna.text: A female name very widespread in the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland and Flanders, often under pet forms: Hanna, Hanne, Jannetje, Anna or Hannie. It also serves as the Latin form of Jeanne in Catholic records. Its name day is often 30 May, the feast of Saint Joan of Arc.

johanne.label: Johanne
johanne.meaning: German, Scandinavian and French form of Johanna, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
johanne.text: A form in use in northern Germany, Denmark and Norway, and more rarely in France and Quebec. It alternates with Johanna in the records for the same woman. Its name day is often 30 May, the feast of Saint Joan of Arc.

johannes.label: Johannes
johannes.meaning: Latin and Germanic form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
johannes.text: A form extremely frequent in records from the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland and Flanders, as an everyday name and as a Latin form. It gave many short forms: Hans, Jan, Johan, Hannes, Joop. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

john.label: John
john.meaning: English form of Jean, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
john.text: The most widespread male name in England, Scotland, Ireland and the United States from the Middle Ages to the mid-20th century, and a poor identifier on its own. Its familiar forms are Jack, Johnny or Jock in Scotland; in Ireland and Wales it renders Seán and Ieuan. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

jonas.label: Jonas
jonas.text: The name of the biblical prophet, found in Protestant records from Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Scandinavia since the 16th century, as well as in Jewish communities. It is also very common in Lithuania (where Jonas is the form of John).

jonathan.label: Jonathan
jonathan.text: A biblical name, that of King Saul's son and David's friend, adopted by English Puritans and frequent in New England from the 17th to the 19th century. In continental Europe it mostly spread in the late 20th century.

joost.label: Joost
joost.meaning: Dutch form of Josse, from Breton "Iodoc", derived from "iud", "lord" or "battle"; the meaning is disputed.
joost.text: An old Dutch and Flemish name, frequent in the 16th and 17th centuries, Latinised as Judocus in the records and corresponding to French Josse. It honours Saint Judoc (Josse), a 7th-century Breton hermit settled in Ponthieu, whose feast is 13 December.

jordane.label: Jordane
jordane.meaning: Feminine of Jordan, from the name of the river Jordan.
jordane.text: A modern name, mostly given in France in the 1980s and 1990s. It is absent from older registers.

jordi.label: Jordi
jordi.meaning: Catalan form of George, from Greek "geôrgos", "farmer, tiller of the soil".
jordi.text: A Catalan name linked to Saint George, patron of Catalonia, whose feast is 23 April (Sant Jordi). Rare in older records, where the Castilian form Jorge is often used, it became very widespread in Catalonia in the second half of the 20th century.

jorge.label: Jorge
jorge.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of George, from Greek "geôrgos", "farmer, tiller of the soil".
jorge.text: A name common in Spain and Portugal since the Middle Ages, in all social classes, and very widespread in the 20th century. Its name day is 23 April, the feast of Saint George the martyr.

jos.label: Jos
jos.meaning: Dutch and Luxembourgish short form of Joseph or Josse, whose origin it shares.
jos.text: A pet form common in Luxembourg, Flanders and the Netherlands in the 19th and 20th centuries, sometimes entered as the official name. The full name (Joseph, Jozef, Josephus) often appears in other records of the same person.

jose.label: José
jose.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
jose.text: The most widespread male name in Spain and one of the most frequent in Portugal since the 18th century, very often in compounds (José María, José Antonio, José Luis). Familiar forms are Pepe in Spanish and Zé in Portuguese; in France and Belgium, José may also be a pet form of Joseph or Joséphine. Its name day is 19 March, the feast of Saint Joseph.

jose_antonio.label: José Antonio
jose_antonio.meaning: Compound name: José, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add", and Antonio, from Latin "Antonius", the name of a Roman family.
jose_antonio.text: One of the most widespread compound names in Spain, especially among men born in the 20th century; the Catalan form is Josep Antoni. In the records the bearer may appear elsewhere simply as José or Antonio.

jose_luis.label: José Luis
jose_luis.meaning: Compound name: José, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add", and Luis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
jose_luis.text: A compound name very widespread in Spain in the 20th century, especially among men born between the 1940s and 1970s, and rarer in older records. The Catalan form is Josep Lluís.

jose_manuel.label: José Manuel
jose_manuel.meaning: Compound name: José, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add", and Manuel, from Hebrew "Immanu El", "God is with us".
jose_manuel.text: A compound name common in Spain and Portugal, especially in the 20th century; the Catalan form is Josep Manuel. The bearer may appear elsewhere simply as José or Manuel.

jose_maria.label: José María
jose_maria.meaning: Compound name: José, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add", and María, from Hebrew "Miryam".
jose_maria.text: A male devotional compound name, joining Saint Joseph and the Virgin Mary, very widespread in Spain and Portugal since the 18th century; it should not be confused with the female María José. It appears in Catalan (Josep Maria), Basque (Joxe Mari) and Latin (Josephus Maria).

josef.label: Josef
josef.meaning: German and Central European form of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josef.text: A name very widespread in the Catholic German-speaking regions (Bavaria, Austria, Switzerland), Bohemia and Luxembourg, especially from the 18th century and the reign of Emperor Joseph II. Familiar forms are Sepp, Seppl or Jupp. Its name day is 19 March, the feast of Saint Joseph.

josefa.label: Josefa
josefa.meaning: Spanish and Germanic feminine of José or Josef, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josefa.text: A female name extremely widespread in Spain in the 18th and 19th centuries, often under the familiar forms Pepa or Pepita; it also occurs in southern Germany, Switzerland and Portugal. In the records it alternates with Josepha, the Latin form.

josefina.label: Josefina
josefina.meaning: Spanish form of Joséphine, feminine diminutive of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josefina.text: A Spanish name widespread in the 19th and early 20th centuries, in Spain and Latin America, and mostly borne by women born before 1960. It sometimes alternates with Josefa for the same woman.

josek.label: Josek
josek.meaning: A Yiddish diminutive of Joseph, "God will add".
josek.text: The form in which 19th-century Polish records register Yiddish Yosl, a diminutive of Joseph. The same man may be called Josek or Józef in different entries.

josep.label: Josep
josep.meaning: Catalan form of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josep.text: One of the most widespread male names in Catalonia, the Balearic Islands and Roussillon since the 18th century, often in compounds (Josep Maria). In Castilian or French records the same man may appear as José or Joseph. Its name day is 19 March, the feast of Saint Joseph.

josepa.label: Josepa
josepa.meaning: Catalan feminine of Josep, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josepa.text: A Catalan female name frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries, today mostly borne by women born before 1950. In Castilian records the same woman often appears as Josefa.

joseph.label: Joseph
joseph.text: The name of the husband of the Virgin Mary, whose cult grew from the 17th century, it became one of the most frequent male names in France, Belgium and Luxembourg in the 18th and 19th centuries, often in compounds (Jean-Joseph, Joseph-Marie). Latin records write it Josephus. Its name day is 19 March, the feast of Saint Joseph.

josepha.label: Josepha
josepha.meaning: Latin feminine form of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josepha.text: A Latin form used in Catholic records in Belgium, Germany and Spain, and an everyday name in southern Germany and Austria. The same woman may appear elsewhere as Josèphe, Josefa or Joséphine.

josephe.label: Josèphe
josephe.meaning: French feminine of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josephe.text: A French and Belgian female name mostly borne in compounds (Marie-Josèphe) in the 18th and 19th centuries. It alternates with Joséphine or the Latin Josepha for the same woman.

josephina.label: Josephina
josephina.meaning: Latinised form of Joséphine, feminine diminutive of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josephina.text: A form used in Catholic records in Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany, and as an everyday name in Flanders and Limburg in the 19th and 20th centuries. The same woman may appear elsewhere as Joséphine, Josepha or Fien.

josephine.label: Josephine
josephine.meaning: French feminine diminutive of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josephine.text: A name made famous by Empress Joséphine, wife of Napoleon, and very widespread in the 19th century in France, Belgium and Luxembourg, among the most given to girls born before 1900; it also occurs in the United States and Britain. It is spelled Josephine in German- and English-speaking countries and shortened to Fine, Jo or Josette.

josephus.label: Josephus
josephus.meaning: Latin form of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josephus.text: A Latin form very frequent in Catholic records in Belgium and the Netherlands, and sometimes kept in Flemish and Dutch civil registration. The same man may appear elsewhere as Joseph, Jozef or Jos. Its name day is 19 March, the feast of Saint Joseph.

josette.label: Josette
josette.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josette.text: A diminutive of Joséphine that became a name in its own right in France in the 20th century, mostly given between the 1930s and 1950s. It is rare in earlier records, where the same woman would be entered as Joséphine.

joshua.label: Joshua
joshua.meaning: From Hebrew "Yehoshua", "God saves", the same name as Jesus.
joshua.text: The name of Moses's successor, adopted by English Puritans and found in England and North America from the 17th to the 19th century. It only became common in the late 20th century; in France its form is Josué.

josiah.label: Josiah
josiah.meaning: From Hebrew "Yoshiyahu", "God supports" or "God heals"; the meaning is disputed.
josiah.text: The name of the reforming king of Judah, adopted by Puritans and frequent in England and New England from the 17th to the 19th century. It is also spelled Josias.

josiane.label: Josiane
josiane.meaning: Feminine derivative of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
josiane.text: A 20th-century French female name, mostly given between the 1940s and 1960s, and absent from older records. It is not tied to any particular saint.

josselin.label: Josselin
josselin.meaning: From Germanic, through Latin "Joscelinus"; disputed meaning.
josselin.text: A medieval male name of Brittany and Normandy, also the name of the town of Josselin. It is distinct from the female Jocelyne, which has its own sheet.

joyce.label: Joyce
joyce.meaning: From Breton "Iodoc" (Saint Judoc), derived from "iud", "lord" or "battle"; the meaning is disputed.
joyce.text: A name first masculine in medieval England, whence the surname Joyce, which later became feminine; it was very popular in England and the United States in the 1920s to 1940s. It is rare in records before 1880.

jozef.label: Józef
jozef.meaning: Polish, Slovak and Flemish form of Joseph, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
jozef.text: One of the most widespread male names in Poland in the 19th and 20th centuries (Józef), and very frequent in Flanders (Jozef); Latin records write it Josephus. Its name day is 19 March, the feast of Saint Joseph.

jozefa.label: Józefa
jozefa.meaning: Polish feminine of Józef, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
jozefa.text: A Polish female name very widespread in the 19th and early 20th centuries, especially in the countryside. In Latin records it appears as Josepha.

juan.label: Juan
juan.meaning: Spanish form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
juan.text: One of the most widespread male names in Spain since the Middle Ages, alone or in compounds (Juan José, Juan Antonio, Juan Bautista); the Galician form is Xoán, the Catalan Joan. Latin records write it Joannes. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

juan_antonio.label: Juan Antonio
juan_antonio.meaning: Compound name: Juan, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious", and Antonio, from Latin "Antonius", the name of a Roman family.
juan_antonio.text: A compound name common in Spain since the 18th century and very widespread in the 20th century; the Catalan form is Joan Antoni. The bearer may appear elsewhere simply as Juan or Antonio.

juan_carlos.label: Juan Carlos
juan_carlos.meaning: Compound name: Juan, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious", and Carlos, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
juan_carlos.text: A compound name rare in older records that became very widespread in Spain and Latin America in the second half of the 20th century. It corresponds to French Jean-Charles.

juan_jose.label: Juan José
juan_jose.meaning: Compound name: Juan, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious", and José, from Hebrew "Yosef", "may God add".
juan_jose.text: A compound name common in Spain since the 18th century and very widespread in the 20th century; the Catalan and Galician forms are Joan Josep and Xoán Xosé. The bearer may appear elsewhere simply as Juan or José.

juana.label: Juana
juana.meaning: Spanish feminine of Juan, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
juana.text: A female name very widespread in Spain from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, borne by Queen Joanna the Mad, and today mostly by women born before 1960. The Galician form is Xoana. Its name day is often 30 May, the feast of Saint Joan of Arc.

juanes.label: Juanes
juanes.meaning: Basque and Navarrese form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
juanes.text: An old form found in records from the Basque Country and Navarre in the 16th to 18th centuries, where the same man may be entered as Juan or Joanes. Its name day is 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

juanita.label: Juanita
juanita.meaning: Spanish diminutive of Juana, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
juanita.text: A diminutive of Juana that became an official name, very widespread in the United States in the 1910s to 1930s, in Hispanic families and beyond. In Spain the same woman is often entered as Juana. Like Juana, its name day is often 30 May, the feast of Saint Joan of Arc.

juda.label: Juda
juda.text: The name of one of Jacob's sons, frequent among European Jews and often paired with Leib (Juda Leib). 19th-century Polish records write Juda or the diminutive Judka.

judicael.label: Judicaël
judicael.text: Saint Judicael, a 7th-century king of Domnonée, is celebrated on 17 December. The name is borne mostly in Brittany; sources write Judikael or Judhael.

judith.label: Judith
judith.text: The name of the biblical heroine of the Book of Judith, borne by Carolingian princesses, then common among Protestants in the Netherlands, Switzerland and England, and in Jewish communities. It was very widespread in the United States and Britain in the mid-20th century. The French calendar marks it on 5 May, the feast of Saint Jutta (Judith) of Kulmsee, patroness of Prussia.

judocus.label: Judocus
judocus.meaning: Latin form of Josse, from Breton "Iodoc", derived from "iud", "lord" or "battle"; the meaning is disputed.
judocus.text: A Latin form frequent in Catholic records from Flanders and northern France, for men called Josse, Joost or Joos in daily life. Its name day is 13 December, the feast of Saint Judoc (Josse), a 7th-century Breton hermit.

judy.label: Judy
judy.meaning: English pet form of Judith, from Hebrew "Yehudit", "woman of Judea".
judy.text: A pet form that became an official name in the United States, very frequent in the 1940s and 1950s. The full name Judith may appear in other records of the same woman.

jules.label: Jules
jules.meaning: From Latin "Julius", the name of Julius Caesar's Roman family.
jules.text: A name very fashionable in the 19th century in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and French-speaking Switzerland, among the most given to boys born before 1900. Latin records write it Julius. Its name day is 12 April, the feast of Pope Saint Julius I.

julia.label: Julia
julia.meaning: From Latin "Julia", the name of a great Roman family (gens Julia).
julia.text: The Latin and international form of the name, common in Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and English-speaking countries, and used in Catholic records for Julie. Its name day is 22 May, the feast of Saint Julia of Corsica, a martyr.

julian.label: Julian
julian.text: A name borne in Spain (Julián), Poland (Julian) and English-speaking countries, frequent in 18th- and 19th-century records; the French form is Julien. Several Saints Julian exist, so the feast day varies by region.

juliana.label: Juliana
juliana.meaning: Feminine of Julianus, from Latin, "of the Julii family".
juliana.text: A medieval name common in Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Spain and England (where it gave Gillian), and the Latin form of Julienne in the records. It honours Saint Juliana of Liège (of Cornillon), who inspired the feast of Corpus Christi, celebrated on 5 April.

juliane.label: Juliane
juliane.meaning: German form of Juliana, from Latin "Julianus", "of the Julii family".
juliane.text: A German name frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries, often shortened to Jule or Liane. In Germany its name day is 16 February, the feast of Saint Juliana of Nicomedia, a martyr.

julie.label: Julie
julie.meaning: French form of Julia, from Latin "Julia", the name of a great Roman family.
julie.text: A name very widespread in France, Belgium and Switzerland in the 19th century, among the most given to girls born before 1900, then very popular again in the late 20th century. Latin records write it Julia. The French calendar marks it on 8 April, the feast of Saint Julie Billiart, a Picard foundress who settled in Namur.

julien.label: Julien
julien.text: An old French name, linked to the cults of Saint Julian of Brioude and Saint Julian of Le Mans, common in records of every period and very popular in the late 20th century. Latin records write it Julianus. The French calendar marks it on 2 August, the feast of Saint Peter Julian Eymard.

julienne.label: Julienne
julienne.meaning: Feminine of Julien, from Latin "Julianus", "of the Julii family".
julienne.text: A female name very common in France and Belgium in the 18th and 19th centuries, among the most given to girls born before 1900. Latin records write it Juliana. Its name day is 16 February, the feast of Saint Juliana of Nicomedia, a martyr.

juliette.label: Juliette
juliette.meaning: French diminutive of Julie, from Latin "Julia", the name of a great Roman family.
juliette.text: A name widespread in France, Belgium, Switzerland and Luxembourg in the 19th century, among the most given to girls born before 1900, and popularised by Shakespeare's Juliet. It sometimes alternates with Julie for the same woman; the feast day varies by calendar.

julio.label: Julio
julio.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Julius, from Latin "Julius", the name of Julius Caesar's family.
julio.text: A name common in Spain and Portugal (Júlio), especially in the 19th and 20th centuries. Its name day is 12 April, the feast of Pope Saint Julius I.

julius.label: Julius
julius.meaning: From Latin "Julius", the name of Julius Caesar's Roman family.
julius.text: The Latin and Germanic form, an everyday name in Germany, Poland, Scandinavia and the Netherlands in the 19th century, and the form used in Catholic records for Jules. Its name day is 12 April, the feast of Pope Saint Julius I.

juliusz.label: Juliusz
juliusz.meaning: Polish form of Julius, from Latin "Julius", the name of Julius Caesar's family.
juliusz.text: A Polish name borne mostly by the nobility and bourgeoisie in the 19th century, like the poet Juliusz Słowacki. In Latin records it appears as Julius. Its name day is notably 12 April, the feast of Pope Saint Julius I.

june.label: June
june.meaning: From English "June", from Latin "Junius", the month dedicated to Juno.
june.text: A 20th-century English name taken from the month, very popular in Britain and the United States in the 1920s and 1930s. It is practically absent from records before 1890.

jurgen.label: Jürgen
jurgen.meaning: Low German form of George, from Greek "geôrgos", "farmer, tiller of the soil".
jurgen.text: A form typical of northern Germany, Schleswig-Holstein and Mecklenburg, found in Lutheran records from the 16th century, then very widespread throughout Germany in the mid-20th century. Its name day is 23 April, the feast of Saint George.

justa.label: Justa
justa.text: A Spanish female name, frequent in rural records and today mostly borne by women born before 1950. It honours Saint Justa, martyred in Seville with her sister Rufina, both celebrated on 17 July.

justin.label: Justin
justin.text: A name common in France and Belgium in the 19th century, among the most given to boys born before 1900, then fashionable again in the late 20th century, also in English-speaking countries. Its name day is 1 June, the feast of Saint Justin, a 2nd-century philosopher and martyr.

justina.label: Justina
justina.meaning: From Latin "Justina", feminine of "Justinus", derived from "justus", "just, righteous".
justina.text: The Latin and Spanish form of the name, used in Catholic records in Belgium and Germany for Justine, and an everyday name in Spain. Its name day is 7 October, the feast of Saint Justina of Padua, a martyr.

justine.label: Justine
justine.meaning: French form of Justina, from Latin "Justinus", derived from "justus", "just, righteous".
justine.text: A name widespread in France, Belgium and Switzerland in the 19th century, among the frequent names of girls born before 1900, then fashionable again in the late 20th century. It honours Saint Justina of Padua, a martyr, whose feast is 7 October; the popular French calendar, however, places it on 12 March.

justo.label: Justo
justo.text: A Spanish name common in rural records, today mostly borne by men born before 1950. It honours Saint Justus, a child martyr of Alcalá de Henares with his brother Pastor, both celebrated on 6 August.

justus.label: Justus
justus.text: A Latin name adopted by German and Dutch humanists and Protestants from the 16th century, borne for instance by the chemist Justus von Liebig. It is also shortened to Just, and several saints bear the name without any one prevailing.

justyna.label: Justyna
justyna.meaning: Polish form of Justina, from Latin "Justina", derived from "justus", "just, righteous".
justyna.text: A Polish name uncommon in older records that became very widespread among women born in the 1970s and 1980s. Its name day is notably 7 October, the feast of Saint Justina of Padua.

kacper.label: Kacper
kacper.meaning: Polish form of Caspar, the traditional name of one of the Magi, often linked to Persian "ganzabara", "treasurer"; the meaning is disputed.
