kacper.text: An old Polish name, found in Latin records as Casparus, which became one of the most given boys' names in Poland in the late 20th century. Its name day is 6 January, Epiphany, together with Melchior and Balthazar.

kalman.label: Kalman
kalman.meaning: Usually linked to Greek Kalonymos, "beautiful name".
kalman.text: A Jewish male name common in central Europe in the 19th century, written Kalman or Kalmen. It is also a Hungarian name (Kálmán) of different origin.

kamil.label: Kamil
kamil.meaning: Polish form of Camillus, from Latin "Camillus", a Roman family name also denoting a young acolyte in religious rites.
kamil.text: A Polish name rare before the 20th century that became very widespread in the second half of the century; Kamil is also a distinct Arabic name ("perfect"). Its name day is 14 July, the feast of Saint Camillus de Lellis, founder of an order devoted to the sick.

karel.label: Karel
karel.meaning: Dutch and Czech form of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
karel.text: A name common in Flanders, the Netherlands and Bohemia, where the same man may appear under the Latin form Carolus or the French Charles depending on the record. Its name day is 4 November, the feast of Saint Charles Borromeo.

karen.label: Karen
karen.meaning: Danish short form of Katherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", of obscure origin, associated with "katharos", "pure".
karen.text: An old Danish and Norwegian name that spread to the United States and Germany in the 20th century, becoming very popular in the 1950s and 1960s. It is rare in older records outside Scandinavia. Like Catherine, its name day is 25 November, the feast of Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

karl.label: Karl
karl.meaning: German form of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
karl.text: A name very widespread in German-speaking lands, Switzerland, Luxembourg and among German speakers in Poland, especially in the 18th and 19th centuries; Latin records write it Carolus. Its name day is often 4 November, the feast of Saint Charles Borromeo.

karol.label: Karol
karol.meaning: Polish and Slovak form of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
karol.text: A Polish name common in the 19th and 20th centuries, Latinised as Carolus in the records. Its name day is 4 November, the feast of Saint Charles Borromeo.

karolina.label: Karolina
karolina.meaning: Polish and Germanic form of Caroline, feminine of Karol, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
karolina.text: A female name widespread in Poland and Germany in the 19th century, then very popular again in Poland in the late 20th century. In Latin records it appears as Carolina.

karoline.label: Karoline
karoline.meaning: German form of Caroline, feminine of Karl, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
karoline.text: A female name very widespread in Germany and Austria in the 18th and 19th centuries, often shortened to Lina or Line. It alternates with Carolina or Caroline in the records.

kaspar.label: Kaspar
kaspar.meaning: German form of Caspar, the traditional name of one of the Magi, often linked to Persian "ganzabara", "treasurer"; the meaning is disputed.
kaspar.text: A name common in Switzerland, southern Germany and Austria from the 16th to the 19th century, also written Caspar or Casper. Its name day is 6 January, Epiphany, together with Melchior and Balthazar.

katarzyna.label: Katarzyna
katarzyna.meaning: Polish form of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", of obscure origin, associated with "katharos", "pure".
katarzyna.text: One of the most widespread female names in Poland in every period, Latinised as Catharina in the records; the familiar form is Kasia. Its name day is 25 November, the feast of Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

katharina.label: Katharina
katharina.meaning: German form of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", of obscure origin, associated with "katharos", "pure".
katharina.text: One of the most frequent female names in German-speaking lands from the 16th to the 19th century, with many short forms: Käthe, Kathrin, Trina, Katrin. It alternates with Catharina in the records. Its name day is 25 November, the feast of Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

katharine.label: Katharine
katharine.meaning: English form of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", of obscure origin, associated with "katharos", "pure".
katharine.text: An English spelling common in Britain and the United States, alternating with Katherine, Catherine or Catharine for the same woman. Its name day is 25 November, the feast of Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

katherine.label: Katherine
katherine.meaning: English form of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", of obscure origin, associated with "katharos", "pure".
katherine.text: A name very widespread in English-speaking countries since the Middle Ages, borne by several queens of England, with many spellings and familiar forms (Kate, Kitty, Kathy). Its name day is 25 November, the feast of Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

kathleen.label: Kathleen
kathleen.meaning: Anglicised form of Irish "Caitlín", itself from Catherine, Greek "Aikaterinê".
kathleen.text: An Irish name very widespread in Ireland and the Irish diaspora, then in England and the United States, among the most given in England around 1910. In Irish records the same woman may be entered as Catherine or Kate.

kathryn.label: Kathryn
kathryn.meaning: Modern English spelling of Catherine, from Greek "Aikaterinê", associated with "katharos", "pure".
kathryn.text: A mainly American spelling, widespread in the 20th century, notably in the 1920s to 1950s. It alternates with Katherine or Catherine for the same woman. Its name day is 25 November, the feast of Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

kazimiera.label: Kazimiera
kazimiera.meaning: Feminine of Kazimierz, from Slavic "kaziti", "to destroy", and "mir", "peace"; the meaning is disputed.
kazimiera.text: A Polish female name very widespread in the first half of the 20th century, especially in the countryside. In Latin records it appears as Casimira.

kazimierz.label: Kazimierz
kazimierz.meaning: From Slavic "kaziti", "to destroy", and "mir", "peace": "destroyer of peace" or "one who imposes peace"; the meaning is disputed.
kazimierz.text: A Polish royal name (Casimir the Great) and one of the most widespread male names in Poland until the mid-20th century. Latin records write it Casimirus. Its name day is 4 March, the feast of Saint Casimir, a Polish prince and patron saint of Poland and Lithuania.

keith.label: Keith
keith.meaning: From a Scottish surname taken from a place, linked to Brittonic "coed", "wood".
keith.text: A Scottish surname (that of the Earls Marischal) that became a given name in the 19th century, very popular in Britain in the mid-20th century. It is rare in earlier records.

kenneth.label: Kenneth
kenneth.meaning: Anglicised form of Gaelic "Coinneach", "handsome", and "Cináed", "born of fire"; the meaning is disputed.
kenneth.text: A Scottish name borne by King Kenneth MacAlpin in the 9th century, common in Scotland and then very popular throughout Britain and the United States in the 1910s to 1940s. It is often shortened to Ken.

keren.label: Keren
keren.text: A modern Hebrew name, mostly given in Israel in the 20th century. It recalls Keren-happuch, a daughter of Job.

kevin.label: Kevin
kevin.meaning: From Irish "Caoimhín", from "caomh", "gentle, handsome", and "gein", "birth": "of gentle birth".
kevin.text: An Irish name long confined to Ireland, then spread to Britain and the United States in the mid-20th century and to continental Europe from the 1960s. It honours Saint Kevin, 6th-century abbot of Glendalough, whose feast is 3 June.

klara.label: Klara
klara.meaning: Polish and Germanic form of Clare, from Latin "clara", "bright, famous".
klara.text: A name borne in Poland, Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands since the Middle Ages, often in Catholic families; it is also written Clara. Its name day is 11 August, the feast of Saint Clare of Assisi.

kleber.label: Kleber
kleber.meaning: From an Alsatian surname, from German "Kleber", "plasterer, gluer".
kleber.text: A French name given in honour of the Revolutionary general Jean-Baptiste Kléber, mostly in the 19th century, and fairly frequent among men born before 1900. It does not correspond to any saint.

konrad.label: Konrad
konrad.text: A medieval name borne by emperors and dukes, very widespread in German-speaking lands and Poland, with the short form Kunz and later Kurt. Its name day is 26 November, the feast of Saint Conrad, 10th-century bishop of Constance.

konstancja.label: Konstancja
konstancja.meaning: Polish form of Constance, from Latin "constantia", "constancy, steadfastness".
konstancja.text: A Polish female name borne mostly by the nobility and bourgeoisie in the 18th and 19th centuries. In Latin records it appears as Constantia.

konstanty.label: Konstanty
konstanty.meaning: Polish form of Constantine, from Latin "constans", "constant, steadfast".
konstanty.text: A Polish name borne mostly by the nobility in the 18th and 19th centuries, and rarer elsewhere. In Latin records it appears as Constantinus.

krystian.label: Krystian
krystian.meaning: Polish form of Christian, from Latin "christianus", "Christian".
krystian.text: A name rare in older Polish records, except in Silesia and families of German origin, then very widespread in the second half of the 20th century. It also appears as Chrystian.

krystyna.label: Krystyna
krystyna.meaning: Polish form of Christina, from Latin "christiana", "Christian".
krystyna.text: A Polish female name very widespread in the 20th century, especially among women born between the 1930s and 1960s, and less frequent in earlier records. Its name day is notably 24 July, the feast of Saint Christina of Bolsena.

krzysztof.label: Krzysztof
krzysztof.meaning: Polish form of Christopher, from Greek "Khristophoros", "Christ-bearer".
krzysztof.text: A Polish name found in records since the 16th century, Latinised as Christophorus, which became one of the most widespread male names in Poland in the second half of the 20th century. Its name day is 25 July, the feast of Saint Christopher.

ksawery.label: Ksawery
ksawery.meaning: Polish form of Xavier, from Basque "Etxeberri", "new house", the name of Saint Francis Xavier's birthplace castle.
ksawery.text: A Polish name of religious origin, first borne in compounds (Franciszek Ksawery), mostly by the nobility in the 18th and 19th centuries. In Latin records it appears as Xaverius. Its name day is 3 December, the feast of Saint Francis Xavier.

kunigunde.label: Kunigunde
kunigunde.text: Saint Cunigunde, wife of Emperor Henry II, is celebrated on 3 March. The name was common in southern Germany (Bavaria, Franconia) from the Middle Ages to the 18th century; records write Kunigonde, Cunégonde, or Cunegundis in Latin.

kurt.label: Kurt
kurt.meaning: German short form of Konrad, from Germanic "kuoni", "bold", and "rad", "counsel".
kurt.text: A German name that became independent in the late 19th century and was very widespread in Germany and Switzerland between 1890 and 1940. It is rarer in older records, where the same man would be entered as Konrad; it is also spelled Curt.

laja.label: Laja
laja.meaning: The Yiddish form (Leye) of Leah; meaning disputed.
laja.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Leye, frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. Leja and the diminutive Lejka also occur.

lambert.label: Lambert
lambert.text: A name very widespread in the former prince-bishopric of Liège, Limburg, Luxembourg and northern France, where it also gave many surnames. Latin records write it Lambertus, and it appears in the Netherlands as Lammert. Its name day is 17 September, the feast of Saint Lambert, bishop of Maastricht martyred at Liège.

lambertus.label: Lambertus
lambertus.meaning: Latin form of Lambert, from Germanic "land", "land", and "berht", "bright, famous".
lambertus.text: A Latin form used in Catholic records in Belgium and the Netherlands, and an everyday name in the Netherlands until the 20th century. The same man may appear elsewhere as Lambert, Lammert or Bert. Its name day is 17 September, the feast of Saint Lambert of Maastricht.

laura.label: Laura
laura.meaning: From Latin "laurus", "laurel", a symbol of victory; sometimes considered the feminine of Laurentius.
laura.text: A name made famous by Petrarch's Laura, widespread in Italy since the Renaissance, then in Spain, Portugal and English-speaking countries in the 19th century. It is not tied to any widely celebrated saint before the 20th century.

laure.label: Laure
laure.meaning: French form of Laura, from Latin "laurus", "laurel", a symbol of victory.
laure.text: A French name common in the 19th century, among the frequent names of women born before 1900, in France, French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium. It also appears as the diminutive Laurette.

laurence.label: Laurence
laurence.meaning: From Latin "Laurentius", "from Laurentum" (a town in Latium), associated with "laurus", "laurel".
laurence.text: Beware of sex: in English, Laurence is a male name (a variant of Lawrence); in French it is mostly the feminine of Laurent, widely given in the mid-20th century. In both cases its name day is 10 August, the feast of Saint Lawrence, deacon and martyr of Rome.

laurens.label: Laurens
laurens.meaning: Dutch form of Lawrence, from Latin "Laurentius", "from Laurentum".
laurens.text: A Dutch name found in records since the 16th century, often shortened to Lau, and Latinised as Laurentius. Its name day is 10 August, the feast of Saint Lawrence, deacon and martyr of Rome.

laurent.label: Laurent
laurent.meaning: From Latin "Laurentius", "from Laurentum" (a town in Latium), associated with "laurus", "laurel".
laurent.text: An old French name found in records of every period in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland, among the frequent names of men born before 1900, then very popular in the 1960s and 1970s. Latin records write it Laurentius. Its name day is 10 August, the feast of Saint Lawrence, deacon and martyr of Rome.

lavinia.label: Lavinia
lavinia.meaning: The name of Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus and wife of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid; its exact meaning is uncertain, perhaps linked to the town of Lavinium.
lavinia.text: A literary name used in Renaissance Italy, then mostly in Britain and the United States in the 18th and 19th centuries. It remains uncommon in the records and is not linked to any well-established saint.

lawrence.label: Lawrence
lawrence.meaning: From Latin "Laurentius", "from Laurentum", a town in Latium whose name is associated with the laurel.
lawrence.text: The English form of Laurent, common in England since the Middle Ages and widespread in the United States in the 20th century; the pet forms Larry and Laurie are often found. It honours Saint Lawrence, a deacon martyred in Rome in 258, whose feast is 10 August.

lazare.label: Lazare
lazare.meaning: From Hebrew "Eleazar", "God has helped", through Greek "Lazaros".
lazare.text: A name found in France under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century without being very common, sometimes written Lazard or Lazar. It refers to Lazarus of Bethany, the friend of Jesus raised from the dead, whom Provençal tradition makes bishop of Marseille and whom the Roman Martyrology commemorated on 17 December.

lazzaro.label: Lazzaro
lazzaro.meaning: From Hebrew "Eleazar", "God has helped", through Greek "Lazaros".
lazzaro.text: The Italian form of Lazarus, found in Italian records since the late Middle Ages; the form Lazaro also occurs. It honours Lazarus of Bethany, the friend of Jesus raised from the dead, whom the Roman Martyrology commemorated on 17 December.

lea.label: Léa
lea.meaning: From Hebrew "Leah", the name of Jacob's first wife, of disputed meaning: "weary" or "wild cow".
lea.text: A biblical name fairly common in France and neighbouring countries in the late 19th century, which became fashionable again much later. It is also written Lea, Leah or Lia. Its name day is that of Saint Lea, a 4th-century Roman widow known from Saint Jerome, on 22 March.

leandre.label: Léandre
leandre.text: An uncommon name, found in France, Belgium and Luxembourg mostly in the 19th century, and in Spain as Leandro. It honours Saint Leander, archbishop of Seville in the 6th century, whose feast is kept on 27 February in France (13 March in Spain).

lee.label: Lee
lee.meaning: From Old English "leah", "clearing, meadow", first a surname that became a given name.
lee.text: A mainly American unisex name, common for boys from the late 19th century and later for girls. It often appears as a middle name and repeats a surname, which may point research towards a maternal line. It is not linked to a saint.

leendert.label: Leendert
leendert.meaning: Dutch form of Leonard, from Germanic "leon", "lion", and "hard", "strong, hardy".
leendert.text: The popular Dutch form of Leonard, very present in the records of Holland and Zeeland, whereas Latin entries often write Leonardus; the pet forms Leen and Leendertje occur. It honours Saint Leonard of Noblac, a 6th-century hermit of the Limousin, whose feast is 6 November.

leger.label: Léger
leger.text: Saint Leodegar, bishop of Autun who died in 678, is celebrated on 2 October. The name was common in French registers under the Ancien Régime; Latin records write Leodegarius.

leib.label: Leib
leib.text: A very frequent Yiddish name, often paired with Judah or Aryeh (Juda Leib). Polish records write Lejb or Lajb, with the diminutive Lewek ("little lion"); German and Alsatian records write Löb or Loeb.

lejzor.label: Lejzor
lejzor.meaning: The Yiddish form of Eliezer, "God is my help".
lejzor.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Leyzer, short for Eliezer, frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. German records write Leiser.

lena.label: Lena
lena.meaning: Short form of several names, mainly Helena and Magdalena, whose etymology it shares.
lena.text: A pet form that became a name in its own right in Germany, the Netherlands, Poland and among immigrants to the United States in the 19th century. In the records the same person may appear as Lena or as Helena or Magdalena, which should also be searched. It has no feast of its own.

leo.label: Leo
leo.text: The German, Dutch and English form of Leon, borne by thirteen popes; it became common in Belgium, Germany, Switzerland and the United States in the late 19th century, partly in honour of Pope Leo XIII. Its name day is that of Pope Saint Leo the Great, on 10 November.

leobald.label: Leobald
leobald.text: A rare Germanic name, found mainly in Alsatian and south-west German registers of the 17th and 18th centuries. It is often latinised as Leobaldus in parish entries.

leokadia.label: Leokadia
leokadia.meaning: A name of Greek origin, probably derived from "leukos", "white, bright"; the etymology remains uncertain.
leokadia.text: A mainly Polish female name, common in the Catholic records of Poland in the 18th and 19th centuries, sometimes shortened to Kada. It honours Saint Leocadia, a virgin martyred in Toledo in the early 4th century, whose feast is 9 December.

leon.label: Léon
leon.text: A very widespread name in France, Belgium and Luxembourg in the 19th and early 20th centuries, also common in Poland and in Jewish communities across Europe. Its name day is that of Pope Saint Leo the Great, on 10 November.

leona.label: Leona
leona.meaning: Feminine form of Leo or Leon, from Latin "leo", "lion".
leona.text: A mainly American name, widely used between 1880 and 1930, and rarer in Belgium and France, where Léonie or Léone are more usual. It has no well-established patron saint.

leonard.label: Leonard
leonard.text: A name widespread in England, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, where it remained common until the early 20th century, notably in the Limousin. It honours Saint Leonard of Noblac, a 6th-century hermit invoked for prisoners and livestock, whose feast is 6 November.

leonarde.label: Léonarde
leonarde.meaning: Feminine of Léonard, from Germanic "leon", "lion", and "hard", "strong".
leonarde.text: A feminine form of Léonard, frequent in Limousin, where Saint Leonard of Noblat is much venerated. Records also spell it Liénarde.

leonardo.label: Leonardo
leonardo.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Leonard, from Germanic "leon", "lion", and "hard", "strong".
leonardo.text: A form common in Italy since the Middle Ages, and also found in Spain and Portugal. It honours Saint Leonard of Noblac, a 6th-century hermit of the Limousin invoked for prisoners, whose feast is 6 November.

leonardus.label: Leonardus
leonardus.meaning: Latin form of Leonard, from Germanic "leon", "lion", and "hard", "strong".
leonardus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic records in the Netherlands and Belgium; in daily life the person was called Leendert, Lenaert or Léonard, and Scandinavian derivatives such as Lennart are related. It honours Saint Leonard of Noblac, whose feast is 6 November.

leonce.label: Léonce
leonce.text: A male name widespread in France and Belgium in the 19th century, borne by several early saints, including a bishop of Fréjus. The French calendar keeps its name day on 18 June, the day of Saint Leontius, a martyr of Tripoli in Phoenicia.

leone.label: Leone
leone.text: The Italian form of Leo, common in Italy and Italian-speaking Switzerland; in France and the United States the same spelling (Léone) is also used as a female name. For men, the name day is that of Pope Saint Leo the Great, on 10 November.

leonel.label: Leonel
leonel.meaning: Portuguese and Spanish form of Lionel, a medieval diminutive built on Latin "leo", "lion".
leonel.text: A mainly Portuguese male name, linked to the character Lionel of the Arthurian romances, and also found in Italy as Leonello. It is not linked to any well-established saint.

leonhard.label: Leonhard
leonhard.meaning: German form of Leonard, from Germanic "leon", "lion", and "hard", "strong".
leonhard.text: A traditional name in southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland, sometimes written Leonhardt, where Saint Leonard was very popular as patron of livestock (the horse processions of the Leonhardifahrt). His feast is 6 November.

leonia.label: Leonia
leonia.meaning: Feminine form derived from Leon, from Latin "leo", "lion".
leonia.text: A form found in Belgium and Poland, mostly in the 19th century, close to the French Léonie. It has no well-established patron saint.

leonide.label: Léonide
leonide.meaning: From Greek "Leonidas", "son of the lion", derived from "leôn", "lion".
leonide.text: A classically inspired name found in France in the 19th century, borne here as a female name although it was also used for men. It has no well-established feast for women.

leonie.label: Léonie
leonie.meaning: Feminine form of Léon, from Latin "leo", "lion".
leonie.text: A very widespread name in France, Belgium and Switzerland in the second half of the 19th century, declining in the 20th. It has no well-established patron saint; it is sometimes celebrated with Saint Leo on 10 November.

leonor.label: Leonor
leonor.meaning: Iberian form of Eleanor (Aliénor), of disputed etymology, possibly Occitan or Germanic.
leonor.text: A name borne by several queens of Castile, Aragon and Portugal, common in Spain and Portugal from the Middle Ages to the 20th century. It has no well-established patron saint.

leonore.label: Leonore
leonore.meaning: Shortened German form of Eleanor, of disputed etymology, possibly Occitan or Germanic.
leonore.text: A mainly German name, popularised by the heroine of Beethoven's "Fidelio" and also found among German emigrants to the United States. It is often shortened to Lore or Lenore. It has no well-established patron saint.

leontine.label: Léontine
leontine.meaning: Feminine form of Léonce, from Latin "Leontius", derived from "leo", "lion".
leontine.text: A very common name in France and Belgium in the 19th century, going out of fashion in the 20th. It has no well-established patron saint.

leopold.label: Leopold
leopold.meaning: From Germanic "liut", "people", and "bald", "bold", later associated with Latin "leo", "lion".
leopold.text: A dynastic name of the Habsburgs and of the kings of the Belgians, very widespread in Austria, southern Germany and Belgium in the 19th century; the Bavarian form Luitpold is a variant. It honours Saint Leopold III, margrave and patron of Austria, whose feast is 15 November.

leopoldina.label: Leopoldina
leopoldina.meaning: Feminine form of Leopold, from Germanic "liut", "people", and "bald", "bold".
leopoldina.text: A Portuguese, Italian and German form, popularised in Portugal and Brazil by Empress Leopoldina of Austria, wife of Pedro I of Brazil. It has no well-established patron saint.

leopoldine.label: Leopoldine
leopoldine.meaning: Feminine form of Leopold, from Germanic "liut", "people", and "bald", "bold".
leopoldine.text: A female name found in Austria, Germany, Belgium and France in the 19th century, often in families attached to the Habsburgs or to the Belgian royal house. It has no well-established patron saint.

leopoldo.label: Leopoldo
leopoldo.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Leopold, from Germanic "liut", "people", and "bald", "bold".
leopoldo.text: A name widespread in northern Italy, notably in Tuscany under the grand dukes of the House of Lorraine, and in Spain and Portugal in the 19th century. It honours Saint Leopold III of Austria, whose feast is 15 November.

leopoldus.label: Leopoldus
leopoldus.meaning: Latin form of Leopold, from Germanic "liut", "people", and "bald", "bold".
leopoldus.text: The Latin form used in Belgian parish records; in daily life the person was called Léopold or Leopold. It honours Saint Leopold III of Austria, whose feast is 15 November.

leroy.label: Leroy
leroy.meaning: From Old French "le roi", "the king", first a nickname, then a surname that became a given name.
leroy.text: A typically American name, very common from the late 19th century to the 1930s, notably in African American families. It is also written LeRoy or Le Roy, which can cause confusion with a surname. It is not linked to a saint.

leslie.label: Leslie
leslie.meaning: From the Scottish surname Leslie, taken from a place in Aberdeenshire; the Gaelic origin of the place name is uncertain.
leslie.text: A mainly male name in Britain and the United States in the early 20th century, which later became mostly female in America. It is not linked to a saint.

lester.label: Lester
lester.meaning: From the English surname Lester, taken from the town of Leicester.
lester.text: A mainly American name, common between the late 19th century and the 1930s. Like other surnames turned given names, it may reflect a surname from the mother's family. It is not linked to a saint.

leszek.label: Leszek
leszek.meaning: A Polish name of uncertain etymology, often linked to Lech, the legendary ancestor of the Poles.
leszek.text: A name borne by several medieval Polish dukes, including Leszek the White, and still in use in Poland, with strong popularity in the 20th century. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

levenez.label: Levenez
levenez.text: A modern Breton name formed from a common noun, given mostly from the second half of the 20th century as part of the Breton name revival. It does not appear in older registers.

lewis.label: Lewis
lewis.meaning: English form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
lewis.text: The English and Scottish form of Louis, common in Scotland and Wales, where it was also used to anglicise the Welsh Llywelyn. It is frequent in the United States in the 19th century. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August.

lidia.label: Lidia
lidia.meaning: From Greek "Lydia", "woman of Lydia", a region of Asia Minor.
lidia.text: The Spanish, Italian and Polish form of Lydia, present in the records from the 19th century and more common in the 20th. It honours Saint Lydia, the purple-cloth merchant of Thyatira converted by Saint Paul, whose feast is 3 August.

lilian.label: Lilian
lilian.meaning: Of disputed etymology: a pet form of Elizabeth, or derived from Latin "lilium", "lily".
lilian.text: An English female name attested from the 16th century and widespread in Britain and the United States in the late 19th century, also spelled Lillian or Lilyan. In France and the Netherlands, Lilian is rather a recent male name. It has no patron saint.

liliane.label: Liliane
liliane.meaning: French form of Lilian, linked to Latin "lilium", "lily", or to a pet form of Elisabeth.
liliane.text: A French name mostly given between the 1920s and the 1950s, so rare in older records; it is sometimes written Lilianne or Lilliane. It has no well-established patron saint.

lillian.label: Lillian
lillian.meaning: Of disputed etymology: a pet form of Elizabeth, or derived from Latin "lilium", "lily".
lillian.text: The most common American spelling of Lilian, very frequent in the United States from the late 19th century to the 1920s. It often alternates with Lillie or Lily for the same person. It has no patron saint.

lillie.label: Lillie
lillie.meaning: Pet form of Lillian or Elizabeth, associated with the name of the lily flower.
lillie.text: An American name very widespread in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, notably in the South. The same woman may appear as Lillie, Lily, Lillian or Elizabeth depending on the record. It has no patron saint.

lilly.label: Lilly
lilly.meaning: Pet form of Elisabeth, or the name of the lily flower (Latin "lilium").
lilly.text: A pet form found in Germany, the Netherlands and Poland, and among immigrants to the United States, often for an Elisabeth or a Caroline; Lili or Lilli also occur. It has no feast of its own.

lily.label: Lily
lily.meaning: The name of the lily flower, from Latin "lilium", a symbol of purity; sometimes also a pet form of Elizabeth.
lily.text: A flower name fashionable in Britain and the United States in the Victorian era, also found in Switzerland, Germany and France as a pet form. It has no patron saint.

lina.label: Lina
lina.meaning: Short form of names ending in "-lina" or "-line" (Carolina, Paolina, Angelina, Karoline...), whose etymology it shares.
lina.text: A pet form that became a name in its own right in Italy, Switzerland, Germany and Poland in the 19th century. In the records, the full name (Carolina, Paolina, Nicolina...) should often be searched as well. It has no feast of its own.

linda.label: Linda
linda.meaning: Probably from the Germanic element "lind", "soft, gentle" (or "linden tree"), later associated with Spanish "linda", "pretty".
linda.text: First a short form of names such as Belinda or Theodelinda, this name became very popular in the United States in the mid-20th century, so it is rare in older records. In Italy it is sometimes linked to the Lombard queen Theodelinda. It has no patron saint.

lionel.label: Lionel
lionel.meaning: A medieval diminutive of "lion", from Latin "leo", "lion".
lionel.text: A name from the Arthurian romances (Lionel, cousin of Lancelot), used in England in the Middle Ages and again in the 19th century, and in France mostly in the 20th century. Lyonel or Lionell also occur. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

lisa.label: Lisa
lisa.meaning: Short form of Elisabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheba", "God is my oath".
lisa.text: A pet form of Elisabeth common in Germany, Switzerland and Poland, where the same woman may also appear as Elisabeth, Liesl or Lisette. Its name day is that of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, 17 November.

lisbeth.label: Lisbeth
lisbeth.meaning: Short form of Elisabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheba", "God is my oath".
lisbeth.text: A shortened form of Elisabeth usual in Germany, Switzerland and Scandinavia, sometimes written Lisbet or Lisebeth. In official records the same person may be entered under the full form Elisabeth. Its name day is that of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, 17 November.

lise.label: Lise
lise.meaning: Short form of Élisabeth, from Hebrew "Elisheba", "God is my oath".
lise.text: A French pet form of Élisabeth, with the variant Lisette, found mostly in the 19th and 20th centuries; the same woman may appear as Élisabeth in her baptism record. Its name day is that of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, 17 November.

livia.label: Livia
livia.meaning: Feminine form of the Roman family name Livius, of uncertain etymology, possibly linked to Latin "lividus", "bluish".
livia.text: A classically inspired name, borne by Livia, wife of the Emperor Augustus, and found mostly in Italy from the Renaissance onward; Liviana or Livietta also occur. It has no well-established patron saint.

livinus.label: Livinus
livinus.meaning: Latin form of the name of a 7th-century missionary, of uncertain etymology, possibly Celtic.
livinus.text: The Latin form of Lieven or Liévin, used in the records of Flanders, where the cult of Saint Livinus, a missionary martyred in Brabant and venerated in Ghent, was very much alive. In daily life the person was called Lieven or Liévin. His feast is 12 November.

lloyd.label: Lloyd
lloyd.meaning: From Welsh "llwyd", "grey", first a nickname, then a surname that became a given name.
lloyd.text: A name of Welsh origin, widespread in Britain and above all in the United States from the late 19th century to the 1930s; the spelling Loyd also occurs. It is not linked to a saint.

lluis.label: Lluís
lluis.meaning: Catalan form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
lluis.text: The Catalan form of Louis, found in Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands, where records kept in Castilian often write Luis. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August.

lluisa.label: Lluïsa
lluisa.meaning: Catalan form of Louise, feminine of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
lluisa.text: The Catalan form of Louise, found in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands, whereas records in Castilian write Luisa. It has no patron saint of its own in older local usage.

lodewijk.label: Lodewijk
lodewijk.meaning: Dutch form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
lodewijk.text: The Dutch form of Louis, common in the Netherlands and Flanders, where Latin records write Ludovicus and French records Louis; Lowie is a Flemish pet form. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August.

lodovico.label: Lodovico
lodovico.meaning: Older Italian form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
lodovico.text: An older Italian form, frequent in the Renaissance, parallel to Ludovico and gradually replaced by Luigi. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August.

lois.label: Lois
lois.meaning: The Greek name of Timothy's grandmother in the New Testament, of uncertain etymology.
lois.text: A biblical name adopted by English and American Protestants, very widespread in the United States in the first half of the 20th century. In Galicia, however, Lois is the Galician male form of Louis. It has no well-established patron saint.

lorena.label: Lorena
lorena.meaning: Spanish and Italian form of Lorraine, from the name of the region, derived from "Lotharingia", the kingdom of Lothair.
lorena.text: A mainly Spanish and Spanish-American name, rare before the 20th century and very common afterwards; it is also found in the United States. It has no patron saint.

lorenz.label: Lorenz
lorenz.meaning: German form of Laurent, from Latin "Laurentius", "from Laurentum".
lorenz.text: The German and Swiss form of Laurent, common in German-speaking Catholic lands; the short forms Lenz or Enz and the Scandinavian Lars are related. It honours Saint Lawrence, a deacon martyred in Rome in 258, whose feast is 10 August.

lorenza.label: Lorenza
lorenza.meaning: Feminine form of Lorenzo, from Latin "Laurentius", "from Laurentum".
lorenza.text: An Italian and Spanish female name, regular in the records of the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no well-established patron saint of its own.

lorenzo.label: Lorenzo
lorenzo.meaning: Italian and Spanish form of Laurent, from Latin "Laurentius", "from Laurentum".
lorenzo.text: A name very widespread in Italy and Spain since the Middle Ages, sometimes shortened to Renzo; older spellings such as Laurenzo occur. It honours Saint Lawrence, a deacon martyred in Rome in 258, whose feast is 10 August.

loretta.label: Loretta
loretta.meaning: Derived from the name of the Marian shrine of Loreto in Italy, or a pet form of Laura.
loretta.text: A mainly American name, fashionable in the 1920s and 1930s, also used in families of Italian or Irish origin. It has no patron saint of its own.

lorraine.label: Lorraine
lorraine.meaning: From the name of the French region, derived from "Lotharingia", the kingdom of Lothair.
lorraine.text: A mainly American female name, very widespread between the 1920s and the 1940s, and rare in France. It has no patron saint.

lothar.label: Lothar
lothar.text: A Carolingian name (Lothair), rare for centuries and then revived in Germany in the 19th and 20th centuries; Latin records write Lotharius. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

lotte.label: Lotte
lotte.meaning: Short form of Charlotte, feminine of Charles, from Germanic "karl", "free man".
lotte.text: A pet form of Charlotte common in Germany and the Netherlands, mostly in the 19th and 20th centuries; in official records the same woman often appears as Charlotte. It has no feast of its own.

louis.label: Louis
louis.text: The name of the kings of France (notably Louis IX / Saint Louis), extremely common across all social classes from the 17th through the 20th century.

louisa.label: Louisa
louisa.meaning: Latinised form of Louise, feminine of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
louisa.text: A mainly English form, fashionable in Britain and the United States in the 18th and 19th centuries, and also found in Belgium and the Netherlands. The same woman may appear as Louisa or Louise depending on the record. It has no well-established patron saint of its own.

louise.label: Louise
louise.meaning: Feminine form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
louise.text: One of the most frequently given female names in France, Belgium and Switzerland in the 19th and early 20th centuries, alone or in compounds (Marie-Louise, Anne-Louise). Its name day is that of Saint Louise de Marillac, co-founder of the Daughters of Charity, on 15 March in the French calendar.

louisette.label: Louisette
louisette.meaning: Pet form of Louise, feminine of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
louisette.text: A pet form of Louise that became a name in its own right in France, mostly in the first half of the 20th century. Its name day is that of Saint Louise de Marillac, 15 March.

loup.label: Loup
loup.text: Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes in the 5th century, is celebrated on 29 July. The name was used in Champagne and Burgundy; the form Leu survives in Saint-Leu place names.

lourdes.label: Lourdes
lourdes.meaning: From the name of the Pyrenean town of Lourdes, site of the Marian apparitions of 1858.
lourdes.text: A Marian name in Spain and Portugal, sometimes written Lurdes, often in compounds (María de Lourdes); it appears only after 1858 and became common in the 20th century. Its feast is that of Our Lady of Lourdes, 11 February.

lourenco.label: Lourenço
lourenco.meaning: Portuguese form of Laurent, from Latin "Laurentius", "from Laurentum".
lourenco.text: The Portuguese form of Laurent, found in Portuguese records since the Middle Ages, and the source of the surname Lourenço. It honours Saint Lawrence, a deacon martyred in Rome in 258, whose feast is 10 August.

lubin.label: Lubin
lubin.meaning: From Latin "Leobinus", of Germanic origin; disputed meaning.
lubin.text: Saint Leobinus, bishop of Chartres in the 6th century, is celebrated on 14 March. The name is characteristic of Beauce and Perche.

luc.label: Luc
luc.meaning: From Latin "Lucas", from Greek "Loukas", "man from Lucania", often associated with "lux", "light".
luc.text: A name found in France since the Middle Ages, but rarer than Jean or Pierre in older records, and much more frequent in the 20th century. It honours Saint Luke the Evangelist, author of the Acts of the Apostles and patron of painters and physicians, whose feast is 18 October.

luca.label: Luca
luca.meaning: Italian form of Luke, from Greek "Loukas", "man from Lucania".
luca.text: The Italian form of Luke, regular in Italian and Ticino records since the Middle Ages. It honours Saint Luke the Evangelist, whose feast is 18 October.

lucas.label: Lucas
lucas.meaning: Latin form of Luke, from Greek "Loukas", "man from Lucania".
lucas.text: The form used in Latin records and in everyday use in the Netherlands, Flanders, Spain and Germany; Lukas and the Dutch Luuk also occur. It honours Saint Luke the Evangelist, whose feast is 18 October.

luce.label: Luce
luce.meaning: French form of Lucia, from Latin "lux", "light".
luce.text: An old French form of Lucia, attested since the Middle Ages and still found in the 19th century. It honours Saint Lucy of Syracuse, a virgin martyred in the 4th century, whose feast is 13 December.

lucette.label: Lucette
lucette.meaning: Pet form of Luce or Lucie, from Latin "lux", "light".
lucette.text: A pet form that became a name in its own right in France, mostly in the early 20th century. Its name day is that of Saint Lucy of Syracuse, 13 December.

lucia.label: Lucia
lucia.meaning: Feminine form of Latin "Lucius", derived from "lux", "light".
lucia.text: The Italian, Spanish, Dutch and German form of Lucy, frequent throughout Catholic Europe since the Middle Ages. It honours Saint Lucy of Syracuse, a virgin martyred in the 4th century, whose feast is 13 December.

luciano.label: Luciano
luciano.meaning: From Latin "Lucianus", derived from "Lucius", itself linked to "lux", "light".
luciano.text: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Lucian, regular in the records of the 18th and 19th centuries. It honours Saint Lucian of Antioch, a 4th-century priest and martyr, whose feast is 7 January.

lucie.label: Lucie
lucie.meaning: Feminine form of Latin "Lucius", derived from "lux", "light".
lucie.text: A name widespread in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland, very frequent in the 19th century; the older form Luce also occurs. It honours Saint Lucy of Syracuse, a virgin martyred in the 4th century, whose feast is 13 December.

lucien.label: Lucien
lucien.meaning: From Latin "Lucianus", derived from "Lucius", itself linked to "lux", "light".
lucien.text: A very widespread name in France, Belgium and Luxembourg in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It honours Saint Lucian of Antioch, a 4th-century priest and martyr, whose feast is 7 January; Saint Lucian of Beauvais is also venerated in northern France.

lucienne.label: Lucienne
lucienne.meaning: Feminine form of Lucien, from Latin "Lucianus", linked to "lux", "light".
lucienne.text: A female name very frequent in France in the early 20th century, and rarer before. It has no well-established patron saint of its own.

lucile.label: Lucile
lucile.meaning: From Latin "Lucilla", a diminutive of "Lucia", derived from "lux", "light".
lucile.text: A French name attested from the 18th century and widespread in the 19th, with the spelling Lucille prevailing in the United States. Its name day is usually that of Saint Lucy of Syracuse, 13 December.

lucille.label: Lucille
lucille.meaning: From Latin "Lucilla", a diminutive of "Lucia", derived from "lux", "light".
lucille.text: A mainly American spelling of Lucile, very widespread in the United States in the 1910s and 1920s, and also found in France. Its name day is usually that of Saint Lucy of Syracuse, 13 December.

lucinda.label: Lucinda
lucinda.meaning: A literary form derived from Lucia, from Latin "lux", "light".
lucinda.text: A literary name used notably by Cervantes in "Don Quixote", found in Portugal, Spain and the English-speaking world. It has no patron saint of its own.

lucja.label: Łucja
lucja.meaning: Polish form of Lucy, from Latin "lux", "light".
lucja.text: The Polish form of Lucy, found in the Catholic records of Poland; Latin records write Lucia. It honours Saint Lucy of Syracuse, whose feast is 13 December.

lucjan.label: Lucjan
lucjan.meaning: Polish form of Lucian, from Latin "Lucianus", linked to "lux", "light".
lucjan.text: The Polish form of Lucian, mostly frequent in the 19th and 20th centuries; Latin records write Lucianus. It honours Saint Lucian of Antioch, whose feast is 7 January.

lucrezia.label: Lucrezia
lucrezia.meaning: From the Roman family name Lucretius, of uncertain etymology.
lucrezia.text: A classically inspired name, recalling Lucretia, heroine of legendary Rome, used in Italy since the Renaissance; the forms Lucrèce and Lucrecia occur in France and Spain. It has no well-established patron saint.

lucy.label: Lucy
lucy.meaning: English form of Lucia, from Latin "Lucia", derived from "lux", "light".
lucy.text: An English name in use since the Middle Ages, frequent in Britain and the United States in the 18th and 19th centuries. It honours Saint Lucy of Syracuse, a virgin martyred in the 4th century, whose feast is 13 December.

lucyna.label: Lucyna
lucyna.meaning: Polish form derived from Lucia or Lucina, from Latin "lux", "light".
lucyna.text: A Polish female name, mostly widespread in the 20th century, close to Łucja, with which it may alternate. It has no well-established patron saint.

ludolf.label: Ludolf
ludolf.text: An old Germanic name, borne by Saxon nobles in the Middle Ages and rare afterwards in Germany, sometimes written Ludolph. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

ludovic.label: Ludovic
ludovic.meaning: From Latin "Ludovicus", the Latinised form of "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior", like Louis.
ludovic.text: A learned doublet of Louis, found in France and Belgium in the 19th century and especially fashionable in the second half of the 20th. In Latin records, Ludovicus usually refers to a Louis. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August.

ludovica.label: Ludovica
ludovica.meaning: Feminine form of Ludovic, from Latin "Ludovicus", from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
ludovica.text: The Italian form of Louise, and the Latin form used in Belgian Catholic records for a Louise. It has no well-established patron saint of its own.

ludovico.label: Ludovico
ludovico.meaning: Italian form of Louis, from Latin "Ludovicus", from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
ludovico.text: An older Italian form of Louis, common in the Renaissance alongside Lodovico, later supplanted by Luigi. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August.

ludovicus.label: Ludovicus
ludovicus.meaning: Latin form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
ludovicus.text: The Latin form used in Catholic records in Belgium, the Netherlands and France; in daily life the person was called Louis, Lodewijk or Ludwig. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August.

ludwig.label: Ludwig
ludwig.meaning: German form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
ludwig.text: A very widespread name in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, notably in Bavaria, several of whose kings bore it in the 19th century. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August.

ludwik.label: Ludwik
ludwik.meaning: Polish form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
ludwik.text: The Polish form of Louis, found in Polish records mostly in the 18th and 19th centuries; Latin records write Ludovicus. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August.

ludwika.label: Ludwika
ludwika.meaning: Polish form of Louise, feminine of Ludwik, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
ludwika.text: A Polish female name, borne notably by Queen Ludwika Maria Gonzaga in the 17th century and frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries; Latin records write Ludovica. It has no well-established patron saint of its own.

luigi.label: Luigi
luigi.meaning: Italian form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
luigi.text: One of the most frequent male names in Italy in the 19th and 20th centuries; Latin records write Aloysius or Ludovicus, and the Veneto has the form Alvise. In Italy the usual name day is that of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga, 21 June.

luigia.label: Luigia
luigia.meaning: Feminine form of Luigi, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
luigia.text: An Italian female name frequent in the 19th century, parallel to Luisa and often shortened to Gina or Gigia; Latin records write Aloysia. It has no well-established patron saint of its own.

luis.label: Luis
luis.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
luis.text: A very widespread name in Spain and Portugal (where Luiz is also written), found in the records since the Middle Ages. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August, although Saint Aloysius Gonzaga is also honoured.

luisa.label: Luisa
luisa.meaning: Feminine form of Luis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
luisa.text: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Louise, frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries, often in compounds (María Luisa, Anna Luisa). It has no old patron saint of its own; it is sometimes celebrated with Saint Louise de Marillac.

luise.label: Luise
luise.meaning: German form of Louise, feminine of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
luise.text: A female name very widespread in Germany and Switzerland in the 18th and 19th centuries, popularised notably by Queen Louise of Prussia; Louise and Luise are both found for the same woman. It has no old patron saint of its own.

luiz.label: Luiz
luiz.meaning: Older Portuguese spelling of Luís, a form of Louis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
luiz.text: The usual Portuguese spelling before the spelling reforms of the 20th century, still common in Brazil; Luiz and Luís are the same name. Its name day is that of Saint Louis, King of France, on 25 August.

lukasz.label: Łukasz
lukasz.meaning: Polish form of Luke, from Greek "Loukas", "man from Lucania".
lukasz.text: The Polish form of Luke, found in the Catholic records of Poland for centuries; Latin records write Lucas. It honours Saint Luke the Evangelist, whose feast is 18 October.

lukrecia.label: Lukrécia
lukrecia.meaning: From the Roman family name Lucretius, of uncertain etymology.
lukrecia.text: A rare spelling of Lucretia (Italian Lucrezia), found in a few records from Italy and Central Europe. It has no well-established patron saint.

lula.label: Lula
lula.meaning: An affectionate pet form of names such as Louisa, Lucy or Tallulah, of varying etymology.
lula.text: A mainly American name, frequent in the southern United States from the late 19th century to the 1920s; the spellings Lulu or Loula also occur. The same woman may appear under another name in official records. It has no patron saint.

luther.label: Luther
luther.meaning: From the surname of the reformer Martin Luther, from an old Germanic given name related to Lothar, "glory" and "army".
luther.text: A mainly American name, given in honour of the reformer in Protestant families, notably Lutheran and Baptist, and frequent from the late 19th century to the 1920s. It is not linked to a saint.

lydia.label: Lydia
lydia.meaning: From Greek "Lydia", "woman of Lydia", a region of Asia Minor.
lydia.text: A biblical name favoured by Protestants in Switzerland, Germany, Britain and the United States from the 17th century, rarer in Catholic lands before the 19th. It honours Saint Lydia, the purple-cloth merchant of Thyatira converted by Saint Paul, whose feast is 3 August.

lydie.label: Lydie
lydie.meaning: French form of Lydia, from Greek "woman of Lydia", a region of Asia Minor.
lydie.text: The French form of Lydia, frequent in France and French-speaking Switzerland in the 19th century, notably in Protestant families. It honours Saint Lydia of Thyatira, converted by Saint Paul, whose feast is 3 August in the Roman and French calendars.

lynn.label: Lynn
lynn.meaning: Disputed: perhaps from Welsh "llyn", "lake", or a short form of names ending in -line (Linda, Carolyn).
lynn.text: A mostly female English-language name, widespread in the United States and Britain in the 20th century, often as a middle name. It was also borne by some men, mainly before 1940.

mabel.label: Mabel
mabel.meaning: Shortened form of Amabel, from Latin "amabilis", "lovable".
mabel.text: A medieval English name, revived in the Victorian era and very frequent in the United States around 1880-1920; Mable or Mabelle also occur. It has no patron saint.

macee.label: Macée
macee.meaning: Feminine of Macé, an old form of Mathieu.
macee.text: A female name frequent in western France (Anjou, Maine, Brittany) in the 15th–17th centuries. Records also spell it Massée.

maciej.label: Maciej
maciej.meaning: Polish form of Matthias, from Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God".
maciej.text: A very common name in Poland since the Middle Ages, shortened to Maciek; Latin records write Mathias. It honours the apostle Saint Matthias, whose feast is 14 May in the current Roman calendar and was 24 February before 1969.

madalena.label: Madalena
madalena.meaning: Portuguese form of Magdalene, from "Magdala", a town in Galilee whose name means "tower" in Hebrew.
madalena.text: The Portuguese form of Magdalene, found in Portuguese records since the Middle Ages. It honours Saint Mary Magdalene, the disciple of Jesus, whose feast is 22 July.

maddalena.label: Maddalena
maddalena.meaning: Italian form of Magdalene, from "Magdala", a town in Galilee whose name means "tower" in Hebrew.
maddalena.text: The Italian form of Magdalene, frequent in Italy from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, often in compounds (Maria Maddalena). It honours Saint Mary Magdalene, whose feast is 22 July.

madeleine.label: Madeleine
madeleine.meaning: From the byname of Mary of Magdala, a town in Galilee whose name means "tower" in Hebrew.
madeleine.text: One of the most frequent female names in France, Belgium and Switzerland, very common from the 17th to the early 20th century; older records often write Magdeleine or Magdelaine. It honours Saint Mary Magdalene, the disciple of Jesus, whose feast is 22 July.

mae.label: Mae
mae.meaning: A variant of May, a pet form of Mary or Margaret.
mae.text: An American name very fashionable from the late 19th century to the 1920s, often as a middle name (Annie Mae, Lillie Mae), especially in the South. It has no feast of its own.

mael.label: Maël
mael.text: An old Breton name, borne by a local saint, that became popular again in France from the 1990s. It is rarely found in 18th- and 19th-century registers.

maelle.label: Maëlle
maelle.meaning: Feminine of Maël, from Old Breton "mael", "prince, chief".
maelle.text: A modern feminine of Maël, given mostly in France since the 1980s. It is absent from older registers.

magda.label: Magda
magda.meaning: Short form of Magdalena, from "Magdala", a town in Galilee whose name means "tower" in Hebrew.
magda.text: A pet form of Magdalena that became a name in its own right in Poland, Germany and Central Europe, mostly in the 20th century; the same woman may appear as Magdalena in her baptism record. Its name day is that of Saint Mary Magdalene, 22 July.

magdalena.label: Magdalena
magdalena.meaning: From the byname of Mary of Magdala, a town in Galilee whose name means "tower" in Hebrew.
magdalena.text: The Latin, Spanish, Polish, German and Dutch form of Magdalene, very frequent in the records of both Catholic and Protestant Europe; Magdalen or the pet form Lena also occur. It honours Saint Mary Magdalene, whose feast is 22 July.

magdalene.label: Magdalene
magdalene.meaning: From the byname of Mary of Magdala, a town in Galilee whose name means "tower" in Hebrew.
magdalene.text: The German form of Magdalene, found in German records and among German emigrants, alternating with Magdalena. It honours Saint Mary Magdalene, whose feast is 22 July.

magdeleine.label: Magdeleine
magdeleine.meaning: Older spelling of Madeleine, from "Magdala", a town in Galilee whose name means "tower" in Hebrew.
magdeleine.text: An older French spelling of Madeleine, very frequent in 17th- and 18th-century records, with the variant Magdelaine; it is the same name as Madeleine. It honours Saint Mary Magdalene, whose feast is 22 July.

magloire.label: Magloire
magloire.text: Saint Magloire, successor of Saint Samson at Dol, is celebrated on 24 October. The name was mostly borne in Brittany and Normandy.

magnus.label: Magnus
magnus.text: A name widespread in Scandinavia since the Middle Ages and traditional in southern Germany and eastern Switzerland, where Saint Magnus (Mang) of Füssen, an 8th-century missionary of the Allgäu, was much venerated. His feast is 6 September.

maiwenn.label: Maïwenn
maiwenn.meaning: A modern Breton name, often linked to Mai (Mary) and "gwenn", "white, pure"; etymology disputed.
maiwenn.text: A Breton name that appeared in the 20th century and has been given mostly since the 1980s. The spellings Maïwenn, Maiwen and Maëwenn coexist; it is absent from older registers.

maja.label: Maja
maja.meaning: Short form of Maria in Slavic and Germanic languages, sometimes associated with the Roman goddess Maia.
maja.text: A name mostly widespread in Poland and Germany in the 20th century, rare in older records, where the same woman generally appears as Maria. It has no well-established feast of its own.

maksymilian.label: Maksymilian
maksymilian.meaning: Polish form of Maximilian, from Latin "Maximilianus", derived from "maximus", "greatest".
maksymilian.text: The Polish form of Maximilian, found in Polish records mostly in the 19th and 20th centuries, often shortened to Maks. Its traditional name day is that of Saint Maximilian of Celeia (or of Lorch), bishop and martyr, on 12 October.

malcolm.label: Malcolm
malcolm.meaning: From Gaelic "Máel Coluim", "devotee of Saint Columba".
malcolm.text: A royal Scottish name, borne by several kings of Scotland, common in Scotland and among people of Scottish descent in Britain and the United States. It is not itself linked to a patron saint.

malgorzata.label: Małgorzata
malgorzata.meaning: Polish form of Margaret, from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
malgorzata.text: One of the most common female names in Poland since the Middle Ages, shortened to Małgosia; Latin records write Margaretha. It traditionally honours Saint Margaret of Antioch, a virgin martyr very popular in the Middle Ages, whose feast is 20 July.

malo.label: Malo
malo.meaning: From Old Breton or Welsh; disputed meaning.
malo.text: Saint Malo, a Welsh monk who became bishop of Aleth, gave his name to the town of Saint-Malo and is celebrated on 15 November. The form Maclou prevails in Normandy; Latin records write Machutus or Maclovius.

manasse.label: Manassé
manasse.text: The name of Joseph's elder son in the Bible. Among the Jews of Alsace and Lorraine it appears in the 18th and 19th centuries in the Yiddish form Manès, while Manassé or Manasseh appear in Protestant and English-language records.

manfred.label: Manfred
manfred.text: A Germanic name used in the Middle Ages (Manfred, King of Sicily), then revived in Germany and Switzerland in the 19th and 20th centuries. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

manoel.label: Manoel
manoel.meaning: Older Portuguese spelling of Manuel, from Hebrew "Immanuel", "God is with us".
manoel.text: An older spelling of Manuel, frequent in Portuguese and Brazilian records until the early 20th century; Manoel and Manuel are the same name. It is not linked to a saint, but to a name given to Christ.

manuel.label: Manuel
manuel.meaning: Shortened form of Emmanuel, from Hebrew "Immanuel", "God is with us".
manuel.text: One of the most widespread names in Spain and Portugal, where Manoel, Manolo or Nelo also occur, and found in Italy and France. It refers not to a saint but to a name of Christ, and so has no patronal feast of its own.

manuela.label: Manuela
manuela.meaning: Feminine form of Manuel, from Hebrew "Immanuel", "God is with us".
manuela.text: A female name common in Spain and Portugal since the 18th century, and rarer elsewhere. It has no well-established patron saint.

marc.label: Marc
marc.meaning: From Latin "Marcus", a Roman first name often linked to the god Mars.
marc.text: A name found in France since the Middle Ages without being very frequent in older records, and very common in the 20th century. It honours Saint Mark the Evangelist, patron of Venice, whose feast is 25 April.

marcantonio.label: Marcantonio
marcantonio.meaning: A compound of Marco and Antonio, recalling the Roman general Mark Antony.
marcantonio.text: An Italian compound name, fashionable in the Renaissance and the 17th and 18th centuries, also written Marc'Antonio or Marco Antonio. It has no feast of its own; it is sometimes linked to Saint Mark or Saint Anthony.

marceau.label: Marceau
marceau.meaning: Old French form of Marcel, from Latin "Marcellus", a diminutive of "Marcus".
marceau.text: An old French name, found in 18th- and 19th-century records as a doublet of Marcel. It has no well-established feast of its own; it is sometimes linked to Saint Marcellus.

marcel.label: Marcel
marcel.text: One of the most frequent male names in France, Belgium and Luxembourg in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its name day is that of Pope Saint Marcellus I, on 16 January.

marcelina.label: Marcelina
marcelina.meaning: Feminine form of Marcellinus, from Latin "Marcellinus", derived from "Marcellus".
marcelina.text: A Spanish and Polish female name, frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no patron saint widely recognised in the usual calendars.

marceline.label: Marceline
marceline.meaning: Feminine form of Marcellin, from Latin "Marcellinus", derived from "Marcellus".
marceline.text: A French female name common in the 19th century, sometimes written Marcelline. It has no patron saint widely recognised in the usual calendars.

marcelino.label: Marcelino
marcelino.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Marcellin, from Latin "Marcellinus", derived from "Marcellus".
marcelino.text: A Spanish and Portuguese male name, frequent in 18th- and 19th-century records. Several saints bore it, but no single feast prevailed.

marcella.label: Marcella
marcella.meaning: Feminine form of Marcellus, a diminutive of "Marcus".
marcella.text: An Italian name, also found in Switzerland, Belgium and the United States, where it was fashionable in the early 20th century. It honours Saint Marcella, a 4th-century Roman widow and friend of Saint Jerome, whose feast is 31 January.

marcelle.label: Marcelle
marcelle.meaning: French feminine form of Marcel, from Latin "Marcellus", a diminutive of "Marcus".
marcelle.text: A very frequent name in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It honours Saint Marcella, a 4th-century Roman widow, whose feast is 31 January.

marcellin.label: Marcellin
marcellin.meaning: From Latin "Marcellinus", derived from "Marcellus", a diminutive of "Marcus".
marcellin.text: A French and Belgian name frequent in the 19th century, also written Marcelin. Several saints bore it, including Pope Marcellinus and Saint Marcellin Champagnat, but no single feast prevailed in older calendars.

marcello.label: Marcello
marcello.meaning: Italian form of Marcel, from Latin "Marcellus", a diminutive of "Marcus".
marcello.text: The Italian form of Marcel, regular in Italian records; the pet form Marcellino also occurs. Its name day is that of Pope Saint Marcellus I, on 16 January.

marcin.label: Marcin
marcin.meaning: Polish form of Martin, from Latin "Martinus", derived from the god Mars.
marcin.text: A very common name in Poland since the Middle Ages; Latin records write Martinus. It honours Saint Martin of Tours, a soldier who became bishop in the 4th century, whose feast is 11 November.

marco.label: Marco
marco.meaning: Italian and Spanish form of Mark, from Latin "Marcus", often linked to the god Mars.
marco.text: A very widespread name in Italy, particularly in Venice, whose patron is Saint Mark, and found in Spain and Italian-speaking Switzerland. It honours Saint Mark the Evangelist, whose feast is 25 April.

marcos.label: Marcos
marcos.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Mark, from Latin "Marcus", often linked to the god Mars.
marcos.text: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Mark, found in the records since the Middle Ages. It honours Saint Mark the Evangelist, whose feast is 25 April.

marcus.label: Marcus
marcus.meaning: The Roman first name "Marcus", often linked to the god Mars.
marcus.text: The Latin form of Mark, used in Latin records and as an everyday name in Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland, where Markus also occurs. It honours Saint Mark the Evangelist, whose feast is 25 April.

marek.label: Marek
marek.meaning: Polish form of Mark, from Latin "Marcus", often linked to the god Mars.
marek.text: The Polish form of Mark, rare in older records and mostly widespread in the 20th century. It honours Saint Mark the Evangelist, whose feast is 25 April.

marga.label: Marga
marga.meaning: Short form of Margarete or Margaretha, from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
marga.text: A pet form of Margarete that became a name in its own right in Germany and Poland, mostly in the 20th century; the same woman may appear as Margarete in official records. Its name day is that of Saint Margaret of Antioch, 20 July.

margaret.label: Margaret
margaret.text: One of the most widespread female names in Britain, Ireland and the United States, with many pet forms (Maggie, Madge, Peggy, Meg). In the British world it chiefly honours Saint Margaret of Scotland, an 11th-century queen whose feast is 16 November; the popular Saint Margaret of Antioch is celebrated on 20 July.

margarete.label: Margarete
margarete.meaning: German form of Margaret, from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
margarete.text: A very frequent name in Germany, Switzerland and Austria, with many shortened forms (Grete, Gretel, Gretchen, Margret). It traditionally honours Saint Margaret of Antioch, a virgin martyr and one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, whose feast is 20 July.

margaretha.label: Margaretha
margaretha.meaning: Latin and Dutch form of Margaret, from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
margaretha.text: A very frequent form in Latin records and in everyday use in the Netherlands, Flanders, Switzerland and Germany; Grietje, Margreta or Margot also occur. It traditionally honours Saint Margaret of Antioch, whose feast is 20 July.

margarethe.label: Margarethe
margarethe.meaning: German form of Margaret, from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
margarethe.text: An older German spelling of Margarete, frequent in German and Swiss records until the early 20th century. It traditionally honours Saint Margaret of Antioch, whose feast is 20 July.

margarida.label: Margarida
margarida.meaning: Portuguese and Catalan form of Margaret, from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
margarida.text: The Portuguese and Catalan form of Margaret, found in the records since the Middle Ages; in the Balearic Islands Margalida also occurs. It traditionally honours Saint Margaret of Antioch, whose feast is 20 July.

margarita.label: Margarita
margarita.meaning: Spanish and Latin form of Margaret, from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
margarita.text: The Spanish form of Margaret, very frequent in Spain, and the Latin form in parish records throughout Europe. It traditionally honours Saint Margaret of Antioch, whose feast is 20 July.

margery.label: Margery
margery.meaning: A medieval English form of Margaret, through Old French "Margerie", from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
margery.text: A medieval English form of Margaret, revived in the 19th and 20th centuries in Britain and the United States, alternating with Marjorie. Its name day is that of Saint Margaret of Scotland, 16 November.

margherita.label: Margherita
margherita.meaning: Italian form of Margaret, from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
margherita.text: A very widespread name in Italy since the Middle Ages, further boosted in the 19th century by Queen Margherita of Savoy; Latin records write Margarita. It traditionally honours Saint Margaret of Antioch, whose feast is 20 July.

margrit.label: Margrit
margrit.meaning: Swiss German form of Margaret, from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
margrit.text: The usual form in German-speaking Switzerland, mostly in the 20th century, while official records may write Margaritha or Margaretha. Its name day is that of Saint Margaret of Antioch, 20 July.

marguerite.label: Marguerite
marguerite.meaning: From Greek "margaritês", "pearl", through Latin "Margarita"; the word also names the daisy.
marguerite.text: One of the most frequently given female names in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland from the Middle Ages to the early 20th century. It traditionally honours Saint Margaret of Antioch, whose feast is 20 July; recent French calendars celebrate it on 16 November, with Saint Margaret of Scotland.

maria.label: Maria
maria.meaning: From Hebrew "Miryam"; disputed meaning — "lady", "one who raises up", or "star of the sea".
maria.text: The Latin, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, German and Dutch form of Mary, by far the most frequent female name throughout Catholic Europe; it is also given to boys as a second name (Josef Maria). Its frequency makes it a poor identifier on its own. Its main feast is the Assumption, 15 August.

maria_angeles.label: Maria Ángeles
maria_angeles.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and the Marian title "Our Lady of the Angels".
maria_angeles.text: A Spanish Marian name, often shortened to Ángeles or Marian, very widespread in the 20th century; María de los Ángeles and the Galician María dos Anxos also occur. Its feast is that of Our Lady of the Angels, 2 August.

maria_antonia.label: Maria Antonia
maria_antonia.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and Antonia, feminine of the Roman name Antonius, of uncertain etymology.
maria_antonia.text: A compound name common in Spain in the 18th and 19th centuries; in daily life the woman might be called simply Antonia or María. It has no feast of its own.

maria_del_carmen.label: María del Carmen
maria_del_carmen.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and the Marian title of Our Lady of Mount Carmel ("karmel", "garden, orchard" in Hebrew).
maria_del_carmen.text: One of the most widespread female names in Spain, especially in the 19th and 20th centuries, with many forms (Carmen, Mari Carmen, the Catalan Maria del Carme). The same woman may appear simply as Carmen. Its feast is that of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, 16 July.

maria_do_carmo.label: Maria do Carmo
maria_do_carmo.meaning: A compound of Maria, from Hebrew "Miryam", and the Marian title of Our Lady of Mount Carmel.
maria_do_carmo.text: The Portuguese form of the Marian name María del Carmen, frequent in Portugal and Brazil, sometimes shortened to Carmo. Its feast is that of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, 16 July.

maria_dolores.label: María Dolores
maria_dolores.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and the Marian title of Our Lady of Sorrows (Spanish "dolores").
maria_dolores.text: A Marian name very widespread in Spain, often shortened to Dolores, Lola or Loli; María de los Dolores and the Catalan Maria Dolors also occur. Its feast is that of Our Lady of Sorrows, 15 September.

maria_isabel.label: María Isabel
maria_isabel.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and Isabel, the Iberian form of Elisabeth, "God is my oath".
maria_isabel.text: A compound name common in Spain, especially in the 20th century; the woman might be called simply Isabel or Maribel. It has no feast of its own.

maria_jesus.label: María Jesús
maria_jesus.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and Jesús, from Hebrew "Yehoshua", "God saves".
maria_jesus.text: A devotional compound name typical of Spain, mostly widespread in the 20th century and often shortened to Chus or Marichu; María de Jesús also occurs. It has no fixed feast of its own.

maria_jose.label: María José
maria_jose.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and José, from Hebrew "Yosef", "he will add".
maria_jose.text: A Spanish compound name joining Mary and Joseph, very widespread in the 20th century and often shortened to Mariajo. In Spain it is celebrated on Saint Joseph's day, 19 March.

maria_josefa.label: María Josefa
maria_josefa.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and Josefa, feminine of José, from Hebrew "Yosef", "he will add".
maria_josefa.text: A compound name very common in Spain in the 18th and 19th centuries; the woman might be called simply Josefa or Pepa. It is celebrated on Saint Joseph's day, 19 March.

maria_josepha.label: Maria Josepha
maria_josepha.meaning: A compound of Maria, from Hebrew "Miryam", and Josepha, the Latin feminine of Joseph, "he will add".
maria_josepha.text: The Latin or Germanic spelling of the compound María Josefa, found in Latin records in Spain and in German-speaking countries. It is celebrated on Saint Joseph's day, 19 March.

maria_juana.label: María Juana
maria_juana.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and Juana, feminine of Juan, "God is gracious".
maria_juana.text: A Spanish compound name, found mostly in the 18th and 19th centuries; the woman might be called simply Juana. It has no feast of its own.

maria_luisa.label: María Luisa
maria_luisa.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and Luisa, feminine of Luis, from Germanic "Hlodwig", "glorious warrior".
maria_luisa.text: A compound name borne by queens and princesses (Marie-Louise), very widespread in Spain and Italy in the 19th and 20th centuries; Maria Lluïsa and Marie-Luise also occur. It has no feast of its own.

maria_pilar.label: Maria Pilar
maria_pilar.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and the Marian title of Our Lady of the Pillar ("pilar") of Zaragoza.
maria_pilar.text: A Spanish Marian name, particularly frequent in Aragon, often shortened to Pilar or Pili; María del Pilar also occurs. Its feast is that of Our Lady of the Pillar, 12 October.

maria_teresa.label: Maria Teresa
maria_teresa.meaning: A compound of María, from Hebrew "Miryam", and Teresa, of uncertain etymology, possibly Greek.
maria_teresa.text: A compound name very widespread in Spain and Italy, also popularised by Empress Maria Theresa of Austria; Maite occurs in Spain and Maria Theresia in German-speaking lands. Its name day is that of Saint Teresa of Ávila, 15 October.

marian.label: Marian
marian.meaning: From Latin "Marianus", "relating to Mary"; in English also a variant of Marion, a pet form of Mary.
marian.text: A unisex name: male in Poland, Romania and Central Europe, mostly in the 19th and 20th centuries, and female in Britain and the United States. The sex should therefore be checked in the record. It has no well-established feast of its own.

mariana.label: Mariana
mariana.meaning: Feminine form of Latin "Marianus", "relating to Mary", often also understood as Mary Anne.
mariana.text: A Portuguese and Spanish female name, common in the 18th and 19th centuries, and also found in Poland and Germany. It has no well-established patron saint in older calendars.

marianna.label: Marianna
marianna.meaning: A compound of Maria and Anna, or feminine form of Latin "Marianus", "relating to Mary".
marianna.text: An Italian, Polish and Dutch form, frequent in 18th- and 19th-century records; the same woman may appear as Maria Anna. It has no feast of its own.

marianne.label: Marianne
marianne.meaning: A contraction of Marie-Anne, from Hebrew "Miryam" and "Hannah", "grace".
marianne.text: A name widespread in Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Britain and France, where it may alternate with Marie-Anne for the same woman; since the Revolution it has also named the figure of the French Republic. It has no feast of its own.

mariano.label: Mariano
mariano.text: A Marian male name common in Spain, Italy and Portugal in the 18th and 19th centuries. Several obscure saints bore it, but no feast prevailed.

marie.label: Marie
marie.meaning: From Hebrew "Miryam"; disputed meaning — "lady", "one who raises up", or "star of the sea".
marie.text: The name of Jesus's mother, Marie was by far the most common female given name in France from the Middle Ages through the 19th century, often used as a first given name paired with a second one (Marie-Anne, Marie-Louise...). Its extreme frequency in the records makes it a poor identifier on its own for genealogical research.

marie_therese.label: Marie-Thérèse
marie_therese.meaning: A compound of Marie, from Hebrew "Miryam", and Thérèse, of uncertain etymology, possibly Greek.
marie_therese.text: A compound name widespread in France, Belgium and Luxembourg in the 18th and 19th centuries, popularised by Empress Maria Theresa of Austria, who then ruled Luxembourg. Its name day is that of Saint Teresa of Ávila, 15 October.

marielle.label: Marielle
marielle.text: A diminutive of Marie that became a name in its own right, given in France mostly between the 1950s and the 1970s. It is rare in records before the 20th century.

marietta.label: Marietta
marietta.meaning: Italian pet form of Maria, from Hebrew "Miryam".
marietta.text: A pet form of Maria common in Italy and among Italian emigrants to the United States; the same woman may appear as Maria in her baptism record. Its feast is that of the Virgin Mary, 15 August.

mariette.label: Mariette
mariette.meaning: French pet form of Marie, from Hebrew "Miryam".
mariette.text: A pet form of Marie that became a name in its own right in France and Belgium, mostly in the 19th and early 20th centuries; Marinette also occurs. Its feast is that of the Virgin Mary, 15 August.

marilyn.label: Marilyn
marilyn.meaning: A modern compound of Mary, from Hebrew "Miryam", and the suffix "-lyn".
marilyn.text: An American name of the 20th century, mostly given in the 1930s and 1940s, so rare in older records. It has no feast of its own.

marin.label: Marin
marin.meaning: From Latin "Marinus", "of the sea", or derived from the Roman name Marius.
marin.text: A French male name, found in older records and frequent in the 19th century. It honours Saint Marinus, the stonemason and legendary founder of San Marino, whose feast is 3 September.

marina.label: Marina
marina.meaning: From Latin "Marina", "of the sea", feminine of Marinus.
marina.text: A name widespread in Italy, Spain and Poland, rarer in Britain before the 20th century. It honours Saint Marina of Antioch, a virgin martyr identified in the West with Saint Margaret, whose feast is 20 July.

marino.label: Marino
marino.meaning: From Latin "Marinus", "of the sea", or derived from the Roman name Marius.
marino.text: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Marinus, found mostly in Italy. It honours Saint Marinus, the legendary founder of the Republic of San Marino, whose feast is 3 September.

marinus.label: Marinus
marinus.meaning: From Latin "Marinus", "of the sea", or derived from the Roman name Marius.
marinus.text: A Latin name that remained in everyday use in the Netherlands and Flanders, notably in Zeeland and Holland, often shortened to Rinus. It honours Saint Marinus, whose feast is 3 September.

mario.label: Mario
mario.meaning: From the Roman family name Marius, probably derived from "mas, maris", "male", or from the god Mars; often wrongly linked to Maria.
mario.text: A very widespread name in Italy, Spain and Portugal, especially from the late 19th century. In Italy its name day is 19 January, with Saint Marius, a Persian martyred in Rome in the 3rd century.

marion.label: Marion
