marion.meaning: A medieval French pet form of Marie, from Hebrew "Miryam".
marion.text: A pet form of Marie attested in France since the Middle Ages (Robin and Marion) and adopted in Scotland, England and the United States, where men also bore it in the late 19th century. For women, its feast is that of the Virgin Mary, 15 August.

marius.label: Marius
marius.meaning: From the Roman family name Marius, probably derived from "mas, maris", "male", or from the god Mars.
marius.text: A classically inspired name very widespread in Provence and south-eastern France in the 19th century, also found in Belgium, the Netherlands and Switzerland. It honours Saint Marius, a Persian martyred in Rome in the 3rd century with his family, whose feast is 19 January.

marjorie.label: Marjorie
marjorie.meaning: A medieval Scottish and English form of Margaret, through Old French "Margerie", from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
marjorie.text: A name borne in Scotland since the Middle Ages, then very fashionable in the United States and Britain in the early 20th century; Marjory or Margery also occur. Its name day is that of Saint Margaret of Scotland, 16 November.

mark.label: Mark
mark.meaning: From Latin "Marcus", a Roman first name often linked to the god Mars.
mark.text: The English form of Mark, found in England since the Middle Ages without being frequent, and very popular in the United States and Britain in the mid-20th century. It honours Saint Mark the Evangelist, whose feast is 25 April.

marlene.label: Marlene
marlene.meaning: A German contraction of Maria and Magdalena.
marlene.text: A name that appeared in Germany in the early 20th century and then spread to Britain, the United States and Spain, mostly in the 1930s; it is therefore rare in older records. It has no feast of its own.

marquise.label: Marquise
marquise.text: A rare female name taken from the noble title, attested in France in the 17th and 18th centuries, especially in the south. It does not necessarily indicate a noblewoman: it is a genuine baptismal name.

marshall.label: Marshall
marshall.meaning: From the English surname Marshall, from Germanic "marh", "horse", and "scalc", "servant", meaning "groom".
marshall.text: A surname turned given name, mainly in the United States, frequent from the late 19th to the mid-20th century. It may reflect a surname in the family. It is not linked to a saint.

marta.label: Marta
marta.meaning: From Aramaic "Marta", "lady, mistress of the house".
marta.text: The Polish, Spanish, Italian and German form of Martha, frequent throughout Catholic Europe. It honours Saint Martha of Bethany, sister of Mary and Lazarus, whose feast is 29 July.

martha.label: Martha
martha.meaning: From Aramaic "Marta", "lady, mistress of the house".
martha.text: A biblical name widespread in Germany, Poland, Switzerland, the Netherlands and among English-speaking Protestants, notably in the United States. It honours Saint Martha of Bethany, sister of Mary and Lazarus, whose feast is 29 July.

marthe.label: Marthe
marthe.meaning: From Aramaic "Marta", "lady, mistress of the house".
marthe.text: A very frequent name in France, Belgium and Switzerland in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and already present under the Ancien Régime, notably in Provence, where Saint Martha is venerated at Tarascon. Its feast is 29 July.

martial.label: Martial
martial.text: A traditional name of the Limousin and west-central France, frequent in older records and in the 19th century. It honours Saint Martial, first bishop of Limoges in the 3rd century, whose feast is 30 June.

martin.label: Martin
martin.meaning: From Latin "Martinus", derived from the god Mars.
martin.text: A very widespread name throughout Europe since the Middle Ages, particularly in Germany (notably among Protestants, in memory of Luther), Switzerland, Spain and Central Europe. It honours Saint Martin of Tours, a soldier who became bishop in the 4th century, whose feast is 11 November.

martina.label: Martina
martina.meaning: Feminine form of Martin, from Latin "Martinus", derived from the god Mars.
martina.text: A female name found in Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium and Poland, mostly in the 18th and 19th centuries, and very fashionable again in the late 20th. It honours Saint Martina, a Roman martyr of the 3rd century, whose feast is 30 January.

martine.label: Martine
martine.meaning: French feminine form of Martin, from Latin "Martinus", derived from the god Mars.
martine.text: A name found in France and Belgium in older records, but above all very widespread in the mid-20th century. It honours Saint Martina, a Roman martyr of the 3rd century, whose feast is 30 January.

martino.label: Martino
martino.meaning: Italian form of Martin, from Latin "Martinus", derived from the god Mars.
martino.text: The Italian form of Martin, common in Italy and Italian-speaking Switzerland since the Middle Ages. It honours Saint Martin of Tours, whose feast is 11 November.

martinus.label: Martinus
martinus.meaning: Latin form of Martin, derived from the god Mars.
martinus.text: The Latin form used in the records and still in everyday use in the Netherlands and Flanders; in daily life Maarten, Marten, Martijn or Tinus occur. It honours Saint Martin of Tours, whose feast is 11 November.

marvin.label: Marvin
marvin.meaning: Probably from Welsh Merfyn, of uncertain etymology, perhaps "eminent"; sometimes linked to Old English.
marvin.text: A mainly American name, very frequent between the 1910s and the 1940s. It is not linked to a saint.

mary.label: Mary
mary.meaning: English form of Marie, from Hebrew "Miryam"; disputed meaning — "lady", "one who raises up", or "star of the sea".
mary.text: The most frequent female name in the English-speaking world for centuries, in England, Ireland and the United States, with many pet forms (Molly, Polly, Mamie, Mae). Its frequency makes it a poor identifier on its own. Its main feast is the Assumption, 15 August.

maryse.label: Maryse
maryse.meaning: A modern derivative of Marie, from Hebrew "Miryam", perhaps a contraction of Marie-Élise.
maryse.text: A French name of the 20th century, mostly given between the 1930s and the 1960s, so rare in older records. Its feast is that of the Virgin Mary, 15 August.

maryvonne.label: Maryvonne
maryvonne.meaning: A compound of Marie, from Hebrew "Miryam", and Yvonne, feminine of Yves, of Germanic origin.
maryvonne.text: A typically Breton compound name, mostly given in the 20th century, joining Marie and Yvonne, the feminine of Yves, the name of Brittany's patron saint. It has no feast of its own.

massimo.label: Massimo
massimo.text: An Italian name, rare in older records and mostly widespread in the 20th century. Several saints named Maximus bore it, including a bishop of Turin, but no single feast prevailed for this name.

mateo.label: Mateo
mateo.meaning: Spanish form of Matthew, from Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God".
mateo.text: The Spanish form of Matthew, found in Spanish records since the Middle Ages; it should not be confused with Matías (Matthias). It honours Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, whose feast is 21 September.

mateusz.label: Mateusz
mateusz.meaning: Polish form of Matthew, from Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God".
mateusz.text: The Polish form of Matthew, found in Polish records; it should not be confused with Maciej (Matthias). Latin records write Matthaeus. It honours Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, whose feast is 21 September.

mathias.label: Mathias
mathias.text: A very widespread name in Luxembourg, the Rhineland and Switzerland, where the Abbey of Saint Matthias in Trier, which claims the apostle's relics, drew pilgrims; Matthias or Mathis also occur. It honours the apostle Saint Matthias, whose feast is 14 May since 1969 and was 24 February before.

mathieu.label: Mathieu
mathieu.meaning: French form of Matthew, from Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God".
mathieu.text: A common name in France, Belgium and Luxembourg since the Middle Ages, written Matthieu or Mathieu depending on the record; it gave rise to many surnames. It honours Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, whose feast is 21 September.

mathilde.label: Mathilde
mathilde.text: A medieval name of princesses and queens, very frequent again in France, Belgium, Switzerland and Germany in the 19th century; Mathilda and the German Mechtild also occur. It honours Saint Matilda, queen of Germany in the 10th century, whose feast is 14 March.

mathildis.label: Mathildis
mathildis.meaning: Latin form of Matilda, from Germanic "maht", "might", and "hild", "battle".
mathildis.text: The Latin form used in Belgian Catholic records; in daily life the person was called Mathilde or Mathilda. It honours Saint Matilda, queen of Germany, whose feast is 14 March.

mathurin.label: Mathurin
mathurin.text: A traditional name of western France, notably in Brittany, very frequent under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century. It honours Saint Maturinus, a 4th-century priest venerated at Larchant and invoked against madness, commemorated on 1 November.

mathurine.label: Mathurine
mathurine.text: A feminine form of Mathurin, very frequent in Brittany, Anjou and Poitou in the 16th–18th centuries.

matias.label: Matías
matias.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Matthias, from Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God".
matias.text: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Matthias, not to be confused with Mateo (Matthew). It honours the apostle Saint Matthias, whose feast is 14 May since 1969 and was 24 February before.

matilda.label: Matilda
matilda.meaning: Latinised form of Matilda, from Germanic "maht", "might", and "hild", "battle".
matilda.text: The English form of Matilda, borne by Norman queens and revived in Britain and the United States in the 19th century; the pet forms Tilda, Tillie and Maud derive from it. It honours Saint Matilda, queen of Germany, whose feast is 14 March.

matilde.label: Matilde
matilde.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Matilda, from Germanic "maht", "might", and "hild", "battle".
matilde.text: A form common in Italy, Spain and Portugal, mostly in the 19th century; in Italy the memory of Countess Matilda of Tuscany may have favoured it. It honours Saint Matilda, queen of Germany, whose feast is 14 March.

matteo.label: Matteo
matteo.meaning: Italian form of Matthew, from Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God".
matteo.text: The Italian form of Matthew, common in Italy since the Middle Ages; it should not be confused with Mattia (Matthias). It honours Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, whose feast is 21 September.

matthaus.label: Matthäus
matthaus.meaning: German form of Matthew, from Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God".
matthaus.text: The German form of Matthew, also written Matthäus or Matthaeus, found in Germany, Switzerland and Austria; it should not be confused with Matthias. It honours Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, whose feast is 21 September.

mattheus.label: Mattheus
mattheus.meaning: Latin and Dutch form of Matthew, from Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God".
mattheus.text: A form used in Latin and Dutch records in the Netherlands and Belgium; the person might be called Matthieu or Mathieu in French records. It honours Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, whose feast is 21 September.

matthew.label: Matthew
matthew.meaning: English form of Matthew, from Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God".
matthew.text: An English name in use since the Middle Ages, common in England, Ireland and the United States, also written Mathew. It honours Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, whose feast is 21 September.

matthias.label: Matthias
matthias.meaning: From Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God", the Greek form of the same name as Matthew.
matthias.text: A very widespread name in Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Poland, notably in the Rhineland, where the Abbey of Saint Matthias in Trier claims the apostle's relics. It honours the apostle Saint Matthias, chosen to replace Judas, whose feast is 14 May since 1969 and was 24 February before.

matthijs.label: Matthijs
matthijs.meaning: Dutch form of Matthias, from Hebrew "Mattityahu", "gift of God".
matthijs.text: The Dutch form of Matthias, common in the Netherlands and Flanders, with the spellings Mathijs, Matthys or Mattijs; Latin records write Mathias. It honours the apostle Saint Matthias, whose feast is 14 May since 1969 and was 24 February before.

mattie.label: Mattie
mattie.meaning: Pet form of Martha, Matilda or Mathilda.
mattie.text: An American name frequent from the late 19th century to the 1920s, notably in the South; the same woman may appear as Martha or Matilda in other records. It has no feast of its own.

maud.label: Maud
maud.meaning: Medieval Anglo-Norman form of Matilda, from Germanic "maht", "might", and "hild", "battle".
maud.text: A medieval form of Matilda, revived in Britain in the Victorian era and also found in France in the late 19th century. Its name day is that of Saint Matilda, 14 March.

maude.label: Maude
maude.meaning: A variant of Maud, a medieval form of Matilda, from Germanic "maht", "might", and "hild", "battle".
maude.text: A spelling of Maud particularly frequent in the United States in the 1880s, and found in Britain and France; the pet form Maudie also occurs. Its name day is that of Saint Matilda, 14 March.

maureen.label: Maureen
maureen.meaning: From Irish "Máirín", a pet form of "Máire", the Irish form of Mary.
maureen.text: An Irish name adopted in Britain and the United States, mostly widespread in the mid-20th century; in Ireland the same woman may appear as Mary in English-language records. Its feast is that of the Virgin Mary, 15 August.

maurice.label: Maurice
maurice.text: A very widespread name in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland in the 19th and early 20th centuries, and found in England since the Middle Ages. It honours Saint Maurice, leader of the Theban Legion martyred at Agaunum (Saint-Maurice, in Valais), whose feast is 22 September.

mauricette.label: Mauricette
mauricette.meaning: A feminine pet form of Maurice, from Latin "Mauritius", "Moor".
mauricette.text: A French female name mostly given in the first half of the 20th century. It has no patron saint of its own.

maurits.label: Maurits
maurits.meaning: Dutch form of Maurice, from Latin "Mauritius", derived from "Maurus", "Moor".
maurits.text: The Dutch form of Maurice, popularised in the Netherlands by the stadtholder Maurice of Nassau; Latin records write Mauritius. It honours Saint Maurice of Agaunum, whose feast is 22 September.

maurizia.label: Maurizia
maurizia.meaning: Italian feminine of Maurizio, from Latin "Mauritius", "Moor".
maurizia.text: The Italian feminine form of Maurice, found in northern Italian and Ticino registers. It remains uncommon.

maurizio.label: Maurizio
maurizio.meaning: Italian form of Maurice, from Latin "Mauritius", derived from "Maurus", "Moor".
maurizio.text: The Italian form of Maurice, found in northern Italy, notably in Piedmont, where Saint Maurice was honoured by the House of Savoy. It honours Saint Maurice of Agaunum, whose feast is 22 September.

mauro.label: Mauro
mauro.text: The Italian and Spanish form of Maurus, found in Italy since the Middle Ages. It honours Saint Maurus, disciple of Saint Benedict, whose feast is 15 January.

mavis.label: Mavis
mavis.meaning: From an old English word for the song thrush ("mavis").
mavis.text: An English name that appeared in the late 19th century under literary influence, and was mostly widespread in Britain in the first half of the 20th century. It has no patron saint.

max.label: Max
max.meaning: Short form of Maximilian or Maxime, from Latin "maximus", "greatest".
max.text: A pet form that became a name in its own right in Germany, Switzerland, Luxembourg and France in the 19th century; the same person may appear as Maximilian or Maxime in other records. It has no feast of its own.

maxime.label: Maxime
maxime.text: A French name rare in older records and in the 19th century, which became very common in the late 20th century. Several saints named Maximus are known, including Maximus the Confessor, but no single feast prevailed everywhere.

maximilian.label: Maximilian
maximilian.text: A name made popular by Emperor Maximilian I of Habsburg and by the electors and kings of Bavaria, frequent in southern Germany and Austria. Its traditional name day in those regions is that of Saint Maximilian of Celeia (or of Lorch), bishop and martyr, on 12 October.

maximilien.label: Maximilien
maximilien.meaning: French form of Maximilian, from Latin "Maximilianus", derived from "Maximus", "greatest".
maximilien.text: The French form of Maximilian, found in France, Belgium and Switzerland, mostly in the 19th century. Its traditional name day is that of Saint Maximilian of Celeia, bishop and martyr, on 12 October.

maximin.label: Maximin
maximin.text: A French name frequent in the 19th century. It refers to several saints, including Saint Maximinus, the legendary first bishop of Aix, and Saint Maximinus of Trier, but no single feast prevailed.

maxine.label: Maxine
maxine.meaning: A modern feminine form of Max, from Latin "maximus", "greatest".
maxine.text: A mainly American name, fashionable in the 1920s and 1930s, and rare in older records. It has no patron saint.

may.label: May
may.meaning: A pet form of Mary or Margaret, associated with the name of the month of May.
may.text: An English and American name widespread from the late 19th century to the 1920s, often as a middle name. The same woman may appear as Mary or Margaret in other records. It has no feast of its own.

maya.label: Maya
maya.meaning: Several origins: Greek (Maia, mother of Hermes), Sanskrit ("illusion"), or a diminutive of Maria.
maya.text: A mostly modern female name in western Europe, rising sharply since the late 20th century. In older central European records it can be a diminutive of Maria.

mecia.label: Mécia
mecia.meaning: A medieval Portuguese name, of uncertain etymology, possibly related to Spanish Mencía.
mecia.text: A rare name, borne in Portugal in the Middle Ages and early modern period, notably among the nobility. It is not linked to a saint.

medard.label: Médard
medard.text: Saint Medard, bishop of Noyon in the 6th century, is celebrated on 8 June, the date of a well-known weather proverb. The name was mostly borne in Picardy and northern France.

meinrad.label: Meinrad
meinrad.text: Linked to Saint Meinrad, a hermit murdered in 861 on the site of Einsiedeln Abbey, and widely given in Catholic Switzerland and southern Germany. It is latinised as Meinradus in parish registers.

meir.label: Meir
meir.text: A frequent Jewish name in central and eastern Europe in the 18th and 19th centuries. Polish records write Majer or Mejer, German and Alsatian ones Mayer or Meyer, spellings that also became surnames.

melaine.label: Mélaine
melaine.meaning: From Latin Melanius, linked to Greek "melas", "black".
melaine.text: The name of Saint Melaine, a 6th-century bishop of Rennes, given in Brittany in older registers. In the 20th century it is sometimes borne by women, by association with Mélanie.

melania.label: Melania
melania.text: The Latin, Polish and Spanish form of Melanie, found mostly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It honours Saint Melania the Younger, a Roman aristocrat who became a nun in Jerusalem in the 5th century, whose feast is 31 December.

melanie.label: Melanie
melanie.text: A very frequent name in France and Belgium in the first half of the 19th century, fashionable again in the late 20th. It honours Saint Melania the Younger, whose feast is 31 December.

melchior.label: Melchior
melchior.meaning: The traditional name of one of the Three Magi, often linked to Hebrew "melek", "king", and "or", "light"; the etymology remains uncertain.
melchior.text: A name used in Switzerland, Germany, Belgium and Poland, mostly from the 16th to the 18th century. It honours Melchior, one of the Three Magi, celebrated at Epiphany, 6 January.

melchor.label: Melchor
melchor.meaning: Spanish form of Melchior, the traditional name of one of the Three Magi, of uncertain etymology.
melchor.text: The Spanish form of Melchior, found in Spanish records, often for a child born or baptised around Epiphany. It honours one of the Three Magi, celebrated on 6 January.

melvin.label: Melvin
melvin.meaning: From the Scottish surname Melville, taken from a place name, or of uncertain Gaelic origin.
melvin.text: A mainly American name, very frequent between the 1910s and the 1940s. It is not linked to a saint.

melvyn.label: Melvyn
melvyn.meaning: A British variant of Melvin, of uncertain etymology, possibly from the Scottish surname Melville.
melvyn.text: A mainly British spelling of Melvin, widespread in the mid-20th century and rare in older records. It is not linked to a saint.

mendel.label: Mendel
mendel.meaning: A Yiddish diminutive, usually linked to Menachem, "comforter".
mendel.text: A very common male Yiddish name in central and eastern Europe in the 19th century, often in compounds (Menachem Mendel). It also became a surname.

merce.label: Mercè
merce.meaning: Catalan form of Mercedes, from Latin "merces", "grace, ransom", referring to Our Lady of Mercy.
merce.text: A Catalan Marian name, closely tied to Barcelona, whose patron is Our Lady of Mercy; records in Castilian write Mercedes. Its feast is 24 September.

mercedes.label: Mercedes
mercedes.meaning: From Spanish "mercedes", "graces", from Latin "merces", referring to Our Lady of Mercy.
mercedes.text: A Spanish Marian name, often from María de las Mercedes, very widespread in Spain in the 19th and 20th centuries and found in Portugal and the Americas. Its feast is that of Our Lady of Mercy, 24 September.

meriadec.label: Mériadec
meriadec.meaning: An old Brittonic name; meaning disputed.
meriadec.text: Borne by Saint Meriadoc (Mériadec), a 7th-century bishop of Vannes, and still associated with the Morbihan. It is rare in older registers and was revived in the 20th century, also in the Breton form Meriadeg.

meta.label: Meta
meta.meaning: A German and Dutch short form of Margarete, from Greek "margaritês", "pearl".
meta.text: A pet form of Margarete that became a name in its own right in northern Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands, and is found among emigrants to the United States; the same woman may appear as Margaretha in other records. Its name day is that of Saint Margaret of Antioch, 20 July.

micaela.label: Micaela
micaela.meaning: Feminine form of Miguel, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?".
micaela.text: A Spanish, Portuguese and Italian female name, found mostly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no patron saint widely celebrated in older calendars.

michael.label: Michael
michael.text: The English, German and Latin form of Michel, frequent in Germany, Switzerland and Austria since the Middle Ages, then in Ireland and the United States. It honours Saint Michael the Archangel, whose feast is 29 September.

michal.label: Michał
michal.meaning: Polish form of Michael, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?".
michal.text: A very widespread name in Poland since the Middle Ages; Latin records write Michael. It honours Saint Michael the Archangel, whose feast is 29 September.

michalina.label: Michalina
michalina.meaning: Polish feminine form of Michał, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?".
michalina.text: A Polish female name, frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries; Latin records write Michaela. It has no patron saint widely celebrated in older calendars.

michel.label: Michel
michel.text: A very widespread name in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland since the Middle Ages, alone or in compounds (Jean-Michel), and the source of many surnames. It honours Saint Michael the Archangel, patron of Mont-Saint-Michel, whose feast is 29 September.

michelangelo.label: Michelangelo
michelangelo.meaning: An Italian compound of Michele, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?", and Angelo, from Greek "angelos", "messenger".
michelangelo.text: An Italian compound name, in honour of the Archangel Michael, found in Italy since the Renaissance and also written Michelangiolo. It has no feast of its own, but is linked to Michaelmas on 29 September.

michele.label: Michele
michele.meaning: Italian form of Michael, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?".
michele.text: A male name very widespread in Italy, notably in the South; in France and the United States the spelling Michèle or Michele is, by contrast, a female name, mostly in the 20th century. For men it honours Saint Michael the Archangel, whose feast is 29 September.

micheline.label: Micheline
micheline.meaning: A feminine pet form of Michel, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?".
micheline.text: A French female name mostly given between the 1920s and the 1950s, so rare in older records. It has no patron saint of its own.

michelle.label: Michelle
michelle.meaning: Feminine form of Michel, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?".
michelle.text: A French and Belgian female name, infrequent before the 20th century and very widespread in its middle decades; Michèle also occurs. It has no patron saint of its own.

michiel.label: Michiel
michiel.meaning: Dutch form of Michael, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?".
michiel.text: The Dutch form of Michael, common in the Netherlands and Flanders; Latin records write Michael. It honours Saint Michael the Archangel, whose feast is 29 September.

mieczyslaw.label: Mieczysław
mieczyslaw.meaning: A Polish name often interpreted as "glory of the sword" ("miecz", "sword", and "sław", "glory"), also linked to the name of Duke Mieszko; the etymology remains disputed.
mieczyslaw.text: A Polish name, rare in older records and mostly widespread in the 19th and 20th centuries, as part of a revival of Slavic names. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

mies.label: Mies
mies.meaning: A Dutch pet form of Maria, from Hebrew "Miryam".
mies.text: A Dutch pet form of Maria; in official records the same woman generally appears as Maria. Its feast is that of the Virgin Mary, 15 August.

miguel.label: Miguel
miguel.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Michael, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?".
miguel.text: A very widespread name in Spain and Portugal since the Middle Ages; the Basque Mikel and the Catalan Miquel are regional forms. It honours Saint Michael the Archangel, whose feast is 29 September.

miguel_angel.label: Miguel Ángel
miguel_angel.meaning: A compound of Miguel, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?", and Ángel, from Greek "angelos", "messenger".
miguel_angel.text: A Spanish compound name in honour of the Archangel Michael, very widespread in the 20th century and rarer before; the Catalan Miquel Àngel and the Galician Miguel Anxo also occur. It is celebrated at Michaelmas, 29 September.

mikolaj.label: Mikołaj
mikolaj.meaning: Polish form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
mikolaj.text: A very widespread name in Poland since the Middle Ages; Latin records write Nicolaus. It honours Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra in the 4th century, whose feast is 6 December.

milagros.label: Milagros
milagros.meaning: From Spanish "milagros", "miracles", referring to Our Lady of Miracles.
milagros.text: A Spanish Marian name, often from María de los Milagros, mostly widespread in the 20th century. Several local shrines bear this title, so no single feast prevailed.

mildred.label: Mildred
mildred.text: An Anglo-Saxon name revived in the 19th century, very widespread in the United States in the 1910s and 1920s; the pet form Millie is often found. It honours Saint Mildred, 8th-century abbess of Minster-in-Thanet, whose feast is 13 July.

milena.label: Milena
milena.meaning: Derived from the Slavic element "mil", "dear, gracious".
milena.text: A Slavic name widespread in Poland, the Czech lands and the Balkans, mostly in the 20th century. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

millicent.label: Millicent
millicent.meaning: From Old French "Melisent", from Germanic "amal", "work", and "swinth", "strong".
millicent.text: A medieval name of Frankish origin, adopted in England and revived in the Victorian era; the pet form Millie is often found. It has no patron saint.

milosz.label: Miłosz
milosz.meaning: Derived from the Slavic element "mił", "dear, gracious".
milosz.text: An old Polish name, rare in older parish records and mostly widespread from the 20th century. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

milton.label: Milton
milton.meaning: From the English surname Milton, taken from a place name meaning "mill farm" or "middle farm".
milton.text: A surname turned given name, mainly in the United States, frequent from the late 19th century to the 1920s, sometimes in honour of the poet John Milton. It is not linked to a saint.

mina.label: Mina
mina.meaning: Short form of names such as Wilhelmina, Hermina or Jacomina, whose etymology it shares.
mina.text: A pet form found in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland, and among emigrants to the United States; the same woman may appear under the full name in other records. It has no feast of its own.

mindla.label: Mindla
mindla.meaning: A Yiddish diminutive of disputed meaning, often linked to Mina.
mindla.text: A female Yiddish name common in Jewish records of Poland and Galicia in the 19th century. Records write Mindla or Mindel.

minna.label: Minna
minna.meaning: Short form of Wilhelmina, associated with Middle High German "minne", "love".
minna.text: A German name fashionable in the 18th and 19th centuries, notably after Lessing's play "Minna von Barnhelm", and found among German emigrants. The same woman may appear as Wilhelmine in other records. It has no feast of its own.

minnie.label: Minnie
minnie.meaning: An English pet form of Wilhelmina, Mary or other names.
minnie.text: An American and British name very widespread in the late 19th century; the same woman may appear as Mary, Wilhelmina or Minerva in other records. It has no feast of its own.

miquel.label: Miquel
miquel.meaning: Catalan form of Michael, from Hebrew "Mikha'el", "who is like God?".
miquel.text: The Catalan form of Michael, frequent in Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands; records in Castilian write Miguel. It honours Saint Michael the Archangel, whose feast is 29 September.

mireille.label: Mireille
mireille.meaning: From Provençal "Mirèio", a name popularised by Frédéric Mistral's poem (1859), of disputed etymology, perhaps linked to "mirar", "to admire".
mireille.text: A Provençal name that spread throughout France after the success of Mistral's "Mirèio" and Gounod's opera, mostly in the early 20th century. It has no patron saint.

miriam.label: Miriam
miriam.meaning: The original Hebrew form of Mary ("Miryam"), of disputed meaning: "lady", "one who raises up", or "star of the sea".
miriam.text: The name of Moses's sister, borne mostly in Jewish communities and among some Protestants, and more widely in the 20th century in Spain, Germany and the English-speaking world. It has no feast of its own.

miroslaw.label: Mirosław
miroslaw.text: A Polish name of Slavic origin, rare in older records and mostly widespread in the 20th century. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

modesto.label: Modesto
modesto.text: A Spanish and Italian name, frequent in 18th- and 19th-century records. Several saints of this name are known, but no single feast prevailed.

mohamed.label: Mohamed
mohamed.text: The name of the prophet of Islam, very widespread in the Muslim world; in older European records it appears mostly in entries for migrants, soldiers or converts, with many transcriptions (Mohamed, Mohammed, Muhammad). It is not linked to a saint.

mohammed.label: Mohammed
mohammed.text: A common English transcription of the name of the prophet of Islam, which varies with the language of the record (Mohamed, Muhammad, Mehmet). In European archives it mostly concerns 20th-century migrants. It is not linked to a saint.

moise.label: Moïse
moise.meaning: French form of Moses, probably of Egyptian origin, "son of", explained in the Bible as "drawn out of the water".
moise.text: A name borne in France in Jewish and Protestant communities, and also by Catholics under the Ancien Régime; Moyse or Moÿse occur in older records. It has no widely celebrated feast.

moises.label: Moisés
moises.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Moses, probably of Egyptian origin, explained in the Bible as "drawn out of the water".
moises.text: A biblical name found in Spain and Portugal, more frequent in the 20th century than in older records. It has no widely celebrated feast.

monica.label: Monica
monica.meaning: Of uncertain etymology, possibly Berber or Punic, later associated with Greek "monos", "alone".
monica.text: A name found in Spain, Italy, Britain and Belgium, mostly in the 20th century. It honours Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine, whose feast is 27 August.

monika.label: Monika
monika.meaning: Polish and German form of Monica, of uncertain etymology, possibly Berber or Punic.
monika.text: The Polish and German form of Monica, mostly widespread in the 20th century. It honours Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine, whose feast is 27 August.

monique.label: Monique
monique.meaning: French form of Monica, of uncertain etymology, possibly Berber or Punic.
monique.text: A French name rare in older records and very widespread in the mid-20th century. It honours Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine, whose feast is 27 August.

montserrat.label: Montserrat
montserrat.meaning: From the name of the Montserrat massif and monastery in Catalonia, "serrated mountain".
montserrat.text: A Catalan Marian name, often shortened to Montse, very widespread in Catalonia; the Black Virgin of Montserrat is the patron of Catalonia. Its feast is 27 April.

mordka.label: Mordka
mordka.meaning: From the biblical Mordecai, probably derived from the Babylonian god Marduk.
mordka.text: The Polish form of Yiddish Mordkhe, Esther's cousin in the Bible, very frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century; Motel is its diminutive. In France, Alsatian and Lorraine records write Mardochée.

moritz.label: Moritz
moritz.meaning: German form of Maurice, from Latin "Mauritius", derived from "Maurus", "Moor".
moritz.text: The German form of Maurice, common in Germany and Switzerland; Latin records write Mauritius. In German Jewish communities it also served as a civil name for Moses (Moshe). It honours Saint Maurice of Agaunum, whose feast is 22 September.

morris.label: Morris
morris.meaning: English form of Maurice, from Latin "Mauritius", derived from "Maurus", "Moor".
morris.text: The English form of Maurice, frequent in the United States in the early 20th century, notably among Jewish immigrants from Central and Eastern Europe, for whom it often replaced Moshe or Moritz. Among Christians it honours Saint Maurice of Agaunum, whose feast is 22 September.

moses.label: Moses
moses.meaning: A biblical name probably of Egyptian origin, "son of", explained in the Bible as "drawn out of the water".
moses.text: A name borne mostly in European Jewish communities (Moshe, Mozes) and among English-speaking and Dutch Protestants, frequent in the United States in the 19th century. It has no widely celebrated feast.

moszek.label: Moszek
moszek.meaning: A Yiddish diminutive of Moses (Moshe), "drawn out of the water" in the biblical explanation.
moszek.text: The form in which 19th-century Polish civil records register Yiddish Moshke, a diminutive of Moshe. In records written in Russian after 1868 it becomes Мошекъ; the same man may be called Moszek, Mosiek or Mojżesz in different entries.

muriel.label: Muriel
muriel.text: A name of Celtic origin, attested in England in the Middle Ages, revived in Britain and the United States in the late 19th century, then in France in the 20th. It has no well-established patron saint.

myrtle.label: Myrtle
myrtle.meaning: The English name of the myrtle plant, from Greek "myrtos".
myrtle.text: A flower name typical of the late 19th century in the United States, very widespread between 1880 and 1920. It has no patron saint.

nadia.label: Nadia
nadia.text: A name of Russian origin that spread to Western Europe in the 20th century, rare in older records. It has no well-established patron saint in Western calendars.

nadine.label: Nadine
nadine.meaning: French form derived from Nadia, from Russian "Nadezhda", "hope".
nadine.text: A French name of the 20th century, mostly given in its middle decades, so rare in older records. It has no well-established patron saint.

nancy.label: Nancy
nancy.meaning: An English pet form of Anne (through "Nan"), from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
nancy.text: An English and American name widespread from the 18th century; in the records the same woman may appear as Ann or Anne. In the 19th and 20th centuries it became a name in its own right. It has no feast of its own.

nanette.label: Nanette
nanette.meaning: A French pet form of Anne, from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
nanette.text: A pet form of Anne found in Switzerland, Germany and France, mostly in the 18th and 19th centuries; in the records the same woman often appears as Anne or Anna. Its name day is that of Saint Anne, 26 July.

nanny.label: Nanny
nanny.meaning: A pet form of Anna, from Hebrew "Hannah", "grace".
nanny.text: A pet form of Anna usual in Switzerland and Germany, where Nanni or Nanette also occur; the same woman generally appears as Anna in official records. Its name day is that of Saint Anne, 26 July.

napoleon.label: Napoléon
napoleon.meaning: An Italian name of disputed etymology, linked to Naples ("Neapolis") or to "leone", "lion".
napoleon.text: A name made famous by Napoleon Bonaparte, widely given in France, Belgium and Poland under the First Empire and in the 19th century. The imperial regime instituted a "Saint Napoleon's day" on 15 August, but this is not a well-established saint.

napoleone.label: Napoleone
napoleone.meaning: An Italian name of disputed etymology, linked to Naples ("Neapolis") or to "leone", "lion".
napoleone.text: An Italian name borne in some families since the Middle Ages, notably the Orsini, then spread by the fame of Napoleon Bonaparte in the 19th century. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

narcis.label: Narcís
narcis.meaning: Catalan form of Narcissus, from Greek "Narkissos", a mythological name associated with "narkê", "torpor".
narcis.text: A Catalan name closely tied to Girona, whose patron is Saint Narcissus; records in Castilian write Narciso. Its feast is 29 October.

narciso.label: Narciso
narciso.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Narcissus, from Greek "Narkissos", a mythological name associated with "narkê", "torpor".
narciso.text: A Spanish and Portuguese name frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries, particularly in Catalonia. It honours Saint Narcissus, bishop of Girona, whose feast is 29 October.

narcisse.label: Narcisse
narcisse.meaning: From Greek "Narkissos", a mythological name associated with "narkê", "torpor".
narcisse.text: A French name frequent in the 19th century. It honours Saint Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem in the 2nd century, whose feast is 29 October.

natale.label: Natale
natale.meaning: From Italian "Natale", "Christmas", from Latin "natalis (dies)", "day of birth".
natale.text: An Italian name often given to a child born or baptised around Christmas, found in Italy and Italian-speaking Switzerland. It refers not to a saint but to the feast of the Nativity, 25 December.

natalia.label: Natalia
natalia.meaning: From Latin "natalis", "of birth", referring to the Nativity of Christ.
natalia.text: A name widespread in Poland, Spain, Portugal and Italy, and in the Orthodox Slavic world; it became especially frequent in the 20th century. It honours Saint Natalia, a 9th-century martyr of Córdoba, whose feast is 27 July.

nathalia.label: Nathalia
nathalia.meaning: A spelling of Natalia, from Latin "natalis", "of birth", referring to the Nativity of Christ.
nathalia.text: A spelling found in Belgian records, where Natalia, Nathalia and Nathalie alternate for the same woman. It honours Saint Natalia, a 9th-century martyr of Córdoba, whose feast is 27 July.

nathalie.label: Nathalie
nathalie.meaning: French form of Natalia, from Latin "natalis", "of birth", referring to the Nativity of Christ.
nathalie.text: A name found in France and Belgium in the 19th century, then extremely widespread in the 1960s and 1970s; Natalie and the Russian forms Natacha or Natasha also occur. It honours Saint Natalia, a martyr of Córdoba, whose feast is 27 July.

nathan.label: Nathan
nathan.text: The name of the prophet Nathan, borne mostly in Jewish communities and among English-speaking and Dutch Protestants, frequent in the United States from the 18th century. It has no widely celebrated feast.

nathaniel.label: Nathaniel
nathaniel.text: A biblical name favoured by English Puritans and very present in New England from the 17th century; Nathanael or Nathanial also occur. The disciple Nathanael is often identified with the apostle Bartholomew, but the name has no established feast of its own.

natividad.label: Natividad
natividad.meaning: From Spanish "natividad", "nativity", referring to the birth of the Virgin Mary.
natividad.text: A Spanish Marian name, often from María de la Natividad, frequent in the 19th and 20th centuries; the pet form Nati occurs. It is celebrated on the Nativity of the Virgin, 8 September.

nazgul.label: Nazgul
nazgul.text: A female name common in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Central Asia. In Europe it appears in recent civil records of families from those regions.

nechama.label: Nechama
nechama.text: A Jewish female name found in 19th-century records of Poland and Lithuania, written Nechama or Nechuma.

neil.label: Neil
neil.meaning: From Irish "Niall", of disputed meaning: "champion" or "cloud".
neil.text: A name of Irish and Scottish origin, widespread in Britain and the United States mostly in the 20th century, with the spellings Neal, Neale or Neill. It is not linked to a saint.

nella.label: Nella
nella.meaning: Short form of names ending in "-nella", such as Antonella, Petronella or Brunella, whose etymology it shares.
nella.text: An Italian pet form that became a name in its own right, also found in Britain and among emigrants to the United States; the same woman may appear under the full name in other records. It has no feast of its own.

nelson.label: Nelson
nelson.meaning: From the English surname Nelson, "son of Neil" (or "son of Nell").
nelson.text: A surname turned given name, popularised in Britain and the United States in the 19th century by the prestige of Admiral Nelson. It is not linked to a saint.

neville.label: Neville
neville.meaning: From the Anglo-Norman surname Neville, taken from a Norman place name, "Neuville", "new town".
neville.text: An aristocratic English surname turned given name, mostly in the 19th and early 20th centuries in Britain. It is not linked to a saint.

niccolo.label: Niccolò
niccolo.meaning: Italian form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
niccolo.text: The Italian form of Nicholas, especially Tuscan, in use since the Middle Ages alongside Nicolò and Nicola. It honours Saint Nicholas, 4th-century bishop of Myra, whose relics are in Bari, and whose feast is 6 December.

nicholas.label: Nicholas
nicholas.meaning: English form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nicholas.text: An English name in use since the Middle Ages, common in Britain and the United States, with the shortened forms Nick or Nichol. It honours Saint Nicholas, 4th-century bishop of Myra, whose feast is 6 December.

nicola.label: Nicola
nicola.meaning: Italian form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nicola.text: A very widespread Italian male name, notably in the South around Bari; in Britain the same spelling is, by contrast, a female name. It honours Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra, whose feast is 6 December.

nicolaas.label: Nicolaas
nicolaas.meaning: Dutch form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nicolaas.text: The Dutch form of Nicholas, very common in the Netherlands and Flanders, with the shortened forms Klaas, Klaasje or Niels; Saint Nicholas (Sinterklaas) is very popular there. His feast is 6 December.

nicolaes.label: Nicolaes
nicolaes.meaning: An older Dutch spelling of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nicolaes.text: An older spelling of Nicolaas, frequent in Dutch and Flemish records of the 16th and 17th centuries. It honours Saint Nicholas, whose feast is 6 December.

nicolas.label: Nicolas
nicolas.text: A very widespread name in France, notably in Lorraine, whose patron is Saint Nicholas, as well as in Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland. It honours Saint Nicholas, 4th-century bishop of Myra, whose feast is 6 December.

nicolasse.label: Nicolasse
nicolasse.meaning: Feminine of Nicolas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nicolasse.text: A popular feminine form of Nicolas, found in registers of northern and eastern France in the 16th–18th centuries. Colasse is its shortened form; Nicole and Colette have their own sheets.

nicolau.label: Nicolau
nicolau.meaning: Portuguese and Catalan form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nicolau.text: The Portuguese and Catalan form of Nicholas, found in the records of Portugal, Catalonia and the Balearic Islands. It honours Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra, whose feast is 6 December.

nicolaus.label: Nicolaus
nicolaus.meaning: Latin form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nicolaus.text: The Latin form used in records throughout Catholic Europe; in daily life the person was called Nicolas, Nikolaus, Klaas or Mikołaj depending on the region. It honours Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra, whose feast is 6 December.

nicole.label: Nicole
nicole.meaning: Feminine form of Nicolas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nicole.text: A female name found in France since the Middle Ages, sometimes written Nicolle, but above all very widespread in the mid-20th century. It has no widely celebrated patron saint.

nicolo.label: Nicolò
nicolo.meaning: Italian form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nicolo.text: An Italian form of Nicholas, frequent notably in the Veneto and Sicily, alongside Niccolò and Nicola. It honours Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra, whose feast is 6 December.

nieves.label: Nieves
nieves.meaning: From Spanish "nieves", "snows", referring to Our Lady of the Snows.
nieves.text: A Spanish Marian name, often from María de las Nieves, frequent in the 19th and 20th centuries; the Catalan Neus and the Basque Edurne are equivalents. Its feast is that of Our Lady of the Snows, 5 August.

nigel.label: Nigel
nigel.meaning: From Medieval Latin "Nigellus", a Latinised form of Irish "Niall", wrongly associated with Latin "niger", "black".
nigel.text: A medieval English name, revived in Britain mostly in the 20th century, so rare in older records. It is not linked to a saint.

niklaus.label: Niklaus
niklaus.meaning: Swiss German form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
niklaus.text: The usual form in German-speaking Switzerland, where it also recalls Nicholas of Flüe (Brother Klaus), hermit and patron of Switzerland, whose feast is 25 September. The traditional name day remains that of Saint Nicholas of Myra, 6 December.

nikodem.label: Nikodem
nikodem.meaning: Polish form of Nicodemus, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "dêmos", "people".
nikodem.text: A biblical name, from the Pharisee who buried Jesus, found in Poland mostly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no widely celebrated feast.

nikola.label: Nikola
nikola.meaning: A form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nikola.text: A unisex name: male in the Balkans and Central Europe, but used in Poland as a female name, mostly from the late 20th century. The sex should therefore be checked in the record. It has no feast of its own for women.

nikolaus.label: Nikolaus
nikolaus.meaning: German form of Nicholas, from Greek "nikê", "victory", and "laos", "people".
nikolaus.text: A very widespread name in Germany, Luxembourg, Austria and Switzerland, with many shortened forms (Klaus, Niklas, Claus). It honours Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra, whose feast is 6 December.

nina.label: Nina
nina.meaning: Short form of names such as Antonina, Giovannina or Anna, also associated with Saint Nino of Georgia.
nina.text: A pet form that became a name in its own right in Italy, Poland, Switzerland and the Russian world, and later throughout Europe; the same woman may appear under the full name in other records. Its name day is that of Saint Nino, who evangelised Georgia in the 4th century, on 14 January.

nino.label: Nino
nino.meaning: An Italian short form of names such as Giovannino, Antonino or Saturnino.
nino.text: An Italian male pet form that became a name in its own right; in the records the same person often appears under the full name. It has no feast of its own.

noa.label: Noa
noa.meaning: Two sources: the Hebrew female name Noa (a daughter of Zelophehad) and a form of Noah (male).
noa.text: A recent name in Europe, given to girls in Israel and the Netherlands and to boys in Spain and France. It is almost absent from records before the late 20th century.

noel.label: Noël
noel.meaning: From Latin "natalis (dies)", "day of birth", naming the feast of Christmas.
noel.text: A name often given to a child born or baptised around Christmas, found in France, Belgium and Britain since the Middle Ages. It refers not to a saint but to the feast of the Nativity, 25 December.

noelia.label: Noelia
noelia.meaning: Spanish feminine form of Noël, from Latin "natalis (dies)", "day of birth".
noelia.text: A recent Spanish name, mostly widespread in the late 20th century, so rare in older records. It refers not to a saint but to Christmas, 25 December.

noelie.label: Noelie
noelie.meaning: Feminine form of Noël, from Latin "natalis (dies)", "day of birth".
noelie.text: A French female name frequent in the 19th century, sometimes given to a girl born around Christmas; Noëlle or Noéline also occur. It refers not to a saint but to Christmas, 25 December.

noemi.label: Noemi
noemi.text: The Spanish, Italian and Polish form of Naomi, the name of Ruth's mother-in-law in the Bible, mostly widespread in the 20th century. It has no widely celebrated feast.

noemie.label: Noémie
noemie.text: A biblical name frequent in France in the 19th century, notably among Protestants and in Jewish communities, and fashionable again in the late 20th. It has no widely celebrated feast.

noor.label: Noor
noor.text: An Arabic female (sometimes male) name, widespread in the Muslim world and common in the Netherlands and Belgium since the late 20th century. The spellings Noor and Nour depend on the transcription language.

nora.label: Nora
nora.meaning: Short form of Eleonora or Honora, whose etymology it shares.
nora.text: A pet form that became a name in its own right in Ireland, Britain, the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland, also popularised by Ibsen's "A Doll's House"; Norah occurs in Ireland. It has no feast of its own.

norbert.label: Norbert
norbert.text: A name widespread in Luxembourg, France, Belgium, Germany and Poland, mostly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It honours Saint Norbert of Xanten, founder of the Premonstratensians and archbishop of Magdeburg in the 12th century, whose feast is 6 June.

norma.label: Norma
norma.meaning: A name popularised by Bellini's opera "Norma" (1831), of uncertain etymology, sometimes linked to Latin "norma", "rule".
norma.text: A name mostly widespread in the United States and Britain in the early 20th century, and also found in Spain. It has no patron saint.

norman.label: Norman
norman.meaning: From Germanic "nord", "north", and "man", "man": "man from the North".
norman.text: An English name, frequent in Scotland and very widespread in the United States and Britain in the early 20th century. It is not linked to a saint.

nuchim.label: Nuchim
nuchim.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Nokhem, the name of the prophet Nahum, frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. It gave rise to the patronymic surname Nuchimowicz.

nuno.label: Nuno
nuno.meaning: A medieval Iberian name, of uncertain etymology, possibly from Latin "Nonius", "ninth".
nuno.text: An old Portuguese name, found among the nobility since the Middle Ages; Latin records write Nunnius. It honours Saint Nuno Álvares Pereira, constable of Portugal who became a Carmelite in the 15th century, whose feast is 6 November.

nuria.label: Nuria
nuria.meaning: From the name of the Marian shrine of Núria, in the Catalan Pyrenees.
nuria.text: A Catalan Marian name, rare in older records and very widespread in Catalonia and throughout Spain in the 20th century. Its feast is that of Our Lady of Núria, 8 September.

nusyn.label: Nusyn
nusyn.meaning: The Yiddish form of Nathan, "he gave".
nusyn.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Nosn, found in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. The same man may be called Nusyn or Natan in different entries.

octave.label: Octave
octave.meaning: From Latin "Octavus", "eighth", a Roman family name (Octavius).
octave.text: A classically inspired name, frequent in France and Belgium in the 19th century. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

octavia.label: Octavia
octavia.meaning: Feminine form of the Roman name Octavius, from Latin "octavus", "eighth".
octavia.text: A classically inspired name, borne by the sister of Augustus, found in Britain, the United States and Belgium in the 19th century. It has no well-established patron saint.

octavie.label: Octavie
octavie.meaning: French form of Octavia, from Latin "octavus", "eighth".
octavie.text: A female name frequent in France and Belgium in the 19th century, later out of fashion. It has no well-established patron saint.

oda.label: Oda
oda.text: An early medieval Germanic name, borne by several saints and Carolingian and Saxon noblewomen. It reappears in Germany and Scandinavia in the 19th and 20th centuries; Ode is the medieval French form.

odette.label: Odette
odette.meaning: A French pet form of Oda, from Germanic "od", "wealth, prosperity".
odette.text: A medieval French name, revived in the late 19th century and very widespread in France in the early 20th. It has no widely celebrated patron saint.

odile.label: Odile
odile.text: A traditional name in Alsace, whose patron is Saint Odile, found in France and Belgium and mostly widespread in the mid-20th century. It honours Saint Odile, 8th-century abbess of Hohenburg (Mont Sainte-Odile), whose feast is 13 December.

odin.label: Odin
odin.meaning: From Old Norse "Óðinn", the chief god of Norse mythology.
odin.text: A name taken from mythology, given mainly in Scandinavia from the Romantic 19th century and more recently elsewhere in Europe. It is rare in older registers.

ofelia.label: Ofelia
ofelia.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Ophelia, perhaps from Greek "ôpheleia", "help, aid".
ofelia.text: A literary name, spread by Ophelia in "Hamlet", found in Spain, Portugal and Latin America, mostly in the 20th century. It has no patron saint.

oksana.label: Oksana
oksana.meaning: Ukrainian form of Xenia, from Greek "xenia", "hospitality".
oksana.text: A Ukrainian and Russian name, found in Poland and Spain mostly among late 20th-century migrants; it is rare in older Western European records. It has no well-established patron saint in Western calendars.

olena.label: Olena
olena.meaning: Ukrainian form of Helen, from Greek "Helenê", of disputed etymology, often linked to "hêlios", "sun".
olena.text: The Ukrainian form of Helen, found in Poland and Spain mostly among recent migrants. It honours Saint Helena, mother of Emperor Constantine, whose feast is 18 August in the Roman calendar.

olga.label: Olga
olga.text: A name of Scandinavian origin adopted in Russia, then fashionable in Western Europe in the late 19th century, in Italy, Poland, Germany, Switzerland and France. It honours Saint Olga, 10th-century princess of Kiev, whose feast is 11 July.

olimpia.label: Olimpia
olimpia.text: A classically inspired name found in Italy, Spain and Poland, notably in the 17th and 18th centuries; Olympia or the French Olympe also occur. It has no widely celebrated patron saint.

olinda.label: Olinda
olinda.meaning: A name of uncertain etymology, possibly Germanic or literary in origin.
olinda.text: A mainly Portuguese and Brazilian name, found in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no patron saint.

olive.label: Olive
olive.meaning: From Latin "oliva", "olive, olive tree", a symbol of peace.
olive.text: A name found in England since the Middle Ages and revived in Britain and the United States around 1900; in France, Olive also appears in the 19th century. It has no widely celebrated patron saint.

oliver.label: Oliver
oliver.meaning: Of disputed etymology: linked to Latin "oliva", "olive tree", or to an altered Germanic or Norse name.
oliver.text: A name known from Oliver, companion of Roland in the chanson de geste, used in England since the Middle Ages; it declined after Oliver Cromwell and returned in the 19th century. It also occurs in Poland. It is not linked to a well-established saint in older records.

olivia.label: Olivia
olivia.meaning: Derived from Latin "oliva", "olive, olive tree", a symbol of peace.
olivia.text: A name made famous by Shakespeare's "Twelfth Night", used in Britain, the United States and Portugal, but mostly widespread in the late 20th century. It has no widely celebrated patron saint.

olivier.label: Olivier
olivier.meaning: Of disputed etymology: linked to Latin "oliva", "olive tree", or to an altered Germanic or Norse name.
olivier.text: A name made popular in the Middle Ages by Oliver, companion of Roland in the "Song of Roland", found in France and Belgium in older records and very widespread in the second half of the 20th century. It is not linked to a well-established early saint; Saint Oliver Plunkett was only canonised in 1975.

olympe.label: Olympe
olympe.text: A fashionable name in 18th-century France, borne notably by Olympe de Gouges. It appears in registers until the 19th century.

omer.label: Omer
omer.meaning: French form of Audomarus, from Germanic "aud", "wealth", and "mar", "famous".
omer.text: A traditional name of northern France and Belgium, frequent in the 19th century. It honours Saint Omer, 7th-century bishop of Thérouanne, who gave his name to the town of Saint-Omer, and whose feast is 9 September.

onofrio.label: Onofrio
onofrio.meaning: Italian form of Onuphrius, a name of Egyptian origin often explained as "he who is always good".
onofrio.text: A name mostly widespread in southern Italy and Sicily. It honours Saint Onuphrius, a hermit of the Egyptian desert in the 4th century, whose feast is 12 June.

opportune.label: Opportune
opportune.text: The name of Saint Opportuna, an 8th-century abbess of Montreuil (Orne), venerated in Normandy and Paris. It is found mainly in Norman registers of the 17th and 18th centuries.

orazio.label: Orazio
orazio.meaning: From the Roman family name Horatius, of uncertain etymology.
orazio.text: An Italian name of classical inspiration, recalling the poet Horace, frequent in Italy since the Renaissance. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

oreste.label: Oreste
oreste.meaning: From Greek "Orestês", derived from "oros", "mountain": "he who comes from the mountains".
oreste.text: A classically inspired name, recalling the hero of Greek tragedy, found in Italy and Italian-speaking Switzerland mostly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

orsola.label: Orsola
orsola.meaning: Italian form of Ursula, from Latin "Ursula", "little she-bear".
orsola.text: The Italian form of Ursula, found in Italian records mostly in the 17th and 18th centuries. It honours Saint Ursula, martyred in Cologne with her companions according to legend, whose feast is 21 October.

oscar.label: Oscar
oscar.meaning: The name of a hero of the Ossian poems, of uncertain Gaelic origin, perhaps "friend of deer".
oscar.text: A name spread across Europe in the late 18th century by the vogue for the Ossian poems, then by King Oscar I of Sweden, Napoleon's godson; it became frequent in Spain, Belgium and the United States. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

oskar.label: Oskar
oskar.meaning: Germanic and Polish form of Oscar, the name of a hero of the Ossian poems, of uncertain Gaelic origin.
oskar.text: The German, Swiss and Polish spelling of Oscar, mostly widespread in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

oswald.label: Oswald
oswald.text: An Anglo-Saxon name whose cult spread widely on the Continent, in Germany, Austria and Switzerland (notably in Zug). It honours Saint Oswald, King of Northumbria, who died in 642 and whose feast is 5 August.

otis.label: Otis
otis.meaning: From the English surname Otis, derived from the Germanic name Otto, "wealth".
otis.text: A surname turned given name in the United States, frequent from the late 19th century to the 1920s. It is not linked to a saint.

ottavio.label: Ottavio
ottavio.meaning: Italian form of Octavius, from Latin "Octavius", derived from "octavus", "eighth".
ottavio.text: An Italian name of classical inspiration, frequent since the Renaissance, sometimes given to an eighth child. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

ottilie.label: Ottilie
ottilie.meaning: German form of Odile, from Germanic "od", "wealth, prosperity".
ottilie.text: A German and Swiss name, frequent in the 19th century; Latin records write Ottilia. It honours Saint Odile, abbess of Hohenburg in Alsace and patron of Alsace, whose feast is 13 December.

otto.label: Otto
otto.text: The name of the Ottonian emperors, common in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands, and very widespread in the late 19th century. It honours Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg and missionary to Pomerania in the 12th century, whose feast is 30 June.

ours.label: Ours
ours.text: Borne by several saints, including Saint Ursus of Solothurn, a martyr of the Theban Legion and patron of that town. The form Urs is very common in German-speaking Switzerland, Ours is found in the Aosta Valley, Savoy and Touraine, Orso in Italy.

owen.label: Owen
owen.meaning: From Welsh "Owain", of disputed etymology, perhaps from Latin "Eugenius", "well-born".
owen.text: A Welsh name, common in Wales and Ireland (where it corresponds to Eoghan), then in Britain and the United States. It is not linked to a well-established saint.

pablo.label: Pablo
pablo.meaning: Spanish form of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small".
pablo.text: A very widespread name in Spain since the Middle Ages; the Catalan Pau is its equivalent. It honours the apostle Saint Paul, celebrated with Saint Peter on 29 June.

palmira.label: Palmira
palmira.meaning: From the name of the ancient city of Palmyra, associated with Latin "palma", "palm".
palmira.text: A female name found in Portugal, Italy and Spain, mostly in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no well-established patron saint.

palmyre.label: Palmyre
palmyre.meaning: From the name of the ancient city of Palmyra, associated with Latin "palma", "palm".
palmyre.text: A female name frequent in Belgium and France in the 19th century, later out of fashion. It has no well-established patron saint.

paloma.label: Paloma
paloma.text: A Spanish name, linked to the Madrid devotion to the Virgin of La Paloma and to the dove as symbol of the Holy Spirit, mostly widespread in the 20th century. It has no patron saint.

pamela.label: Pamela
pamela.meaning: A name coined by the poet Philip Sidney in the 16th century, perhaps from Greek "pan", "all", and "meli", "honey".
pamela.text: A literary name popularised by Richardson's novel "Pamela" (1740), but mostly widespread in Britain and the United States in the mid-20th century. It has no patron saint.

pancrace.label: Pancrace
pancrace.text: The name of Saint Pancras, a young 4th-century Roman martyr and one of the May "ice saints". Registers latinise it as Pancratius; it is Pankraz in Bavaria and Austria, Pancrace in France.

paola.label: Paola
paola.meaning: Italian form of Paula, feminine of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small".
paola.text: An Italian female name, found in older records and very widespread in the 20th century. Its name day is that of Saint Paula, a 4th-century Roman widow and disciple of Saint Jerome, on 26 January.

paolina.label: Paolina
paolina.meaning: Italian pet form of Paola, feminine of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small".
paolina.text: An Italian female name frequent in the 19th century, borne notably by Pauline Bonaparte (Paolina); the short form Lina occurs. It has no widely celebrated early patron saint.

paolo.label: Paolo
paolo.meaning: Italian form of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small".
paolo.text: A very widespread name in Italy and Italian-speaking Switzerland since the Middle Ages. It honours the apostle Saint Paul, celebrated with Saint Peter on 29 June.

pascal.label: Pascal
pascal.meaning: From Church Latin "paschalis", "of Easter", from Hebrew "pesach".
pascal.text: A name often given to a child born around Easter, found in France and Belgium in older records and very widespread in the mid-20th century. It honours Saint Paschal Baylon, a 16th-century Spanish Franciscan friar, whose feast is 17 May.

pascaline.label: Pascaline
pascaline.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Pascal, from Latin "paschalis", "of Easter".
pascaline.text: A feminine of Pascal given in France, rare in older registers and mostly 20th-century. It was sometimes chosen for a child born around Easter.

pascual.label: Pascual
pascual.meaning: Spanish form of Pascal, from Latin "paschalis", "of Easter".
pascual.text: A Spanish name frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries, notably in Aragon and Valencia, where Saint Paschal Baylon lived. Its feast is 17 May.

pasquale.label: Pasquale
pasquale.meaning: Italian form of Pascal, from Latin "paschalis", "of Easter".
pasquale.text: A very widespread name in southern Italy, often shortened to Lino or Pasqualino, and frequent among Italian emigrants to the United States. It honours Saint Paschal Baylon, whose feast is 17 May.

pasquier.label: Pasquier
pasquier.text: A name often given to children born around Easter, common in western France until the 17th century, then mostly a surname.

patrice.label: Patrice
patrice.meaning: French form of Patrick, from Latin "patricius", "patrician, noble".
patrice.text: A name found in France and Belgium in older records and mostly widespread in the mid-20th century. It honours Saint Patrick, who evangelised Ireland in the 5th century, whose feast is 17 March.

patricia.label: Patricia
patricia.meaning: Feminine form of Patrick, from Latin "patricius", "patrician, noble".
patricia.text: A name rare before the 20th century, which became very widespread in Britain, the United States and Spain in its middle decades. It has no widely celebrated patron saint.

patrick.label: Patrick
patrick.text: The emblematic name of Ireland, very frequent among the Irish and their descendants in Britain and the United States; Pádraig is the Gaelic form. It honours Saint Patrick, who evangelised Ireland in the 5th century, whose feast is 17 March.

patsy.label: Patsy
patsy.meaning: A pet form of Patricia or Martha, and in Ireland of Patrick, from Latin "patricius", "noble".
patsy.text: A mainly female American name, frequent between the 1920s and the 1940s; in Ireland and among Italian Americans, Patsy was also used as a male pet form (Patrick, Pasquale). It has no feast of its own.

pau.label: Pau
pau.meaning: Catalan form of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small".
pau.text: The Catalan form of Paul, used in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands, whereas records in Castilian write Pablo; it is mostly widespread in the late 20th century. It honours the apostle Saint Paul, celebrated with Saint Peter on 29 June.

paul.label: Paul
paul.text: A very widespread name in France, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Belgium and Germany, particularly frequent in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, alone or in compounds (Jean-Paul). It honours the apostle Saint Paul, celebrated with Saint Peter on 29 June.

paula.label: Paula
paula.meaning: Feminine form of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small".
paula.text: A female name common in Germany, Poland, Switzerland, Spain and Italy, mostly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It honours Saint Paula, a 4th-century Roman widow and disciple of Saint Jerome in Bethlehem, whose feast is 26 January.

paule.label: Paule
paule.meaning: French feminine form of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small".
paule.text: A French and Belgian female name, frequent in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It honours Saint Paula, a 4th-century Roman widow, whose feast is 26 January.

paulette.label: Paulette
paulette.meaning: A feminine pet form of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small".
paulette.text: A French name very widespread between the two World Wars, so rare in older records. It has no patron saint of its own; it is sometimes celebrated with Saint Paula on 26 January.

paulin.label: Paulin
paulin.text: A French male name frequent in the 19th century. It honours Saint Paulinus of Nola, an Aquitanian senator who became bishop of Nola in the 5th century, whose feast is 22 June.

paulina.label: Paulina
paulina.meaning: Feminine form of Paulinus, from Latin "Paulina", derived from "Paulus", "small".
paulina.text: A name frequent in Poland, Belgium, the Netherlands and Spain in the 18th and 19th centuries; the same woman may appear as Pauline or Paulina depending on the language of the record. It has no widely celebrated early patron saint.

pauline.label: Pauline
pauline.meaning: Feminine form of Paulinus, from Latin "Paulina", derived from "Paulus", "small".
pauline.text: A very frequent name in France, Belgium and Switzerland in the 19th century, also found in Germany and the United States. It has no widely celebrated early patron saint; it is sometimes celebrated with Saint Paula on 26 January.

paulino.label: Paulino
paulino.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Paulinus, from Latin "Paulinus", derived from "Paulus", "small".
paulino.text: A Spanish and Portuguese male name, frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries. It honours Saint Paulinus of Nola, bishop of Nola in the 5th century, whose feast is 22 June.

paulo.label: Paulo
paulo.meaning: Portuguese form of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small, humble".
paulo.text: The Portuguese and Galician form of Paul, found in records from Portugal and, later, from Portuguese emigrant communities. The name refers to the apostle Saint Paul, celebrated with Saint Peter on 29 June.

paulus.label: Paulus
paulus.text: The Latin form of Paul, very frequent in Latin parish registers in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany, where it names the same person recorded as Paul or Pauwel in vernacular documents. The name refers to the apostle Saint Paul, celebrated on 29 June.

pawel.label: Paweł
pawel.meaning: Polish form of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small, humble".
pawel.text: The Polish form of Paul, common in Catholic registers in Poland; Latin records write it Paulus and transcriptions without diacritics give Pawel. The name refers to the apostle Saint Paul, celebrated on 29 June.

pearl.label: Pearl
pearl.meaning: From English "pearl", the name of the gem used as a given name.
pearl.text: An English-language female name that emerged with the late 19th-century fashion for gem and flower names, especially in the United States. It is rare before about 1870 and has no particular patron saint.

pedro.label: Pedro
pedro.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Peter, from Greek "petros", "stone, rock".
pedro.text: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Peter, one of the most widespread male names in the Iberian Peninsula for centuries. It also appears as Petrus in Latin registers and as Pere in Catalan. It refers to the apostle Saint Peter, celebrated on 29 June.

pelagia.label: Pelagia
pelagia.meaning: From Greek "pelagos", "the open sea", hence "she of the sea".
pelagia.text: A name of Greek origin borne by several early saints, found mainly in Catholic registers in Poland, where it is long established, and more rarely in Belgium. The best known is Saint Pelagia of Antioch, virgin martyr, celebrated on 9 June.

percival.label: Percival
percival.meaning: From medieval French "Perceval", the Grail knight in Chrétien de Troyes; the etymology is disputed, sometimes read as "pierce the valley".
percival.text: A name taken from the Arthurian romances, used mainly in England, notably among the gentry from the early modern period, spelled Percival or Perceval. It has no patron saint.

percy.label: Percy
percy.meaning: From the Percy family surname, taken from the Norman place name Percy; also a pet form of Percival.
percy.text: An English aristocratic surname turned given name, mainly in the 19th century in Britain and the United States. It also serves as a pet form of Percival and has no patron saint.

pere.label: Pere
pere.meaning: Catalan form of Peter, from Greek "petros", "stone, rock".
pere.text: The Catalan form of Peter, very frequent in Catalonia, the Balearic Islands and the Valencia region; Castilian or Latin documents often render it as Pedro or Petrus. The name refers to the apostle Saint Peter, celebrated on 29 June.

peregrin.label: Pérégrin
peregrin.text: A rare name borne by several saints, including Saint Peregrine Laziosi, an Italian Servite invoked against cancer. It is latinised as Peregrinus in central European registers and is Pellegrino in Italy.

perpetua.label: Perpétua
perpetua.text: A rare name, found mainly in Portuguese and Italian registers. It refers to Saint Perpetua, martyred at Carthage in 203 with Saint Felicity, celebrated on 7 March.

perrine.label: Perrine
perrine.meaning: French diminutive built on Pierre, merged with Petronilla, from Latin "Petronius".
perrine.text: A female name very common in French records, especially in the west (Brittany, Anjou, Maine) from the 15th to the 18th century, spelled Perrine, Périne or Perrinne. It is traditionally linked to Saint Petronilla, celebrated on 31 May.

pesa.label: Pesa
pesa.meaning: Disputed: linked to Passover (Pesach) or to Batya.
pesa.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Pesye, with the diminutive Pesla, found in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century.

peter.label: Peter
peter.meaning: From Greek "petros", "stone, rock", the name Jesus gave the apostle Simon.
peter.text: The English, German and Dutch form of Pierre, borne continuously in the records of these countries since the Middle Ages; it also appears as Petrus (Latin), Pieter (Dutch) or Peder. The name refers to the apostle Saint Peter, celebrated on 29 June.

petra.label: Petra
petra.meaning: Feminine form of Peter, from Greek "petros", "stone, rock".
petra.text: The feminine of Petrus, long used in Spain and in Germany mainly from the 20th century onward. It has no well-established saint of its own.

petronella.label: Petronella
petronella.meaning: From the Roman family name "Petronius", of uncertain etymology, associated early on with Peter.
petronella.text: A female name frequent in Dutch and Flemish registers, found as Petronella, Petronilla, Pieternella or the pet form Nel. It refers to Saint Petronilla, a Roman martyr whom tradition called the daughter of Saint Peter, celebrated on 31 May.

petronille.label: Pétronille
petronille.meaning: From Latin "Petronilla", derived from "Petronius" and popularly linked to Peter.
petronille.text: Saint Petronilla is celebrated on 31 May. The name was widespread in the Middle Ages in its popular forms Péronnelle, Perrenelle or Péronne, still found in 16th- and 17th-century registers.

petrus.label: Petrus
petrus.meaning: Latin form of Peter, from Greek "petros", "stone, rock".
petrus.text: The Latin form of Peter, ubiquitous in parish registers kept in Latin in Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and France. A Petrus in a baptism record is the Pieter, Peter or Pierre of civil records. The name refers to the apostle Saint Peter, celebrated on 29 June.

pharailde.label: Pharaïlde
pharailde.meaning: Of Germanic origin, with a disputed etymology; the second element is linked to "hild", "battle".
pharailde.text: A typically Flemish female name, found mainly around Ghent, where Saint Pharaildis (Veerle in Dutch) is patron of the city. It appears as Pharaïlde, Pharaildis or Veerle; the saint is celebrated on 4 January.

philibert.label: Philibert
philibert.text: An old male name, frequent in Burgundy, Savoy and the Lyon area under the Ancien Régime, notably among the Savoyard nobility. It refers to Saint Philibert, founder of Jumièges Abbey, celebrated on 20 August.

philiberte.label: Philiberte
philiberte.meaning: Feminine of Philibert, from Germanic "filu", "much", and "berht", "bright".
philiberte.text: A feminine form of Philibert, found mostly in Burgundy, Bresse and Savoy under the Ancien Régime.

philip.label: Philip
philip.text: The English form of Philippe, used in England since the Middle Ages and common in British and American records, with the variant Phillip. The name refers to the apostle Saint Philip, celebrated on 3 May with Saint James the Less.

philipp.label: Philipp
philipp.text: The German form of Philippe, common in German and Swiss registers, particularly in the Rhineland and Hesse. Latin records write it Philippus. The name refers to the apostle Saint Philip, celebrated on 3 May.

philippe.label: Philippe
philippe.text: A royal name in France (Philip Augustus, Philip the Fair), given steadily in French records from the Middle Ages to the 20th century, though less often than Jean or Pierre. Latin records write it Philippus. It refers to the apostle Saint Philip, celebrated on 3 May.

philippine.label: Philippine
philippine.meaning: Feminine form of Philip, from Greek "Philippos", "lover of horses".
philippine.text: The feminine of Philippe, found in France and the Netherlands, and as Philippina or Filippine in German and Polish registers. It has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

philippus.label: Philippus
philippus.meaning: Latin form of Philip, from Greek "Philippos", "lover of horses".
philippus.text: The Latin form of Philip, frequent in parish registers kept in Latin in Belgium, the Netherlands and France; it corresponds to Philippe, Philip or Filips in vernacular records. The name refers to the apostle Saint Philip, celebrated on 3 May.

philomena.label: Philomena
philomena.meaning: From Greek "philos", "friend", and "menos", "strength", or read as "beloved"; the etymology is disputed.
philomena.text: A name that became very popular in the 19th century, notably in Belgium, Ireland and Italy, following the cult of Saint Philomena, whose relics were found in Rome in 1802. Her feast on 11 August was removed from the Roman calendar in 1961.

philomene.label: Philomene
philomene.meaning: From Greek "philos", "friend", and "menos", "strength", or read as "beloved"; the etymology is disputed.
philomene.text: The French form of Philomena, very fashionable in France and Belgium in the 19th century thanks to the cult of Saint Philomena, promoted notably by the Curé of Ars. Her feast on 11 August was removed from the Roman calendar in 1961.

phoebe.label: Phoebe
