phoebe.text: A mainly Protestant female name, found in English and American registers from the 17th century, often spelled Phebe. It refers to Phoebe, the deaconess of Cenchreae mentioned by Saint Paul, celebrated on 3 September.

phyllis.label: Phyllis
phyllis.meaning: From Greek "phyllon", "leaf", the name of a figure in Greek mythology.
phyllis.text: A name from pastoral poetry that became common in Britain and the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also spelled Phillis and has no patron saint.

pia.label: Pia
pia.text: An Italian and German female name, the feminine of Pio, made popular by the popes named Pius in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no well-established saint of its own.

pier.label: Pier
pier.meaning: Short Italian form of Peter, from Greek "petros", "stone, rock".
pier.text: A short form of Pietro, used mainly in Italy in compounds such as Pier Luigi or Pier Paolo; in Dutch, Pier is also a Frisian form of Pieter. The name refers to Saint Peter, celebrated on 29 June.

pierina.label: Pierina
pierina.meaning: Italian feminine diminutive of Pietro, from Greek "petros", "stone".
pierina.text: A feminine diminutive of Piera, common in Italian registers of the 19th and early 20th centuries, especially in the north. It has no well-established saint of its own.

piero.label: Piero
piero.meaning: Italian form of Peter, from Greek "petros", "stone, rock".
piero.text: The Tuscan form of Pietro, old and frequent in Florence from the Renaissance. Records also give it as Pietro or, in Latin, Petrus. The name refers to Saint Peter, celebrated on 29 June.

pierre.label: Pierre
pierre.text: The name Jesus gave the apostle Simon ("you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church"), very popular in France from the early Middle Ages to today.

pierrette.label: Pierrette
pierrette.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Pierre, from Greek "petros", "stone".
pierrette.text: The feminine of Pierre, already found under the Ancien Régime as Perrette, then more frequent in France in the 20th century. It has no well-established saint of its own.

pieter.label: Pieter
pieter.meaning: Dutch form of Peter, from Greek "petros", "stone, rock".
pieter.text: One of the most frequent male names in the Netherlands and Flanders from the 16th to the 20th century, often shortened to Piet; Latin registers write it Petrus. In Dutch patronymics it gives Pieterse or Pietersz. The name refers to Saint Peter, celebrated on 29 June.

pieternella.label: Pieternella
pieternella.meaning: Dutch feminine built on Pieter, influenced by Petronella.
pieternella.text: A Dutch female name, widespread especially in Zeeland and South Holland in the 18th and 19th centuries, often interchanged with Petronella in records. It has no distinct saint of its own.

pietro.label: Pietro
pietro.meaning: Italian form of Peter, from Greek "petros", "stone, rock".
pietro.text: One of the most common male names in Italy since the Middle Ages, also used in Italian-speaking Switzerland; Latin records write it Petrus and the Tuscan form is Piero. It refers to Saint Peter, celebrated on 29 June.

pilar.label: Pilar
pilar.meaning: From Spanish "pilar", "pillar", referring to Our Lady of the Pillar in Zaragoza.
pilar.text: A Spanish female name, the short form of María del Pilar, very widespread in Aragon and then throughout Spain. It honours Our Lady of the Pillar, patroness of Zaragoza and of the Hispanic world, celebrated on 12 October.

pinkus.label: Pinkus
pinkus.meaning: From Hebrew "Pinchas" (Phinehas), a biblical name probably of Egyptian origin.
pinkus.text: The name of Aaron's grandson in the Bible, written Pinkus or Pinkas in 19th-century Polish records. The Yiddish form is Pinkhes.

pio.label: Pio
pio.text: An Italian name given mainly in honour of the popes called Pius, particularly from the long reign of Pius IX (1846-1878). The longest-established saint pope of that name is Pius V, celebrated on 30 April.

piotr.label: Piotr
piotr.meaning: Polish form of Peter, from Greek "petros", "stone, rock".
piotr.text: The Polish form of Peter, common in Catholic registers in Poland; Latin records write it Petrus and Russian-language records (1868-1917) transcribe it in Cyrillic. It refers to Saint Peter, celebrated on 29 June.

placido.label: Placido
placido.text: A male name found in Italy, Spain and Portugal, often in families linked to Benedictine monasteries. It refers to Saint Placidus, disciple of Saint Benedict, celebrated on 5 October.

pol.label: Pol
pol.meaning: Breton, Catalan and Luxembourgish form of Paul, from Latin "Paulus", "small, humble".
pol.text: A regional form of Paul used in Luxembourg, Brittany, Catalonia and Belgium, which official records often render as Paul or Paulus. In Brittany it also recalls Saint Paul Aurelian, founder of Saint-Pol-de-Léon; here the name is linked to the apostle Saint Paul, celebrated on 29 June.

polyxene.label: Polyxène
polyxene.text: The name of a daughter of Priam in mythology, borne by the Bohemian and central European nobility in the 16th and 17th centuries as Polyxena. It remains rare in ordinary registers.

pompeo.label: Pompeo
pompeo.meaning: From the Roman family name "Pompeius", perhaps from an Oscan word meaning "five".
pompeo.text: A name of the Italian Renaissance, inspired by the Roman general Pompey and used in Italy mainly in educated or noble families. It has no widely celebrated saint.

pons.label: Pons
pons.meaning: From Latin "Pontius", a Roman family name.
pons.text: Saint Pontius, a martyr of Cimiez, is celebrated on 14 May. The name was widely used in Languedoc and Provence in the Middle Ages, notably by the counts of Toulouse.

porzia.label: Porzia
porzia.meaning: From the Roman family name "Porcius", perhaps linked to "porcus", "pig".
porzia.text: The Italian form of Portia, a rare name given under humanist influence in memory of Porcia, wife of Brutus. It appears mainly in Italian registers of the 16th to 18th centuries and has no patron saint.

prigent.label: Prigent
prigent.meaning: An old Breton name; meaning disputed.
prigent.text: A medieval Breton name, still given in Lower Brittany until the 16th and early 17th centuries, after which it survived mainly as a surname. Its use as a given name helps date the oldest entries.

privat.label: Privat
privat.text: Saint Privatus, a martyred bishop of Gévaudan, is celebrated on 21 August. The name is characteristic of Gévaudan and Languedoc.

prix.label: Prix
prix.text: Saint Praejectus, bishop of Clermont in the 7th century, is celebrated on 25 January. The name was mostly borne in Auvergne.

prosper.label: Prosper
prosper.text: A male name frequent in France, Belgium and Luxembourg in the 19th century and rarer before. It refers to Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, a 5th-century theologian, celebrated on 25 June.

prospero.label: Prospero
prospero.text: The Italian form of Prosper, found in Italian registers mainly from the 16th to the 19th century. It refers to Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, celebrated on 25 June; Emilia also honours a Saint Prosper, bishop of Reggio.

protais.label: Protais
protais.text: Saints Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs of Milan, are celebrated on 19 June. The name is rare and often found in parishes under their patronage.

prudence.label: Prudence
prudence.text: A virtue name given in France and England, notably in Protestant circles in the 17th and 18th centuries. In France it is borne by women and, more rarely, by men (as Prudent).

przemyslaw.label: Przemysław
przemyslaw.text: An old Polish name, borne by medieval dukes of the Piast dynasty, then rare until its revival in the 20th century. Records without diacritics write it Przemyslaw; it has no patron saint.

purificacion.label: Purificación
purificacion.text: A Spanish female name, short for María de la Purificación, given in honour of the Purification of the Virgin (Candlemas). It is celebrated on 2 February; the Catalan and Basque forms are Purificació and Garbiñe.

quentin.label: Quentin
quentin.text: Saint Quentin, a martyr in Vermandois, gave his name to the town of Saint-Quentin and is celebrated on 31 October. The name was mostly borne in Picardy under the Ancien Régime and became very popular at the end of the 20th century.

quitterie.label: Quitterie
quitterie.text: Saint Quiteria, venerated at Aire-sur-l'Adour, is celebrated on 22 May. The name is characteristic of Gascony and the Landes.

rachel.label: Rachel
rachel.text: The name of Jacob's wife in Genesis, used in Jewish and Protestant families, notably in the Netherlands, England and the United States; it is rarer in older Catholic registers. It has no saint in the calendar.

rachele.label: Rachele
rachele.meaning: Italian form of Rachel, from Hebrew "Rahel", "ewe".
rachele.text: The Italian form of Rachel, found in Italian registers mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no saint in the calendar.

radegonde.label: Radegonde
radegonde.text: Saint Radegund, the Frankish queen who founded the Holy Cross abbey in Poitiers, is celebrated on 13 August. The name is mostly borne in Poitou.

rafael.label: Rafael
rafael.text: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Raphael, frequent in Iberian and Latin American records. The name refers to the archangel Raphael, celebrated on 29 September with Michael and Gabriel (on 24 October before 1969).

rafaela.label: Rafaela
rafaela.meaning: Feminine of Rafael, from Hebrew "Rephael", "God heals".
rafaela.text: The feminine of Rafael, used in Spain and Portugal and more rarely in Germany. It has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

rafal.label: Rafał
rafal.meaning: Polish form of Raphael, from Hebrew "Rephael", "God heals".
rafal.text: The Polish form of Raphael, found in Catholic registers in Poland; Latin records write it Raphael and transcriptions without diacritics Rafal. The name refers to the archangel Raphael, celebrated on 29 September.

raffaele.label: Raffaele
raffaele.meaning: Italian form of Raphael, from Hebrew "Rephael", "God heals".
raffaele.text: The Italian form of Raphael, particularly frequent in southern Italy (Campania, Apulia). It is also spelled Raffaelle or, in Latin, Raphael. The name refers to the archangel Raphael, celebrated on 29 September.

raffaello.label: Raffaello
raffaello.meaning: Italian form of Raphael, from Hebrew "Rephael", "God heals".
raffaello.text: A Tuscan variant of Raffaele, made famous by the painter Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio). It is less frequent than Raffaele in the records. The name refers to the archangel Raphael, celebrated on 29 September.

rahel.label: Rahel
rahel.meaning: German form of Rachel, from Hebrew "Rahel", "ewe".
rahel.text: The German form of Rachel, used mainly in Jewish and Protestant families in German-speaking lands. It has no saint in the calendar.

raimondo.label: Raimondo
raimondo.meaning: Italian form of Raymond, from Germanic "ragin", "counsel", and "mund", "protection".
raimondo.text: The Italian form of Raymond, found in Italian and Ticino registers. The name refers to Saint Raymond of Penyafort, a Catalan Dominican celebrated on 7 January; Saint Raymond Nonnatus (31 August) is also honoured.

raimundo.label: Raimundo
raimundo.meaning: Portuguese and Spanish form of Raymond, from Germanic "ragin", "counsel", and "mund", "protection".
raimundo.text: A learned form of Raymond, common in Portugal and found in Spain alongside Ramón; Latin records write it Raymundus. The name refers to Saint Raymond of Penyafort, celebrated on 7 January.

rajzla.label: Rajzla
rajzla.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Reyzl, "little rose", frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. The plain form Rojza (Royze) is the same name.

ralph.label: Ralph
ralph.text: The English form of Raoul, brought by the Normans and used in England since the Middle Ages; it is common in Britain and the United States in the 19th and 20th centuries. Older records also spell it Rafe or, in Latin, Radulphus. There is no widely celebrated saint of this name.

ramiro.label: Ramiro
ramiro.text: A name of Visigothic origin, borne by medieval kings of Asturias and León, then found in Spain and Portugal. It has no widely celebrated saint.

ramon.label: Ramón
ramon.meaning: Spanish and Catalan form of Raymond, from Germanic "ragin", "counsel", and "mund", "protection".
ramon.text: The Spanish and Catalan form of Raymond, very frequent in Catalonia and throughout Spain; Latin records write it Raymundus. It was often given in honour of Saint Raymond Nonnatus, patron of childbirth, celebrated on 31 August; Saint Raymond of Penyafort is celebrated on 7 January.

ramona.label: Ramona
ramona.meaning: Feminine of Ramón, from Germanic "ragin", "counsel", and "mund", "protection".
ramona.text: The Spanish feminine of Ramón, found in Spain and, from the late 19th century, in the United States. It has no saint of its own.

raoul.label: Raoul
raoul.text: An old French name, common in the Middle Ages, then rarer before coming back into favour in the late 19th century. Latin records write it Radulphus or Rodulphus, which links it to Rodolphe. It is associated with Saint Raoul (Rodulf), 9th-century archbishop of Bourges, celebrated on 21 June.

raphael.label: Raphaël
raphael.text: A biblical name found in France, Belgium, Switzerland and Germany, more frequent in the records from the 19th century; it is also used in Jewish families. The name refers to the archangel Raphael, celebrated on 29 September with Michael and Gabriel (on 24 October before 1969).

raquel.label: Raquel
raquel.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Rachel, from Hebrew "Rahel", "ewe".
raquel.text: The Iberian form of Rachel, found in Spain and Portugal and more frequent in the 20th century. It has no saint in the calendar.

raul.label: Raul
raul.meaning: Portuguese and Spanish form of Raoul, from Germanic "Radulf", "counsel wolf".
raul.text: The Iberian form of Raoul, used in Portugal and Spain, mainly in the 20th century; in Spanish it is written Raúl. There is no widely celebrated saint of this name in the peninsula.

ray.label: Ray
ray.meaning: Short form of Raymond, from Germanic "ragin", "counsel", and "mund", "protection".
ray.text: An English-language pet form of Raymond, used as a name in its own right in the United States mainly from the late 19th century. The same person often appears as Raymond in other records; it has no saint of its own.

raymond.label: Raymond
raymond.text: A name widely used in southern France in the Middle Ages (the counts of Toulouse), then throughout France, Belgium and Luxembourg in the 19th and 20th centuries, and also in England and the United States. Latin records write it Raymundus. It is celebrated on 7 January in honour of Saint Raymond of Penyafort.

raymonde.label: Raymonde
raymonde.meaning: Feminine of Raymond, from Germanic "ragin", "counsel", and "mund", "protection".
raymonde.text: The feminine of Raymond, frequent in France mainly in the first half of the 20th century. It has no saint of its own.

rebecca.label: Rebecca
rebecca.meaning: From Hebrew "Rivqah", of disputed meaning, often linked to "tie" or "bind".
rebecca.text: The name of Isaac's wife in Genesis, used in Jewish and Protestant families, notably in England, the Netherlands and the United States from the 17th century. It also appears as Rebekah, Rebekka or Rébecca and has no saint in the calendar.

recha.label: Recha
recha.meaning: Of disputed origin; probably a German-Jewish familiar form of a Hebrew name such as Rachel or Rebecca.
recha.text: A female name found mainly in Jewish families in Germany and Poland in the 18th and 19th centuries, sometimes recorded as the civil counterpart of a Hebrew name. It has no patron saint.

regina.label: Regina
regina.text: A female name common in Poland, Germany, Switzerland and Belgium, often linked to the Marian title of Queen of Heaven. It refers to Saint Regina of Alise, a virgin martyr venerated in Burgundy, celebrated on 7 September.

reginald.label: Reginald
reginald.text: An English name of Norman origin, rare until its Victorian vogue in the 19th century in Britain and the United States. It is related to Reynold, Renaud and Rinaldo and has no widely celebrated saint.

regine.label: Régine
regine.meaning: French form of Regina, from Latin "regina", "queen".
regine.text: The French form of Regina, used in France and Belgium mainly in the 20th century, and found as Regine in German and Polish registers. It refers to Saint Regina of Alise, celebrated on 7 September.

regis.label: Régis
regis.meaning: From the name of Saint John Francis Regis, linked to Latin "rex, regis", "king".
regis.text: A French name born of the cult of Saint John Francis Regis, a Jesuit missionary of the Velay and Vivarais canonised in 1737; it is most frequent in the Massif Central, around Lalouvesc and Le Puy. The saint is celebrated on 16 June in French calendars.

regula.label: Regula
regula.text: A typically Swiss German female name, especially in Zurich. It refers to Saint Regula, martyred with her brother Saint Felix, patrons of Zurich, celebrated on 11 September.

reine.label: Reine
reine.text: A French and Belgian female name, frequent under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century, notably in Burgundy; Latin records write it Regina. It refers to Saint Regina of Alise, celebrated on 7 September.

reinhard.label: Reinhard
reinhard.text: An old German name, found in Germany, Switzerland and among German speakers in Poland, with the spellings Reinhardt or Reinhart. It is most frequent in the 20th century and has no widely celebrated saint.

reinhold.label: Reinhold
reinhold.text: A German name found in Germany, Switzerland and among German speakers in Poland and the Baltic, also spelled Reinold. It refers to Saint Reinold, a monk of Cologne and patron of Dortmund, celebrated on 7 January.

reinier.label: Reinier
reinier.meaning: Dutch form of Rainier, from Germanic "ragin", "counsel", and "hari", "army".
reinier.text: An old Dutch name, found in registers of the Netherlands from the 16th to the 20th century and the source of patronymics such as Reiniers. It has no widely celebrated saint in the Netherlands.

remedios.label: Remedios
remedios.meaning: From Spanish "remedios", "remedies, help", referring to Our Lady of Remedies.
remedios.text: A Spanish female name, short for María de los Remedios, given in honour of Our Lady of Remedies, venerated in many shrines. Her feast varies from place to place; the Catalan form is Remei.

remi.label: Remi
remi.text: An old French and Belgian name, particularly linked to Champagne and Reims. Latin records write it Remigius; Rémy or Remy also occur. It refers to Saint Remigius, the bishop of Reims who baptised Clovis, celebrated on 15 January (and traditionally on 1 October).

remy.label: Rémy
remy.text: A French spelling of Remi, common in records where Rémy, Remy and Remi alternate, with Remigius in Latin. It refers to Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, celebrated on 15 January (and traditionally on 1 October).

renata.label: Renata
renata.meaning: From Latin "renatus", "born again", an allusion to baptism.
renata.text: A female name found in Poland, Italy and Germany, most frequent in the 20th century. It has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

renato.label: Renato
renato.meaning: From Latin "renatus", "born again", an allusion to baptism.
renato.text: The Italian form of René, found in Italian registers and more frequent from the late 19th century. There is no widely celebrated saint of this name in Italy.

rene.label: René
rene.meaning: From Latin "renatus", "born again", an allusion to baptism.
rene.text: A French name attested since the Middle Ages, especially in Anjou and western France (King René of Anjou), then very frequent in France, Belgium, Switzerland and Luxembourg in the first half of the 20th century. Latin records write it Renatus. It is celebrated on 19 October, with Saint René Goupil, a martyr in New France.

renee.label: Renée
renee.meaning: Feminine of René, from Latin "renatus", "born again".
renee.text: The feminine of René, found in France since the Renaissance (Renée of France) and very frequent in the first half of the 20th century in France, Switzerland and Belgium. It has no saint of its own.

reto.label: Reto
reto.meaning: Usually linked to the Raetians, an ancient Alpine people (Raetia); etymology disputed.
reto.text: A characteristically Swiss name, mostly from Graubünden and German-speaking Switzerland, given mainly in the 20th century. It is rare outside Switzerland.

ricard.label: Ricard
ricard.meaning: Catalan form of Richard, from Germanic "rīc", "powerful", and "hard", "strong".
ricard.text: The Catalan form of Richard, rare in older registers and more frequent in the 20th century; Castilian documents render it as Ricardo. It refers to Saint Richard of Chichester, celebrated on 3 April.

ricardo.label: Ricardo
ricardo.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Richard, from Germanic "rīc", "powerful", and "hard", "strong".
ricardo.text: The Iberian form of Richard, found in Spain and Portugal and more frequent from the 19th century; Latin records write it Ricardus. It refers to Saint Richard of Chichester, celebrated on 3 April.

riccardo.label: Riccardo
riccardo.meaning: Italian form of Richard, from Germanic "rīc", "powerful", and "hard", "strong".
riccardo.text: The Italian form of Richard, found in Italy since the Middle Ages (the Norman princes of the south) and common in modern registers. It refers to Saint Richard of Chichester, celebrated on 3 April.

richard.label: Richard
richard.text: A name very widespread in England since the Norman Conquest, then in the United States; it is also found in Germany, France and, as Ryszard, in Poland. Latin records write it Ricardus and English pet forms are Dick or Rick. It refers to Saint Richard of Chichester, celebrated on 3 April.

richarde.label: Richarde
richarde.meaning: Feminine of Richard, from the Germanic elements "ric" (powerful) and "hard" (hard, strong).
richarde.text: The name of Saint Richardis, wife of Emperor Charles the Fat and founder of Andlau Abbey in Alsace. It is rare, found in Alsatian and Lorraine registers as Richarde and Richardis.

rie.label: Rie
rie.meaning: Dutch pet form, most often of Maria, sometimes of other names ending in "-rie"; the origin follows the full name.
rie.text: A Dutch familiar form, mainly of the 19th and 20th centuries, which usually corresponds to a Maria or Marie in the birth record. The full name should therefore be sought in official records; this pet form has no saint of its own.

rina.label: Rina
rina.meaning: Italian pet form of names ending in "-rina" such as Caterina, Marina or Rosarina; the origin follows the full name.
rina.text: An Italian short form used on its own mainly in the 20th century; in older records it often stands for a Caterina or a Marina. It has no saint of its own.

rinaldo.label: Rinaldo
rinaldo.meaning: Italian form of Reynold, from Germanic "ragin", "counsel", and "wald", "rule".
rinaldo.text: An Italian name made famous by the chivalric poems (Rinaldo in Ariosto and Tasso), found in Italian registers as Rainaldo or Renaldo. It has no widely celebrated saint.

rita.label: Rita
rita.meaning: Short form of Margherita, from Latin "margarita", "pearl".
rita.text: A name that became independent through the cult of Saint Rita of Cascia (Margherita Lotti), canonised in 1900 and very popular in Italy, Portugal and Spain in the 20th century. The saint is celebrated on 22 May.

robert.label: Robert
robert.text: A name widely used in France since the Capetians and in England since the Norman Conquest, then in the United States, Luxembourg and Germany. Latin records write it Robertus; the English pet forms Bob or Rob appear in recent records. It is celebrated on 30 April in honour of Saint Robert of Molesme, founder of Cîteaux.

roberta.label: Roberta
roberta.meaning: Feminine of Robert, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "berht", "bright".
roberta.text: The feminine of Robert, found in the United States, Britain and Italy, mainly in the 20th century. It has no saint of its own.

roberto.label: Roberto
roberto.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Robert, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "berht", "bright".
roberto.text: The southern European form of Robert, common in Italy, Spain and Portugal and more frequent in the 20th century. In Italy it is mainly celebrated on 17 September, the day of Saint Robert Bellarmine, a Jesuit cardinal canonised in 1930.

robin.label: Robin
robin.meaning: Medieval pet form of Robert, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "berht", "bright".
robin.text: An English pet form of Robert, known since the Middle Ages (Robin Hood) and used as a name in its own right in Britain. In older records the same person may appear as Robert; it has no saint of its own.

rocco.label: Rocco
rocco.meaning: Italian form of Roch, of disputed etymology, perhaps from Germanic "hrok", "rest" or "cry".
rocco.text: A name very widespread in southern Italy (Basilicata, Calabria, Apulia) and in Ticino, and carried abroad by many Italian emigrants. It refers to Saint Roch of Montpellier, a pilgrim invoked against the plague, celebrated on 16 August.

roch.label: Roch
roch.text: Saint Roch, a pilgrim born in Montpellier and invoked against the plague, is celebrated on 16 August. The name was widespread throughout France under the Ancien Régime; Latin records write Rochus.

rodney.label: Rodney
rodney.meaning: From an English place name in Somerset, which became a surname and then a given name.
rodney.text: An English surname turned given name, especially after the fame of Admiral Rodney in the 18th century, and common in Britain and the United States in the 20th century. It has no patron saint.

rodolfo.label: Rodolfo
rodolfo.meaning: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Rudolph, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "wulf", "wolf".
rodolfo.text: The southern European form of Rudolph, found in Italy, Portugal, Spain and Ticino, more frequent in the 19th and 20th centuries. There is no widely celebrated saint of this name in those countries.

rodolphe.label: Rodolphe
rodolphe.text: The French form of Rudolf, used in French-speaking Switzerland, France and Belgium, and often interchangeable with Raoul in older records (Rodulphus in Latin). It is celebrated on 21 June in honour of Saint Rodulf (Raoul), 9th-century archbishop of Bourges.

rodrigo.label: Rodrigo
rodrigo.text: A name of Visigothic origin, borne by the last Visigothic king and by El Cid (Rodrigo Díaz), common in Spain and Portugal; Latin records write it Rodericus and the short forms are Ruy or Rui. It refers to Saint Roderick, a 9th-century martyr of Córdoba, celebrated on 13 March.

roelof.label: Roelof
roelof.meaning: Dutch form of Rudolf, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "wulf", "wolf".
roelof.text: A Dutch name widespread mainly in the north-east of the Netherlands (Drenthe, Groningen, Overijssel) and the source of patronymics such as Roelofs. It has no widely celebrated saint.

rogatien.label: Rogatien
rogatien.meaning: From Latin Rogatianus, derived from "rogatus", "asked for".
rogatien.text: The name of Saint Rogatian, martyred in Nantes with his brother Donatian around the end of the 3rd century. It is found mainly in registers of Loire-Atlantique and Vendée.

rogelio.label: Rogelio
rogelio.meaning: From Latin "Rogellus", of uncertain etymology, often wrongly linked to Roger.
rogelio.text: A Spanish name linked to the memory of Saint Rogellus, a 9th-century martyr of Córdoba, and most frequent in the 20th century. The martyr's cult remained local; the Catalan form is Rogeli.

roger.label: Roger
roger.text: An old name in France and in England since the Normans, again very frequent in France, Luxembourg and Belgium in the first half of the 20th century. Latin records write it Rogerius; the forms Rogier or Rodger also occur. It is celebrated on 30 December in honour of Saint Roger, bishop of Cannae in Apulia.

rogerio.label: Rogério
rogerio.meaning: Portuguese form of Roger, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "gār", "spear".
rogerio.text: The Portuguese form of Roger, most frequent in the 20th century in Portugal and Brazil. There is no widely celebrated saint of this name in Portugal.

roland.label: Roland
roland.text: A name made famous by the Song of Roland, used in France since the Middle Ages and frequent in the 20th century in France, Switzerland, Britain and the United States. Latin records write it Rolandus; the corresponding Italian form is Orlando. French calendars celebrate it on 15 September, the day of Blessed Roland de' Medici.

rolande.label: Rolande
rolande.meaning: Feminine of Roland, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "land", "land".
rolande.text: The feminine of Roland, rare before the 20th century and used mainly in France and Belgium. It refers to Saint Rolande, venerated at Gerpinnes in Belgium, where a folk procession honours her, and celebrated on 13 May.

romain.label: Romain
romain.text: A French name used since the Middle Ages, particularly in the Jura and Normandy, rarer in the 18th and 19th centuries and later back in favour. Latin records write it Romanus. It is celebrated on 28 February in honour of Saint Romanus, founder of the abbey of Condat (Saint-Claude).

roman.label: Roman
roman.text: The Polish, German and Spanish form of Romain, common in Poland and the Slavic countries; in Spanish it is written Román. Several saints bear this name and feast dates vary from country to country.

romolo.label: Romolo
romolo.meaning: Italian form of Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome, of disputed etymology.
romolo.text: An Italian name inspired by the founder of Rome, given mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries, notably in Tuscany and Lazio. A Saint Romulus is venerated as first bishop of Fiesole, but his cult remains local.

romuald.label: Romuald
romuald.text: A name found in Poland and Germany and more rarely in France. It refers to Saint Romuald, an Italian hermit and founder of the Camaldolese order, celebrated on 19 June.

ronald.label: Ronald
ronald.meaning: From Old Norse "Rögnvaldr", from "regin", "counsel (of the gods)", and "valdr", "ruler".
ronald.text: A name of Scandinavian origin established in Scotland, which became common in Britain and the United States mainly in the 20th century. Its Gaelic forms are Raghnall or Ranald; it has no widely celebrated saint.

ronan.label: Ronan
ronan.meaning: From Irish "rón", "seal", with a diminutive suffix.
ronan.text: Saint Ronan, an Irish hermit settled at Locronan, is celebrated on 1 June. The name is used in Brittany and spread widely in the second half of the 20th century.

ronnie.label: Ronnie
ronnie.meaning: Pet form of Ronald, from Old Norse "Rögnvaldr", "ruler by counsel".
ronnie.text: An American pet form of Ronald, sometimes used on its own as a name in the 20th century. The same person may appear as Ronald in other records; it has no saint of its own.

rosa.label: Rosa
rosa.text: A female name widespread in Italy, Spain, Portugal, Germany and Poland (Róża), often associated with Marian devotion (Rosa Mystica). It refers to Saint Rose of Lima, the first saint of the Americas, celebrated on 23 August (30 August in the older calendar).

rosalia.label: Rosalia
rosalia.meaning: From Latin "rosa", "rose", perhaps via the Roman festival of the Rosalia; the etymology is disputed.
rosalia.text: A female name particularly linked to Sicily, where Saint Rosalia is patroness of Palermo, and also found in Spain, Belgium and the Netherlands. The saint is celebrated on 4 September, and on 15 July in Palermo.

rosalie.label: Rosalie
rosalie.meaning: French and German form of Rosalia, from Latin "rosa", "rose".
rosalie.text: A female name frequent in the 19th century in Belgium, France, Switzerland, Germany and Poland. It refers to Saint Rosalia of Palermo, celebrated on 4 September.

rosario.label: Rosario
rosario.meaning: From Spanish and Italian "rosario", "rosary", from Latin "rosarium", "rose garden".
rosario.text: In Spain a female name, short for María del Rosario (pet form Charo); in southern Italy it is on the contrary mostly male. It honours Our Lady of the Rosary, celebrated on 7 October.

rose.label: Rose
rose.text: An old female name in France, often in compounds (Marie-Rose, Rose-Marie), and frequent in Britain and the United States in the 19th and 20th centuries. It is celebrated on 23 August (30 August in the older calendar) in honour of Saint Rose of Lima.

rosemary.label: Rosemary
rosemary.meaning: From English "rosemary", the herb (from Latin "ros marinus", "sea dew"), associated with Rose and Mary.
rosemary.text: An English-language name of the 20th century, widespread mainly in Britain and the United States, sometimes written Rose Marie or Rosemarie. It has no saint of its own.

roser.label: Roser
roser.meaning: Catalan form of Rosario, "rosary", from Latin "rosarium".
roser.text: A Catalan female name, short for Maria del Roser, equivalent to the Castilian Rosario. It honours Our Lady of the Rosary, celebrated on 7 October.

rosina.label: Rosina
rosina.text: A diminutive of Rosa, common in Italy and in German-speaking lands, notably Switzerland, mainly in the 19th century. It has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

rosine.label: Rosine
rosine.text: The French form of Rosina, found in French-speaking Switzerland, France and Germany, mainly in the 19th century. French calendars celebrate it on 11 March, the day of a Saint Rosina whose cult remained local.

rowland.label: Rowland
rowland.meaning: English form of Roland, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "land", "land".
rowland.text: The English form of Roland, found in England and Wales since the Middle Ages and also used as a surname. It has no widely celebrated saint.

roy.label: Roy
roy.meaning: From Scottish Gaelic "ruadh", "red-haired", sometimes wrongly linked to French "roi", "king".
roy.text: A name of Scottish origin that became common in Britain and the United States in the late 19th and 20th centuries. It has no patron saint.

royston.label: Royston
royston.meaning: From an English place name in Hertfordshire, which became a surname and then a given name.
royston.text: An English place name and surname used as a given name, mainly in Britain in the 20th century. It has no patron saint.

rozalia.label: Rozalia
rozalia.meaning: Polish form of Rosalia, from Latin "rosa", "rose".
rozalia.text: The Polish form of Rosalie, frequent in Catholic registers in Poland in the 18th and 19th centuries; Latin records write it Rosalia. It refers to Saint Rosalia of Palermo, celebrated on 4 September.

ruben.label: Ruben
ruben.text: The name of Jacob's eldest son in Genesis, used in Jewish and Protestant families, then in Spain (Rubén) and the United States mainly in the 20th century. It has no saint in the calendar.

ruby.label: Ruby
ruby.meaning: From English "ruby", the gem, from Latin "ruber", "red".
ruby.text: An English-language name that appeared with the late 19th-century fashion for gem names, mainly in the United States and Britain. It has no patron saint.

ruchla.label: Ruchla
ruchla.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Rokhl, very frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. Records in Russian after 1868 write Рухля; Rochla and Ruchel also occur.

rudolf.label: Rudolf
rudolf.text: A name widely used in Switzerland, Germany, the Netherlands and Central Europe (the Habsburg dynasty), with the pet forms Ruedi in Swiss German and Roelof in Dutch. Latin records write it Rudolphus; it has no widely celebrated saint.

rudolph.label: Rudolph
rudolph.meaning: Variant of Rudolf, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "wulf", "wolf".
rudolph.text: A spelling of Rudolf frequent in older German and Dutch records and among German-speaking emigrants to the United States. It has no widely celebrated saint.

rufus.label: Rufus
rufus.text: A Roman nickname turned given name, used mainly in the United States, notably in New England and the South, in the 18th and 19th centuries. Several obscure saints bear the name, without a widely observed feast.

ruggero.label: Ruggero
ruggero.meaning: Italian form of Roger, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "gār", "spear".
ruggero.text: The Italian form of Roger, linked to the Norman kings of Sicily (Roger II) and found mainly in southern Italy. It refers to Saint Roger, bishop of Cannae and patron of Barletta, celebrated on 30 December.

rui.label: Rui
rui.meaning: Portuguese short form of Rodrigo, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "rīc", "powerful".
rui.text: A Portuguese pet form of Rodrigo, used as a name in its own right since the Middle Ages and very frequent in Portugal in the 20th century. The same person may sometimes appear as Rodrigo; it has no saint of its own.

russell.label: Russell
russell.text: An English surname of Norman origin turned given name, mainly in the United States and Britain in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no patron saint.

ruth.label: Ruth
ruth.meaning: From Hebrew "Rut", of disputed meaning, often rendered "friend, companion".
ruth.text: The name of the heroine of the Book of Ruth, adopted by Protestants from the 17th century and frequent in the United States, Britain, Switzerland and Germany. It has no saint in the calendar.

ruy.label: Ruy
ruy.meaning: Medieval short form of Rodrigo, from Germanic "hrod", "glory", and "rīc", "powerful".
ruy.text: An old pet form of Rodrigo, frequent in Portuguese and Castilian documents of the medieval and early modern periods (modern spelling Rui in Portugal). The same person may appear as Rodrigo; it has no saint of its own.

ryszard.label: Ryszard
ryszard.meaning: Polish form of Richard, from Germanic "rīc", "powerful", and "hard", "strong".
ryszard.text: The Polish form of Richard, most frequent in Poland in the 20th century. It refers to Saint Richard of Chichester, celebrated on 3 April.

rywka.label: Rywka
rywka.meaning: The Yiddish form of Rebecca (Rivka); meaning disputed, often given as "bond".
rywka.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Rivke, very common in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. Rywka, Ryfka and Riwka alternate for the same person.

sabina.label: Sabina
sabina.meaning: From Latin "Sabina", "Sabine woman", of the Sabine people of central Italy.
sabina.text: A female name found in Poland, Germany, Belgium, Spain and Italy. It refers to Saint Sabina, a Roman martyr who gave her name to the basilica of Santa Sabina, celebrated on 29 August.

sabine.label: Sabine
sabine.meaning: French and German form of Sabina, "Sabine woman", of the Sabine people.
sabine.text: The French and German form of Sabina, found in Germany, Belgium, France and Poland and most frequent in the 20th century. It refers to Saint Sabina, a Roman martyr celebrated on 29 August.

sala.label: Sala
sala.meaning: A common Polish-record form of Jewish female names; linked to Sara or to Salomea depending on the family.
sala.text: A very frequent female name in Jewish civil records of Poland in the 19th and 20th centuries. The same person may appear as Sala, Sura or Sara in different entries, which must be checked case by case.

salomea.label: Salomea
salomea.text: An old female name in Poland, borne from the Middle Ages in the Piast dynasty. Blessed Salomea of Kraków, a 13th-century Poor Clare, is venerated there, but she has not been canonised.

salomon.label: Salomon
salomon.text: The name of King Solomon, used in Jewish families (Shlomo) as well as Protestant ones, notably in the Netherlands, Switzerland and Germany. It also appears as Solomon and has no saint in the calendar.

salvador.label: Salvador
salvador.meaning: From Spanish "salvador", "saviour", from Latin "salvator", referring to Christ.
salvador.text: A Spanish and Portuguese name given in honour of Christ the Saviour, frequent notably in Catalonia, the Valencia region and Andalusia. It does not refer to a particular saint.

salvatore.label: Salvatore
salvatore.meaning: From Italian "salvatore", "saviour", from Latin "salvator", referring to Christ.
salvatore.text: One of the most frequent male names in Sicily and southern Italy, very common among Italian emigrants to the United States. It honours Christ the Saviour rather than a particular saint; pet forms are Turi, Totò or Salvo.

samson.label: Samson
samson.text: Saint Samson, a Welsh monk who founded Dol-de-Bretagne, is celebrated on 28 July. The name was used in Brittany and Normandy, and as a biblical name in Protestant registers.

samuel.label: Samuel
samuel.meaning: From Hebrew "Shemuel", "his name is God" or "God has heard"; the etymology is disputed.
samuel.text: A biblical name widely used by Protestants (England, United States, Switzerland, Netherlands) from the 16th century, as well as in Jewish families (Shmuel). It refers to the prophet Samuel, celebrated on 20 August.

sandra.label: Sandra
sandra.meaning: Short form of Alessandra or Alexandra, from Greek "alexein", "to defend", and "anêr, andros", "man".
sandra.text: An Italian pet form of Alessandra that became a name in its own right, very frequent in the 20th century in the United States, Spain, Britain and Poland, and rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

sandrine.label: Sandrine
sandrine.meaning: A diminutive of Sandra, short for Alexandra, "defender of men".
sandrine.text: A French name very fashionable in the 1960s and 1970s and almost absent from earlier registers. It is a typical marker of that generation.

santiago.label: Santiago
santiago.meaning: From Spanish "Sant Iago", "Saint James"; James comes from Hebrew "Yaaqov", of disputed meaning ("heel-holder" or "may God protect").
santiago.text: A Spanish name built on the invocation "Santiago", the apostle James the Greater being patron of Spain and of Compostela. In records it coexists with Diego, Jaime, Iago or Yago, and Latin Jacobus. The apostle is celebrated on 25 July.

santina.label: Santina
santina.meaning: Italian diminutive of Santa, from Latin "sanctus", "holy".
santina.text: An Italian female name, frequent in the 19th and early 20th centuries, especially in Sicily, Calabria and the north-east. It has no saint of its own and was sometimes given to a child born around All Saints' Day.

santos.label: Santos
santos.meaning: From Spanish "santos", "saints", referring to the feast of All Saints.
santos.text: A Spanish name, sometimes short for Todos los Santos, often given to a child born or baptised around All Saints' Day. It is celebrated on 1 November; it is also a very common surname in Spain and Portugal, not to be confused with the given name.

sara.label: Sara
sara.text: A form of Sarah used in the Netherlands, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Italy, more frequent in Protestant and Jewish registers before the 19th century. Abraham's wife has no widely observed feast in the Latin calendar.

sarah.label: Sarah
sarah.text: The name of Abraham's wife, widely used by English and American Protestants from the 17th century, with the pet forms Sally or Sadie, and in Jewish families. It has no widely observed feast in the Latin calendar.

saturnin.label: Saturnin
saturnin.meaning: From Latin "Saturninus", derived from the god Saturn.
saturnin.text: Saint Saturninus (or Sernin), first bishop of Toulouse, is celebrated on 29 November. The name is used around Toulouse and in Languedoc.

saturnino.label: Saturnino
saturnino.text: An old Spanish name particularly linked to Navarre, where Saint Saturninus (San Cernin) is patron of Pamplona. The saint, first bishop of Toulouse (Saint Sernin), is celebrated on 29 November.

sauveur.label: Sauveur
sauveur.text: A name given in honour of Christ the Saviour, frequent in Provence, Corsica and the Basque Country under the Ancien Régime.

saverio.label: Saverio
saverio.meaning: Italian form of Xavier, from Basque "etxe berri", "new house", the name of Saint Francis Xavier's birthplace castle.
saverio.text: An Italian name, frequent alone or in the compound Francesco Saverio, especially in southern Italy from the 17th century. It refers to Saint Francis Xavier, the Jesuit missionary celebrated on 3 December.

scholastique.label: Scholastique
scholastique.text: Saint Scholastica, sister of Saint Benedict, is celebrated on 10 February. The name appears in French registers of the 17th and 18th centuries, often spelled Scolastique.

scipione.label: Scipione
scipione.text: A name of the Italian Renaissance, inspired by the Scipios of Roman history and used mainly in noble or educated families. It has no patron saint.

sebastian.label: Sebastian
sebastian.text: The German, Polish and Spanish (Sebastián) form of Sébastien, common in these countries since the 16th century; the short form Bastian also occurs. It refers to Saint Sebastian, a Roman martyr invoked against the plague, celebrated on 20 January.

sebastiana.label: Sebastiana
sebastiana.text: The Spanish feminine of Sebastián, found mainly in Spanish registers of the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

sebastiano.label: Sebastiano
sebastiano.meaning: Italian form of Sebastian, from Greek "sebastos", "venerable".
sebastiano.text: The Italian form of Sebastian, common in Italy and Ticino, with the short form Bastiano. It refers to Saint Sebastian, a Roman martyr celebrated on 20 January.

sebastiao.label: Sebastião
sebastiao.meaning: Portuguese form of Sebastian, from Greek "sebastos", "venerable".
sebastiao.text: The Portuguese form of Sebastian, popularised by King Sebastian I (16th century) and frequent in Portuguese registers. It refers to Saint Sebastian, celebrated on 20 January.

sebastien.label: Sébastien
sebastien.text: A name found in France, French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium under the Ancien Régime, then very frequent in France in the 1970s. Latin records write it Sebastianus. It refers to Saint Sebastian, celebrated on 20 January.

sebastienne.label: Sébastienne
sebastienne.text: A feminine form of Sébastien, found in French registers under the Ancien Régime, also as the shortened Bastienne.

selina.label: Selina
selina.meaning: Of disputed origin: linked to Greek "selênê", "moon", or to Latin "caelum", "heaven".
selina.text: An English name attested since the 17th century and more frequent in 19th-century Britain, with the variants Selena or Celina. It has no saint of its own.

selma.label: Selma
selma.meaning: Of disputed origin: popularised by the Ossian poems, perhaps shortened from Germanic names ending in "-selma"; the etymology is uncertain.
selma.text: A female name widespread in Scandinavia, Germany and the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries; it is also found in Poland. It has no patron saint.

serafin.label: Serafín
serafin.meaning: From Hebrew "seraphim", the name of the seraph angels, linked to "saraf", "to burn".
serafin.text: The Spanish form of Seraphin, found in Spain and in Franciscan orders. It refers to Saint Seraphin of Montegranaro, a Capuchin brother celebrated on 12 October.

serafino.label: Serafino
serafino.meaning: From Hebrew "seraphim", the name of the seraph angels, linked to "saraf", "to burn".
serafino.text: The Italian form of Seraphin, found mainly in the Marche and central Italy. It refers to Saint Seraphin of Montegranaro, a Capuchin of the Marche, celebrated on 12 October.

seraphin.label: Séraphin
seraphin.meaning: From Hebrew "seraphim", the name of the seraph angels, linked to "saraf", "to burn".
seraphin.text: An infrequent French and Belgian name, attested mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It refers to Saint Seraphin of Montegranaro, a Capuchin brother celebrated on 12 October.

seraphina.label: Seraphina
seraphina.meaning: Feminine of Seraphin, from Hebrew "seraphim", the name of the seraph angels.
seraphina.text: The Latin and Flemish form of Séraphine, found in Belgian registers of the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint.

seraphine.label: Seraphine
seraphine.meaning: Feminine of Seraphin, from Hebrew "seraphim", the name of the seraph angels.
seraphine.text: A female name found in Belgium, the Netherlands and France, mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint.

serge.label: Serge
serge.meaning: From the Roman family name "Sergius", of uncertain etymology.
serge.text: A French name most frequent in the 20th century, partly under Russian influence (Sergei), also found in French-speaking Switzerland. It is celebrated on 7 October, the day of Saint Sergius, martyred in Syria with Saint Bacchus.

sergio.label: Sergio
sergio.meaning: From the Roman family name "Sergius", of uncertain etymology.
sergio.text: The Spanish and Italian form of Serge, most frequent in the 20th century; the Catalan form is Sergi. It refers to Saint Sergius, martyred with Saint Bacchus, celebrated on 7 October.

severin.label: Séverin
severin.text: Saint Severinus, a hermit of Paris, is celebrated on 27 November. The name appears in French registers under the Ancien Régime.

seweryn.label: Seweryn
seweryn.meaning: Polish form of Severinus, from Latin "severus", "stern, austere".
seweryn.text: The Polish form of Severinus, found in Catholic registers in Poland; Latin records write it Severinus. It refers to Saint Severinus of Noricum, 5th-century apostle of the Danube, celebrated on 8 January.

sharon.label: Sharon
sharon.meaning: From Hebrew "Sharon", the name of a coastal plain in Israel mentioned in the Bible.
sharon.text: An English-language name widespread mainly in the United States in the mid-20th century, inspired by the "rose of Sharon" of the Song of Songs. It has no patron saint and is rare in older records.

sheila.label: Sheila
sheila.meaning: Anglicised form of Irish "Síle", itself from Latin Caecilia (Cecilia).
sheila.text: A name of Irish origin that became common in Britain and the United States in the 20th century. In older Irish records the same woman may be entered as Cecilia or Celia; it has no distinct saint of its own.

shirley.label: Shirley
shirley.meaning: From Old English "scīr", "shire", and "lēah", "clearing"; a place name turned surname.
shirley.text: An English surname that became a female name after Charlotte Brontë's novel (1849), very frequent in the United States and Britain in the 1930s. It has no patron saint.

sibylla.label: Sibylla
sibylla.text: An old female name in Germany and Switzerland, borne by princesses from the Middle Ages, spelled Sibilla or Sybilla. It has no widely celebrated saint.

sibylle.label: Sibylle
sibylle.text: The French and German form of Sibylla, found in Germany and France, rare in older records and more frequent in the 20th century. It has no widely celebrated saint.

sidney.label: Sidney
sidney.meaning: From the English surname Sidney, probably from an English place name meaning "wide island"; the French "Saint-Denis" origin is a folk etymology.
sidney.text: An English surname turned given name, common in Britain and the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries, also spelled Sydney. It has no patron saint.

sidoine.label: Sidoine
sidoine.text: Saint Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of Clermont in the 5th century, is celebrated on 21 August. The name is rare and found mostly in Auvergne.

sidonia.label: Sidonia
sidonia.meaning: From Latin "Sidonius", "from Sidon", a city of Phoenicia.
sidonia.text: The Latin and Flemish form of Sidonie, found in Belgian registers of the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint.

sidonie.label: Sidonie
sidonie.meaning: From Latin "Sidonius", "from Sidon", a city of Phoenicia.
sidonie.text: A female name found in Belgium, France, Germany and Poland, mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint; Saint Sidonius Apollinaris is a man.

sidrac.label: Sidrac
sidrac.meaning: French form of Shadrach, the Babylonian name given to Hananiah in the Book of Daniel; meaning disputed.
sidrac.text: A rare biblical name taken from the episode of the three young men in the furnace. It appears occasionally in French registers, mostly Protestant ones.

siegfried.label: Siegfried
siegfried.text: A German name made famous by the hero of the Nibelungenlied, most frequent in Germany in the late 19th and 20th centuries. It is linked to Saint Sigfrid, an English missionary in Sweden, celebrated on 15 February, whose cult is mainly Scandinavian.

siegmund.label: Siegmund
siegmund.text: The German form of Sigismund, found in Germany and among German speakers in Poland. It refers to Saint Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, celebrated on 1 May.

sigismondo.label: Sigismondo
sigismondo.meaning: Italian form of Sigismund, from Germanic "sigu", "victory", and "mund", "protection".
sigismondo.text: The Italian form of Sigismund, borne mainly in noble families of the Renaissance and rarer afterwards. It refers to Saint Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, celebrated on 1 May.

sigismund.label: Sigismund
sigismund.text: A name of emperors and kings (Emperor Sigismund, the kings of Poland), found in Germany, Poland, Switzerland and the Netherlands; Latin records write it Sigismundus. It refers to Saint Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, celebrated on 1 May.

sigmund.label: Sigmund
sigmund.meaning: Contracted form of Sigismund, from Germanic "sigu", "victory", and "mund", "protection".
sigmund.text: A short form of Sigismund, used in Germany, Switzerland and Poland, notably in German-speaking Jewish families in the 19th century. It refers to Saint Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, celebrated on 1 May.

silvestro.label: Silvestro
silvestro.text: The Italian form of Sylvester, found in Italian registers and sometimes given to a child born at the end of December. It refers to Pope Saint Sylvester I, celebrated on 31 December.

silvia.label: Silvia
silvia.meaning: From Latin "silva", "forest"; the name of Rhea Silvia, legendary mother of Romulus.
silvia.text: A female name found in Spain, Italy and Belgium, rare in older records and frequent in the 20th century. It refers to Saint Silvia, mother of Pope Gregory the Great, celebrated on 3 November.

silvine.label: Silvine
silvine.text: A rare female name of the Sylvain and Sylvie family, found in 19th-century French registers. The spellings Silvine and Sylvine alternate.

silvio.label: Silvio
silvio.text: An Italian name, found mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries, with the variant Sylvio. It has no widely celebrated saint.

simao.label: Simão
simao.meaning: Portuguese form of Simon, from Hebrew "Shimon", "he has heard".
simao.text: The Portuguese form of Simon, found in Portuguese registers since the Middle Ages. It refers to the apostle Saint Simon the Zealot, celebrated with Saint Jude on 28 October.

simeon.label: Simeon
simeon.text: A biblical form close to Simon, borne by the son of Jacob and by the old man who welcomed Jesus at the Temple; it is found in France, Switzerland and among English-speaking Protestants. Several saints named Simeon exist, without a dominant feast in the Latin calendar.

simon.label: Simon
simon.text: A biblical name borne continuously in the Netherlands, Germany, France and Switzerland since the Middle Ages, and the source of many surnames. It refers to the apostle Saint Simon the Zealot, celebrated with Saint Jude on 28 October.

simone.label: Simone
simone.meaning: Feminine of Simon, from Hebrew "Shimon", "he has heard".
simone.text: The French feminine of Simon, very frequent in France and Belgium in the first half of the 20th century; in Italy, by contrast, Simone is a male name. It has no saint of its own.

simonne.label: Simonne
simonne.meaning: Spelling variant of Simone, from Hebrew "Shimon", "he has heard".
simonne.text: A spelling of Simone frequent in France and Belgium in the early 20th century; the same person may be recorded as Simone in other documents. It has no saint of its own.

slawomir.label: Sławomir
slawomir.text: A Polish name of Slavic origin, rare before the 20th century and very frequent after 1945. Records without diacritics write it Slawomir; it has no patron saint.

sofia.label: Sofia
sofia.text: The Italian, Portuguese, Spanish and German form of Sophie, long present in princely families and common from the 19th century. It refers to Saint Sophia, a Roman martyr celebrated on 15 May.

sofie.label: Sofie
sofie.text: A German, Scandinavian and Polish spelling of Sophie, found mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It refers to Saint Sophia, a Roman martyr celebrated on 15 May.

solange.label: Solange
solange.meaning: From Latin "sollemnia", "solemn feasts"; the etymology is disputed.
solange.text: A French female name, long confined to Berry, where Saint Solange, a 9th-century shepherdess martyr, is the regional patroness, then widespread in France in the 20th century. The saint is celebrated on 10 May.

soledad.label: Soledad
soledad.meaning: From Spanish "soledad", "solitude", referring to Our Lady of Solitude.
soledad.text: A Spanish female name, short for María de la Soledad, given in honour of the Virgin alone after the Crucifixion on Holy Saturday. Her feast is tied to Holy Week and varies from place to place.

soline.label: Soline
soline.meaning: Meaning disputed; often linked to Latin "sol", "sun".
soline.text: A female name rare in older registers and mostly given in France since the 1990s. It is associated with the Poitou village of Sainte-Soline.

sonia.label: Sonia
sonia.meaning: Russian pet form of Sofia, from Greek "sophia", "wisdom".
sonia.text: A name of Russian origin (Sonia, Sonya), spread in Western Europe by literature in the 19th century and frequent in Spain and Poland in the 20th century. It has no saint of its own distinct from Sophia.

sophia.label: Sophia
sophia.text: The learned form of Sophie, frequent in Dutch, Belgian, German and English registers, notably in Latin records. It refers to Saint Sophia, a Roman martyr celebrated on 15 May, one of the "Ice Saints" of German folk tradition.

sophie.label: Sophie
sophie.text: A female name very widespread in Germany, Switzerland, Belgium and the Netherlands in the 18th and 19th centuries, and also in France. It is celebrated on 15 May in honour of Saint Sophia, a Roman martyr; French calendars celebrate it on 25 May, the day of Saint Madeleine-Sophie Barat.

stanislao.label: Stanislao
stanislao.meaning: Italian form of Stanislaus, from Slavic "stani", "become, establish", and "slava", "glory".
stanislao.text: The Italian form of Stanislaus, rare and spread mainly through the cult of Saint Stanislaus Kostka, a Polish Jesuit who died in Rome. The name refers to Saint Stanislaus, the martyred bishop of Kraków, celebrated on 11 April in the Roman calendar.

stanislas.label: Stanislas
stanislas.text: A name of Polish origin that spread in Lorraine and France in the 18th century thanks to Duke Stanislas Leszczyński, father-in-law of Louis XV, and also found in Belgium. It refers to Saint Stanislaus, the martyred bishop of Kraków, celebrated on 11 April.

stanislaw.label: Stanisław
stanislaw.text: One of the most frequent male names in Poland, linked to the country's patron saint; Latin records write it Stanislaus and transcriptions without diacritics Stanislaw, with the pet forms Staś or Stach. In Poland, Saint Stanislaus of Szczepanów is celebrated on 8 May (11 April in the Roman calendar).

stanislawa.label: Stanisława
stanislawa.meaning: Feminine of Stanisław, from Slavic "stani", "become", and "slava", "glory".
stanislawa.text: The feminine of Stanisław, frequent in Poland in the 19th and 20th centuries; transcriptions without diacritics write it Stanislawa. It has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

stanley.label: Stanley
stanley.meaning: From Old English "stān", "stone", and "lēah", "clearing"; a place name turned surname.
stanley.text: An English surname turned given name in the 19th century, very frequent in Britain and the United States around 1900. In the United States it sometimes served as an Americanised form of Stanisław among Polish immigrants. It has no patron saint.

stefan.label: Stefan
stefan.text: The German, Polish, Dutch and Scandinavian form of Stephen, common in Poland, Germany and Switzerland; older Polish also has Szczepan. It refers to Saint Stephen, the first martyr, celebrated on 26 December.

stefania.label: Stefania
stefania.text: The Italian and Polish feminine of Stephen, found in Poland and Italy, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

stefano.label: Stefano
stefano.meaning: Italian form of Stephen, from Greek "stephanos", "crown".
stefano.text: The Italian form of Stephen, common in Italy and Ticino since the Middle Ages; Latin records write it Stephanus. It refers to Saint Stephen, the first martyr, celebrated on 26 December.

stella.label: Stella
stella.meaning: From Latin "stella", "star", echoing the Marian title "Stella Maris", "star of the sea".
stella.text: A female name rare before the 19th century, then used in Portugal, the Netherlands, Britain and the United States. It has no saint of its own; it evokes the Virgin under the title Star of the Sea.

stephan.label: Stephan
stephan.text: A German spelling of Stephen, frequent in Germany, Switzerland and among German speakers in Poland and Lorraine; Latin records write it Stephanus. It refers to Saint Stephen, the first martyr, celebrated on 26 December.

stephane.label: Stéphane
stephane.meaning: Learned form of Étienne (Stephen), from Greek "stephanos", "crown".
stephane.text: A modern French name, the learned form of Étienne, rare before the 20th century and very frequent in the 1960s and 1970s. In older records the same name appears as Étienne or, in Latin, Stephanus. It refers to Saint Stephen, celebrated on 26 December.

stephanie.label: Stephanie
stephanie.text: The feminine of Stephen, used in Belgium, France and Germany from the 19th century, then very frequent in the second half of the 20th century. It also appears as Stefanie or Stephania and has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

stephen.label: Stephen
stephen.meaning: English form of Stephen (Étienne), from Greek "stephanos", "crown".
stephen.text: The English form of Stephen, common in England since the Middle Ages (King Stephen) and in the United States. Latin records write it Stephanus; short forms are Steve or Steven. It refers to Saint Stephen, the first martyr, celebrated on 26 December.

steven.label: Steven
steven.text: An English and Dutch form of Stephen, frequent in the United States in the 20th century and old in the Netherlands (Steven, Stevens). It refers to Saint Stephen, the first martyr, celebrated on 26 December.

stuart.label: Stuart
stuart.meaning: From Old English "stigweard", "steward"; the name of the Scottish royal house of Stuart.
stuart.text: A Scottish surname, that of the royal dynasty, which became a given name in the 19th century in Britain and then the United States. It also appears as Stewart and has no patron saint.

sulpice.label: Sulpice
sulpice.meaning: From Latin "Sulpicius", a Roman family name.
sulpice.text: Saint Sulpicius the Pious, bishop of Bourges in the 7th century, is celebrated on 17 January. The name was common under the Ancien Régime, notably in central France, where many parishes bear his name.

sura.label: Sura
sura.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Sore, among the most frequent Jewish female names in 19th-century Poland, alone or in compounds (Chaja Sura). The same woman may be called Sura, Sara or Sala in different entries.

susan.label: Susan
susan.meaning: English form of Suzanne, from Hebrew "Shoshannah", "lily".
susan.text: The English form of Susanna, common in England and North America since the 17th century and very frequent in the mid-20th century; the longer forms Susannah or Susanna occur in older records. It is celebrated on 11 August in honour of Saint Susanna, a Roman martyr.

susana.label: Susana
susana.meaning: Spanish form of Susanna, from Hebrew "Shoshannah", "lily".
susana.text: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Susanna, found in Iberian registers and more frequent in the 20th century. It refers to Saint Susanna, a Roman martyr celebrated on 11 August.

susanna.label: Susanna
susanna.text: The biblical and Latin form of Susanna, heroine of the Book of Daniel, common in Swiss, Dutch, German and English registers, notably Protestant ones. It refers to Saint Susanna, a Roman martyr celebrated on 11 August.

susanne.label: Susanne
susanne.meaning: German form of Susanna, from Hebrew "Shoshannah", "lily".
susanne.text: The German form of Susanna, frequent in Switzerland and Germany, and very widespread in the 20th century. It refers to Saint Susanna, a Roman martyr celebrated on 11 August.

suzanna.label: Suzanna
suzanna.text: A Dutch and Flemish spelling of Susanna, found in registers of the Netherlands and Belgium. It refers to Saint Susanna, a Roman martyr celebrated on 11 August.

suzanne.label: Suzanne
suzanne.text: A female name found in France since the Middle Ages, with the Latin form Susanna and the pet form Suzette, and very frequent in France, Switzerland and Belgium in the early 20th century. It is celebrated on 11 August in honour of Saint Susanna, a Roman martyr.

suze.label: Suze
suze.meaning: Dutch pet form of Susanna, from Hebrew "Shoshannah", "lily".
suze.text: A Dutch familiar form of Susanna, sometimes used alone; in official records the same person is usually entered as Susanna. It refers to Saint Susanna, celebrated on 11 August.

sybil.label: Sybil
sybil.text: The English form of Sibylla, used in England since the Middle Ages and back in fashion in the late 19th century, spelled Sibyl or Sybilla. It has no widely celebrated saint.

sydney.label: Sydney
sydney.meaning: From the English surname Sidney, probably from an English place name meaning "wide island".
sydney.text: A spelling of Sidney, an English surname turned male name, common in Britain and the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no patron saint.

sylvain.label: Sylvain
sylvain.meaning: From Latin "Silvanus", "of the woods", the name of a Roman woodland god.
sylvain.text: A French and Belgian name used under the Ancien Régime, then frequent in the 20th century; Latin records write it Silvanus. French calendars celebrate it on 4 May, the day of Saint Sylvanus of Gaza, a martyred bishop.

sylvestre.label: Sylvestre
sylvestre.text: Saint Sylvester, a 4th-century pope, is celebrated on 31 December. The name appears in French registers under the Ancien Régime, often spelled Silvestre.

sylvia.label: Sylvia
sylvia.meaning: From Latin "silva", "forest"; the name of Rhea Silvia, legendary mother of Romulus.
sylvia.text: A spelling of Silvia widespread in Britain, Belgium, the United States and Germany, mainly in the 20th century. It refers to Saint Silvia, mother of Pope Gregory the Great, celebrated on 3 November.

sylviane.label: Sylviane
sylviane.meaning: Derived from Sylvie or feminine of Sylvain, from Latin "silva", "forest".
sylviane.text: A French name most frequent in the mid-20th century and rare in older records. It has no saint of its own.

sylvie.label: Sylvie
sylvie.meaning: French form of Silvia, from Latin "silva", "forest".
sylvie.text: A French and Belgian name rare before the 20th century, then among the most given in France in the 1960s. It refers to Saint Silvia, mother of Pope Gregory the Great, celebrated on 3 November (5 November in some French calendars).

sylwester.label: Sylwester
sylwester.meaning: Polish form of Sylvester, from Latin "silvester", "of the woods".
sylwester.text: The Polish form of Sylvester, found in Catholic registers in Poland; in Polish, "Sylwester" also means New Year's Eve. It refers to Pope Saint Sylvester I, celebrated on 31 December.

symphorien.label: Symphorien
symphorien.text: Saint Symphorian, a martyr of Autun, is celebrated on 22 August. The name was mostly borne in Burgundy and east-central France under the Ancien Régime.

szaja.label: Szaja
szaja.meaning: The Yiddish form of Isaiah (Yeshayahu), "God saves".
szaja.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Shaye, a diminutive of Isaiah, common in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century.

szejndla.label: Szejndla
szejndla.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Sheyndl, common in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. Szejndla and Szajndla alternate.

szlama.label: Szlama
szlama.meaning: The Yiddish form (Shloyme) of Solomon, from Hebrew "shalom", "peace".
szlama.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Shloyme, very frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. After 1868, records in Russian write Шляма; the Hebrew form is Shlomo.

szmul.label: Szmul
szmul.meaning: The Yiddish form of Samuel, "name of God" or "God has heard".
szmul.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Shmuel, very frequent in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century. German records write Schmul.

szprynca.label: Szprynca
szprynca.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Shprintse, a name that came from Spanish through Sephardic communities. It is found in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century.

szulim.label: Szulim
szulim.text: The Polish spelling of Yiddish Sholem, common in Jewish records of Poland in the 19th century.

szymon.label: Szymon
szymon.meaning: Polish form of Simon, from Hebrew "Shimon", "he has heard".
szymon.text: The Polish form of Simon, found in Catholic registers in Poland; Latin records write it Simon. It refers to the apostle Saint Simon the Zealot, celebrated with Saint Jude on 28 October.

tadeusz.label: Tadeusz
tadeusz.meaning: Polish form of Thaddeus, of Aramaic origin and disputed meaning (often rendered "heart, chest" or "courageous").
tadeusz.text: A very popular name in Poland, notably in honour of Tadeusz Kościuszko from the late 18th century; Latin records write it Thaddaeus. It refers to the apostle Saint Jude Thaddeus, celebrated with Saint Simon on 28 October.

tanguy.label: Tanguy
tanguy.text: Saint Tanguy, the legendary founder of Saint-Mathieu abbey, is celebrated on 19 November. The name was used in Brittany, notably by the du Chastel family in the form Tanneguy.

tarcisius.label: Tarcisius
tarcisius.meaning: A Latin name of disputed etymology.
tarcisius.text: The name of Saint Tarcisius, a young Roman martyr of the Eucharist, popularised in the 19th century by Catholic youth movements. It is found in Belgium, France and Switzerland, and as Tarcisio in Italy.

tauba.label: Tauba
tauba.text: A female Yiddish name, written Tauba in Polish records and Taube in German records of the 19th century.

teodor.label: Teodor
teodor.text: The Polish and Catalan form of Theodore, found in Poland and Spain; the East Slavic forms are Fedor or Fyodor. It refers to Saint Theodore of Amasea, a soldier martyr, celebrated on 9 November.

teodora.label: Teodora
teodora.meaning: Feminine of Teodor, from Greek "theos", "god", and "dôron", "gift".
teodora.text: The feminine of Theodore, found in Poland and Spain. Several saints of this name exist, without a dominant feast in the Latin calendar.

teodoro.label: Teodoro
teodoro.meaning: Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Theodore, from Greek "theos", "god", and "dôron", "gift".
teodoro.text: The southern European form of Theodore, found in Spain, Italy, Portugal and Ticino. It refers to Saint Theodore of Amasea, a soldier martyr, celebrated on 9 November.

teofil.label: Teofil
teofil.meaning: Polish form of Theophilus, from Greek "theos", "god", and "philos", "friend": "friend of God".
teofil.text: The Polish form of Theophilus, found in registers in Poland in the 18th and 19th centuries; Latin records write it Theophilus. Several saints bear this name, without a dominant feast.

teofilo.label: Teófilo
teofilo.meaning: Iberian and Italian form of Theophilus, from Greek "theos", "god", and "philos", "friend".
teofilo.text: The Portuguese, Spanish and Italian form of Theophilus, infrequent in the records. Several saints bear this name, without a dominant feast.

teotonio.label: Teotónio
teotonio.text: A typically Portuguese name, linked to the cult of Saint Theotonius, prior of Santa Cruz in Coimbra and the first canonised Portuguese saint. He is celebrated on 18 February.

terence.label: Terence
terence.meaning: From the Roman family name "Terentius", of uncertain etymology.
terence.text: An English and Irish name, often used in Ireland to anglicise Gaelic names, and frequent in Britain in the 20th century. It has no widely celebrated saint.

teresa.label: Teresa
teresa.meaning: Of disputed origin: perhaps from Greek "therizein", "to harvest", or from the island of Thera.
teresa.text: A name first Spanish, spread throughout Catholic Europe after the canonisation of Saint Teresa of Ávila in 1622, and very frequent in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Poland. The saint, reformer of the Carmelites, is celebrated on 15 October.

teresina.label: Teresina
teresina.meaning: Italian pet form of Teresa, of disputed origin.
teresina.text: An Italian pet form of Teresa, used as a name in the 19th and 20th centuries; the Portuguese form Teresinha rather evokes Saint Thérèse of Lisieux. In official records the same woman may be entered as Teresa.

terry.label: Terry
terry.meaning: Short form of Terence or of Theodoric, of disputed origin.
terry.text: An English-language name, most frequent in the United States and Britain in the 20th century, often as a pet form of Terence. It has no saint of its own.

thais.label: Thaïs
thais.meaning: An ancient Greek name; meaning disputed.
thais.text: The name of an Athenian courtesan and of a penitent saint of Egypt, popularised in France by Anatole France's novel (1890) and Massenet's opera (1894). It is rare in registers before the late 19th century.

thea.label: Thea
thea.meaning: From Greek "thea", "goddess", or short for Theodora or Dorothea.
thea.text: A German, Dutch and Scandinavian female name, often a pet form of Dorothea or Theodora, used on its own mainly in the 20th century. It has no saint of its own.

thecle.label: Thècle
thecle.text: Saint Thecla, a disciple of Saint Paul according to tradition, is celebrated on 23 September. The name is rare in France and found mostly in the 17th and 18th centuries.

thekla.label: Thekla
thekla.text: A female name found in Germany and Poland (Tekla), also spelled Thecla. It refers to Saint Thecla of Iconium, a disciple of Saint Paul according to tradition, celebrated on 23 September.

thelma.label: Thelma
thelma.meaning: Of disputed origin: popularised by Marie Corelli's novel "Thelma" (1887), perhaps from Greek "thelema", "will".
thelma.text: An English-language name that appeared in the late 19th century, frequent in the United States and Britain in the early 20th century. It has no patron saint.

theo.label: Theo
theo.meaning: Short form of Theodore or Theophilus, from Greek "theos", "god".
theo.text: A pet form used as a name in Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland, mainly from the late 19th century. In official records the same person often appears as Theodorus, Theodor or Théophile; it has no saint of its own.

theodoor.label: Theodoor
theodoor.meaning: Dutch form of Theodore, from Greek "theos", "god", and "dôron", "gift".
theodoor.text: The Dutch form of Theodore, found in the Netherlands and Flanders, where Latin records write it Theodorus; the usual pet form is Door. It refers to Saint Theodore of Amasea, a soldier martyr, celebrated on 9 November.

theodor.label: Theodor
theodor.text: The German form of Theodore, found in Germany, Switzerland, Luxembourg and Poland, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It refers to Saint Theodore of Amasea, a soldier martyr, celebrated on 9 November.

theodora.label: Theodora
theodora.meaning: Feminine of Theodore, from Greek "theos", "god", and "dôron", "gift".
theodora.text: A female name found in the Netherlands, Britain, Germany and Belgium, rare before the 19th century; it was also borne by the Byzantine empress Theodora. Several saints bear the name, without a dominant feast in the Latin calendar.

theodore.label: Theodore
theodore.text: A name found in Luxembourg, France, Belgium and the United States, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries; Latin records write it Theodorus. It refers to Saint Theodore of Amasea, a soldier martyr, celebrated on 9 November.

theodoros.label: Theodoros
theodoros.meaning: Greek form of Theodore, "gift of God".
theodoros.text: A Hellenising spelling of Theodore found in some Belgian registers, probably a hypercorrection of Latin Theodorus; it is the same name as Theodoor or Théodore. It refers to Saint Theodore of Amasea, celebrated on 9 November.

theodorus.label: Theodorus
theodorus.meaning: Latin form of Theodore, from Greek "theos", "god", and "dôron", "gift".
theodorus.text: The Latin form of Theodore, frequent in Dutch and Flemish parish registers, where it corresponds to the vernacular forms Theodoor or Door; it should not be confused with Theodoricus, which gives Dirk. It refers to Saint Theodore of Amasea, a soldier martyr, celebrated on 9 November.

theophile.label: Théophile
theophile.text: A French, Belgian, Luxembourgish and Swiss name, most frequent in the 19th century; Latin records write it Theophilus and German records Theophil. Several saints bear this name, without a dominant feast in the Latin calendar.

theresa.label: Theresa
theresa.meaning: Of disputed origin: perhaps from Greek "therizein", "to harvest", or from the island of Thera.
theresa.text: The English and German form of Teresa, found in the United States, Britain, Italy and Spain in records written in English or Latin. It refers to Saint Teresa of Ávila, reformer of the Carmelites, celebrated on 15 October.

therese.label: Thérèse
therese.meaning: Of disputed origin: perhaps from Greek "therizein", "to harvest", or from the island of Thera.
therese.text: The French form of Teresa, widespread in France, Belgium and Germany from the 17th century, often in compounds (Marie-Thérèse). It refers to Saint Teresa of Ávila, celebrated on 15 October; after 1925 it was also given in honour of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, celebrated on 1 October.

theresia.label: Theresia
theresia.meaning: Latin and Germanic form of Teresa, of disputed origin.
theresia.text: The Latin and German form of Teresa, very widespread in Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Germany, notably under the influence of Empress Maria Theresa in the 18th century. It refers to Saint Teresa of Ávila, celebrated on 15 October.

thibault.label: Thibault
thibault.text: The name of the counts of Champagne, common in France from the Middle Ages to the 17th century. Saint Theobald of Provins is celebrated on 8 July in the French calendar; records write Thibaut, Thibaud or Theobaldus.

thierry.label: Thierry
thierry.text: The French form of Theodoric, borne by Merovingian kings. Saint Theodoric, abbot near Reims, is celebrated on 1 July; present in the Middle Ages, the name was very fashionable in the 1960s.

thomas.label: Thomas
thomas.text: A name borne continuously throughout Europe since the Middle Ages, particularly frequent in England, the Netherlands and Germany; Latin records write it Thomas, and English pet forms are Tom or Tommy. It refers to the apostle Saint Thomas, celebrated on 3 July (21 December before 1969).

thomasse.label: Thomasse
thomasse.text: A feminine form of Thomas, common in French registers from the 15th to the 17th century, then rare.

tilly.label: Tilly
tilly.meaning: Pet form of Matilda or Ottilie, from Germanic "maht", "might", and "hild", "battle" (Matilda).
tilly.text: A Dutch, German and English familiar form, used on its own mainly in the late 19th and 20th centuries. In official records the same woman is often entered as Mathilde, Matilda or Ottilie; this pet form has no saint of its own.

timothy.label: Timothy
