timothy.text: A biblical name adopted by English and American Protestants after the Reformation, then common in the United States and Britain; it is also frequent in Ireland. It refers to Saint Timothy, disciple of Saint Paul, celebrated on 26 January with Saint Titus.

tina.label: Tina
tina.meaning: Short form of names ending in "-tina" (Christina, Martina, Albertina…); the origin follows the full name.
tina.text: A pet form used as a name in Italy, Switzerland, Germany and Poland, mainly in the 20th century. In older records the same woman often appears under a full name such as Christina or Martina; it has no saint of its own.

tine.label: Tine
tine.meaning: Dutch pet form of names ending in "-tine" or "-tina" (Christina, Martina, Albertine…); the origin follows the full name.
tine.text: A Dutch familiar form, sometimes used on its own; in official records the same woman is usually entered under a full name such as Christina or Albertina. This pet form has no saint of its own.

tiphaine.label: Tiphaine
tiphaine.meaning: From Greek "Theophania", "manifestation of God", that is, Epiphany.
tiphaine.text: A medieval name of Brittany and Normandy, borne by Tiphaine Raguenel, wife of Du Guesclin, and often given to children born around Epiphany. Rare under the Ancien Régime, it became fashionable again at the end of the 20th century.

titia.label: Titia
titia.meaning: Of disputed origin: a Frisian name, perhaps linked to Latin "Titia", feminine of Titus.
titia.text: A traditional female name of Friesland and the northern Netherlands, borne notably in prominent Frisian families in the 17th and 18th centuries. It has no patron saint.

tito.label: Tito
tito.meaning: Italian form of Titus, a Roman first name of uncertain etymology.
tito.text: An Italian name, found mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries, sometimes in homage to figures of Roman antiquity. It refers to Saint Titus, disciple of Saint Paul, celebrated on 26 January with Saint Timothy.

titouan.label: Titouan
titouan.meaning: A modern Breton name of disputed origin.
titouan.text: A recent name, given in France mostly since the 1990s, first in Brittany. It is absent from older registers.

tobias.label: Tobias
tobias.text: A biblical name from the Book of Tobit, used in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands, frequent among both Protestants and Catholics; in French it becomes Tobie. Tobias has no widely observed feast in the Latin calendar.

tomas.label: Tomás
tomas.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Thomas, from Aramaic "te'oma", "twin".
tomas.text: The Iberian form of Thomas (Tomás), found in Spain and Portugal since the Middle Ages, often also in honour of Saint Thomas Aquinas. The name refers to the apostle Saint Thomas, celebrated on 3 July (21 December before 1969).

tomasa.label: Tomasa
tomasa.text: The Spanish feminine of Tomás, found mainly in Spanish registers of the 18th and 19th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

tomasz.label: Tomasz
tomasz.meaning: Polish form of Thomas, from Aramaic "te'oma", "twin".
tomasz.text: The Polish form of Thomas, found in Catholic registers in Poland; Latin records write it Thomas. It refers to the apostle Saint Thomas, celebrated on 3 July (21 December before 1969).

tome.label: Tomé
tome.meaning: Old Portuguese form of Thomas, from Aramaic "te'oma", "twin".
tome.text: A popular Portuguese form of Thomas, frequent in older registers alongside the learned form Tomás; it gave its name to the island of São Tomé. It refers to the apostle Saint Thomas, celebrated on 3 July (21 December before 1969).

tommaso.label: Tommaso
tommaso.meaning: Italian form of Thomas, from Aramaic "te'oma", "twin".
tommaso.text: The Italian form of Thomas, common in Italy and Ticino, often also in honour of Saint Thomas Aquinas; older records spell it Tomaso. It refers to the apostle Saint Thomas, celebrated on 3 July (21 December before 1969).

toni.label: Toni
toni.meaning: Short form of Antonia (or Anton), from the Roman family name "Antonius", of uncertain etymology.
toni.text: In German and Polish registers, a female familiar form of Antonia, used on its own mainly in the 20th century; elsewhere Toni is often male (a pet form of Anton). In official records the same person is usually entered under the full name.

toussaint.label: Toussaint
toussaint.meaning: From French "Toussaint", the feast of All Saints.
toussaint.text: A French and Belgian name given to a child born or baptised around 1 November, mainly from the 17th to the 19th century; it also became a surname. It is celebrated on All Saints' Day, 1 November.

toussainte.label: Toussainte
toussainte.text: Often given to a girl born around All Saints' Day (1 November), attested in France in the 17th and 18th centuries, notably in Brittany and Normandy. It remains rare.

traugott.label: Traugott
traugott.meaning: A German name built on "trau Gott", "trust in God".
traugott.text: A Lutheran Pietist name that appeared in Germany in the 18th century, used in Germany, Switzerland and among German-speaking Protestants in Poland. It has no patron saint.

trevor.label: Trevor
trevor.meaning: From Welsh "tref", "village", and "mawr", "large"; a place name turned surname.
trevor.text: A Welsh surname turned given name, most frequent in Britain in the 20th century; the Welsh form is Trefor. It has no patron saint.

trinidad.label: Trinidad
trinidad.text: A Spanish female name, short for María de la Trinidad, given in honour of the Holy Trinity. Its feast, Trinity Sunday, is movable; the Catalan form is Trinitat.

tristan.label: Tristan
tristan.meaning: The name of the hero of the Arthurian legend; etymology disputed (Brittonic Drustan).
tristan.text: A medieval name from the legend of Tristan and Isolde, rare in early modern registers and popular again in France from the 1990s. The English form is Tristram.

tugdual.label: Tugdual
tugdual.text: Saint Tugdual, one of the seven founding saints of Brittany and first bishop of Tréguier, is celebrated on 30 November. The name is used in Brittany, especially in the Trégor.

tullio.label: Tullio
tullio.meaning: From the Roman family name "Tullius", of uncertain etymology.
tullio.text: An Italian name inspired by Cicero (Marcus Tullius Cicero), given mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint.

ugo.label: Ugo
ugo.meaning: Italian form of Hugh, from Germanic "hugu", "mind, spirit".
ugo.text: The Italian form of Hugh, found in Italy and Ticino since the Middle Ages. It refers to Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble and protector of Saint Bruno, celebrated on 1 April.

ulisse.label: Ulisse
ulisse.meaning: Italian form of Ulysses, from Latin "Ulixes", the Latin name of the Greek hero Odysseus.
ulisse.text: An Italian name of classical inspiration, given mainly in the 19th century. It has no patron saint.

ulrich.label: Ulrich
ulrich.text: A name very widespread in German-speaking Switzerland and southern Germany, with the Swiss pet form Ueli; Latin records write it Udalricus or Ulricus. It refers to Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, celebrated on 4 July.

ulrike.label: Ulrike
ulrike.meaning: Feminine of Ulrich, from Germanic "uodal", "heritage", and "rīc", "powerful".
ulrike.text: The German feminine of Ulrich, found in Germany and Poland, mainly in the 20th century; the older form is Ulrica or Ulrika. It has no saint of its own.

ulysse.label: Ulysse
ulysse.meaning: From Latin "Ulixes", the Latin name of the Greek hero Odysseus.
ulysse.text: A rare French name of classical inspiration, given mainly in the 19th century in France and French-speaking Switzerland. It has no patron saint.

umberto.label: Umberto
umberto.meaning: Italian form of Humbert, from Germanic "hun", "giant" or "bear cub", and "berht", "bright".
umberto.text: An Italian name linked to the House of Savoy (Umberto I, King of Italy), very frequent in Italy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Blessed Humbert III of Savoy has not been canonised.

urbain.label: Urbain
urbain.text: A French, Belgian and Luxembourgish name, used under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century, notably in wine-growing regions. It refers to Pope Saint Urban I, patron of winegrowers, celebrated on 25 May.

urbaine.label: Urbaine
urbaine.meaning: Feminine of Urbain, from Latin "urbanus", "of the city".
urbaine.text: The feminine of Urbain, found in registers of western France (Maine, Anjou, Brittany) in the 17th and 18th centuries. Priests wrote Urbaine, Urbane or Urbanne.

ursula.label: Ursula
ursula.text: A female name very widespread in Switzerland and Germany, particularly linked to Cologne, and also found in Belgium and Spain; the French form is Ursule. It refers to Saint Ursula, martyred at Cologne with her companions, celebrated on 21 October.

urszula.label: Urszula
urszula.meaning: Polish form of Ursula, from Latin "ursula", "little she-bear".
urszula.text: The Polish form of Ursula, found in Catholic registers in Poland since the early modern period; Latin records write it Ursula. It refers to Saint Ursula of Cologne, celebrated on 21 October.

uszer.label: Uszer
uszer.text: The name of one of Jacob's sons, written Uszer or Oszer in 19th-century Polish records. German records write Ascher.

valentin.label: Valentin
valentin.text: A name found in Spain (Valentín), Germany, France and Switzerland, mainly in Catholic regions; Latin records write it Valentinus. It refers to Saint Valentine, a Roman martyr, celebrated on 14 February.

valentina.label: Valentina
valentina.meaning: Feminine of Valentine, from Latin "valens", "strong, vigorous".
valentina.text: The feminine of Valentine, found in Italy, Spain and Poland (Walentyna), mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

valentine.label: Valentine
valentine.meaning: French feminine of Valentin, from Latin "valens", "strong, vigorous".
valentine.text: A French female name, also used in French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium, found in the 19th century and back in favour in the late 20th century; in English, Valentine is mostly male. It has no saint of its own.

valentino.label: Valentino
valentino.meaning: Italian form of Valentine, from Latin "valens", "strong, vigorous".
valentino.text: The Italian form of Valentine, found throughout Italy, particularly in Umbria, where Terni venerates its saintly bishop. It refers to Saint Valentine, celebrated on 14 February.

valeria.label: Valeria
valeria.meaning: From the Roman family name "Valerius", from "valere", "to be strong, healthy".
valeria.text: A female name found in Italy, Belgium and Spain, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. Several saints bear the name; French calendars celebrate Valérie on 28 April.

valerie.label: Valerie
valerie.meaning: French form of Valeria, from Latin "valere", "to be strong, healthy".
valerie.text: A French and Belgian female name, rare before the 19th century and very frequent in the second half of the 20th century, also used in Luxembourg and Britain. It is celebrated on 28 April in honour of Saint Valeria of Milan, a martyr.

valerien.label: Valérien
valerien.meaning: From Latin Valerianus, derived from Valerius, "to be strong".
valerien.text: Borne by several saints and martyrs, including the husband of Saint Cecilia. It appears in French registers mostly in the 19th century.

valerio.label: Valerio
valerio.meaning: From the Roman family name "Valerius", from "valere", "to be strong, healthy".
valerio.text: The Italian form of Valerius, found in Italy mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. Several saints bear the name, without a dominant feast.

vanessa.label: Vanessa
vanessa.meaning: A name coined by Jonathan Swift in the early 18th century.
vanessa.text: Invented by Swift for his poem Cadenus and Vanessa, it remained rare until the 20th century. It was widely given in France and Europe in the 1970s and 1980s.

vasco.label: Vasco
vasco.meaning: Of disputed origin: from medieval Spanish "Velasco", perhaps from Basque "bela", "crow".
vasco.text: A typically Portuguese name, made famous by Vasco da Gama and found in Portuguese registers since the Middle Ages. It has no patron saint.

vera.label: Vera
vera.meaning: Of disputed origin: from Russian "vera", "faith", or Latin "verus", "true".
vera.text: A female name widespread in Russia and Central Europe, which became common in Britain, the United States, Germany and Poland in the late 19th and 20th centuries. It has no saint of its own in the Latin calendar.

verena.label: Verena
verena.meaning: Of disputed origin: perhaps from a Coptic name or linked to Latin "verus", "true".
verena.text: A typically Swiss female name, with the Swiss German pet form Vreni, very frequent in German-speaking Switzerland. It refers to Saint Verena, who came from Egyptian Thebes according to tradition and is venerated at Zurzach, celebrated on 1 September.

vernon.label: Vernon
vernon.meaning: From the Anglo-Norman surname Vernon, from a Norman place name linked to Gaulish "vern", "alder".
vernon.text: An English aristocratic surname of Norman origin turned given name, mainly in the United States and Britain in the late 19th and 20th centuries. It has no patron saint.

veronica.label: Veronica
veronica.meaning: Probably from Greek "Berenikê", "bringer of victory", linked by folk etymology to Latin "vera icon", "true image".
veronica.text: A name popularised by the tradition of the woman who wiped Christ's face on the way to Calvary, common in Italy, Spain, Britain and Belgium. There is no universal feast for this Veronica; in Italy the name is celebrated on 9 July with Saint Veronica Giuliani, a Capuchin nun canonised in 1839.

veronique.label: Véronique
veronique.meaning: From Latin "Veronica", associated with "vera icon", "true image"; disputed meaning.
veronique.text: Saint Veronica, who according to tradition wiped the face of Christ, is celebrated on 4 February in the French calendar. The name appears in registers under the Ancien Régime and was very fashionable in the 1960s.

vicenc.label: Vicenç
vicenc.meaning: Catalan form of Vincent, from Latin "vincens", "conquering".
vicenc.text: The Catalan form of Vincent, used in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands; Castilian documents render it as Vicente and Latin ones as Vincentius. It refers to Saint Vincent of Saragossa, a martyred deacon, celebrated on 22 January; Saint Vincent Ferrer (5 April) is also highly honoured in the Catalan lands.

vicent.label: Vicent
vicent.meaning: Valencian form of Vincent, from Latin "vincens", "conquering".
vicent.text: The Valencian form of Vincent, very frequent in the Valencia region, where Saint Vincent Ferrer, born in Valencia, is especially venerated (feast on 5 April). The name also refers to Saint Vincent of Saragossa, martyred at Valencia, celebrated on 22 January.

vicenta.label: Vicenta
vicenta.text: The Spanish feminine of Vicente, frequent in Spanish registers of the 18th and 19th centuries, notably in the Valencia region. It has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

vicente.label: Vicente
vicente.meaning: Spanish and Portuguese form of Vincent, from Latin "vincens", "conquering".
vicente.text: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Vincent, very widespread in the Iberian Peninsula; Latin records write it Vincentius. It refers to Saint Vincent of Saragossa, a martyred deacon and patron of Lisbon, celebrated on 22 January.

victoire.label: Victoire
victoire.text: A French and Belgian female name, frequent in the 18th and 19th centuries, and occasionally borne by men in older records. Several saints named Victoria exist, without a dominant feast in the Latin calendar.

victor.label: Victor
victor.text: A name found in Belgium, Luxembourg, France and Britain, most frequent in the 19th and early 20th centuries (Victor Hugo). French calendars celebrate it on 21 July, the day of Saint Victor of Marseille, a soldier martyr.

victoria.label: Victoria
victoria.text: A female name long used in Spain and Belgium, then very widespread in Britain and the British Empire from the reign of Queen Victoria (1837-1901). Several saints bear the name, without a dominant feast in the Latin calendar.

victoriano.label: Victoriano
victoriano.text: A Spanish name, found mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries, with the variants Vitoriano or, in Basque, Bitoriano. It has no widely celebrated saint.

victorin.label: Victorin
victorin.text: A rare French name, attested mainly in the 19th century. Several saints named Victorinus exist, without a dominant feast in the Latin calendar.

victorina.label: Victorina
victorina.text: A Spanish and Flemish female name, found mainly in the 19th century. It has no widely celebrated saint.

victorine.label: Victorine
victorine.text: A female name frequent in Belgium and France in the 19th century. It has no widely celebrated saint.

viktor.label: Viktor
viktor.meaning: Germanic and Slavic form of Victor, from Latin "victor", "conqueror".
viktor.text: The German, Swiss and Polish form of Victor, most frequent in the 19th and 20th centuries. In Germany the name is celebrated on 10 October in honour of Saint Victor of Xanten, a martyr of the Theban Legion.

viktoria.label: Viktoria
viktoria.text: The German form of Victoria, found in Germany and Poland, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint.

vincent.label: Vincent
vincent.text: An old name in France, particularly frequent in the wine-growing regions whose patron Saint Vincent is, and also found in Britain, the United States and Luxembourg; Latin records write it Vincentius. It is celebrated on 22 January in honour of Saint Vincent of Saragossa; Saint Vincent de Paul (27 September) also inspired many baptisms.

vincenza.label: Vincenza
vincenza.text: The Italian feminine of Vincent, frequent in southern Italy and Sicily. It has no widely celebrated saint of its own.

vincenzo.label: Vincenzo
vincenzo.meaning: Italian form of Vincent, from Latin "vincens", "conquering".
vincenzo.text: One of the most frequent male names in southern Italy, also used in Ticino and by Italian emigrants. It refers to Saint Vincent of Saragossa, celebrated on 22 January; Saint Vincent Ferrer and Saint Vincent de Paul are also honoured there.

viola.label: Viola
viola.text: An English-language female name known since Shakespeare, common in the United States and Britain in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; it is also found in Italy and Germany. It has no widely celebrated saint.

violante.label: Violante
violante.meaning: Iberian and Italian form of Yolanda, of disputed origin, perhaps Germanic or linked to Latin "viola", "violet".
violante.text: A name borne by medieval queens and princesses (Violant of Aragon), found in Portugal and Italy, mainly in noble families. It has no widely celebrated saint.

violet.label: Violet
violet.text: An English-language female name, most frequent in Britain and the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with the fashion for flower names. It has no patron saint.

violette.label: Violette
violette.text: A French and Swiss female name, given mainly in the early 20th century with the fashion for flower names. It has no patron saint.

virgil.label: Virgil
virgil.meaning: From the Roman family name "Vergilius", of uncertain etymology, borne by the poet Virgil.
virgil.text: An American name of classical inspiration, most frequent in the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint in the United States.

virgilio.label: Virgilio
virgilio.meaning: From the Roman family name "Vergilius", of uncertain etymology, borne by the poet Virgil.
virgilio.text: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Virgil, found mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries. Saint Virgil of Salzburg is honoured in Austria, but without a widely observed feast in these countries.

virginia.label: Virginia
virginia.meaning: From the Roman family name "Verginius", linked to Latin "virgo", "maiden".
virginia.text: A female name found in Italy, Portugal, the United States and Belgium, inspired by Verginia of Roman history and, in the United States, by the state of that name. No early saint bore it; Virginia Centurione Bracelli was only canonised in 2003.

virginie.label: Virginie
virginie.meaning: French form of Virginia, linked to Latin "virgo", "maiden".
virginie.text: A French and Belgian female name, popularised by the novel "Paul et Virginie" (1788) and frequent in the 19th century, then again in the late 20th century. It has no early saint.

vital.label: Vital
vital.text: A name found in France, Belgium, Switzerland and Portugal, mainly under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century; Latin records write it Vitalis. It refers to Saint Vitalis of Milan, a martyr, celebrated on 28 April.

vito.label: Vito
vito.text: A name very widespread in southern Italy, notably in Apulia and Sicily, and frequent among Italian emigrants. It refers to Saint Vitus, a young martyr and one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, celebrated on 15 June.

vitor.label: Vítor
vitor.meaning: Portuguese form of Victor, from Latin "victor", "conqueror".
vitor.text: The Portuguese form of Victor, found in Portugal and more frequent in the 20th century; the older spelling is Victor. There is no widely celebrated saint of this name in Portugal.

vitoria.label: Vitória
vitoria.meaning: Portuguese form of Victoria, from Latin "victoria", "victory".
vitoria.text: The Portuguese form of Victoria, found in Portugal; the older spelling is Victoria. It has no widely celebrated saint.

vitorino.label: Vitorino
vitorino.meaning: Portuguese form of Victorinus, from Latin "Victorinus", derived from "victor".
vitorino.text: A Portuguese name, found in registers of the 18th to 20th centuries, with the older spelling Victorino. It has no widely celebrated saint.

vittoria.label: Vittoria
vittoria.meaning: Italian form of Victoria, from Latin "victoria", "victory".
vittoria.text: An Italian female name, used since the Renaissance (Vittoria Colonna) and frequent in the 19th and 20th centuries. It has no widely celebrated saint.

vittorina.label: Vittorina
vittorina.meaning: Italian diminutive of Vittoria, from Latin "victoria", "victory".
vittorina.text: A diminutive of Vittoria used as a name in Italy, mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no saint of its own.

vittorio.label: Vittorio
vittorio.meaning: Italian form of Victor, from Latin "victor", "conqueror".
vittorio.text: An Italian name very widespread after the Risorgimento in honour of King Victor Emmanuel II; older records also give Vittore. There is no widely celebrated saint of this name in Italy.

vivian.label: Vivian
vivian.text: An English-language name once male in Britain, which became mainly female in the United States in the 20th century, with the spellings Vivien or Vivienne. It has no widely celebrated saint.

viviane.label: Viviane
viviane.meaning: From Latin "Viviana", derived from "vivus", "alive"; associated with Bibiana.
viviane.text: A French female name, linked to the fairy Viviane of the Arthurian legends and most frequent in the 20th century. French calendars celebrate it on 2 December, the day of Saint Bibiana, a Roman martyr.

waclaw.label: Wacław
waclaw.meaning: Polish form of Wenceslaus, from Slavic "więcej", "more", and "sława", "glory".
waclaw.text: A Polish name of Czech origin, frequent in Poland; Latin records write it Wenceslaus and transcriptions without diacritics Waclaw. It refers to Saint Wenceslaus, the martyred duke of Bohemia, celebrated on 28 September.

walburga.label: Walburga
walburga.meaning: From the Germanic elements "walt" (to rule) and "burg" (protection).
walburga.text: The name of Saint Walpurga, an 8th-century Anglo-Saxon abbess of Heidenheim, widely given in Bavaria, Austria and Alsace. Registers spell it Walburga, Walpurga or Waltburga.

waldemar.label: Waldemar
waldemar.meaning: From Germanic "wald", "rule", and "mēri", "famous"; Scandinavian form Valdemar.
waldemar.text: A name of Germanic and Scandinavian origin (the Valdemar kings of Denmark), found in Poland, Germany and Switzerland, mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries; Woldemar also occurs in the Baltic lands. It has no patron saint.

walenty.label: Walenty
walenty.meaning: Polish form of Valentine, from Latin "valens", "strong, vigorous".
walenty.text: The Polish form of Valentine, frequent in Catholic registers in Poland in the 18th and 19th centuries; Latin records write it Valentinus. It refers to Saint Valentine, celebrated on 14 February.

wallace.label: Wallace
wallace.meaning: From Anglo-Norman "waleis", "Welsh, foreigner"; a Scottish surname.
wallace.text: A Scottish surname, made famous by William Wallace, which became a given name in the 19th century in the United States and Britain. It has no patron saint.

wally.label: Wally
wally.meaning: German pet form of Walburga or of names beginning with "Wal-"; the origin follows the full name.
wally.text: A German female familiar form, known from the novel "Die Geier-Wally" (1875), used on its own mainly in the 20th century; in English, Wally is rather a male pet form of Walter. In official records the same person is usually entered under the full name.

walter.label: Walter
walter.text: An old name in England, Germany and Switzerland, with the forms Walther, Wouter (Dutch) or Gauthier (French); it is very frequent in the United States and Britain around 1900. It has no widely celebrated saint in these countries.

walther.label: Walther
walther.meaning: Older German form of Walter, from Germanic "wald", "rule", and "hari", "army".
walther.text: The traditional German spelling of Walter (Walther von der Vogelweide), found in Germany, Switzerland and among German speakers in Poland. It has no widely celebrated saint.

wanda.label: Wanda
wanda.meaning: Of disputed origin: the name of the legendary princess of Kraków, perhaps linked to the name of the Vandals.
wanda.text: A Polish name taken from the legend of Princess Wanda, daughter of Krakus, popularised in the 19th century by Romanticism and later used in the United States, Germany and France. It has no patron saint.

warren.label: Warren
warren.meaning: From the Anglo-Norman surname Warren, from a Norman place name or Old French "garenne", "game preserve".
warren.text: An English surname turned given name, mainly in the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no patron saint.

wayne.label: Wayne
wayne.meaning: From the English surname Wayne, from Old English "wægn", "wagon", denoting a cartwright.
wayne.text: An English surname that became a given name in the United States, mainly in the mid-20th century. It is rare in older records and has no patron saint.

wendelin.label: Wendelin
wendelin.meaning: Derived from the Germanic element "Wandal", the name of the Vandals; meaning disputed.
wendelin.text: The name of Saint Wendelin, a 6th-century hermit near Trier and patron of shepherds and livestock, widely given in the Saarland, German-speaking Lorraine, Alsace and southern Germany. Registers write Wendelinus, the genitive Wendelini, and the dialect form Wendling.

wendy.label: Wendy
wendy.meaning: A name popularised by J. M. Barrie's play "Peter Pan" (1904), perhaps from a childish nickname; also a pet form of Gwendolen.
wendy.text: An English-language name widespread mainly in the 20th century in Britain and the English-speaking world, and rare before. It has no patron saint.

werner.label: Werner
werner.meaning: From Germanic "warin", "protection", or the name of the Warini people, and "hari", "army".
werner.text: An old German name, found in Germany, Switzerland, Poland and Belgium, and most frequent in the 20th century. The formerly local cult of Werner of Oberwesel has been suppressed; the name has no recognised saint.

wesley.label: Wesley
wesley.meaning: From Old English "west", "west", and "lēah", "clearing"; a place name turned surname.
wesley.text: An English surname that became a given name in honour of John and Charles Wesley, founders of Methodism, mainly in Methodist families in Britain and the United States from the late 18th century. It has no patron saint.

wieslaw.label: Wiesław
wieslaw.text: A Polish name of Slavic origin, rare before the 20th century and then very frequent in the mid-20th century. Transcriptions without diacritics write it Wieslaw; it has no patron saint.

wieslawa.label: Wiesława
wieslawa.meaning: Feminine of Wiesław, from Slavic "więcej", "more", and "sława", "glory".
wieslawa.text: The feminine of Wiesław, most frequent in Poland in the mid-20th century. Transcriptions without diacritics write it Wieslawa; it has no patron saint.

wiktor.label: Wiktor
wiktor.meaning: Polish form of Victor, from Latin "victor", "conqueror".
wiktor.text: The Polish form of Victor, found in Catholic registers in Poland; Latin records write it Victor. Several saints named Victor exist, without a dominant feast in the Polish calendar.

wiktoria.label: Wiktoria
wiktoria.meaning: Polish form of Victoria, from Latin "victoria", "victory".
wiktoria.text: The Polish form of Victoria, found in Polish registers in the 19th and 20th centuries; Latin records write it Victoria. It has no widely celebrated saint.

wilbur.label: Wilbur
wilbur.meaning: From the English surname Wilbur, of disputed etymology, perhaps from Old English "wil", "will", and "burh", "fortress".
wilbur.text: An English surname turned given name, mainly in the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries (Wilbur Wright). It has no patron saint.

wilfred.label: Wilfred
wilfred.text: A spelling of Wilfrid, brought back into fashion in the 19th century in Britain and the United States by the medieval revival. It refers to Saint Wilfrid, 7th-century bishop of York, celebrated on 12 October.

wilfrid.label: Wilfrid
wilfrid.text: An Anglo-Saxon name used in England and, more rarely, in France (Wilfried) in the 19th and 20th centuries. It refers to Saint Wilfrid, 7th-century bishop of York, celebrated on 12 October.

wilhelm.label: Wilhelm
wilhelm.text: One of the most widespread male names in Germany, Switzerland and among German speakers in Poland and the Netherlands, especially under the Emperors Wilhelm in the 19th century; Latin records write it Guilielmus or Wilhelmus. Several saints named William exist, without a dominant feast in the German calendar.

wilhelmina.label: Wilhelmina
wilhelmina.meaning: Feminine of Wilhelm, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
wilhelmina.text: A female name very widespread in the Netherlands, especially from the reign of Queen Wilhelmina (1890-1948), and found in Germany, Britain and Belgium; the usual Dutch pet form is Mien. It has no saint of its own.

wilhelmine.label: Wilhelmine
wilhelmine.meaning: Feminine of Wilhelm, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
wilhelmine.text: The German and French form of Wilhelmina, found in Luxembourg, Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland, mainly in the 19th century. It has no saint of its own.

wilhelmus.label: Wilhelmus
wilhelmus.meaning: Latin form of William, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
wilhelmus.text: The Latinised form of Willem, very frequent in Dutch and Flemish parish registers, where it corresponds to the vernacular forms Willem or Wim. Several saints named William exist, without a dominant feast in the Netherlands.

willard.label: Willard
willard.meaning: From the English surname Willard, from Old English "wil", "will", and "heard", "hardy".
willard.text: An English surname turned given name, mainly in the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no patron saint.

willem.label: Willem
willem.meaning: Dutch form of William, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
willem.text: One of the most frequent names in the Netherlands and Flanders, borne by William of Orange; Latin records write it Wilhelmus and the usual pet form is Wim. It is the source of patronymics such as Willems. Several saints named William exist, without a dominant feast in the Netherlands.

william.label: William
william.meaning: English form of Guillaume, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet, protection".
william.text: A name introduced to England by William the Conqueror and still one of the most frequent in Britain and the United States; Latin records write it Gulielmus and pet forms are Will, Bill or Billy. Several saints named William exist (of York, of Bourges, of Gellone), without a dominant feast in English-speaking countries.

willibald.label: Willibald
willibald.text: A German name widespread mainly in Bavaria and Franconia, also found in Poland. It refers to Saint Willibald, an Anglo-Saxon missionary and first bishop of Eichstätt, celebrated on 7 July.

willis.label: Willis
willis.meaning: From the English surname Willis, "son of Will", a pet form of William.
willis.text: An English surname turned given name, mainly in the United States in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It has no patron saint.

willy.label: Willy
willy.meaning: Pet form of Wilhelm or Willem, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet".
willy.text: A familiar form used as a name in Luxembourg, Germany, Switzerland and Belgium, mainly in the early 20th century, also spelled Willi. In official records the same person may appear as Wilhelm or Guillaume; it has no saint of its own.

wilma.label: Wilma
wilma.meaning: Short form of Wilhelmina, from Germanic "wil", "will", and "helm", "helmet".
wilma.text: A female name most frequent in the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, often in families of German or Dutch origin. It has no patron saint.

wilson.label: Wilson
wilson.meaning: From the English surname Wilson, "son of Will", a pet form of William.
wilson.text: A very common English surname turned given name, mainly in Britain and the United States in the 19th century. It has no patron saint.

wincenty.label: Wincenty
wincenty.meaning: Polish form of Vincent, from Latin "vincens", "conquering".
wincenty.text: The Polish form of Vincent, frequent in Catholic registers in Poland; Latin records write it Vincentius. It refers to Saint Vincent of Saragossa, celebrated on 22 January; Saint Vincent de Paul (27 September) is also honoured.

winifred.label: Winifred
winifred.meaning: Anglicised form of Welsh "Gwenfrewi", from "gwen", "white, blessed", and "frewi", "reconciliation"; associated with Old English Winfrith.
winifred.text: A name of Welsh origin, common in Britain and the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It refers to Saint Winifred, whose well at Holywell in Wales is an old pilgrimage site, celebrated on 3 November.

witold.label: Witold
witold.meaning: Polish form of Lithuanian "Vytautas", of disputed etymology, linked to Germanic "wid", "wood", and "wald", "rule".
witold.text: A name linked to Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania (Witold in Polish), used in Poland mainly from the 19th century; Latin records write it Vitoldus. It has no patron saint.

wladyslaw.label: Władysław
wladyslaw.text: A name of Polish kings (Władysław Jagiełło), very frequent in Poland in the 19th and 20th centuries; Latin records write it Ladislaus and transcriptions without diacritics Wladyslaw. It corresponds to the sainted King Ladislaus of Hungary, whose feast varies between calendars.

wladyslawa.label: Władysława
wladyslawa.meaning: Feminine of Władysław, from Slavic "vladi", "to rule", and "slava", "glory".
wladyslawa.text: The feminine of Władysław, frequent in Poland in the 19th and 20th centuries; transcriptions without diacritics write it Wladyslawa. It has no saint of its own.

wlodzimierz.label: Włodzimierz
wlodzimierz.meaning: Polish form of Vladimir, from Slavic "vladi", "to rule", and "mir", "peace" or "world".
wlodzimierz.text: A Polish name of East Slavic origin, rare before the 19th century and then frequent in the 20th century; transcriptions without diacritics write it Wlodzimierz. It refers to Saint Vladimir, Prince of Kiev, honoured mainly in the Eastern Churches.

wojciech.label: Wojciech
wojciech.text: A very old and frequent Polish name; Latin records render it as Adalbertus and German records as Adalbert, which can be confusing. It refers to Saint Adalbert (Wojciech) of Prague, martyr and patron of Poland, celebrated on 23 April.

wolf.label: Wolf
wolf.meaning: From Germanic "wulf", "wolf", or short for Wolfgang.
wolf.text: An old German name, found in Germany, Switzerland and Poland, frequent notably in German-speaking Jewish families (Wolf, Wulf, Welwel); it is also a pet form of Wolfgang. It has no saint of its own.

wolfgang.label: Wolfgang
wolfgang.text: A name widespread in southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland, borne by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart; it is also found in Poland. It refers to Saint Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg, celebrated on 31 October.

wouter.label: Wouter
wouter.meaning: Dutch form of Walter, from Germanic "wald", "rule", and "hari", "army".
wouter.text: An old Dutch name, found in the Netherlands and Flanders since the Middle Ages; Latin records write it Walterus or Gualterus. It is the source of patronymics such as Wouters. It has no widely celebrated saint.

xaver.label: Xaver
xaver.meaning: German form of Xavier, from Basque "etxe berri", "new house", the name of Saint Francis Xavier's birthplace castle.
xaver.text: A German and Swiss name, often in compounds (Franz Xaver), frequent in Bavaria, Catholic Switzerland and Poland. It refers to Saint Francis Xavier, the Jesuit missionary celebrated on 3 December.

xavier.label: Xavier
xavier.meaning: From Basque "etxe berri", "new house", the name of Saint Francis Xavier's birthplace castle.
xavier.text: A name born of the cult of Saint Francis Xavier after his canonisation in 1622, often in compounds (François-Xavier), frequent in France, Portugal, Spain and Luxembourg. The saint, a Jesuit missionary, is celebrated on 3 December.

yolanda.label: Yolanda
yolanda.meaning: Spanish form of Yolande, of disputed origin, perhaps Germanic or linked to Greek "ion", "violet".
yolanda.text: A Spanish female name, borne by medieval queens (Violante) and most frequent in the 20th century in Spain and the United States. It has no widely celebrated canonised saint.

yolande.label: Yolande
yolande.meaning: Of disputed origin, perhaps Germanic or linked to Greek "ion", "violet".
yolande.text: A female name borne by the medieval aristocracy (Yolande of Aragon), then rare in the records before coming back into favour in France in the 20th century. It has no widely celebrated canonised saint.

yrieix.label: Yrieix
yrieix.text: Saint Aredius, a 6th-century abbot in Limousin, gave his name to Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche and is celebrated on 25 August. The name is specific to Limousin.

yvan.label: Yvan
yvan.meaning: French spelling of Ivan, the Slavic form of John, from Hebrew "Yohanan", "God is gracious".
yvan.text: A modern French name, most frequent in the 20th century, borrowed from Russian Ivan. It belongs with John and hence with Saint John the Baptist, celebrated on 24 June.

yves.label: Yves
yves.meaning: From Germanic "iv", "yew", the wood used for bows.
yves.text: A name closely linked to Brittany, where Saint Ivo is the patron of the province, and frequent in France in the 20th century; the Breton form is Erwan or Youenn. It refers to Saint Ivo Hélory of Kermartin, a 13th-century priest and lawyer, celebrated on 19 May.

yvette.label: Yvette
yvette.meaning: Feminine diminutive of Yves, from Germanic "iv", "yew".
yvette.text: A French female name, most frequent in the first half of the 20th century. It refers to Saint Yvette (Juetta) of Huy, a 12th-century recluse, celebrated on 13 January.

yvon.label: Yvon
yvon.meaning: Derived form of Yves, from Germanic "iv", "yew".
yvon.text: A variant of Yves, mainly Breton, frequent in France in the 20th century; the corresponding Breton form is Erwan. It refers to Saint Ivo of Kermartin, celebrated on 19 May.

yvonne.label: Yvonne
yvonne.text: A female name very frequent in France, Switzerland, Belgium and Britain in the first half of the 20th century and rare before. It has no saint of its own.

zacharias.label: Zacharias
zacharias.text: The Latin, German and Dutch form of Zachary, found in Germany, the Netherlands, Poland and Belgium, and frequent among Protestants. It refers to Saint Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, celebrated on 5 November with Saint Elizabeth.

zbigniew.label: Zbigniew
zbigniew.meaning: From Slavic "zbyć", "to get rid of", and "gniew", "anger": "one who dispels anger".
zbigniew.text: An old Polish name, borne by a 12th-century Piast prince, rare afterwards and then very frequent in the mid-20th century. It has no patron saint.

zdzislaw.label: Zdzisław
zdzislaw.meaning: From Slavic "zdzieść", "to accomplish", and "sława", "glory"; the etymology is disputed.
zdzislaw.text: A Polish name of Slavic origin, attested in the Middle Ages and frequent mainly in the 20th century. Transcriptions without diacritics write it Zdzislaw; it has no patron saint.

zelie.label: Zélie
zelie.meaning: Of disputed origin: short for Azélie, perhaps linked to Latin "zelus" or Greek "zêlos", "zeal".
zelie.text: A French and Belgian female name most frequent in the 19th century. Zélie Martin, mother of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, was only canonised in 2015; the name has no early saint.

zelig.label: Zelig
zelig.text: A male Yiddish name, written Zelik or Zelig in Polish records and Selig in German records of the 19th century.

zelman.label: Zelman
zelman.meaning: A Yiddish form derived from Solomon (Shlomo).
zelman.text: A Yiddish name written Zelman or Zalman in Polish and Lithuanian records of the 19th century.

zenon.label: Zenon
zenon.meaning: From Greek "Zênôn", derived from the name of Zeus.
zenon.text: A name of Greek origin, used in Poland mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries and also found in Luxembourg. It refers to Saint Zeno, bishop and patron of Verona, celebrated on 12 April.

zlata.label: Zlata
zlata.text: A name of Slavic origin adopted by the Jews of Poland and Russia, frequent in 19th-century records, written Zlata or Złata. It is also borne by Christian women in South Slavic countries.

zoe.label: Zoé
zoe.text: A female name rare in older records, found in Belgium, France and Britain in the 19th century and back in favour in the late 20th century. Several saints named Zoe exist, without a dominant feast in the Latin calendar.

zofia.label: Zofia
zofia.meaning: Polish form of Sophia, from Greek "sophia", "wisdom".
zofia.text: A female name widespread in Poland since the Middle Ages (Queen Sophia of Halshany), with the pet form Zosia; Latin records write it Sophia. It is celebrated on 15 May in honour of Saint Sophia, a Roman martyr.

zuzanna.label: Zuzanna
zuzanna.meaning: Polish form of Susanna, from Hebrew "Shoshannah", "lily".
zuzanna.text: The Polish form of Susanna, found in Catholic registers in Poland; Latin records write it Susanna. It refers to Saint Susanna, a Roman martyr celebrated on 11 August.

zygmunt.label: Zygmunt
zygmunt.meaning: Polish form of Sigismund, from Germanic "sigu", "victory", and "mund", "protection".
zygmunt.text: The name of Polish kings of the Jagiellonian and Vasa dynasties (Sigismund I, II and III), frequent in Poland; Latin records write it Sigismundus. It refers to Saint Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, celebrated on 1 May.
